stories.Headline: Judge urges expert witnesses to declare AI use right away
stories.Summary:
Joanna Smith, interim deputy president of the UK High Court's business and property division, has told expert witnesses to disclose their use of artificial intelligence now rather than wait for a formal rule. She made the point at the Bond Solon Expert Witness Conference at Church House in Westminster, as reported by the Law Society Gazette on 7 November 2026. Her warning was that experts whose evidence is shaped by AI they have not declared could face searching questions under cross-examination. She told the audience that there is currently no rule requiring such disclosure, but that experts who stay silent may find themselves open to criticism.

The instruction follows a report from the Civil Justice Council published in late October 2026, on AI and the preparation of court documents. Smith co-chaired the working group behind it. The council recommended that experts make a declaration where AI tools have generated or influenced the substantive content of a report, and that this requirement be added to the 2014 guidance on instructing experts in civil claims. Smith said the declaration should give enough information to allow effective scrutiny, which could include the method used, confirmation that AI was appropriate for that purpose, and, in exceptional cases, the tool itself. She also advised experts to check at the point of instruction whether AI use is permitted, citing intellectual property, data protection and regulatory compliance.

Smith placed the responsibility on experts themselves, reminding them that their credibility depends on their fundamental duties to the court. She said AI has not changed those duties, and that the obligations of independence, objectivity, transparency and professional competence remain exactly as they were. In her keynote she identified the main danger as the erosion of independent judgment, where experts hand their opinions over to an AI agent and lose their integrity. She listed practical risks including inadequate oversight, poor training, and a weak understanding of what AI can do. She also advised experts to disclose intended AI use to their instructing solicitors even when the instructions say nothing about it.

The context includes a recent case, Cornwall Council v M & Ors [2026] EWFC 306, in which an independent social worker used Microsoft Copilot to prepare a parenting assessment, assessments of potential kinship carers and an addendum report. The judge found that AI use had influenced a significant part of the report and therefore gave the evidence limited weight. The articles do not say whether a formal rule will follow or when. Smith concluded that experts who understand both the capabilities and limits of AI, and use it transparently where necessary, will be best placed to meet their overriding duty to the court.

stories.Headline: Legal AI Adoption Highlights Need for Better Lawyer Training
stories.Summary:
Legal AI use is growing fast, and a new report argues that lawyers need better training to use it safely. Wolters Kluwer's 2026 Future Ready Lawyer survey, published in November 2026, looked at how attorneys use AI and what gets in their way. The survey gathered responses from 810 lawyers working in law firms and corporate legal departments in the United States, China, and eight European countries. It ran online from August 8 to August 25, 2025. Ninety-two percent of respondents said they use at least one AI tool in their daily work.

Even with that wide adoption, lawyers still face obstacles. The survey found that ethical and data privacy concerns and a lack of training each drew 39% of responses, making them the most common barriers. The findings suggest that using AI well requires more than learning how a tool works. Lawyers must check the results they get, protect client information, and follow professional rules. The report's authors, Wolters Kluwer, present the results as evidence that training should keep pace with the technology.

The article itself, published by a legal career site, draws practical lessons from the survey. It says lawyers should verify every case and source an AI tool produces, check quotes and facts, know which tools their firm permits, and protect confidential client data. Those habits matter across litigation, business law, research, and legal operations. The piece also suggests that job candidates explain in interviews how they check AI output and handle privacy, and that they ask prospective employers how they train staff and supervise AI-assisted work.

It notes, however, that not every firm uses the same tools, so candidates should rely on current postings and firm materials. The broader message is that AI can speed up legal work but does not replace professional judgment. The article argues that as more firms adopt the technology, proper training will matter even more. The sources provided do not describe any specific regulatory changes, deadlines, or enforcement actions tied to this survey, so the outlook beyond these recommendations remains unclear.

stories.Headline: Health researchers warn proposed federal privacy law could expose sensitive medical data
stories.Summary:
Health researchers have warned that Canada's proposed federal privacy legislation contains gaps that could leave sensitive medical information open to commercial exploitation as artificial intelligence spreads through the health-care system. Their concerns centre on Bill C-36, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, which the Carney government introduced in June as part of an effort to modernize private-sector privacy rules. The critics published their commentary in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, arguing that some provisions would let companies collect, use or disclose personal information without direct consent in certain circumstances. One provision in particular allows organizations to rely on a legitimate business interest when they judge that the expected benefits outweigh reasonably foreseeable harm to individuals.

Dr. Sheryl Spithoff, a clinician scientist at Women's College Hospital in Toronto and a co-author of the commentary, says this gives companies too much discretion over how personal data is used. She argues that firms should have to inform regulators from the start and that the clause should apply only in rare cases, with higher standards for sensitive information such as health records. The researchers also point to the European Union's data protection regulation, which sets a higher bar of proof and says legitimate interest does not override the fundamental rights of data owners. Teresa Scassa, a research chair in information law at the University of Ottawa and another co-author, warns that advances in AI may make it impossible to fully anonymize data, since records can be linked with other information and used to profile people as high-risk for costly conditions. Under the bill, deliberately re-identifying personal information would be an offence, though Scassa noted that this could be hard to prove.

The bill requires that personal information be de-identified by modifying details such as names and health card numbers, but it does not protect anonymized data, which is stripped of personal information so that no reasonably foreseeable risk of identification remains. The researchers say anonymized data often carries societal biases that can be built into AI systems and lead to discrimination, and they cite a widely used American hospital algorithm that allocated fewer resources to Black patients. Ottawa's position is that the legislation would strengthen privacy protection, improve corporate accountability and introduce safeguards on automated decision-making. AI Minister Evan Solomon's office repeated the bill's definition of legitimate interest and said organizations relying on it would have to assess and mitigate privacy risks, without detailing those safeguards. Some physicians, including Dr. Amol Verma of St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto, argue that de-identified health data is valuable for research and hospital efficiency when handled safely, and that privacy protection and innovation can go hand in hand.

Bill C-36 remains before Parliament, and the debate reflects a broader tension between technological innovation, commercial use of data and Canadians' privacy rights. Other jurisdictions are facing similar problems, including a class-action lawsuit filed earlier this year against Chicago-based Tempus AI, which the plaintiffs allege obtained patients' genetic and clinical data and sold it without consent. Last year, a study that Spithoff worked on found that millions of Canadians' de-identified health records, including medical histories and prescriptions, were being sold to pharmaceutical companies. The study's authors warned that such sharing could improve care but could also let drug companies put their economic interests ahead of patients' and push up prices. Critics say stronger restrictions and independent oversight are needed to prevent commercial misuse of sensitive information, and the bill's path through Parliament will determine whether those changes are made.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang’s Troubles Leave the AI Industry Reeling
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, long one of the most influential figures in the artificial intelligence boom, now faces a serious threat to his position. Reports published on November 9, 2026, say Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence services concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia's board said it would investigate the matter, and Huang said he fully supports the review and will cooperate with it. The incident has also drawn the attention of a US congressional investigation, according to Asian business reporting on the matter.

The stakes for the industry are large. Nvidia controls about 90 percent of the market for chips used to train frontier AI models, and it has invested billions in companies that buy those chips, including OpenAI and Anthropic. Corporate filings show Huang earned $36 million last year and owned about 3.5 percent of the company as of March, and he is an at-will employee who can be dismissed at any time without severance. Analysts note that Nvidia has no other executive of comparable prominence and no apparent successor. Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday while broader market indices rose.

Experts say the board's inquiry will likely focus on whether Huang broke company policy, though the FBI could examine whether any laws were broken. Congress may also look into whether the affair influenced US policy on chip sales to China, and some analysts say it raises questions about whether sensitive information about AI companies or US strategy reached China. Huang has been outspoken against tougher export controls on China, which could leave his credibility on that issue in doubt. The Trump administration loosened some restrictions in its second term, giving China access to older Nvidia chips.

Researchers at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology expect the scandal to speed efforts to tighten chip exports, with more scrutiny from the Commerce Department over shipments routed through third countries such as Singapore and the Middle East. In South Korea, semiconductor and manufacturing firms that have built plans around Nvidia's AI technology are watching closely, and analysts say the impact on memory chipmakers may be limited given ongoing shortages. Some observers also warn that possible changes in Congress after the US midterm elections could bring stricter rules on AI data centers, which could affect investment across the supply chain. Nvidia's board has not yet said how long its investigation will take.

stories.Headline: Samsung, Hyundai Motor Deepen Physical AI Alliance
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics and Hyundai Motor Group, two long-standing rivals that have cooperated across three generations of their founding families, have announced a deeper strategic alliance aimed at future industries. The partnership, which began in semiconductors, batteries and automotive electronics, now extends to robots and artificial intelligence. On November 9, Samsung hosted an event called "HMG Appreciation Day" at its Seocheon Training Institute, inviting key Hyundai executives in what was the first large-scale invitation of its kind from Samsung to a major domestic conglomerate. The gathering was held under the theme "One Harmony Toward the Future" and drew 177 people, including Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun and Hyundai Vice Chair Chang Jae-hoon.

The cooperation is already producing business results. Samsung Electronics agreed to supply its Exynos Auto V920 in-vehicle infotainment chip to Hyundai Motor Company, and Samsung SDI signed its first long-term electric vehicle battery supply contract with Hyundai in 2023. Its high-nickel prismatic batteries are slated for Kia's compact electric SUV, Hyundai's Ioniq 3, and the Genesis GV90 flagship. The two sides have also begun jointly developing batteries for robots, widening their work into the robotics sector. Analysts quoted in the report suggest that combining Samsung's semiconductor, sensor and battery technology with Hyundai's robotics and autonomous driving know-how could strengthen their future mobility competitiveness.

Jun Young-hyun said in his welcoming speech that the two groups are reliable partners that have written Korean industrial history together, and he hoped their combined strengths would open up new possibilities. Chang Jae-hoon said that cooperation now reaches beyond vehicle components into robots and energy, and that the strengths built over three generations would create greater synergy. The article also recounts the history between the groups, including a 1985 birthday visit by Samsung founder Lee Byung-chull to Hyundai founder Chung Ju-yung, and a 2020 meeting between Lee Jae-yong and Euisun Chung to discuss next-generation electric vehicle batteries. Observers quoted in the report describe the groups as moving from eternal rivals to pragmatic strategic partners.

A separate report from the same period describes Nvidia's AI Day Seoul 2026 at COEX, where the company outlined its physical AI cooperation with South Korean firms, including Hyundai Motor Group, Doosan, SK Hynix and LG Electronics. Nvidia is working with Hyundai on robot simulation for automotive production lines using its Omniverse and Isaac platforms, and with Doosan on robotic precision polishing of car body surfaces. Dipu Talla, Nvidia's vice president of robotics and edge AI, said South Korea would play a very important role in physical AI over the next decade. Nvidia positions itself as a platform company supplying core technology rather than building robots itself, with South Korea serving as a proving ground.

stories.Headline: The impact of AI on youth unemployment
stories.Summary:
The London Assembly's Economy, Culture and Skills Committee is holding a public meeting on the effect of artificial intelligence on youth unemployment in the capital. The session, chaired by Bassam Mahfouz AM, is set for Tuesday 10 November at 10am in the Chamber at City Hall. The background is a Greater London Authority report from April 2026, which estimates that around 46 per cent of London's workforce is in roles that could be at risk of automation, compared with 38 per cent across the wider UK. Media and members of the public are invited to attend, and the meeting can be watched live or later by webcast or on YouTube.

The Milburn Review's interim report found that AI and automation are likely to add further pressure to the entry-level labour market. A key concern is that the vacancies traditionally filled by young first-time job seekers are often the same roles most exposed to automation. The Committee will continue its investigation into youth unemployment in London with a focus on how AI is affecting job availability. It will also hear from employers about the barriers and opportunities facing young people looking for work in the capital. Panel speakers include representatives from the West London Alliance, NHS North East London, UKHospitality, the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development, and the Institute for the Future of Work, along with GLA officials.

The material supplied does not set out any policy change, legal requirement or formal finding from the Committee, so it is not clear what the session will produce beyond the hearing itself. The Assembly describes its role as investigating issues that matter to Londoners and acting as a check and balance on the Mayor. The page is an announcement from the London Assembly and the GLA, and it attributes the workforce estimate to a GLA Economics report and the entry-level concern to the Milburn Review's interim report. Further detail on the Committee's findings, if any are published, is not covered in these articles. For media enquiries, the Assembly Media Office contact details are given on the page.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Still Plans to Go Public as Soon as Next Week: Report
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company, still plans to go public later this month, according to a Wall Street Journal report cited by Gizmodo, even as investor anxiety about AI valuations has grown. Shares could begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT as soon as October 19 or 20, the Journal reported. The expected valuation has fallen sharply, from speculation of about $2 trillion earlier in the year to a range of $1 trillion to $1.25 trillion, according to CNBC. The drop followed a rough October for AI-adjacent stocks, when the Nasdaq had one of its worst months in a while.

The company's regulatory filings show it brought in $33 billion in revenue from January through September 2026. Those filings also warn that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. Separately, Anthropic has announced plans to commit 5 per cent of its shares to an Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, with additional contributions tied to the company's growth in value. The company says the fund would support people affected by AI rather than go toward executive pay. Gizmodo noted that the company's own data shows hiring of junior technical workers fell sharply last year as it expanded its use of Claude AI agents.

Economists and policy experts quoted by The Globe and Mail are skeptical that the fund would do much for affected workers. Rafael Gomez, director of the Centre for Industrial Relations and Human Resources at the University of Toronto, called the proposal very conceptual and said it could pre-empt government regulation by defining rules on the company's own terms. Barry Eidlin, a McGill University sociologist, described such funds as a public-relations effort to keep control over how regulation is shaped. Rosalie Wyonch of the C.D. Howe Institute argued the funds could instead signal commitment to investors and reduce the chance of forceful political action. Anthropic did not respond to the Globe's questions about these criticisms.

The debate sits against a backdrop of limited regulation, since neither Canada nor the United States has a comprehensive AI law like the European Union's AI Act. Canada's federal AI minister, Evan Solomon, has warned against governments ceding control of AI regulation to frontier platforms. OpenAI, Anthropic's rival, filed confidentially to go public in June but will not list before the end of the year, Gizmodo reported. In May, OpenAI's foundation announced a $250 million commitment to help workers, of which $50 million has been distributed so far. Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed a one-time 50 per cent tax on the equity of large AI companies, and Gomez pointed to past labour and industry coalitions as a model for consultation.

stories.Headline: Exclusive: Former Meta and OpenAI Contractor Sama Liquidates, Citing Lawsuits
stories.Summary:
Sama, a data annotation firm that had worked for Meta and OpenAI, is winding down its operations and liquidating its assets, according to a letter to creditors dated November 6, 2026 that TIME reviewed. The letter blames declining revenue, driven by competition and by class-action litigation that would have taken years and significant resources to defend. It does not name the lawsuit it means, though Sama has faced separate class actions in Kenya and the United States. An unaudited balance sheet attached to the letter lists about $1 million in assets against $17 million in liabilities as of October. On October 23, the U.S. entity operating as Sama, Samasource Impact Sourcing, Inc., transferred its assets to a newly formed company, Sama ABC, to oversee their sale and distribute proceeds to creditors.

The letter says Sama ABC is run by professionals who specialize in liquidating financially distressed companies, and that it is not corporately affiliated with Sama despite the similar name. A bank holds a priority claim to substantially all of the company's assets, according to the letter. Earlier reporting by TIME found that Sama performed content moderation for Meta and data labeling for OpenAI, work that employees said exposed them to traumatic content without adequate safeguards. Sama and Meta also face Kenyan lawsuits from former content moderators who allege they were exploited, illegally fired after raising concerns, and blocked from unionizing. The letter does not say what the liquidation means for that case.

Those Kenyan cases include a 2022 suit by Daniel Motaung, a former moderator fired in 2019 after trying to organize a strike, which alleges violations of constitutional rights, forced labor and human trafficking. It has since been consolidated with a separate petition from former moderators who say they were unlawfully made redundant and blacklisted. Sama has said it complied with Kenyan labor law, and Meta has denied responsibility for the working conditions. Separately, Sama drew criticism earlier this year over its handling of footage from Meta's AI-powered smart glasses, after workers told Swedish newspapers they had to review private content, including people using the toilet and having sex. Plaintiffs dropped their claims against Sama in August, and Meta says it will fight the privacy claims against it.

The letter praises Sama's model of deliberately hiring people from marginalized communities in East Africa, saying it reached more than seventy thousand people with training and well-paid digital work. Sama's CEO, Wendy Gonzalez, did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and an email to the company's press inbox bounced. Sama ABC representatives did not respond to emails or calls. Whether the liquidation ends the Kenyan litigation, or how the claims against Sama will be handled through the winding-down process, is not addressed in the articles.

stories.Headline: Missoula AI company files lawsuit challenging city's data center restrictions
stories.Summary:
A Missoula artificial intelligence company, CubCloud AI, has sued the City of Missoula over zoning rules that restrict data centers. The lawsuit was filed in Missoula County District Court, according to the reporting, and the company's complaint says the city's ordinance is unconstitutionally vague. The Missoulian and Montana Free Press both reported the filing on November 9, 2026. The articles describe the lawsuit as the company's challenge to the city's new local zoning rules. The company says it has 16 employees and has put money into research and development that it says would be wasted under the restrictions.

Its leaders told reporters they want the city to allow the project to proceed while the case is decided. The company is also seeking to build a new 4,200-square-foot research facility in the area, a plan the Missoulian says is tied to the changes the city has proposed. The city has said it intends to tweak its data center regulations, but the articles say the city will not comment on pending litigation. The city's rules were adopted after a city council discussion, and the company argues that the restrictions amount to a de facto ban on data centers in parts of town. Its representatives say the city was working toward a new proposal that would give them a path to build.

Officials with the city defended the ordinance as a legitimate exercise of local land-use authority. The Goldwater Institute, a Phoenix-based free-market think tank, is representing the company, the articles report, and says the restrictions go beyond what the law allows. The case comes as Missoula weighs how to handle data centers and other high-energy uses, a question many Montana communities are also debating. The articles do not say when a hearing is scheduled or when the court might rule. The city has indicated it will revise its regulations, and the outcome of the lawsuit could determine whether CubCloud AI can move ahead with its planned facility.

stories.Headline: Claude Personal Finance vs ChatGPT Finances: 5 key differences in privacy, features and bank access
stories.Summary:
Anthropic and OpenAI are each offering AI tools that connect to users' bank accounts to help with budgeting and financial planning. Anthropic's Claude Personal Finance and OpenAI's ChatGPT Finances both rely on Plaid to link accounts, and both provide read-only access, so neither chatbot can move money or change account details. Claude can view bank names, account names and types, the last four digits of account numbers, balances, credit limits and up to two years of transaction history. OpenAI's Finances feature can pull balances, transactions, investments and liabilities. The articles say neither tool is meant to replace a professional financial advisor.

The biggest difference between the two is how they handle user data. Anthropic says conversations in Claude's Personal Finance hub are not used to train its AI models by default, and removing a bank account stops Claude from using the data previously shared. OpenAI applies the user's existing ChatGPT data controls to financial conversations, and model improvement is enabled by default unless users turn off the "Improve the model for everyone" option in Settings. OpenAI also says financial account data is deleted from its systems within 30 days after a user disconnects an account. Anthropic states that Claude Personal Finance contains no advertisements or product suggestions and offers no credit cards, loans or savings accounts of its own.

The articles report that OpenAI has not set out a clear advertising policy for its Finances feature, though it began testing ads on selected lower-priced ChatGPT plans in January 2026. OpenAI's Finances was rolled out in May 2026, and it is planning a tie-up with Intuit that could add help with credit card applications and tax questions. Anthropic plans to work with banks, wealth managers and other financial firms to expand Claude Personal Finance. The articles note that both tools currently offer largely the same tracking options, but Claude's default privacy stance may appeal to users concerned about their financial information.

stories.Headline: NAVER's $9 Billion AI Factory Is Built on a Fee Contract Banks Can Lend Against
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA paid $1 billion for a 4.13% stake in NAVER on November 6, completing the final step of a deal that began with a condition. The chipmaker would invest only after NAVER secured at least $9 billion in separate committed financing for computing infrastructure. Brookfield signed that infrastructure agreement with NAVER on October 27. The headline frames this as an equity story, but the articles describe a credit structure underneath it.

Under that structure, a Brookfield-funded company will buy the GPUs and data center assets and lease computing to NAVER Cloud. NAVER Cloud will run the facilities and pay usage fees, which NAVER says are tied to its business revenue. Korean banks plan to lend against those fees, with KB Kookmin Bank announcing on November 1 a mandate to arrange about KRW 10.7 trillion of loans for a KRW 12.6 trillion project. Hana Bank, Shinhan Bank, Woori Bank and NH Investment & Securities are reported as participants, though final commitments have not been disclosed. NAVER also guarantees NAVER Cloud's fee obligations for up to eight years, with a nominal amount of KRW 18.74 trillion, but the guarantee does not cover the syndicated loan itself.

The articles also set out the capacity plan and what remains unsettled. At the GAK Sejong data center, capacity is staged at 55 MW in the first half of 2027, 100 MW by the end of 2027 and 200 MW in 2028, within a wider project NAVER describes as a 1-gigawatt-scale global AI factory. NAVER issued a little over 6.5 million new shares on November 6, raising about KRW 1.3 trillion. The articles say the fee formula, including any minimum payment and how fees move when sales are slow, is not disclosed. NAVER is expected to consolidate the Brookfield-owned company as a subsidiary under K-IFRS, so its borrowings and assets would appear in NAVER's own accounts.

NAVER has not named customers for the capacity, though it targets enterprise and government clients in Asia, Europe and the Middle East. In October, NAVER Cloud and Vietnam's FPT announced cooperation on AI factories and GPU-as-a-service across Asia-Pacific. The articles say no purchase commitment for this capacity has been disclosed. Separately, NVIDIA and NAVER are expanding their AI model work, with NAVER Cloud taking part in NVIDIA's Nemotron Alliance and using related technology for its HyperCLOVA X model, according to a November 9 report.

stories.Headline: Lawyers need AI education, not AI legislation
stories.Summary:
Nicole Black, a Rochester, New York attorney and legal technology writer, argues that lawyers do not need new AI laws or ethics rules, but more education. Her column responds to California's SB 574, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed on September 30, 2026, and which will likely take effect January 1, 2027. Black notes that bar associations have issued at least twenty ethics opinions and guides on AI since ChatGPT's public release in November 2022. She frames the debate as a question of whether generative AI use warrants new rules at all. Her answer is no, because AI is simply another technology that existing ethics guidance already covers.

The California law, she says, mostly repeats duties lawyers already have. It bars lawyers from delegating the practice of law to AI and restricts entering confidential or nonpublic information into systems not restricted to authorized persons. It requires lawyers to verify the accuracy of AI outputs, correct hallucinated content, and personally verify every citation in a court filing, including those generated by AI. It also requires disclosure of AI use in documents submitted to the court and consideration of disclosure when AI helps create public-facing content. Black argues that the disclosure requirement is duplicative of many recent ethics opinions and that courts should simply assume lawyers have used AI, since it is built into most legal and general software.

Black's central complaint is that the law adds complication and discourages adoption without adding protection. She points to earlier technologies such as email, the internet, social media, and cloud computing, whose initial requirements, such as client consent, eventually faded as the tools became routine. She expects AI to follow that path more quickly, since it is already embedded in nearly every technology used in law firms, sometimes without lawyers realizing it. In her view, duplicative laws hurt lawyers' ability to compete in a fast-changing market. She writes that the wiser course is to invest in education that helps lawyers use technology to serve clients, and she hopes other states will not follow California's lead, though she says she is not optimistic.

stories.Headline: UC Law SF scholars drive solutions to AI legal challenges - UC Law San Francisco | (Formerly UC Hastings)
stories.Summary:
UC Law San Francisco scholars are developing legal and policy proposals for artificial intelligence, and some of their ideas have already drawn interest from lawmakers. Professors Prithika Balakrishnan, Dave Owen, Seema N. Patel and Robin Feldman are at the center of this work, which examines how AI affects workers, artists, consumers, political debate and criminal evidence. Their recommendations include new laws to encourage AI innovation, stronger consumer rights, clear liability standards and a greater role for employees in workplace technology decisions. Chancellor and Dean David Faigman said the school's scholars are proposing concrete measures to protect people's rights and promote accountability while still encouraging innovation. The articles describe the research as an effort to give policymakers a workable path forward.

Professor Robin Feldman, who directs the AI Law & Innovation Institute at the Center for Innovation, has focused on who should answer for harm caused by AI agents. She asks whether the developer, the deployer or another party is responsible when such a system causes damage. Feldman suggests Congress could create clearer rules and "safe harbors" that shield companies from liability when they follow them, which she says would promote accountability while reducing litigation risk. The Institute receives more than 50 requests a year from government officials, she said, increasingly about AI regulation. Her broader work includes a 2025 book, "AI Versus IP: Rewriting Creativity," and a forthcoming book, "The Human Zone," which proposes a New Deal-style patronage and licensing system to support new human-generated creative work.

Professor Ben Depoorter, who has studied copyright for more than 15 years, argues in a forthcoming paper that it is too early to decide whether training AI models on copyrighted works counts as fair use. He says more evidence is needed on whether AI can produce innovative work or only lower-quality imitations, and on its effect on the creative economy. He recommends that judges and lawmakers keep copyright rules flexible as that evidence develops. Professor Dave Owen, working with Alexandra Klass of the University of Michigan, proposes requiring data centers to accept power interruptions during peak demand, which could help keep household and business electricity costs from rising. Owen said the study has drawn inquiries from state lawmakers and attorneys general's offices.

Professor Prithika Balakrishnan, a former public defender, questions how AI-enabled license plate and analytical tools decide that a pattern of travel is suspicious. She cites a 2022 case in which New York police stopped David Zayas after software flagged his vehicle for possible drug trafficking based on nine trips between Massachusetts and New York over about two years. To guard against errors, she proposes requiring a warrant to search a vehicle's license plate location history and expert testimony to help judges assess algorithm-driven conclusions. Professor Seema N. Patel, meanwhile, examines how low-wage workers' personal data is collected, sold and used to train AI without their consent or compensation. She notes that 94% of low-wage workers lack union representation and recommends stronger data rights and new laws and enforcement strategies at the federal, state and local levels.

stories.Headline: How to get started with AI agents, which are best for specific tasks
stories.Summary:
Associated Press technology writer Kaitlyn Huamani reported on November 8, 2026, that AI agents designed to act for users on tasks such as buying groceries or managing to-do lists have become popular this year, with Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic and other companies competing in the market. The article offers beginners guidance on choosing and testing these tools, since their offerings differ in cost, availability and focus. It notes that some agents are free, some need a monthly subscription, and others remain in testing or are unavailable in countries outside the United States. Experts say the choice depends on what a user needs, and the article describes the agents as either colleague-style tools or personal-assistant-style tools.

Writers and consultants quoted in the piece recommend using several agents together, which they call a "stack." Jose Artigas, a business consultant working on AI strategy, said there is not yet one agent that can do everything. Clara Gigling, founder of Oudae Labs, described having one agent do the work while another critiques it so that mistakes are caught and corrected. Artigas suggested Claude Duet for side projects or new businesses, Dots for specialized technical problems, Instinct for tedious emails and travel bookings, and Muse as a user-friendly starting point for newcomers. Gigling advised giving agents specific goals along with the context and tools they need.

Both experts stressed trial and error, with users testing agents on one repeated online task they have been putting off, such as writing a long email or booking a flight. The article notes that agents work best with access to a person's inbox, calendar, identification details and even credit card and bank information, which has raised privacy concerns. Gigling urged users to be curious but mindful about what they share, and the article says many companies have published privacy policies describing dedicated cloud computers and how users can control memory retention. Artigas said agents cannot handle offline chores like folding laundry. The article invites readers to suggest future topics for its One Tech Tip series.

stories.Headline: Stavian Group Showcases Its Infrastructure Vision for the AI Era at the Inaugural Fortune SEA500 Summit 2026
stories.Summary:
Stavian Group, a Vietnam-headquartered infrastructure enterprise, took part as a Partner in the inaugural Fortune SEA500 Summit 2026, held in Ho Chi Minh City under the theme "New Horizons, Enduring Growth." The summit brought together policymakers, investors and business leaders to discuss innovation, infrastructure and long-term competitiveness as Southeast Asia grows under the influence of artificial intelligence and digital transformation. The reporting, published on November 9, 2026, describes the event as a gathering focused on the foundations businesses need in a more interconnected, technology-driven economy. Stavian used the occasion to present its view of infrastructure as the defining enabler of growth in the AI era.

A highlight of Stavian's participation was a panel titled "Building the AI Growth Engine," where Le Dang Dung, Chairman of Stavian High Tech Infrastructure, spoke about what sustainable AI-driven growth requires. He argued that success depends not only on technology but also on strong underlying infrastructure, which the articles list as digital connectivity, energy resilience, investment capacity and talent development. The summit also recognized Stavian Chemical in the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 2026 ranking for the second consecutive year. Tony Dinh Duc Thang, Founder and Chairman of Stavian Group, accepted the ranking certificate on the company's behalf.

Stavian describes the recognition as reflecting years of international expansion, operational excellence and the trust of customers and partners across global markets. The company says it is pursuing infrastructure-led growth through four strategic pillars: Industry, Technology, Energy and Trade. It treats infrastructure not only as physical assets but also as the networks, technologies, energy systems and platforms that connect industries and accelerate innovation. The company says it sees significant opportunities to contribute to infrastructure ecosystems supporting growth across Vietnam, Southeast Asia and the wider Asia-Pacific region.

Looking ahead, Stavian says it will build on the strength of its business ecosystem, including Stavian Chemical, while expanding its role in future-ready infrastructure, innovation and sustainable development. The company states that it aims to become a Global Top 500 enterprise and to help shape a connected, sustainable and resilient future across Southeast Asia and beyond. The articles present these goals as the company's own stated intentions. They do not report any specific projects, investment figures or timelines tied to them.

stories.Headline: Has Wales already lost the AI revolution?
stories.Summary:
Wales has been slow to capture the growth of artificial intelligence businesses since ChatGPT launched in November 2022, according to a column by Dylan Jones-Evans published on 8 November 2026. He argues that the launch signalled a major technological shift that gave entrepreneurs a chance to start new firms and sell products internationally almost overnight. Wales, which has long tried to build a more inventive economy, should have seen this as a chance to create a new group of fast-growing companies. Almost four years on, he says, the country has not made the most of that chance.

The column draws on the Artificial Intelligence Sector Study 2025, published by the UK Government the week before, which counts 10,488 AI businesses across the UK. Those firms generate £33.6 billion in revenue and employ more than 130,000 people. Wales accounts for just 1.6% of them, compared with 3.7% in Scotland, 5.9% in the North West of England and 4% in the West Midlands. Only Northern Ireland and the North East of England have smaller shares. Jones-Evans notes that AI differs from older industries, where advantages built up over generations, because regions could build new strengths in it relatively quickly.

Jones-Evans says Wales has useful assets for this work, including talented researchers, established universities and specialist expertise in semiconductors, cybersecurity and financial technology. He points out that AI firms do not need expensive factories and that small teams can build competitive products with modest initial investment. In his view, Wales could have set up a national programme in early 2023 to find, develop and back hundreds of AI businesses, drawing on universities, entrepreneurs, investors and economic development agencies. He suggests such a programme could have focused on healthcare, manufacturing, education and financial services.

He is critical of the response so far, noting that the Welsh Government published its AI Plan in November 2025, almost three years after ChatGPT appeared. Earlier this year it announced £2.1 million to support AI adoption, including £600,000 for Business Wales, £1 million for skills and £500,000 for tourism and events. Jones-Evans welcomes these measures but says they mainly help existing companies use AI rather than creating firms that build and sell the technology. He argues that both approaches matter, but a Welsh company developing products for world markets could create jobs, intellectual property, exports and wealth on a much larger scale. He says there is still time to change course, but that this requires the Welsh Government, Business Wales and the Development Bank to act.

stories.Headline: From Fake CEO Calls To Garland Police Briefings: Texas And Federal Moves Against AI Impersonation
stories.Summary:
A familiar voice on the phone and an urgent request for money no longer prove that the caller is a company executive, attorney, or government official. Criminals can now use artificial intelligence to imitate identities and persuade victims to hand over funds or sensitive information. A recent federal case involving an alleged $129 million international fraud scheme shows how far these tactics have reached. Meanwhile, the Trump administration, Texas lawmakers, and North Texas police have each pursued different responses, ranging from prosecutions to new laws and public education.

Federal prosecutors in New York unsealed charges on November 5 against Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42. The Justice Department alleges that the conspirators targeted companies worldwide between 2024 and 2026, using AI tools to imitate corporate executives and lawyers. According to the indictment, they posed as chief executives, used synthetic voices or images during calls, and sent employees to supposed attorneys who directed large wire transfers into accounts they controlled. Prosecutors say the scheme took more than $129 million from businesses, including hospital systems and financial firms. Authorities arrested the defendants in Spain and the United Kingdom between June and September, and extradition requests were still pending when the charges were announced.

President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14390 on March 6, directing agencies to develop measures against international scam centers and cyber-enabled financial fraud. The order calls for stronger coordination, prosecution priorities, and recommendations for returning money to victims from recovered criminal proceeds. On November 5, the Justice Department also announced a Super Intelligence Task Force to address harmful uses of emerging technology by foreign actors and criminal groups. The FBI, for its part, warned in July that criminals were using AI-generated videos resembling its personnel to lure earlier fraud victims toward fake complaint websites with promises of recovering lost money.

In Texas, Senate Bill 2373 took effect September 1, 2025, criminalizing specified financial abuse carried out with artificially generated media or phishing and creating a civil route for some victims to seek damages. House Bill 149, the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, took effect January 1, 2026, setting rules for certain AI uses and giving the attorney general enforcement power. Closer to home, Garland police scheduled a November 5 presentation at the West Garland Library on deceptive calls, messages, and AI voice cloning. The FBI advises people to verify unexpected requests through a previously trusted phone number and to use multi-factor authentication, while businesses can stop scams by confirming large payments through a separate channel before releasing funds.

stories.Headline: Cathie Wood Just Sold AMD Stock and Bought This AI Chip Stock Instead
stories.Summary:
Cathie Wood's Ark Invest firm reportedly sold its position in AMD and bought shares in Broadcom instead, a move reported around early November 2026. The Motley Fool analysis published November 9, 2026, argues that Broadcom, not AMD or Intel, poses the bigger competitive threat to Nvidia. The argument rests on the growing trend of AI hyperscalers designing their own custom chips, known as application-specific integrated circuits, to lower costs and improve performance on specific workloads. Broadcom is the partner helping build these chips for large customers including Alphabet, Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic. Together those relationships place Broadcom at the center of a shift that could draw spending away from Nvidia's general-purpose GPUs.

Broadcom's financial results show that demand for custom silicon is accelerating. In its fiscal third quarter, which ended August 2, AI semiconductor revenue more than tripled year over year to $16.7 billion, with custom chips making up roughly 73 percent of that total. Management guided AI semiconductor revenue to $21.7 billion for the fourth quarter. Broadcom expects AI semiconductor revenue of roughly $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and about $230 billion in fiscal 2028. Broadcom also expects Anthropic to deploy 5 gigawatts of eighth-generation TPU capacity in 2027 and an additional 10 gigawatts in 2028, while its OpenAI agreement targets 5 gigawatts of processors by the end of 2028.

The Motley Fool analyst, Adam Spatacco, makes the case that these developments could challenge Nvidia's dominance as inference workloads grow, because specialized processors are often more efficient for repetitive tasks. Spatacco notes that Broadcom's stock, which traded near $294 in early November, had fallen about 39 percent from its all-time high and carried a forward price-to-earnings multiple of about 15, its cheapest level since the AI boom began. He also points out that Broadcom sells networking and connectivity technology that helps AI accelerators work together, so it can benefit even if customers keep buying Nvidia GPUs. A separate Motley Fool article in The Globe and Mail, dated November 8, 2026, instead favors Nvidia over AMD, citing Nvidia's cheaper valuation relative to next year's expected earnings. Nvidia is scheduled to report its fiscal third-quarter results on November 17, 2026.

stories.Headline: Ethical governance of medical AI: a qualitative study of stakeholder perspectives in Shenzhen’s innovation ecosystem
stories.Summary:
A study published on November 9, 2026, in BMC Medical Ethics examines how stakeholders in Shenzhen view the ethical challenges of medical artificial intelligence. Its authors, Ping Ji, Teck Chuan Voo and Haihong Zhang, ran focus group interviews with 45 participants drawn from government agencies, industry, research institutions and medical institutions. The Shenzhen Biomedical Ethics Review Committee approved the work, which followed the Declaration of Helsinki. The study was funded by Shenzhen's Sanming Project and was released early, pending final edits. The authors analyzed the interview material by thematic analysis using NVivo 11 software.

The findings describe a set of concerns that the study says need attention. Participants worried about the safety and reliability of AI in healthcare, the lack of regulatory clarity in day-to-day practice, how responsibility should be divided among parties, and how well different disciplines work together. The authors conclude that more explicit ethical guidance is needed, along with better regulatory coordination, stronger cross-sector collaboration and more institutional support. They also note that the Chinese government and local authorities already include ethical governance in their plans to promote the AI industry. The study argues that all stakeholders should address these ethical issues in both the development and use of medical AI.

The study's authors present Shenzhen's position in China's healthcare AI sector as a possible model for policy and practice in the city and in other fast-growing regions. The paper itself is an academic qualitative study and does not set out specific new rules or deadlines. Its recommendations are framed as needs rather than enforceable requirements. The article notes that the work is open access under a Creative Commons license, and it lists the authors' affiliations with a clinical research institute and a geriatrics department in Shenzhen.

A separate opinion piece in China Daily, written by professors Yin Yunqiang and Wang Dujuan, makes a broader argument about building AI innovation ecosystems rather than isolated projects. The authors say computing power, data, models, real-world testing, talent, capital and rules should reinforce one another. They recommend that governments set strategic direction and fund shared infrastructure without dictating technical paths. They also argue that clear rules on intellectual property, data use and liability give businesses the confidence to invest and experiment. The piece does not address medical AI specifically.

stories.Headline: ‘AI rebounding’: Nearly 20% of U.S. workers replaced by AI are being asked back
stories.Summary:
Nearly one in five U.S. workers say their employer replaced them with AI and later asked them to come back, a pattern a talent assessment firm called "AI rebounding." The finding comes from a survey by SHL conducted in June and July and reported by Fortune on November 9, 2026. Across the U.S. and U.K. the figure was 16%, and 19.1% of American respondents reported having been replaced and then recalled. Younger workers reported the reversal more often, with 24% of respondents aged 18 to 24 saying they had been rehired after being replaced.

Returning workers have been setting conditions before they agree to come back. SHL found that 51% wanted a substantial pay increase, 42% wanted written guarantees about future job security, and 40% wanted to know how AI would be used in their positions. A Robert Half survey from July found that 32% of U.S. hiring managers had to reinstate the same or similar roles after cutting them for AI, with 40% of that group saying the jobs needed institutional knowledge that AI could not replace. Lucy Beaumont, a senior vice president at SHL, said companies often automate roles before they have assessed the human capability inside them. Klarna and Ford have also brought people back after AI tools fell short, with Klarna rehiring human customer service staff and Ford adding 350 experienced engineers in June.

Even so, employers are still citing AI for job cuts at a fast pace. Outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas counted 121,401 announced job cuts linked to AI through October, more than double the 54,836 planned layoffs for all of 2025. A Stanford Digital Economy Lab study found that employment among workers aged 22 to 25 in highly AI-exposed occupations sat 19% below where it would have been at the pace of less-exposed peers. Ford's representative said AI contributed to quality gains but needed to be paired with experienced engineering teams.

A separate global survey from G-P, drawing on 7,100 leaders and workers in six economies, suggests the pressure extends to hiring as well. It found that 58% of employees would reject a job offer if the employer's AI values conflicted with their own, and 73% of those likely to job hunt want their next employer to treat AI as a core part of operations. G-P's Laura Maffucci said employees want employers that pair innovation with chances to build distinctly human skills. The same research found that 92% of executives believe their AI strategy affects their ability to attract and retain talent.

stories.Headline: BREAKING: AI images, deceased persons: 'INEC has cleansed voter register' - Amupitan
stories.Summary:
INEC has announced that it completed a cleansing exercise to remove irregularities from the national voter register ahead of the 2027 general election. INEC Chairman Prof. Joash Amupitan made the announcement at a press briefing in Abuja on Monday, after the commission displayed the preliminary register between October 9 and 15, 2026. The exercise followed public complaints about suspected duplicate registrations, manipulated photographs, unusual names and deceased persons remaining on the register. Amupitan said the commission waited for the 14-day statutory period under the Electoral Act 2026 to expire before reviewing the complaints and acting on them.

The commission processed 11,088,238 registration records from the three phases of the 2025-2026 Continuous Voter Registration using its biometric identification system. The system initially flagged 1,545,052 records for further examination, and 1,277,052 of these were confirmed invalid and excluded before publication. Another 268,000 cases were adjudicated after the display period, with 217,722 removed and 50,278 kept. A further 113,886 invalid registrations were identified and removed following complaints and findings from INEC's technology department. Amupitan also said a nationwide revalidation exercise was postponed until after the elections, while biometric screening and adjudication continue, and the final register is due for publication on December 15, 2026.

Amupitan attributed many multiple-registration complaints to historical records dating back to 2011 and 2023, which were created under different technologies and standards. Separately, INEC's ICT Director, Dr Lawrence Bayode, told Punch that internal and field registration officers used their login credentials to introduce AI-generated images into the register. Bayode said photographs merely enhanced by AI phone applications would not lead to exclusion, while fully AI-generated images would be removed. He also said a special registration option for persons with incomplete or no fingers had been exploited to create questionable profiles.

The reports also place the register within wider concern about AI-generated content in Nigerian elections, following fake images circulated during the June 20, 2026 Ekiti governorship election. Amupitan has said AI is not an enemy of democracy, while warning that generative tools can be used to clone voices and fake official announcements. Experts quoted by Punch said AI could help detect duplicates and misinformation, but they urged safeguards, deepfake detection tools and coordination with social media platforms. The reports do not say what action, if any, will be taken against the officials who used their credentials beyond removal of the records.

stories.Headline: RBA’s Hunter says AI has yet to deliver productivity boost, trigger job losses By Reuters
stories.Summary:
Australian Reserve Bank Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter said on Monday, November 9, 2026, at a UBS conference in Sydney, that there was limited evidence artificial intelligence had meaningfully raised productivity or caused widespread job losses. She also warned that the technology could pose growing risks to financial stability. Hunter spoke as part of a broader discussion of how AI is affecting the economy. Her remarks were reported by Reuters. On inflation, Hunter said the effect from AI would likely change over time, first boosting demand and adding to price pressures while the economy was supply constrained.

She expected supply to catch up as data centre capacity and related sectors expanded, easing current bottlenecks. If AI produced broader productivity gains, she argued, the economy could make more with the same inputs, and the early inflationary pressure from AI investment would likely fade. A boom in domestic data centre investment has added to demand pressure, and it is one reason the central bank has raised interest rates five times this year, to an 18-year high of 4.85%. Hunter described tentative signs of adjustment in the labour market, including weaker job advertisement postings and weaker employment outcomes in occupations more exposed to AI. She also noted stronger growth in areas where the technology has had less impact, particularly for younger workers.

Her comments were made in a speech, and the articles do not indicate any formal policy response linked to them. On financial stability, Hunter warned that AI could increase risks because asset prices may face sharp repricing or disorderly adjustment if returns on AI investment fall short of expectations. The articles do not say whether the central bank plans specific measures in response. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Jesse Eisenberg "experiments" with AI to make sure it's still bad at writing
stories.Summary:
Jesse Eisenberg, the writer, director and actor, told Variety in a new interview that he sometimes tests AI to see whether it can write well yet. He said he remains paranoid about the technology, but he checks it regularly and finds it still writes badly, which relieves him for now. The interview was conducted alongside his co-star Julianne Moore, who is in his new A24 film The Debut, and both were asked how they feel about AI shaping Hollywood. Eisenberg said that when he asks AI to write a scene, the results remain poor.

The articles frame his concern as a question of how far the technology is from producing good work. Eisenberg described a scenario in which a child could put on a headset and watch a made-to-order movie, and he said that possibility worries him. One article notes that AI has already entered the entertainment industry, citing Netflix's use of some form of AI on 300 titles and its recently launched AI Discover feature. It also mentions an AI bot that used actress Mia Goth's name and likeness in viral posts, and efforts to promote the AI actor Tilly Norwood. Eisenberg's remarks sit within a broader Hollywood debate in which some creatives strongly oppose AI, others are skeptical, and some embrace it.

Eisenberg responded to the threat by pointing to the staying power of human creativity. He said the creative spirit will keep finding ways to entertain people and to speak about things in a way that computers may not. He also cited the Greek plays written about 2,500 years ago, which are still performed in much the same way, as evidence that lasting art endures. He said people still want to gather in the same room to watch and hear stories, a habit he compared to cave dwellers around a campfire. He added, however, that his real worry is whether artists will still be able to earn a living from their work, and he said he is not fully sure about that.

The articles place these comments within a wider pattern of entertainers speaking out about AI. Masako Nozawa, the voice of Goku in Dragon Ball, criticized people who used AI to imitate her voice, and Nicolas Cage said he would probably not work with Amazon again after declining to sign its AI waiver. Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto said Nintendo would prefer to take a different direction on the subject. Eisenberg's next film, The Debut, is set to arrive on December 11, 2026.

stories.Headline: Wall Street rallies on falling oil prices despite Nvidia and artificial intelligence fears
stories.Summary:
Wall Street rallied on Monday, November 9, 2026, recovering part of the steep losses it had suffered the previous week as oil prices fell. The S&P 500 climbed 2.3%, putting it on track for a second straight gain, while the Dow rose about 2% and the Nasdaq gained 2.6%. The gains came even though Nvidia, one of the market's most influential stocks, dropped 4.7%. The advance followed a sell-off driven by worries that Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections could slow the construction of AI data centers.

Oil prices were a major driver of the rally, with Brent crude falling 4.8% to $93.59 a barrel, down from above $112 earlier in the month amid uncertainty over the war with Iran. President Donald Trump told CNN over the weekend that a resumption of strikes is "highly unlikely" if negotiations make progress, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Iranian demands to end the war "outrageous and ridiculous." Airlines and cruise operators benefited from expectations of lower fuel costs, with United Airlines up 5.9% and Carnival up 3.4%. Strong earnings from some major companies also lifted sentiment, and Constellation Energy jumped 9.5% after beating analyst expectations on the back of deals to supply power to Big Tech data centers. Advanced Micro Devices and CoreWeave also gained after losses the week before.

The main concern for AI-linked companies is that new government restrictions could reduce purchases of AI chips, power and related infrastructure, since Democratic victories in statehouses across the country saw voters blame data centers for rising electricity bills. Nvidia's drop came after the company said it was investigating CEO Jensen Huang over an intimate relationship with an executive who, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China. Nvidia's board said it has "no reason to believe" national security or company secrets were compromised but that the inquiry will review all available information. China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun dismissed the allegations as "nothing but smears against China." Analysts at Morgan Stanley and UBS had argued that last week's AI sell-off went too far, since the feared extreme regulation of data centers under a Democrat-controlled Congress seemed unlikely to materialize.

Markets remained on edge as investors looked toward the coming days, with the Labor Department scheduled to release its October Consumer Price Index report on Tuesday and economists polled by Reuters expecting a 2.7% year-over-year increase. Fears of a December interest rate hike persisted after stronger-than-expected October jobs data. Treasury yields were steady, with the 10-year yield at 4.88%, below the peak of over 5.30% reached last month, a level not seen in two decades. The recent pullback in yields has eased borrowing rates for mortgages and loans, which has helped equity markets. Analysts suggested that the focus on Nvidia could fade once investors turn to the inflation data later in the week.

stories.Headline: DeepSeek’s AI agent push gains speed as Harness tops 1.5 million daily users
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek, the Hangzhou-based Chinese AI start-up, said on Sunday that its Harness agent framework had reached 1.54 million daily active users less than three months after launch. The company reported that, as of November 4, users of Harness through its official application programming interface were consuming about 92 trillion tokens a day, roughly 1.1 billion tokens per second. The announcement was reported by the South China Morning Post, with reporter Minxiao Chang filing from Shenzhen. The growth was described as rapid in a new contest between leading Chinese and American AI firms over agents.

A harness, according to the article, is the software infrastructure that turns a large language model into an AI agent able to carry out tasks on its own for users rather than only answering prompts. The article frames the effort as DeepSeek ramping up work to monetise its powerful foundation models as the agent platform gains traction. It also asks whether DeepSeek can challenge OpenAI and Anthropic in AI agents as adoption of Harness takes off. The figures above are the company's own disclosures, and the article does not independently verify them.

The company itself is the source of the usage numbers, and the article relays them as DeepSeek's statement rather than as audited data. Beyond the user and token figures, the article gives no further detail on who is accountable for the platform's direction or what specific pricing or product changes were announced. The surrounding context is a competitive race in which Chinese and American AI giants are both pushing into agent products. The article does not say what comes next for Harness or what regulatory or commercial steps are planned, so the outlook remains open.

stories.Headline: Meta expands Instagram’s AI age-guessing tech globally
stories.Summary:
Meta announced on Monday, November 9, 2026, that it is rolling out its AI-powered age-estimation technology on Instagram worldwide. The system is designed to identify users it suspects are teenagers, even when those users entered an adult birthday when they signed up. Once flagged, those accounts are moved into Teen Accounts, which carry stricter settings. Mashable reported the same expansion, noting that Meta first began using the technology on Instagram in April 2025.

The Teen Account settings limit who can send direct messages to a teen, hide harmful comments, and make accounts private by default. To find likely teens, Meta's tools analyze whole profiles for contextual clues such as birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades, looking across posts, comments, bios and captions. The company also examines visual cues from photos and videos, including a person's height or bone structure. Meta says the same technology will expand to Facebook, with a similar global rollout planned for Threads later this year. In the United States, parents will begin seeing an in-feed video on Instagram explaining how their teens are placed in age-appropriate protections.

Meta said it is acting partly under its agreements with state officials. The company reached settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every U.S. state and territory in August, resolving lawsuits alleging its platforms harm teens, and agreed to improve how it identifies teens and children under 13. Under its agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general, Meta said it is investing in stronger technology to catch accounts that may belong to children under 13 and strengthening detection of accounts belonging to users aged 13 to 17. In a blog post, the company said it would continue doing its part to keep teens in age-appropriate experiences. Meta has also urged TikTok and YouTube to adopt the same practices, arguing that teens remain inconsistently protected unless other companies follow suit.

The expansion comes amid continued legal pressure on the company. In March, a jury found Meta liable in a case brought by the state of New Mexico, which alleged that its design features helped predators exploit children, and Meta said it would fight the decision. Mashable also reported that Meta sued the California attorney general last week to block a new law aimed at reducing youth social media addiction, which is set to take effect in January. Governments elsewhere are also tightening rules, including Australia's ban on social media for users under 16. Mashable noted that child safety groups have generally welcomed Meta's proposed fixes, though they continue to criticize the company's Teen Accounts.

stories.Headline: David Ellison Is Very Bullish On AI’s Creative Potential
stories.Summary:
Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison said on his company's first earnings call as head of both Paramount and Warner Bros. that artificial intelligence could become the biggest creative breakthrough in modern Hollywood history. The remarks came on November 9, 2026, and drew on his view that AI would help studios make content faster and more cheaply. He also drew a line against what he called low-quality "AI slop," saying premium, hand-crafted storytelling would remain valuable. The comments were made while he was pitching the merged company as a tech-forward enterprise.

Ellison compared AI to the arrival of CGI and digital composites in the early 1990s, which he credited with enabling films such as Jurassic Park and Terminator 2. He argued that the tools could make budgets more manageable, using James Cameron's original Terminator, made for about $4 million in 1983, as an example. By his estimate, a shot-for-shot remake today would cost $60 million to $70 million. He said these tools could help the company take bigger creative risks on original stories. Skydance plans to spend $30 billion a year across its content portfolio.

Ellison framed AI as a tool for artists rather than a replacement for them, and he said the company has been building its own AI tools. He also said that franchise intellectual property, which he described as the company having 40 franchises worth $1 billion each, would act as a protective barrier against the flood of AI-generated content. Skydance is also seeking about $6 billion in cost savings from combining Paramount and Warner Bros., with AI workflows scaled across the company. He said that merging Paramount+ and HBO Max within a year was an "ambitious target" made possible by the latest AI tools. He has also been backed publicly by Cameron, whose own studio recently bought an AI-driven 3D post-production firm.

Industry reaction is divided, as the technology is widely seen as a threat to traditional Hollywood production methods while also being adopted by studios. Netflix has used AI on more than 300 titles through a VFX firm associated with Ben Affleck, according to the reporting. The articles do not say how the combined company will balance these competing pressures in practice. The companies have also said that a bundle of HBO Max and Paramount+ would launch in early 2027.

stories.Headline: Google Unveils TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx: A Dual-Chip TPU and a Confidential TPU
stories.Summary:
Google has added two new systems to its eighth-generation TPU lineup, announced on November 9, 2026. The first, TPU 8i Max, is a dual-chip package made from two TPU 8i chips and is aimed at very large context windows and higher rack density. The second, TPU 8tx, is aimed at secure, confidential inference. Both arrive alongside the TPU 8t and TPU 8i that Google announced in April. The new systems reuse existing eighth-generation silicon and change the packaging, hosts, memory and networking around it.

TPU 8i Max combines two low-latency TPU 8i chips into one package, which the articles say doubles compute, on-chip SRAM and HBM bandwidth compared with a single TPU 8i. Each TPU 8i chip is rated at 10.1 PFLOPS of FP4, 288 GB of HBM, 8,601 GB/s of bandwidth and 384 MB of on-chip SRAM, so the doubled figures would imply roughly 20.2 PFLOPS, 768 MB of SRAM and 17.2 TB/s per package, though Google has not published these absolute numbers. TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as TPU 8t, paired with 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU hosts and the Boardfly network from TPU 8i. Google claims TPU 8tx cuts latency by up to 2x versus TPU 8t with a near-zero security penalty, and it lets teams fine-tune, distill and run reinforcement learning on one system without moving sensitive data between clusters. The articles note that neither system has published benchmarks, prices or regions, and that both are slated for 2027 availability according to Bloomberg via Quartz.

Google is the company behind both systems, and its team describes TPU 8i Max as a way to fit twice the silicon in the existing rack footprint for agents working across whole codebases or hours of video. TPU 8tx is positioned for regulated enterprises and governments that need data and model weights protected even while in active use, which normally requires decrypting data in memory during processing. The articles also list several accompanying software releases: TorchTPU, open-sourced last month, which runs PyTorch and Hugging Face models natively; a TPU agent suite in preview; TPU Sync, an open-source library for tiering KV cache across memory levels; and Agent Compute Engine, which is expected to enter preview in the coming months. Google's own tests of TPU Sync on Ironwood, not the new systems, reportedly cut median KV transfer latency on Qwen3 235B to about 230 ms.

stories.Headline: The realities of scaling AI agents: ‘You don't have an AI problem, you have a content problem’
stories.Summary:
Sifted published an article on 9 November 2026 about the challenges of scaling autonomous AI agents, drawing on a Sifted Talks panel held in partnership with the content management platform Box. The piece describes a shift from AI copilots, which wait for human instructions, to agents that can access databases, draft and send emails, process invoices, organise files and make decisions in real time. Because these agents work at high speed, the article notes, a single mistake can affect business operations within seconds. The panel discussion focused on how businesses can integrate such agents safely through a plan for data, security and governance.

The article says the main difference between copilots and autonomous agents is that the latter make decisions without human prompting, so trust and autonomy must be earned over time. One panellist compared deployment to onboarding a new salesperson, starting with a defined scope, limited system access and ongoing supervision, and said agents should never receive full autonomy across business management systems on day one. Another panellist warned that an agent's speed and capacity make the potential for damage much larger than a human employee's mistake, and said that when agents can reach databases, the potential blasts of an error escalate significantly. The panel also stressed that humans must remain accountable, since people provide agents with their capabilities and the right to act.

The article states that the panellists want organisations to organise their business data and context before an agent carries out any task, because agents can hallucinate and fail when fed disorganised data, duplicates or outdated files. Chief AI officer Hanah-Marie Darley of Geordie AI argued that "human-in-the-loop" has become an overused term because it does not specify who the reviewer is or what information that person needs. Panellists also described a zero-trust approach in which the model is assumed to be compromised and the business defines and enforces what the agent can and cannot do. The article adds that access should be task-specific, time-bounded and context-aware, and that controls must be applied at the content level to stop agents from exposing restricted information. Darley, according to the article, identified a "silent failure" in which agents operate without alarm bells and without any real-time understanding of their behaviour.

The article credits Hébrard, from Box, with the central point that "you don't have an AI problem, you have a content problem," and attributes to panellist McNeil the view that governance, compliance and risk teams should be involved before pilots begin, since they will either enable or hinder successful scaling. The article also reports that McNeil said companies often focus too heavily on technology rather than on the underlying business process. Hébrard, it says, recommended that organisations log every prompt and reasoning step so they can explain what happened during audits. The article frames these recommendations as the practical response to the risk that unsanctioned tools spread when employees lack sanctioned options that work.
