stories.Headline: Japan government to create AI-based Japanese-learning app for anime, manga fans
stories.Summary:
Japan's government plans to build an artificial intelligence-powered app that helps people learn Japanese through the anime and manga characters they already love. According to Nikkei, the app will be developed by the Japan Foundation at the request of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, after budget approval for the next fiscal year. The Japan Times reports that it is expected to be finished by fiscal 2028 and will mainly aim at young people overseas who are interested in anime and manga. Users will be able to practice conversations with popular characters, and it will be the first time the foundation has used AI in its language-learning services.

The app marks a shift from earlier foundation tools, which used original characters because of copyright limits. For this project, the foundation plans to negotiate with rights holders to use well-known characters instead. The ministry has requested ¥1.83 billion, about $11.6 million, for fiscal 2027 to support the overseas expansion of Japanese content. The Japan Times also notes that the ministry hopes the app will widen access to Japanese-language education in areas where schools and qualified teachers are scarce. It is also described as a lower-cost option than setting up more overseas teaching facilities.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs asked for the project, and the Japan Foundation will carry it out. The reports describe the effort as part of a wider push to strengthen Japan's soft power, meaning its influence through culture rather than force. Officials are seeking to turn growing overseas interest in Japanese pop culture into a larger base of fans, particularly in emerging and developing economies in Africa and Central and South America. Other measures in the same effort include building networks between Japanese and local content professionals, promoting legal distribution to fight piracy, and supporting translators.

The context is a 2024 foundation survey, which found that 61.3% of students at overseas Japanese-language institutions cited anime, manga, J-pop or J-fashion as their reason for studying the language. The same survey counted a record 4 million overseas learners, up 5.4% from its 2021 edition. Interest in studying or working in Japan was also rising, with 37.3% citing study there and 36.4% citing future employment. Both outlets present the app as a planned project with a target completion date of fiscal 2028, and the reports do not say how the rights negotiations will turn out.

stories.Headline: Arab News | Who will reinvent education for the AI age?
stories.Summary:
On November 8, 2026, Arab News senior editor Arnab Neil Sengupta published a column asking whether the long-standing family advice to study hard, earn a good degree and land a well-paying job will still be enough in an economy shaped by artificial intelligence. He argued that nobody can say with confidence which occupations will shrink, flourish or emerge over the next decade, but that schools and universities cannot wait for the picture to clear before asking whether they are preparing young people for the world outside the classroom. The piece was also carried by The Frontier Post. It is an opinion column rather than a news report, so it sets out the author's view of what education systems should do.

The column leans on several figures. The World Economic Forum's 2025 employer survey estimated that 39 percent of workers' existing skills would change or become outdated by 2030, and 46 percent in the Middle East and North Africa. The International Labour Organization estimates that one in four workers holds an occupation with some exposure to generative AI, though it sees changes to how people work as more likely than outright job replacement. A 2025 study by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Stanford found that support agents using an AI reply tool resolved 15 percent more queries per hour, with the biggest gains among less experienced staff. An OECD 2026 digital education review cited a high school math experiment in which students who used a general purpose chatbot did better in practice but scored lower on a test taken without it.

On what should change, Sengupta says primary schools should keep their focus on reading, writing, mathematics and getting along with others, while teaching children that a computer can sound authoritative and still be wrong. He says secondary schools must work out whether homework still shows what a pupil knows, and that universities should add entrepreneurship, risk assessment and teamwork to subject knowledge, especially in Saudi Arabia and its Gulf neighbors. He points to King Abdullah University of Science and Technology's Venture Studio and TAQADAM accelerator, and to the UAE's Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, as models, and notes that Singapore and Khan Academy's Khanmigo tutor offer lessons elsewhere. He also cautions that entrepreneurship should not become a fashionable slogan, since societies will still need teachers, nurses, technicians and public servants.

Several officials are cited. Prince Turki Al-Faisal, the former Saudi diplomat and intelligence chief, said at an event in Bahrain on November 1 that Gulf economies will need AI and robotics to offset aging populations and labor shortages, even though the same tools could cut opportunities for young graduates, and he urged closer links between technology, education and employment policy along with retraining programs. Egypt's education minister, Mohammed Abdel Latif, told a parliamentary committee earlier this year that coding and AI are already being taught, especially to first-year secondary students, and in September reported that work was finished on 11 subjects for the second year of secondary school under the Egyptian Baccalaureate, including programming and AI. The UAE's acting higher education minister, Abdulrahman Al-Awar, speaking in Abu Dhabi last month, said new technologies are changing the skills the market needs. Looking ahead, the author urges schools to ask whether an AI tool helps children learn, to train teachers and trial it in a few classrooms first, and to keep time for reading novels and debating history.

stories.Headline: Children need AI that helps them think, not think for them
stories.Summary:
Korean policy commentary published on November 10, 2026 by Kim Hyun-cheol, a professor at Yonsei University College of Medicine, argues that schools need age-based rules for students' use of generative AI. The piece notes that 68 percent of students from fourth grade through high school reported using generative AI in the previous week, including 82 percent of high school students. It cites American data showing that 63 percent of teenagers using AI for schoolwork have obtained answers from it, while 25 percent have copied them directly. Separately, a second opinion piece from Hindustan Times, published on November 8, 2026 by Shishir Jaipuria, raises a similar concern about learners relying on AI for ready-made answers.

The columnist recommends that Korea limit AI in elementary schools, supervise it in middle schools and teach critical use in high schools. Under this approach, elementary pupils would not independently use general-purpose AI to complete assignments, and reading, writing, arithmetic and basic reasoning would come first. Middle school students would use AI designed to encourage independent thinking under teacher guidance. Authorities would need to set standards for age suitability, safety, privacy and learning outcomes, while high schools would teach how to use general-purpose AI critically and disclose its role in work.

The author draws on research to support the case for careful design. In a Turkish study of nearly 1,000 high school students, an ordinary chatbot raised practice scores by 48 percent but lowered later unaided test results by 17 percent compared with textbooks, while a hint-based tutor showed no significant difference. A two-year trial of Khan Academy's Khanmigo tutor at 18 Tennessee middle schools produced only modest gains in mathematics. The author also notes that a 44 percent share of teenagers encountered device or network blocks, and that 59 percent of them then switched to personal devices, so enforcement alone is unlikely to work.

The commentary proposes that assessment change so that students must show their reasoning, solve problems in class and explain their answers orally. It also calls for pilot programs compared against control schools, with results measured for achievement, reasoning, teacher workload and gaps between students, and for publicly released findings. The author concludes that children need AI that helps them think rather than thinking in their place. The Hindustan Times piece likewise advises a "Think, Ask, Verify, Create, Reflect" approach to using AI in learning.

stories.Headline: RBA's Sarah Hunter says the AI boom is pushing up Australian inflation
stories.Summary:
The Reserve Bank of Australia's Sarah Hunter has said that the AI boom is adding to inflation pressure in Australia in the near term. She made the remarks at a UBS conference in Sydney on Monday, November 9, while the RBA's cash rate sat at 4.85%, an 18-year high after five rate increases this year. Hunter called AI "likely to be one of the most significant technological developments of our time," and said it is already reshaping business investment and demand. Her comments came alongside new RBA staff research on AI's effects on jobs, inflation, data centres and household wealth.

The central bank's concern is that a strong boost to demand, set against limited supply, pushes prices up before capacity catches up. Data centre investment has expanded roughly tenfold in three years, according to RBA staff, and the construction, labour and materials it draws on are already stretched. RBA staff project a further $115 billion in data centre investment by the end of 2028, about two per cent of GDP, though they warned that figure could be overstated if power, water or construction constraints grow. Export prices for a South Korean memory chip called DRAM rose more than 200 per cent in the year to September, and Australian buyers are likely to feel that through higher tech costs. Two developments in recent weeks, Stockland shelving a Kogarah data centre and community opposition to projects in Melbourne and Sydney, show the constraints are already biting.

Hunter has said that AI-driven demand should eventually be matched by expanded capacity, and that productivity gains could let the economy produce more from the same inputs, leaving the long-run effect on inflation broadly neutral. She has also said there is limited evidence so far that AI has lifted productivity or caused widespread job losses, though weaker job postings in AI-exposed roles suggest some labour market adjustment. The RBA's research estimates that household exposure to AI-related shares rose from two per cent of financial wealth at the end of 2022 to 5.3 per cent by June 2026, mainly through superannuation. A 30 per cent fall in those share prices would cut household wealth by about 1.6 per cent, according to the same estimates. Hunter also warned that if returns on AI investment disappoint, some asset prices could face sharp or disorderly repricing.

The RBA's stance points in one direction for borrowers and founders: the central bank is not signalling near-term rate relief, and funding costs are likely to stay high. The articles note that the picture could shift if AI spending slows, which would ease demand pressure on inflation while hurting the shares of companies whose earnings depend on that spending. Capital Economics has expected US AI investment to keep growing next year at a slower pace before falling in 2028. The next RBA policy decision and the next quarterly CPI release will show whether the central bank's reading of AI as a temporary inflation push holds.

stories.Headline: Capgemini to Lead EU Consortium on Advanced AI Cyber Risks
stories.Summary:
Capgemini has been selected to lead a consortium working for the European Commission's AI Office, which sits within DG CNECT, to assess cyber threats from advanced AI systems. The work falls under the EU's AI Safety program and the AI Act, and it focuses on cyber offence risks linked to general-purpose AI models. Capgemini announced the award on Thursday, November 5, 2026, and the contract is one of six lots in a call for tenders on technical assistance for AI safety. This lot covers the modeling and evaluation of cyber offence risks. The award was made under Lot 2 of the EC-CNECT-2025-OP-0032 procurement procedure.

The consortium is meant to address concerns that these models are gaining autonomous abilities relevant to hacking. Those abilities include finding software flaws automatically, generating exploit code and coordinating large-scale attacks. Capgemini said Europe needs harmonized evaluation frameworks so that such technologies can be deployed safely across the bloc. The announcement did not disclose a contract value or any direct revenue figure. Its stated purpose is to support enforcement of the AI Act against providers of general-purpose AI models.

Capgemini leads the group alongside Wavestone, a consulting firm, and LNE, the French public body for metrology and testing. The partners bring expertise in cybersecurity risk management, operational security, AI evaluation and conformity assessment. Their tasks include modeling emerging risks, building evaluation tools and designing technical methods for checking compliance. They will also carry out technical assessments on request from the AI Office. Capgemini's chief responsibility is to help the AI Office identify systemic risks and enforce the Act's obligations.

The award came shortly after Capgemini's earnings update on October 30. The company reported third-quarter revenue of 6,073 million euros, up 11.7 percent at constant exchange rates. It raised its full-year constant-currency growth target to 9.0 to 9.5 percent, from about 8.5 to 9.0 percent, and expects fourth-quarter growth of 3 to 4 percent. The articles do not describe any further milestones or next steps for the consortium beyond the tasks already outlined.

stories.Headline: Google AI school policy
stories.Summary:
Google has announced that, in the coming months, Google Search and its Gemini chatbot will be turned off by default for schools, and will only be available to schools that opt in to artificial intelligence. The Los Angeles Unified School District said it is reviewing the announcement and what it means for schools, educators and students. Earlier this school year, the district had already barred students from using generative AI on district-issued devices. Currently, students can still search with Google, but the AI chat mode is off. Its Ad Hoc Committee on Generative AI meets on November 13.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, said search and AI are deeply integrated, so a school that bans AI would lose access to search. Google has said schools should control AI in their classrooms, and it plans a "guided learning" tool for student accounts in schools that opt in. Advocates have objected sharply, with Lila Byock of Schools Beyond Screens urging district leaders to divest from Google. The district has also asked Google to let schools turn off AI-generated search summaries.

In a separate matter, the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority told staff on Friday to stop work, shut down their computers and stay off agency systems while it looked into a potential security issue. Interim CEO Gita O'Neill said the agency did not yet know whether sensitive personal information had been accessed. The shutdown was still in place Monday evening, and the agency said it had hired outside cybersecurity specialists. The agency holds sensitive records on people experiencing homelessness, including Social Security numbers and health histories. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Wearable sleep trackers are using your brainwaves to train AI models without explicit user consent — tens of millions of hours of EEG data harvested
stories.Summary:
Wearable sleep trackers from several companies have been using the brain-wave recordings they collect to train AI models, according to an investigation by Science with the Pulitzer Center's AI Accountability Network, published on November 9, 2026. The investigation found that these firms have gathered tens of millions of hours of electroencephalography (EEG) data, which measures electrical activity in the brain. Several of them are using those recordings to build what are called brain foundation models, even though their privacy policies at first did not clearly say so. One example is Interaxon, the Canadian maker of the Muse headband, which has already trained an AI model on about 50,000 hours of recordings. Using the data for training was not made particularly clear to customers.

Interaxon says it strips out identifying details such as names, email addresses and home addresses before using the data. Its Chief Marketing Officer, Nadia Kumentas, said the company aims to use as much of its eligible data as possible. She also acknowledged that users should be explicitly informed, and the company has since updated its privacy policy to say so. Customers whose recordings had already been used were told only after the fact, which could expose the company to potential lawsuits.

The article also notes that more than two-thirds of the companies Science studied allowed their data to be transferred to other companies without user consent, a concern if a small firm is acquired. Colorado and California have amended their consumer privacy laws to cover neural data, while other states have not. Emotiv, another wearable EEG maker, is training its Large Brain model partly on recordings from customers who use its high-end devices. After questions from Science, the company updated its privacy policy to disclose the use of de-identified neural data for model training, subject to opt-in consent.

The approach differs from training a large language model, since developers feed these systems recordings of brain activity rather than text, and the models learn recurring patterns that can be adapted to recognize brain states or support research. AI startup Piramidal has trained its model on more than 4 million hours of EEG data in partnership with the Cleveland Clinic, and after fine-tuning it correctly identified nine out of 10 seizures in a pilot study. The article stresses that consumer headbands, which typically use one to six electrodes compared with 19 to 25 in clinical systems, cannot read people's thoughts. It also points to a February incident in which an engineer found he could access other users' brain-wave recordings through a smart sleep mask because of hardcoded credentials in its Android app.

stories.Headline: Adobe’s CX Enterprise Coworker Gets Embedded Within Leading AI Platforms
stories.Summary:
Adobe announced on November 6 that its CX Enterprise Coworker, an agentic AI teammate for customer experience orchestration, will be embedded in ChatGPT as a plugin, Claude, Databricks Genie, Gemini for business, and Microsoft Copilot. The company said availability in Amazon Quick, IBM, and Snowflake is expected soon. The system is designed to manage the full customer lifecycle, from acquiring clients to growing their lifetime value. It is built on open standards, including the model context protocol and Agent2Agent, so it can connect with the tools marketers already use.

Adobe also introduced new connectors that provide prebuilt integrations with ecosystem partners such as Microsoft Work IQ, RainFocus, Snowflake Cortex AI, Amazon Ads, Databricks Genie, and Demandbase. These connectors allow marketers to link their existing partner systems without doing any integration work. A single request can then pull data and take action across several systems at once. The goal is to smooth the customer experience from start to finish inside familiar AI tools.

Anjul Bhambhri, Adobe's senior vice president of engineering for customer experience orchestration, said that marketers often use AI tools in isolation without the organizational context they need. She argued that the Coworker connects those tools and workflows using brand, customer, and channel intelligence to produce better business results. Rao Surapaneni, a vice president at Google Cloud, said that integrating the system into Gemini lets organizations use customer data securely where they already work. Rob Howard of Microsoft described the approach as putting agentic AI to work across the customer experience.

Global systems integrators such as Accenture, Capgemini, Cognizant, Deloitte Digital, EY, IBM, Infosys, PwC, and TCS are building ready-to-use industry solutions on the platform. Agencies including Dentsu, Havas, Omnicom, Publicis, Stagwell, and WPP are customizing it with their own tools and expertise for shared clients. Together, these partners aim to link Adobe with wider corporate technology stacks and turn AI pilots into measurable business results. The articles present this as a shift toward collaborative productivity in modern enterprises.

stories.Headline: What to Buy After the AI Stock Plunge? Oppenheimer: Focus on the 'Realization of Returns' Theme, with Microsoft, Oracle, and SAP as Top Picks
stories.Summary:
Microsoft is winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing capacity from Oracle, according to a Bloomberg News report published on a Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The decision is part of a broader reassessment of Microsoft's cloud partnerships, which involve billions of dollars. Microsoft had been gradually cutting back its rented capacity from Oracle in recent months and declined to renew the contract. The report also said the Oracle hardware relied on an older generation of Nvidia chips that became less valuable to Microsoft as its needs evolved.

An Oracle spokesperson told Reuters that demand for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure's AI infrastructure remains strong, even for earlier-generation GPUs. Microsoft is rethinking how it secures computing capacity so it can get the most from its large AI investments. Separately, AI cloud company IREN said on a Thursday that it had delayed some infrastructure deliveries because Microsoft asked for changes to its network design. That shift moved IREN's target for bringing more than $4 billion in annualized revenue capacity online from year-end to January, with a possible further delay until late February. Bloomberg also reported that day that Microsoft is tightening oversight of data center projects run by neocloud providers, including IREN, Nebius, and Nscale, because of delays and rising costs.

Oracle and Microsoft had announced a multi-year deal in 2023 under which Microsoft would use Oracle's AI infrastructure to power the AI-assisted version of its Bing search engine. The financial terms of that agreement were not disclosed. The articles do not say how much capacity Microsoft is shedding or when the wind-down will be complete. They also do not indicate whether the Bing arrangement is affected by the reassessment.

stories.Headline: Lunit to Supply AI Imaging Software to Saudi National Guard Health Affairs
stories.Summary:
Lunit, the Korean medical AI company listed as 328130.KQ, said on November 10, 2026 that it will supply its AI imaging analysis software to the Ministry of National Guard Health Affairs (MNGHA) in Saudi Arabia. The products are Lunit INSIGHT CXR, which analyzes chest X-rays, and Lunit INSIGHT MMG, which analyzes mammography. The deal will be carried out through stc Group's ICT subsidiary, Solutions by stc, which will act as systems integrator while Lunit supplies the AI licenses. The tools will connect to MNGHA's existing picture archiving and communication system, so local medical staff can see AI results inside their current reading environment without using a separate system.

MNGHA is the medical organization under the Ministry of National Guard, which oversees the Saudi Arabian National Guard. Established in 1982, it serves National Guard personnel, their families and the general public through hospitals and medical centers in major regions, centered on Riyadh and Jeddah. According to Lunit, the agency is recognized for its global competitiveness in digital healthcare. King Abdulaziz Medical City Riyadh, which operates under MNGHA, became the first in the world to reach Stage 7, the highest grade, in four categories of the HIMSS digital maturity assessment in 2022.

Lunit has been building its presence in Saudi Arabia for some time. In 2023 it took part in the SEHA Virtual Hospital project and a healthcare sandbox program, both tied to Vision 2030, the Saudi government's national development strategy. The same year, it supplied Lunit INSIGHT MMG to Dr. Sulaiman Al Habib Medical Group, the largest private healthcare group in the kingdom. The company says the new agreement broadens its local references.

Lunit's chief executive, Suh Beom-seok, said MNGHA has some of the most advanced digital infrastructure in the world and chose Lunit based on its technology and its ability to integrate with large medical systems. Suh also said the company will expand its Saudi healthcare business through its partnership with a leading local ICT firm and extend AI cancer screening across the Middle East. Lunit plans to accelerate its push into Saudi Arabia and the wider region, in step with the kingdom's effort to digitize healthcare as a core part of Vision 2030. stories.Headline: Here’s a look into student and faculty opinions on AI use
stories.Summary:
Some professors at San Diego State University and Penn are mixing firm bans with cautious openness about AI, according to recent campus reporting. The Daily Aztec reported that SDSU partnered with OpenAI to give students free ChatGPT memberships, and that Google Gemini held a two-day pop-up on campus. The same report noted that the California State University system's annual AI survey, run by researchers David Goldberg and Elisa Sobo, was most recently collected in 2025. It also said that 49 percent of American adults report using AI chatbots, and 66 percent of those users are between 18 and 29.

The survey found that students in SDSU's Colleges of Professional Studies and Fine Arts, Arts and Letters, and Education reported the lowest rates of AI use, while the Fowler College of Business reported the highest. Among Fowler business students, 80.5 percent agreed that AI will play a significant role in their future careers. At Penn, the Daily Pennsylvanian reported that its PennChat portal, launched in July after a pilot phase finished a month later, gives members access to select Claude and ChatGPT models within the university's network. Penn's technology leader, Tiffany Hanulec, said the portal has nearly 6,000 registered users and that web search and image generation have been added. Penn's guidance asks users to avoid entering identifiable health information unless it is necessary for the task.

At SDSU, professors take very different positions on AI in their courses. John Francis, a management professor, bars generative AI in his course unless the instructor approves it, but he argues that rules should focus on using AI well in professional settings. Eunice Uhm, an art history professor, bars AI-generated ideas or writing submitted as a student's own, and she argues that such tools are not ethically situated or intellectually committed. Benjamin Gonzalez O'Brien, a political science professor, says any generative AI use violates his academic honesty policy. Crosby Noricks, a public relations professor, takes a middle path, treating AI as a baseline research skill while keeping academic honesty expectations.

At Penn, professors and students are similarly divided over the portal's value and risks. Matthew O'Donnell, an Annenberg lecturer, sees PennChat as a potentially useful teaching tool because it could make AI use easier to track and document. Etienne Jacquot, an Annenberg systems administrator, stressed that enterprise licenses keep university data under the university's control, while commercial subscriptions may use the data for training. Engineering senior Thomas Fanjul said he prefers PennChat for document work but rarely uses it because it requires Penn's Wi-Fi or a VPN connection. Both campuses' reporting suggests the debate over AI policy is likely to keep evolving as the technology spreads through professional fields.

stories.Headline: Predictions 2027: Why the future of work is 'AI and human' adjacent
stories.Summary:
Angela Vidler, Managing Director and Co-Founder at Hyvid, has set out her predictions for how work will change in 2027, in a piece published by IT Brief Australia on 9 November 2026. She argues that businesses will have to rethink who does the work, how it gets done and who takes responsibility for the outcome as AI agents take on more of the execution. In her view, the shift will put AI onto the board's workforce agenda, speed up the redesign of workflows and raise expectations of global talent. She adds that capability and output will become stronger measures of value than labour cost alone.

On the board agenda, Vidler says directors have long governed people through headcount, pay, capability, succession and structure, while AI sat with technology. She expects that split to break down, with boards asking whether they truly know what their AI workforce is doing and who is accountable when it gets something wrong. An organisation might have 500 employees, she notes, yet its real capacity will come from people, AI-augmented people and autonomous systems working together. Boards will need visibility into where AI assists people, where it adds to individual capacity and where it runs defined workflows alone, and will need a workforce plan for their AI as well as their people.

Vidler backs her case with research from Microsoft and Deloitte. Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index found that active agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem grew 15 times year on year, and 18 times in large enterprises, and that the biggest gains go to organisations that redesign workflows rather than simply hand out AI tools. It also found that organisational factors such as culture, manager support and talent practices account for more than twice the reported AI impact of individual factors. Deloitte's 2026 research found that 74% of surveyed leaders expect nearly half of their business processes to be redesigned or rebuilt around AI agents within four years, and 61% expect most of their agents to be generally autonomous with humans overseeing them. Only 5% of organisations say their processes are currently highly prepared for AI agents, while 75% of executives say human and agent collaboration creates more value than agent automation alone.

Vidler stresses that this will not be a simple story of AI replacing employees, and expects one person to supervise, validate and manage far more work, with humans supplying judgement, accountability, context and exception handling. For global and offshore talent, she predicts the focus will move from finding the cheapest capable person to building AI-integrated teams that deliver much more output per person. She also points to Deloitte's work naming workforce planning as one of four priorities for adopting agentic AI, alongside governance, strategy and trust, with planning shifting from headcount towards skills, tasks, roles and capacity. In her view, 2027 will be the year businesses treat AI agents as part of workforce planning and organisational design, deciding how much capacity they need and which mix of people and AI will deliver it.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence: A New Security Threat to Central Asia?
stories.Summary:
On November 6, Astana hosted an Aqaba Process summit on security in the field of artificial intelligence. The meeting brought together the presidents of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, King Abdullah II of Jordan, Kyrgyzstan's foreign minister, the speaker of Azerbaijan's parliament and other officials. Jordan's king launched the Aqaba Process in 2015 as an international initiative to counter terrorism and violent extremism. Participants discussed threats including deepfakes, disinformation, cyberattacks and the use of AI for extremist and terrorist purposes.

Several concrete steps and rules came up. Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev said his country is ready to host a regional office of the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism, which could help train specialists and address terrorist content in Central Asia, though that office remains a proposal and has not been set up. Kazakhstan's AI law, in force since January 2026, defines synthetic content as images, video, audio, text or combinations of these that an AI system creates or alters to imitate people or events. Uzbekistan introduced administrative liability in January 2026 for the unlawful processing and spreading of personal data using artificial intelligence, a provision that concerns data protection and does not make every deepfake an offence.

Responsibility for the response is spread across governments. Kazakhstan's government has warned that criminals use fake images and voices of bank staff, police officers, company executives and relatives, and says tackling this requires cooperation among law enforcement, banks and financial regulators. In February 2026, Kyrgyzstan's Interior Ministry reported fake videos impersonating the president, made with deepfake technology to deceive citizens, and urged people to check such messages against official sources. The ministry later issued more warnings about fraudulent AI-generated videos, and the country is investigating high-tech fraud cases in which criminals pose as state representatives. Tajikistan and Turkmenistan took part in the Astana talks, but the available information does not show what specific anti-deepfake measures either has introduced.

The article, an opinion piece by Saken Mukan, argues that recognition of the problem is only a first step. It says readiness will depend on trained specialists, working channels for sharing information and clear incident procedures, along with closer cooperation among agencies, banks, technology companies, media and research centres. It also notes that detection tools may work less well in Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, Tajik or Turkmen than in English or Russian, and that security measures need clear rules, data protections and ways to challenge mistaken decisions. What concrete decisions will follow the Astana meeting is not yet known.

stories.Headline: WATCH: OC students showcase AI innovations at annual convening
stories.Summary:
Orange County students gathered on November 6, 2026, at the Orange County Department of Education's third annual Student AI Convening, held at the OCDE Conference Center in Costa Mesa. About 100 middle and high school students and 20 adults, including educators, parents and community members, attended the event, which was designed and led by students. The program included an opening keynote, six interactive breakout sessions and a closing panel. Topics ranged from machine learning and AI-powered study tools to educational games, computer programming and responsible technology use.

Beyond the tools on display, the convening aimed to help students connect with peers, exchange ideas and reflect on what they learned while building their own projects. Presenters included students who showed an AI-powered study tool and an educational game meant to strengthen writing skills. Separately, a summit convened by State Superintendent Tony Thurmond in Sacramento on November 9, 2026, looked at how AI can support literacy and math instruction while protecting student privacy and safety. California is also advancing a statewide framework through Senate Bill 1288, which established an AI working group to develop guidance and a model policy for local school agencies. Students in grades seven through 12 who want to join OCDE's Student AI Network can learn more at the address listed in the coverage.

OCDE AI Education Lead Wes Kriesel said the students led the day rather than simply attending it. He described how students on the closing panel talked about pushing through frustration, working late to finish a game and gaining confidence in themselves. Kriesel also shared a student reflection that a person in motion beats a person at rest, even if the resting person is far smarter. Superintendent Thurmond said California has an opportunity to lead the nation in using AI responsibly, but he stressed that innovation cannot come at the cost of student safety, privacy or human connection. He argued that educators should remain central to instructional decisions and that technology should show evidence of improving student outcomes.

The two events reflect a broader push to shape how young people and schools use artificial intelligence, with attention to both opportunity and risk. At the county level, OCDE's Student AI Network connects students across Orange County to share projects and learn from one another. At the state level, the working group created under Senate Bill 1288 is developing guidance on privacy, data security, academic integrity and the appropriate role of AI in classrooms. The coverage does not describe a timeline for when that state guidance or model policy will be finished. It also does not detail how the Orange County network will expand beyond its current membership.

stories.Headline: ChatGPT Enterprise now available in AWS Marketplace
stories.Summary:
On November 9, 2026, OpenAI announced that ChatGPT Enterprise is now available through AWS Marketplace. The listing lets organizations find, buy, and manage the product using their existing AWS purchasing and billing relationship, and eligible spend can count toward their AWS commitments. The same day, Consilient, a provider of federated AI-powered financial crime technology, said its solutions are also available in AWS Marketplace, including for use in AWS GovCloud (US). Both announcements aim to make buying these tools simpler for enterprises, financial institutions, and government organizations.

OpenAI says ChatGPT Enterprise brings its familiar experience to work, covering ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, Codex, and dots. AWS customers receive the same models and features available directly from OpenAI, with new features released at the same time. The company notes that these products complement the OpenAI models in Amazon Bedrock, so developers can build applications and agents while teams use ChatGPT Enterprise in daily work. Consilient's offering includes four products: Federated Learning Models and Exchange, Federated Synthetic Data, SAR Analyzer, and OSINT Agent. Customers can deploy these within their AWS environment while their data stays local and private.

Matt Yanchyshyn, Vice President of AWS Marketplace and Partner Services, said enterprises want to deploy AI across teams without adding new procurement layers. Chris Grusz, Managing Director of Cloud Partnerships at OpenAI, said joint customers can bring ChatGPT to their teams through a cloud provider they already trust. John Peterson, Chief Technology Officer at Sophos, said buying through a single channel and applying existing AWS commitments reduces friction that often slows AI adoption. Ajit Tharaken, Chief Executive Officer of Consilient, said the company's solutions have improved efficiency by 75% and increased detection effectiveness by 4x in deployments at Tier-1 financial institutions.

OpenAI also said eligible customers can access ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Financial Services through AWS Marketplace. Consilient described growing demand from U.S. government agencies and regulated institutions for financial crime detection that meets high security and compliance standards. The company said industry estimates suggest existing rules-based systems can generate false positive rates of up to 98%, and it positions its federated approach as a way to reduce that burden. Customers who want to confirm eligibility or get started with ChatGPT Enterprise are directed to contact their OpenAI or AWS account team.

stories.Headline: Forrester warns of shadow AI governance gap in Asia Pacific
stories.Summary:
Forrester, a research and advisory firm, published its 2027 Asia Pacific predictions report on November 9, 2026, warning that one in three large enterprises in the region will face a shadow AI agent governance problem. The firm expects large organisations to find at least 10 employee-built shadow AI agents for every officially sanctioned agent, as staff-built tools, embedded software features and locally chosen AI platforms spread faster than internal controls. Forrester says this will create a new layer of technical debt linked to unmanaged risk, weaker governance, duplicated functions and undocumented dependencies. The report argues that executives in the region should focus less on how quickly AI is deployed and more on control, governance and accountability.

The report also forecasts that one in five large regulated enterprises will approve Chinese open-weight models, reflecting a wider view of sovereignty that extends beyond data residency to control over models and inference. Greater visibility into model weights and bias could lead some firms to approve self-hosted Chinese models where they meet operational sovereignty requirements, despite lingering concerns about provenance and geopolitics. Forrester further predicts that a personal AI agent belonging to an employee will trigger an incident at a Fortune 500 company. As consumer AI use grows, more workers may bring personal agents into the office, giving them access to corporate devices, credentials and data. Existing security systems tend to verify identity and access rather than intent, so an agent performing a seemingly routine task could misuse its privileges or expose sensitive information.

Forrester also expects 10 of Asia Pacific's largest consumer-facing brands to differentiate themselves through human assurance, making human oversight standard in high-consequence interactions such as those involving financial risk, emotional vulnerability or complex decisions. Sectors like financial services and healthcare are likely to keep pairing AI-led experiences with access to human experts and licensed advisers where trust is critical. Frederic Giron, Vice President and Senior Research Director at Forrester, said the region's diversity makes governance a central issue for companies scaling AI. He said organisations that adapt governance to local sovereignty requirements while building long-term trust with customers will be better placed to capture AI's value. The report suggests governance in Asia Pacific may need to be more localised than in other regions, since companies operating across several jurisdictions must navigate different rules on data handling, model hosting and accountability.

stories.Headline: Data Doctors: Can I trust AI shopping agents?
stories.Summary:
Meta launched its Muse shopping agent in early September, and within 40 days 10 million people in the U.S. had downloaded it. Buying was the app's most popular task, with purchases averaging more than $200. OpenAI followed a few weeks later with Dots, its own always-on agent, and both companies promised a tireless assistant that could check a hundred sites for the cheapest flight while its owner slept. The pitch was appealing, but the internet was built for people, and the arrival of these agents quickly created friction.

Agentic web traffic roughly tripled from August to September, and most of it went to e-commerce sites, forcing retailers to decide how to respond. Amazon blocked Muse almost immediately, citing security and privacy, though its shopping business also depends on knowing who its customers are and what they buy. Walmart took a different approach, announcing a system that gives each agent its own profile, with shoppers able to require approval for every purchase or set a spending limit. JPMorgan said it would not let outside agents into customer accounts, and several large banks reported customers sharing credentials in ways that broke their terms of service.

Even sites that welcomed agents ran into trouble. The RealReal, a luxury resale site, holds items in a shopper's cart for 20 minutes, and a reporter instructed Muse to keep re-adding a brand's newest pieces, which the agent did for hours. The company said within days that it had updated its anti-bot filters, so agents could still browse but had a much harder time logging in or buying. Shoppers gained help with chores they disliked, such as chasing refunds and canceling forgotten subscriptions, but they also faced more bot checks that caught real people too.

The larger question is whose interests an agent serves. Meta has partnerships with Walmart, Sephora and others, and its chief executive said the company would take a commission on purchases, so shoppers have little way to tell whether recommendations are impartial. In a recent preprint, researchers at Carnegie Mellon and Cisco gave agents the inboxes of invented users, and the agents inferred finances from clues like tax and stock emails, then recommended pricier options to wealthier users. Economist Lindsay Owens, author of the book Gouged, argues that AI shopping agents should be held to a fiduciary standard like financial advisers, so they would be legally bound to act for the shopper. Until the law settles that, the article suggests shoppers must rely on the word of the agent and the company that profits from it.

stories.Headline: Sources: John Ternus wants more urgency in Apple's AI efforts, pushing Craig Federighi to move beyond Siri AI tweaks to agentic and other advanced capabilities (Mark Gurman/Bloomberg)
stories.Summary:
Apple CEO John Ternus held a closed-door meeting with software chief Craig Federighi in recent weeks, according to a Bloomberg report by Mark Gurman published on Sunday, November 8, 2026. Ternus is said to have pressed Federighi to speed up Apple's AI road map and to look beyond improvements to Siri, amid concern that the company is falling behind its rivals. Sources say the goal is to turn Siri into a true AI agent, one that moves past answering commands to proactively managing tasks on a user's behalf. Apple has not publicly confirmed the meeting or announced any change to Federighi's role.

On the product side, Apple is reportedly eyeing an autonomous, agentic Siri as early as next year, to compete with offerings such as ChatGPT Dots, Meta Muse and Grok. Gurman also notes that Apple has another gap to close in computer use, since OpenAI and Anthropic already have agents that can operate software, click buttons and finish tasks, while Apple, despite controlling the Mac, iPhone and iPad, lacks a comparable capability. Separate coverage says Siri will not get more control of Apple apps until spring 2027. Apple is also changing how it develops iOS 28, iPadOS 28 and macOS 28, giving engineers more time to explore and build new features before those features are locked in. Federighi is said to focus on software plans of roughly 12 to 18 months, while hardware planning typically runs several years ahead.

The reports put Federighi's management style under scrutiny. He is described as staying closely involved in major technical decisions and as encouraging vigorous debate over competing ideas, which has reportedly frustrated some employees who feel their ideas get limited consideration. The shorter planning horizon has also sometimes complicated development. The reports do not say Federighi will leave or be replaced, and instead suggest Ternus wants changes in how software projects are developed, reviewed and approved. Separately, Mike Rockwell, who helped rescue Siri AI and now serves as Siri chief, is said to be seriously considering leaving that role, or Apple altogether, next year, though no departure has been announced.

Ternus succeeded Tim Cook as chief executive in September 2026, and Reuters reported that month that he was weighing organisational changes to make Apple more engineering-focused and able to release products more often. Apple's AI push has already faced scrutiny over delays to promised Siri capabilities, while Google, Microsoft and OpenAI have rolled out increasingly capable services. Apple is also exploring how AI-assisted coding tools might cut time spent on some engineering tasks, though their output still needs checks for errors and security flaws. No timetable has been confirmed for changes to Apple's software management structure, and Apple has not said whether the discussions will alter release dates for upcoming operating system updates.

stories.Headline: ‘NVIDIA AI Day Seoul’ Kicks Off... Samsung, LG and SK Said to Be Turning Out in Force
stories.Summary:
Nvidia opened its two-day "AI Day Seoul 2026" event at COEX in Samseong-dong, Seoul, on November 9, with the program running through November 10. About 2,000 developers, startup representatives, company employees and researchers were expected, along with 20 partner companies including several major Korean firms. Samsung Electronics, LG Electronics and SK hynix were reported to be attending in force to present their research so far. The event focuses on physical AI, which lets robots or machines perceive the real world and carry out physical tasks, agentic AI, which plans and carries out multi-step work toward a user's goal, and AI infrastructure.

Samsung Electronics plans to show how it uses Nvidia's PhysicsNeMo tool to speed fluid, thermal and structural analyses to near-real-time and to automate design exploration with AI agents. LG Electronics will present a robot learning system built on the Isaac GR00T platform, covering data collection, training, simulation and real-world validation, along with factory examples. SK hynix will show how it accelerates semiconductor device and process simulations using CUDA-X and PhysicsNeMo. Naver Cloud, LG AI Research, SK Telecom and Upstage will discuss developing and running AI models, and AIM Intelligence will explain how to deploy AI agents safely. Industry insiders say simulation accuracy, access to real-world data and robot reliability will shape whether these technologies can be commercialized.

Madison Huang, Nvidia's senior director and the eldest daughter of CEO Jensen Huang, had been expected to attend but her trip was canceled the day before the event opened. The company did not disclose a specific reason, though it was reported to be family-related, and some speculated that recent foreign media reports alleging that people close to Jensen Huang were involved in Chinese espionage may have played a part. In an official statement dated November 8, the Nvidia board said it had launched an independent investigation into recent reports that Jensen Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence agencies. Separately, one report noted that Deputy Prime Minister and Science and ICT Minister Bae Kyung-hoon had been scheduled to meet Madison Huang, and that the meeting was also dropped, while the event itself was to proceed as planned.

The event also draws attention to talks between the South Korean government and Nvidia about hosting a GTC Korea conference by late 2027, after Jensen Huang said at GTC Taipei in June that he would hold a Seoul event "if Seoul wants it." Bae Kyung-hoon told a parliamentary audit last month that the two sides were discussing a late-next-year event as part of spreading AI infrastructure in Korea. Seoul's COEX and Goyang's KINTEX are cited as likely venues. For Korean companies, the cancellation reduces chances for face-to-face talks with Nvidia's management, though the technical sessions are still going ahead.

stories.Headline: JPMorgan drops Alphabet from focus list, adds Meta on AI advertising gains
stories.Summary:
On November 9, 2026, JPMorgan removed Alphabet from its Analyst Focus List and added Meta Platforms, with analyst Doug Anmuth citing stronger near-term earnings momentum at Meta after its third-quarter results. Meta and Amazon are now the bank's preferred internet picks. Shares of Meta and Amazon each rose more than 5% that Monday, while the bank kept its Overweight rating on Alphabet. The bank's reasoning was that AI-driven advertising gains make Meta the more attractive stock right now.

The bank's view rests on several figures from the quarter. Meta's advertising revenue rose 26% year over year in the third quarter, with North American growth reaching 33%, and JPMorgan estimated Meta generated about $13 billion in incremental advertising revenue, roughly twice the extra dollars Google Search produced. The bank expects Meta's Family of Apps advertising revenue to surpass Google Search in the fourth quarter and beyond. It also pointed to Meta's Muse assistant, which has drawn 10 million sign-ups in the U.S. and Canada with a 25% daily-to-monthly active user ratio, and to enterprise potential in Meta Model API and Muse Code. On Amazon, JPMorgan expects AWS revenue growth above 40% in both 2027 and 2028, after AWS grew 39% in the quarter.

Anmuth attributed Meta's strength to AI-driven improvements in ad retrieval, ranking and targeting, which are lifting advertiser conversions. The bank's Alphabet concern is about the pace of AI monetization rather than a broader decline in its outlook, and it warned that AI-powered search could take time to produce comparable advertising economics. Google Search revenue growth slowed to 12% in the third quarter from 19% in the first quarter and 17% in the second, with management citing foreign exchange as the largest factor. JPMorgan also flagged that Alphabet's free cash flow was negative for a second straight quarter, that its 2026 capital expenditure forecast stands at $195 billion to $205 billion, and that spending will rise significantly in 2027. Google Cloud revenue grew 103% with a backlog of $561 billion, though the bank noted TPU system sales contributed meaningfully to that growth and that margins may face pressure through at least the first quarter of 2027.

The bank sees AI investments producing increasingly tangible returns across the sector, particularly in cloud and advertising, with the combined AWS and Google Cloud backlogs exceeding $1.1 trillion. Its preference for Meta reflects a view that Meta can capture those returns sooner through its core advertising business. Stocktwits reported that retail sentiment toward Meta and Google was bullish, while sentiment toward Amazon was neutral. Year to date, Meta shares were down about 1% and Google shares down more than 7%, while Amazon had gained nearly 20%.

stories.Headline: SK hynix to expand U.S. workforce to deepen ties with key clients
stories.Summary:
SK hynix, a South Korean chipmaker, is preparing to expand its U.S. workforce, according to its parent company SK Group, which made the announcement on Monday, November 9, 2026. The move appears aimed at strengthening ties with major American clients, including Nvidia Corp. The company plans additional executive appointments and a reorganization of its U.S. operations around December 3. The timing follows a recent executive reshuffle at SK Group, a Korean conglomerate with interests in semiconductors, construction and other sectors. SK hynix had created a new executive-level post to oversee its U.S. operations and named Ahn Hyun, its president in charge of development, to fill it. Ahn has led development of artificial intelligence memory products, including high bandwidth memory, known as HBM.

The appointment represents a change in how the company manages its U.S. business, which has traditionally been run by executives with sales and marketing backgrounds. Industry sources said the shift reflects how HBM contracts are now won, since memory makers increasingly work with customers from the early stages of product development to tailor chips to their AI infrastructure. An industry insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said companies can no longer stay competitive without close collaboration with customers from the research and development stage. The articles attribute the plans to SK Group, which confirmed the expansion and the timing of the executive appointments and reorganization. The articles do not name a specific individual who made the decision beyond the appointment of Ahn Hyun.

The industry insider's comments were given without attribution, so the view is presented as coming from unnamed sources. The company itself is described as a major supplier in the AI memory market, where its customers include Nvidia. The reporting places the expansion within a broader context of rising demand for AI chips and closer cooperation between memory suppliers and their largest customers. The articles do not say what size the expanded U.S. workforce will reach or how many new positions will be created. They also do not describe the outcome of the December 3 reorganization, which remains a planned step.

stories.Headline: Trump tells 60 Minutes he doesn't mind AI guardrails, as Democrats prepare hearings
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump told CBS's "60 Minutes" that the risks of artificial intelligence are not as real as critics claim and can be managed, and that he does not mind guardrails, Reuters reported on Sunday, November 8. Correspondent Ross Douthat asked the question, and Trump added that he does not want to put the United States in "a deep second position" because it is leading number one. Reuters also reported that Trump said he would work with Democrats on safeguards, following the party's wins in the midterm elections. No bill, executive order or agency rule accompanied the remarks, and it remains unclear what kind of guardrails he has in mind.

Democrats are already lining up legislation. Rep. Ted Lieu, a member of the House Democratic leadership, said the new majority will hold AI hearings and push for reasonable guardrails, according to The National Desk. Common Sense Media named two bills as priorities, the GUARD Act, which covers AI companions and minors, and the AI LEAD Act, which sets liability standards for AI systems. Legislation on frontier models, including safety audits before release, is also on the table, though the hearings Lieu promised have no dates and the new Congress has not yet been seated.

The comments mark a notable change in tone for Trump. In September he wrote that the only guardrails AI needs is a strong and smart president, and he described a "SICK conspiracy" against AI and data centers. When he left the White House in June, tech adviser Sriram Krishnan said Trump would never back a US AI regulator, according to Crypto Briefing, and Trump had signed an executive order to override state AI laws in favour of one federal standard. His new openness comes with a condition tied to China, as he said Xi Jinping is "all in" on what he called superintelligence and framed any rule as a question of whether it slows the US.

The administration is also moving on a separate track. The Justice Department announced a Super Intelligence Task Force this month, co-chaired by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss, to prosecute foreign governments, criminal groups and companies that use advanced AI to break the law. That is enforcement against misuse, not a rulebook for how labs build models. The timing is awkward for the industry, since market reports put the Nasdaq's 5.5% one-day drop on November 5 at the biggest in about 19 months, driven by doubts that AI spending will earn its money back. Child-safety and liability bills would land hardest on companies selling chatbots and companions to consumers, while pre-release audits would fall on the frontier labs, and Trump did not say which guardrails he would sign.

stories.Headline: Pflugerville approves SAFE resolution to set rules for AI and surveillance technology - KEYE
stories.Summary:
The headline on the KEYE piece concerns Pflugerville approving a SAFE resolution, but the articles supplied to me cover a different event: the 7th World Media Summit in Beijing, which opened on a Saturday and was organized by Xinhua and the Beijing municipal government. The summit ran from Thursday to Monday and brought together nearly 500 representatives from 330 mainstream media outlets, think tanks and government bodies from 112 countries and regions, along with the United Nations and other international organizations. Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and head of its Publicity Department, gave the keynote speech at the opening ceremony. The gathering took the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action."

The summit adopted the 7th World Media Summit Beijing Consensus, which calls for joint efforts to advance the transformation and development of the global media industry in the age of artificial intelligence. Under it, signatories commit to the inclusive and responsible use of AI in media so that its benefits reach organizations at every stage of development and in every country. The summit also released the Global Media Initiative for the Joint Development of AI Application Standards, which Xinhua launched and which brings together major outlets and professional bodies. Its stated aims are to safeguard the authenticity of information, protect data security and uphold media ethics in order to keep public trust in the media. The first 22 participants include Russia's TASS, Malaysia's Bernama, South Africa's Independent Media, China's People's Daily and China Media Group.

Participants in the initiative plan to work together for about two years to develop a set of standards covering different media uses of AI, which outlets would then validate. The initiative also calls for a global database of AI applications. Xinhua and the Beijing government are the organizers named in the reporting, and the consensus and initiative were presented as the summit's outcomes. The World Media Summit was started in 2009 and has become a major global platform for media exchange and cooperation. The previous summit took place in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region in Northwest China, in 2024.

stories.Headline: IBM Pushes Deeper Into Quantum and AI Governance as Shares Edge Lower - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
IBM's stock slipped 0.1% on a Friday, a move that media coverage did not tie to any clear company-specific catalyst. Meanwhile, the day brought several developments: a new quantum error-correction platform, a quantum system commissioned in Chicago, and the general availability of identity controls for AI agents. Taken together, these items painted a much busier picture than the flat share price suggested. On the research side, IBM is building a joint platform for quantum error correction with AMD and the Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The setup connects IBM quantum hardware, including its 120-qubit Nighthawk processor, to Oak Ridge's Umbra high-performance computing system, which runs on AMD chips.

The effort is placed under the U.S. Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission. Separately, IBM unveiled its first quantum system in Illinois, the IBM Quantum System Two, which is already operating at Hyde Park Labs and is slated to move to the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park once that campus is finished. On the AI side, IBM made Agent Identity generally available in watsonx Orchestrate on a Tuesday, giving AI agents their own identities along with audit logs and a kill switch. The launch builds on controls IBM announced about two weeks earlier, spanning HashiCorp Vault and watsonx Orchestrate, which covered access controls and tools to detect, contain and assess agents. IBM-owned Confluent also announced its Streamhouse architecture, aimed at keeping business context current for AI agents, applications and analytics.

Roughly two weeks ago, IBM and the USTA extended their partnership by five years, keeping IBM as the official AI and cloud partner of the US Open through 2031. The articles do not say that any of these announcements moved the share price, and they describe the stock's slight dip as muted and unexplained. The U.S. Open partners reported that the tournament's digital offerings recorded more than 270 million interactions in 2026. The articles give no further guidance on what comes next for these projects, beyond the planned relocation of the Illinois system and the wider rollout of agent controls.

stories.Headline: Nvidia scandal raises export risks for Korean chipmakers
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital relationship with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, whom US investigators reportedly suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. The disclosure came in an email to employees on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026, in which he apologized to his family and pledged to cooperate with an internal review. The reports that prompted the scrutiny say US authorities had been looking into her former employer, Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, since 2024 over suspicions it diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China. Those intelligence suspicions have not been established as fact, and Nvidia had earlier described the contacts as routine business dealings.

The controversy could lead Washington to tighten oversight of AI chip exports through third countries, which would mean more verification of end users, intended applications and possible reexports. Such checks could raise compliance costs and delay shipments for Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, and any limits on Nvidia's sales to China could indirectly reduce demand for the high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, used in its accelerators. No new restrictions had been announced in connection with the case. Some analysts see a possible upside as Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta develop their own AI processors, which could widen the customer base for HBM. An industry official said the short-term compliance burden must be managed without losing sight of that opportunity.

Nvidia's independent directors, advised by outside counsel, will examine whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised and expressed confidence in him, and he remains CEO. Three US House committee chairs have asked for a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 about his contacts with Alice Huang and the company's safeguards against espionage. South Korea's government said Monday it expects Nvidia GPU deliveries under existing contracts to proceed as scheduled, while Vice Science Minister Ryu Je-myung said the investigation's impact remains uncertain.

The episode also drew attention to the leadership question at Nvidia, which commands 80% to 90% of the GPU market. One report noted that a possible divorce could affect Huang's stake of about 3.58 percent, and that the company lacks a formal CEO succession plan. Separately, Madison Huang, Jensen Huang's daughter and a senior Nvidia executive, canceled a planned visit to Seoul that included meetings with officials and the Korean AI chipmaker Rebellions. Nvidia's AI Day in Seoul went ahead on Monday and Tuesday with Vice President Deepu Talla taking her place at a startup partnership forum. Korean markets were also under pressure, with the KOSPI closing at 5,018.85 after a third straight decline.

stories.Headline: AI adoption matures, but still uneven in OECD firms
stories.Summary:
The OECD released its Digital Economy and Society Outlook 2026 report on November 9, 2026, finding that artificial intelligence adoption among member countries is maturing but remains uneven across firms of different sizes. The report found that 20 per cent of all firms use AI tools, compared with 52 per cent of large firms with 250 or more employees. It warned that this gap could persist without targeted support, and projected that AI uptake among large firms could reach nearly 80 per cent higher than the average across all firms by the end of the decade. Separately, a DoubleVerify report released the same day found that 97 per cent of marketers plan to use AI in some part of media planning, buying and optimisation in 2026, though adoption across individual workflows is uneven.

The OECD report calls for policies that spread AI use to firms of every size, pointing to wider access to cloud services, targeted support for AI and big data analytics, and stronger interoperability and open standards. The report says policies should address several constraints at once, including skills development, clarity on legal and data protection frameworks, and support for integration costs, particularly for firms with limited digital capabilities. The DoubleVerify report recommends that advertisers build on current adoption by integrating AI more deeply into campaign planning, activation and optimisation. Its survey of 2,020 marketers found that AI use for summarising media briefs rose from 28 per cent in 2024 to 37 per cent in 2025, with 40 per cent expected in 2026. Use of AI for mid-flight campaign optimisation climbed from 21 per cent to 31 per cent over the same period, and is expected to reach 36 per cent in 2026.

OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann said in a statement that AI adoption among firms continues to expand, and that the aim is to make sure adoption reaches firms of every size so they can benefit from its potential for productivity and competitiveness. The OECD report attributes the wider uptake among large firms to their greater resources and capacity to integrate the technology across business functions. It names marketing and sales, business administration and management, accounting and finance, and ICT security as the leading reasons for deployment among member countries. DoubleVerify, in turn, said marketers rank the accuracy and effectiveness of AI recommendations highest when judging AI optimisation tools, followed by data privacy and security compliance and cost and return on investment, each cited by 29 per cent of respondents. Stuart Flint, its senior vice president and managing director for EMEA, said accuracy, transparency and measurable outcomes will be essential to building confidence in these tools.

The OECD report notes that growth has slowed in 2025 in some sectors, including information and communication, administrative and support services, retail trade, and professional, scientific and technical activities. It attributes the slowdown partly to a lack of in-house expertise, implementation costs, difficulties integrating AI into existing infrastructure, and concerns about data protection, privacy and the legal and regulatory implications of AI use. The DoubleVerify report adds that 98 per cent of marketers using AI-powered bidding reported performance improvements, suggesting the next phase will see these capabilities play a larger role in campaign management. Neither report sets out specific steps beyond the recommendations described above.

stories.Headline: Paras Semiconductors partners with US firm BroadPak for advanced chip packaging in India
stories.Summary:
Paras Semiconductors, a subsidiary of Paras Defence and Space Technologies, has announced a technology partnership with the US-based BroadPak Corporation to develop advanced semiconductor packaging in India. The announcement was made in a release on Monday, November 10, 2026. The two firms plan to set up an advanced heterogeneous integration and 3D packaging outsourced semiconductor assembly and test facility in the country. The announcement was reported by PTI and carried by The Hindu BusinessLine.

The proposed unit will focus on 2.5D and 3D packaging, chiplet integration, hybrid bonding, wafer-level and panel-level fan-out packaging, co-packaged optics, and testing and qualification. Through the tie-up, Paras Semiconductors will gain access to BroadPak's design, manufacturing and integration intellectual property, along with technology transfer and process know-how. The two firms will also explore joint development of packaging platforms for AI and high-performance computing, and collaborate on training Indian engineers. The facility is meant to serve high-volume manufacturing and strategic electronics needs, including devices for optical and optronic systems, networking and data centres.

Paras Semiconductors presents the move as a strategic expansion into a technology area that is growing in importance for India's AI, data centre and industrial capabilities. Munjal Sharad Shah, Managing Director of Paras Defence and Space Technologies, described it that way. Santosh Kumar, CEO of Paras Semiconductors, said the company intends to build a packaging platform that can meet the performance, connectivity and thermal needs of next-generation applications. BroadPak, which is headquartered in San Jose, California, and was founded in 2007, is led by Farhang Yazdani, who said India's growing semiconductor ecosystem offers an important opportunity in heterogeneous integration and system-level packaging.

The deal comes as packaging has become a central bottleneck in the AI chip market. A separate report published on November 8, 2026, explains that the technology used to be a final protective step but now determines how quickly AI processors can exchange data with memory. TSMC dominates the advanced method known as CoWoS, but its capacity has not kept pace with demand, which has pushed chip designers and suppliers to look for additional partners. That report says Nvidia is funding new CoWoS lines at Siliconware Precision Industries, and that Taiwan's Powertech Technology is pursuing panel-level packaging alongside TSMC. The articles do not say when the India facility will begin operating.

stories.Headline: U.S. Commerce Dept. Inquiry Into Megaspeed Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention
stories.Summary:
A Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed, a Singaporean data center company suspected of smuggling Nvidia's artificial intelligence chips into China, was abruptly halted late last year and transferred to the Justice Department. Investigators had spent months on the case, which centered on a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. officials now believe to be a Chinese spy with a relationship to Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang. The transfer followed an email that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, sent to Commerce Department investigators asking for information about the inquiry. Contact between agents and a company's representatives is not unusual in itself, but this message stood out because of what it said.

Teter said that Jeff Kessler, a top Commerce Department official, had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case. The agents were alarmed because Kessler, their superior, was nominated to his role by President Trump, and Nvidia had invoked his name. Current and former officials and others familiar with the incident said some viewed Kessler's interaction with Nvidia as violating government procedure and potentially tainting the case. The articles do not say what prompted Teter to contact the department. They do note that the case was shifted to the Justice Department last year, and that the agents' concerns have been raised in the reporting.

Nvidia has been under closer scrutiny since Huang acknowledged an affair with a Megaspeed executive, which has intensified attention on the company's role in shaping policy on chip sales to China. The New York Times reported last month that the U.S. government had concluded that Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a top executive at the firm, was a spy working for the Chinese government. The Times also reported that Nvidia said on Sunday it was opening an investigation into Huang's conduct. The articles describe the circumstances around the halted inquiry but do not say what outcome either government body will reach.

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s $895 Billion AI Gamble Could Become Wall Street’s Next Debt Nightmare
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the private AI company, has committed $895.4 billion to future computing power, equipment leases and other infrastructure agreements, according to an amended IPO filing released November 2, 2026. The articles describe this as a contractual spending commitment rather than reported debt or revenue. About $447.5 billion is expected to be spent by the end of 2030, and $69.8 billion comes due within the next 12 months. Because Anthropic is still private, public-market investors carry this exposure through the companies on the other side of those contracts.

The commitments are concentrated among a few suppliers. They include $161.2 billion in equipment leases with Broadcom, at least $121.3 billion owed to Google, a unit of Alphabet, and at least $110 billion owed to Amazon. Some of these agreements require payment regardless of how much Anthropic actually uses. Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of about $17 billion, infrastructure costs of $9.9 billion and a $567 million operating loss. It also raised its revolving credit commitments from $3.3 billion to $15.0 billion and lifted its minimum liquidity covenant to $5.0 billion.

The suppliers are already spending heavily to build this capacity, and the articles say the strain is most visible in companies that borrowed to build for Anthropic. Oracle holds $664 billion in remaining performance obligations, but its free cash flow was negative $5.40 billion and its interest expense rose 55% to $1.4 billion. CoreWeave reported free cash flow of negative $5.743 billion, and its quarterly interest expense rose to $640 million from $267 million a year earlier. Broadcom's own filing flags dependence on a limited number of significant customers, while NVIDIA's Colette Kress said on an August earnings call that frontier AI labs are growing faster than their balance sheets and credit profiles can support. Anthropic's IPO valuation has reportedly fallen from about $2 trillion toward $1.5 trillion.

Some of the exposure is less severe than the headline figure suggests, the articles note. About $213.8 billion of the total carries termination rights or contingent conditions, and some obligations run through 2045. Still, the termination rights leave suppliers holding assets built for demand that may not arrive. The stocks of the six named suppliers fell over the month through November 6, with CoreWeave down 47.54% and Broadcom down 22%, while Amazon held up best. The articles say investors should watch Anthropic's IPO pricing next, since it will show how much financing the company can actually raise.
