stories.Headline: Former House Speaker Paul Ryan: 'Hard time seeing' federal AI bill getting done in divided government
stories.Summary:
Former House Speaker Paul Ryan said he has a hard time seeing a federal bill on artificial intelligence get done in a divided government. He made the remarks in a conversation with CNBC's David Faber at the CNBC Connect: Balance of Power event in New York City on November 5, 2026, shortly after the midterm elections. The discussion was broadcast on November 9, 2026. The article frames the question as whether lawmakers can reach bipartisan answers on AI's broad effects on society. The article describes those effects as wide-ranging, touching on the data center buildout, AI regulation and the retraining of workers.

Ryan was asked where lawmakers may find common ground on these issues and where they may not. The piece presents his comments as a view on the prospects for federal action rather than as a report of any legislation being passed or advanced. Little else in the material spells out specific provisions or deadlines. Ryan is the responsible voice here, and he was speaking as a former lawmaker rather than a current office holder. According to the article, he weighed in on where Congress might agree and where it might not, and he expressed doubt about a federal AI bill getting done under current political conditions.

The article does not report a response from current lawmakers or from any agency on his comments. The article also carries a set of unrelated CNBC video teasers on other stories, which do not bear on the AI question. Beyond the interview itself, the material does not say what steps, if any, are planned in Congress. The source offers no further details on what might follow.

Articles.Title: Former House Speaker Paul Ryan: 'Hard time seeing' federal AI bill getting done in divided government

stories.Headline: Cal Poly unveils NVIDIA-powered 'AI Factory' to expand AI education, research
stories.Summary:
Cal Poly, the California Polytechnic State University in San Luis Obispo, unveiled a new AI Factory in October to give students and faculty direct access to advanced AI computing on campus. The facility was unveiled during AI Day on October 22, when a ribbon cutting was held as part of a full-day event on the San Luis Obispo campus. The NVIDIA-powered facility uses four NVIDIA DGX B200 systems, and it was funded by a $3 million investment from the Noyce School of Applied Computing. The university says the setup lets students work directly with large systems while giving it more control over how students learn and how faculty conduct AI research.

The articles describe the AI Factory as a way to bring computing power that once exceeded what a typical laptop could handle onto campus. Bringing that capacity on-site, the university argues, makes proprietary research more effective and efficient and lowers costs compared with buying advanced AI systems from outside providers. Faculty are already using it, including computer science professor Jonathan Ventura, whose machine learning system analyzes drone imagery of eelgrass in Morro Bay and processes images roughly 10 times faster than hand annotation while matching its quality. Professor Paul Anderson is using it for spinal cord injury and genetic risk projects, since protected patient data cannot be sent to outside AI services. Anderson said the facility gives his team compute it previously lacked to train frontier models.

Cal Poly President Jeffrey D. Armstrong took part in the ribbon cutting alongside NVIDIA Vice President, Americas, Charlie Wuischpard, who delivered the keynote speech on AI's growth and its new opportunities for students, researchers and educators. Alex Bisberg, an assistant professor of computer science and software engineering, said that owning the hardware means owning the university's digital destiny, and he argued that training models themselves helps students learn about them and research ways to improve them. The university said in its release that graduates will need to understand AI well enough to question its output and recognize its limits, given public concern about the technology, ethical questions, and the environmental impact of large data centers. The articles also note that the Noyce School was created in 2024 after a $60 million gift from the Robert N. Noyce Trust, and that Noyce co-founded Intel and passed away in June 1990.

Articles.Title: Cal Poly unveils NVIDIA-powered 'AI Factory' to expand AI education, research

stories.Headline: ‘Highly selective’: Singapore banks see strong AI financing demand but stay alert to debt risks
stories.Summary:
Singapore's three largest banks, OCBC, UOB and DBS, say they remain eager to finance the booming data centre sector in South-east Asia, but they are picking their borrowers carefully. The banks made these points during their third-quarter results briefings, where all three stressed prudent lending standards and a focus on financially strong customers. Industry watchers said established operators with solid financial backing and long-term customer contracts continue to attract funding, while smaller developers are facing tighter liquidity conditions. The cautious stance follows a sharp sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday, November 5, led by stocks tied to artificial intelligence. Fears that the data centre boom could stall followed the midterm election results, and those worries have added to growing unease about debt-funded spending on AI infrastructure.

The banks' approach therefore reflects both the strong demand for financing and the wariness about how much debt the sector can carry. The article does not give figures for lending volumes or loan sizes. The banks themselves framed the message as one of discipline rather than retreat, with each emphasising that it is prioritising sponsors with strong balance sheets and reliable cash flows. The article attributes these positions to the lenders' briefings and does not offer further detail on individual loan decisions.

Its coverage of the bankers' remarks is paraphrased rather than quoted at length. The article does not say how long the selective approach will last or whether lending standards are likely to tighten further. It also does not indicate what outcome the banks expect if the Wall Street sell-off deepens or if AI spending slows. Readers should watch for further guidance from the banks and for signs of whether smaller developers begin to lose access to funding.

Articles.Title: ‘Highly selective’: Singapore banks see strong AI financing demand but stay alert to debt risks - The Business Times

stories.Headline: Ioan Gruffudd Calls for A.I. Regulation After Fan Gets Scammed By Imposter
stories.Summary:
Actor Ioan Gruffudd has called for regulation of artificial intelligence after a fan was deceived by an imposter who used A.I. to pose as him. According to TMZ, which reported on November 9, 2026, the actor spoke to reporters at LAX on Monday, and the story was posted that day at 5:00 PM Pacific time. Gruffudd said a woman he met at a convention had believed for over a year that she was in an affair with him. He said she had been shown hundreds of A.I.-generated photos and videos, which he described as explicit and disturbing, of someone pretending to be him.

Gruffudd made the situation public on social media, and TMZ reports that he explained how he handled the uncomfortable encounter with the fan. He made clear that the relationship was fake, but he said the feelings of those affected are very real. The articles do not say what specific regulation he is proposing or which laws would change. He did, however, say he hopes whoever is behind the scam is prosecuted, and TMZ reports that he gave an impassioned plea for artificial intelligence to be brought under control.

The articles do not name the person behind the scam, and they do not say whether any investigation or charges have been filed. TMZ's report is based on Gruffudd's own account and on his remarks to the outlet, so the details come from him rather than from any independent source. The same page carries several unrelated stories, including reports on Bill Gates and A.I. and on a celebrity's plans for politics, but none of them bear on this case. The articles do not say whether Gruffudd plans further public action or whether any platform or lawmaker has responded.

Articles.Title: Ioan Gruffudd Calls for A.I. Regulation After Fan Gets Scammed By Imposter

stories.Headline: The rise of sovereign AI factories: Why the C-suite is rejecting cloud dependency
stories.Summary:
Sovereign AI data centers have become the fastest-growing segment of accelerated computing, according to Intersect360 Research, as organizations move away from relying on the public cloud for advanced AI work. The firm reported that spending on national sovereign AI data centers rose from $1.6 billion in 2023 to $7.2 billion in 2024, an increase of 349 percent, and projected the market would reach $122.8 billion by 2026 at a 90.4 percent compound annual growth rate. The article, published by CIO and sponsored by HPE and AMD on November 9, 2026, presents this as a structural shift in how executives treat data sovereignty and strategic autonomy. It also notes that the infrastructure at these sites is largely a merger of high-performance computing and AI, since 62.5 percent of surveyed organizations run both kinds of workloads on the same systems.

Shared storage is used by 67.1 percent of them for the same purpose. The article ties this consolidation to a demand for on-premises control, which it describes as a mandatory constraint for projects such as Japan's AI Bridging Cloud Infrastructure and the G42 cloud in the UAE. According to the data cited, 56.3 percent of sites keep active compute entirely on-premises and 68.2 percent do the same for storage. Buyers rated cloud integration lowest among features for their next purchase, giving it 2.25 out of 5, and 36 percent called it not important at all.

The piece argues that regulatory, jurisdictional and security boundaries prevent offloading data, so these systems must perform without a cloud fallback. It identifies memory bandwidth as the feature buyers value most after GPU performance, with a satisfaction gap of 0.86 that the article calls the largest in the industry. Storage performance with small files, a common trait of AI training data, shows a gap of 0.98. The article is written as sponsored content by HPE and AMD, and the figures come from Intersect360 Research and the HPC-AI Leadership Organization.

HPE and AMD are described as partners that combine large-scale system design with AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct accelerators to build such platforms. The authors advise executives to treat storage locality as a security strategy, to prioritize node bandwidth over raw processing speed, and to seek co-design partners rather than simple product vendors. The piece points readers to the full Intersect360 report for the complete data set. It does not describe any specific regulatory change or deadline, and it does not report on outcomes at the named national projects beyond their existence.

Articles.Title: The rise of sovereign AI factories: Why the C-suite is rejecting cloud dependency

stories.Headline: Google rolls out a Googlebook update that frees up 3GB to 6GB of RAM via on-device AI optimizations, reduces Chrome crashes, patches ~60 Android flaws, and more (Jay Bonggolto/Android Central)
stories.Summary:
Google has begun rolling out its November update for Googlebook, a set of fixes meant to make the platform more reliable and less frustrating to use. The most significant change concerns memory used by Googlebook's on-device AI services. According to a Reddit post by Google's Mishaal Rahman, Google updated its NPU driver and optimized AICore memory management, which frees up 3GB to 6GB of system RAM. The article notes that this is a meaningful gain for laptops with 16GB of RAM, particularly when users switch among many apps and browser tabs. The update also changes how the system reclaims memory when background AI services conflict with browser processes, which should reduce unexpected tab reloads and Chrome crashes.

The release covers a wide range of other hardware and software issues. Convertibles should no longer lose keyboard and touchpad input when switching between tablet and laptop modes, and Zoom crashes that occurred with simulated backgrounds, filters, blur effects, and 3D avatars have been fixed. External displays can now play DRM-protected streaming content such as Netflix instead of showing a black screen. USB microphones and multichannel audio interfaces should work as expected, and Bluetooth users may see lower audio-video synchronization delays and more reliable reconnection for wireless mice.

Developers are also covered by the release. The Linux Terminal beta gains more reliable shell sessions after sleep, better SSH port forwarding, and improved multi-window management, along with a fix for a memory leak when closing terminal tabs. Linux VM updates are now less destructive, preserving user storage and custom SSH configurations. On security, the Android security patch dated November 1, 2026 resolves around 60 vulnerabilities, and Google has updated the Linux 6.18 kernel and Ti50 security chip firmware.

These updates address unexpected restarts, boot loops, and noisy fans. The article is written by Jay Bonggolto for Android Central and was last updated on November 9, 2026. The author describes the memory fix as the kind of change that arguably should have been in place before Googlebook launched, though it is better late than never. The article does not indicate any further phased rollout details or future plans beyond this November release.

Articles.Title: Google rolls out a Googlebook update that frees up 3GB to 6GB of RAM via on-device AI optimizations, reduces Chrome crashes, patches ~60 Android flaws, and more (Jay Bonggolto/Android Central)

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang maintains deep control over Nvidia, managing 60+ direct reports and owning a 3.56% stake, presenting a challenge for Nvidia's 10-person board (New York Times)
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board of directors opened an investigation on Sunday into the conduct of chief executive Jensen Huang, after he admitted to a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence agencies have determined to be a spy for China. The Financial Times reported that Nvidia's shares fell about 5 percent in pre-market trading on Monday, November 9, following the announcement. The company had earlier dismissed the interactions as nothing unusual or unexpected. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led its rise during the artificial intelligence boom.

Under the arrangement described by the New York Times, the company's independent board members will choose an outside counsel to carry out the inquiry, and a company spokesman said Huang will take no part in picking that counsel. The board said its review will examine all available information. Huang, the board said, fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The headline attached to the Times report puts his stake in the company at 3.56 percent and says he manages more than 60 direct reports, while the board that must oversee him has 10 members.

In its statement, the board said it has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised. The Times described the challenge facing the directors as stemming from the sweeping control Huang holds over the company. It reported that he manages all aspects of the business as chief executive and that members of his family have steadily risen through the company's ranks. Few Silicon Valley executives, apart from Elon Musk at Tesla and Steve Jobs at Apple, have been as closely identified with their companies, the paper said.

The stakes extend well beyond one executive's conduct, given Nvidia's position in the industry. The Times estimates that the company controls about 90 percent of the market for the computer chips used in the large artificial intelligence projects now driving the U.S. economy. That dominance has made Huang one of the wealthiest people in the world and an ally of President Trump. A separate Motley Fool piece published days earlier showed Nvidia shares trading at $186.64 on November 6, and quoted Huang as saying the energy needed for AI computing could be roughly 1,000 times what exists today. The articles do not say how long the board's investigation will take or what outcomes it could produce.

stories.Headline: Anwar says AI Governance Bill to complement cybersecurity, data laws
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the Malaysian government is finalising an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance Bill that will work alongside existing laws such as the Cybersecurity Act and data protection regulations. He made the remarks at the launch of Ant International's Global Development Centre in Kuala Lumpur. At the event, he said the government would ask technology companies, including Ant International, for input as the Bill is drafted. He said officials and the relevant ministry would hold discussions with the company because of its expertise and familiarity with regulations in many countries.

Anwar said the Bill would form part of the final phase of the Malaysian Digital Economy Blueprint and that digital trust is the foundation for building a digital nation. He said artificial intelligence and large language models would change how businesses operate, how credit is assessed, how risks are managed and how markets connect across borders. He said that when applied responsibly, such models could remove barriers, aid communication and open new opportunities for trade and innovation. He also warned that these technologies could concentrate large amounts of power among those who control data platforms and digital infrastructure. He stressed that human judgment must remain at the centre of decision-making as machines become more capable.

The Prime Minister said trust and security must remain central to the digital finance industry, arguing that customers need assurance that their money and information are protected and that decisions about them are fair. The AI Governance Bill was first flagged in mid-2025 by Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo, who said he hoped to table the legislation in the second half of 2026. The articles do not give further details on the Bill's contents or a firm date for its tabling in Parliament. The article was published by the New Straits Times on November 8, 2026.

Articles.Title: Anwar says AI Governance Bill to complement cybersecurity, data laws - NST Online

stories.Headline: Embodied AI’s AIR: Wheeled Humanoid Built for Factory Floors
stories.Summary:
Swiss robotics company Embodied AI has unveiled AIR, a wheeled humanoid robot designed to work alongside people on factory floors. The article, published on 9 November 2026 by AI Magazine and written by Adam Pond, describes the machine as built around compliant hardware and AI that learns from human demonstrations. The firm is a Google DeepMind partner and part of the NVIDIA Inception startup accelerator program. AIR's arms are light, moved by tendons, and designed to give way safely on contact with people.

Each job begins under the control of a human operator, and every run is recorded so that the company's AI stack can learn from those demonstrations. According to the company, AIR can then perform the task on its own, typically within a month, with the operator remaining available for unfamiliar situations. The robot runs on wheels rather than legs because factory floors are flat and wheels offer more stability. Its motors, gearboxes and electronics sit in the torso. The company says AIR is designed under the ISO/TS 15066:2016 standard, with CE marking planned for 2027.

CEO Francesco Stella says the team built AIR around the principle that humanoid robots must be safe and reliable enough to work beside people in factories. He argues that the combination of compliant hardware and learning from human demonstrations lets AIR take on repetitive, high-dexterity tasks while existing teams focus on work that needs their skills. The company points to a trial in which a leading consumer electronics manufacturer tested five funded startups on a cable-handling task, and says Embodied AI was the only one to meet its targets, reaching 98% reliability against a 90% goal. Stella also argues that a robot error that injures someone is a very different matter from a poor software recommendation.

The article places the launch within a growing market for physical AI. McKinsey partner Ani Kelkar is quoted predicting that robotics and physical AI could create at least a trillion dollars in economic value by 2040, mostly in manufacturing and logistics. The Manufacturing Leadership Council is cited as finding that 22% of manufacturers plan to use physical AI, such as humanoid robots, within two years, more than double the 9% using it today. The article does not disclose Embodied AI's valuation, and it describes the firm's earlier funding round as undisclosed but led by Faber VC.

Articles.Title: Embodied AI’s AIR: Wheeled Humanoid Built for Factory Floors

stories.Headline: The industrialization of AI: 8 critical considerations for building an AI gigafactory
stories.Summary:
The European Commission is working to establish multiple AI gigafactories, centralized facilities built to train next-generation AI models with trillions of parameters. A standard corporate AI setup might use a few hundred or thousand GPUs, while a gigafactory scales to tens or hundreds of thousands of nodes. Its power needs are measured in megawatts or gigawatts rather than as an ordinary budget line item. The article, a sponsored piece based on a white paper from HPE and AMD and published on November 9, 2026 by CIO, frames this as a generational infrastructure shift. It is written for CIOs and technology leaders who must plan these investments to run for about a decade.

The article lists eight considerations for planning such a facility. Power and land come first, since many organizations find late that the existing grid cannot support their compute plans, and the sites must sit near strong grids and independent backup generation. Liquid cooling is needed because dense AI chips make air cooling obsolete, and liquid systems can carry up to 3,000 times more heat than air while using less energy. Networking must be overbuilt, because bandwidth has to grow far faster than compute to keep costly GPUs from sitting idle. The remaining points cover designing for hardware and software failure with self-healing fault domains, deploying orchestration and governance before the hardware goes live, choosing suppliers with high-performance computing experience and open ecosystems to avoid vendor lock-in, keeping utilization high to justify the capital cost, and running a proactive communications plan with transparent reporting for public stakeholders.

The article attributes this guidance to HPE and AMD, the sponsors, who argue that their large-scale system design expertise and their processors and accelerators can support these facilities. The piece itself is promotional, and the article does not provide independent verification of the figures or claims it makes. It frames the gigafactory as a launchpad for economic progress, scientific discovery, and national competitiveness, and it states that addressing these constraints early lets technology leaders deliver lasting value and operational sovereignty. The article does not describe a specific timeline for the European facilities or outline next steps beyond pointing readers to a companion white paper.

Articles.Title: The industrialization of AI: 8 critical considerations for building an AI gigafactory

stories.Headline: Can financial institutions keep pace with the changing landscape of AI regulation?
stories.Summary:
The article is a feature interview rather than breaking news, so the account below covers what it actually reports. LexisNexis Regulatory Compliance published a report mapping the state of AI regulation across the UK, EU, US, China and Australia, and RegTech Analyst editor Daniel Willis spoke with Daveena Suri, the firm's UK/EU content manager, about it. The piece was published on November 9, 2026. Its central finding is a growing gap between how fast AI is deployed and how well regulators can oversee it, a gap the article describes as widening as the technology expands across industries.

Suri's view is that firms should stop asking whether regulation can match every technological breakthrough and focus instead on building governance, accountability and oversight. She said the more useful test is whether companies know who is accountable when a system fails and whether their governance frameworks change as risks evolve. On the differing approaches of the UK and EU, she said the UK's model allows more flexibility while the EU's risk-based framework offers more consistent expectations, and that neither guarantees faster innovation. Firms that can run one system across several jurisdictions will gain an edge, she argued. She also said that human oversight must be real, with tighter permissions and escalation thresholds as a system's potential consequences grow, and that someone must own the decision to deploy a system and respond when its limits are breached.

Suri pointed to an EU Court of Justice ruling that individuals subject to automated decisions under the GDPR must receive an intelligible explanation of the procedure and principles applied to their data. She cited the European Banking Authority's mapping of AI requirements against banking and payments rules, including DORA, as an example of overlapping obligations that firms must assess. On self-regulation, she said she would judge it by whether it changes decisions, even commercially inconvenient ones, and whether customers can challenge outcomes and obtain real remedies. She also said RegTech should close the gap between regulatory change and verified operational change, and that she expects future rules to stress that AI stays controlled throughout its operational life, including after model approvals, supplier changes, service updates and data shifts. The article does not report any specific enforcement action or new legal deadline.

Articles.Title: Can financial institutions keep pace with the changing landscape of AI regulation?

stories.Headline: Europe should lead on a global AI incident reporting compact
stories.Summary:
A Bruegel commentary by Mario Mariniello argues that Europe should lead on a global mechanism for sharing information about artificial intelligence failures across borders. The piece notes a growing sense that AI needs more oversight, pointing to an AI selloff after United States midterm election results amid fears of stricter regulation, China's plan to impose mandatory domestic AI safety standards, and EU leaders discussing how Europe can contribute to international AI governance. It also says the interests of major countries overlap little, and that a Global Dialogue on AI governance launched by the United Nations has produced no negotiated outcome. The article was published on 9 November 2026.

The author proposes a well-defined structure for sharing information about AI incidents, which would be activated when a failure crosses borders. Using the example of banks in Berlin, Rio de Janeiro, Singapore and Washington relying on the same Chinese-developed model to score mortgage applicants, the piece argues that an early warning shared by the first affected bank would stop others from being harmed and give the model developer a chance to fix the bias. The mechanism would need to be sustainable, so that joining does not force countries to slow AI development or lose ground in capability rankings, and it should avoid creating security risks or imposing foreign values. The article cites the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), which requires providers of powerful models and high-risk applications, the latter from December 2027, to report serious incidents.

The author suggests the European Commission should not act alone, since a unilateral move could be seen as "regulatory colonialism," and should instead build a coalition. Mariniello names India, Canada, the United Kingdom and Brazil, a co-founder of China's World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, as possible partners that could pilot the mechanism from early 2027 before taking it to the UN and G20. The goal would be a common floor for reporting AI failures using shared protocols and formats, with countries that do not report receiving less from the shared pool. The article compares this to the Montreal Protocol, which grew out of the 1985 Vienna Convention and was accepted by every state by 2009. It concludes that the common floor would not stop the race at the AI frontier, but would let governments report future failures in a common language.

Articles.Title: Europe should lead on a global AI incident reporting compact

stories.Headline: AI Makes Contracting Faster Yet Businesses Are Struggling to Show the ROI
stories.Summary:
A new report from World Commerce & Contracting, produced with support from Deloitte and the contract lifecycle management provider Ironclad, finds that artificial intelligence is speeding up the work of legal and contracting professionals but has not yet produced clear business results for many organizations. The research, published in November 2026, found that 62% of the organizations surveyed saw greater individual productivity from AI without being able to show a matching impact on the wider business. Individuals are finishing tasks faster, yet those gains are not adding up to better outcomes at the organization level. The findings were reported by Tony Thompson on law.com on November 9, 2026.

The report also shows that AI use in contracting remains concentrated on individual tasks rather than shared processes. Only 4% of the organizations surveyed use AI as a cross-functional platform that spans teams. The authors suggest that fragmented systems and processes may be limiting returns, since AI layered on top of disconnected workflows can speed up pieces of the job without changing the whole. The implication is that organizations need to rethink how contracting work is structured before AI can deliver measurable value.

Simply making existing work faster is not enough to show a return. Tim Cummins of World Commerce & Contracting and Craig Conte of Deloitte Legal are the named voices in the coverage, and both argue that businesses should point AI at commercial outcomes rather than treating it as a tool to accelerate current contracting routines. In their view, the question for organizations is what the contracting function is meant to achieve for the business, and AI should be measured against that goal. Their comments, as reported, reflect a call for a shift in focus from activity to results.

The article attributes these positions to them without adding further detail on specific recommendations. The findings arrive as many companies are investing heavily in AI tools and face growing pressure from executives to justify those costs. The gap between personal productivity and organizational return is a central tension in the report, and the coverage does not go beyond what the survey and the commentary describe. The article does not specify any follow-up steps, timelines or planned changes by the organizations involved, so the practical next moves for businesses remain open to them.

Articles.Title: AI Makes Contracting Faster Yet Businesses Are Struggling to Show the ROI - Law.com

stories.Headline: Europe’s AI Factories Are Switching On – And Raw Power Won’t Decide the Race
stories.Summary:
Europe is building a new generation of AI factories, and the article argues that raw computing power alone will not decide who leads. EuroHPC has selected thirteen AI Factories since December 2024, six of which have signed procurement contracts, while consortia are preparing AI GigaFactories. The piece frames Europe's effort around three pillars: an integrated AI environment, sustainability and sovereignty. It also notes that a complementary global race for scale is measured in gigawatts, whereas Europe asks what each watt actually delivers.

The article says performance gains are limited by memory and storage bandwidth, network delays as clusters grow, and Amdahl's law, under which a program with 5% sequential code cannot run more than 20 times faster however many processors it uses. It proposes hybrid systems that pair GPUs and AI accelerators with CPUs, and eventually quantum processors, orchestrated by software so users do not have to manage the mix. Infrastructure spending should be tied to measurable goals such as scientific discovery, medical research and digital twins, with utilisation, efficiency and return on investment weighed alongside peak performance. Energy is treated as a design criterion, since an AI rack can exceed 120 kW against about ten for a typical enterprise rack, and an AI factory may draw 100 MW or more.

The author attributes much of this thinking to Bull, the French supercomputer maker, and its executives. Bruno Lecointe, SVP HPC, AI and Quantum Business Line, presented a metric called Science Usage Efficiency at the Teratec Forum in Paris, measuring useful science per unit of energy, such as simulated nanoseconds per megajoule in molecular dynamics. Bull says it has more than ten years of experience building facilities with a PUE below 1.2, and that its LUMI-AI system, due in Finland in the second half of 2027, will feed excess heat into Kajaani's district heating network on entirely renewable electricity. The article also notes that Germany's Energy Efficiency Act requires a PUE of 1.2 for new data centres.

The article presents sovereignty as a goal shared by every country, one that requires secure, trusted systems that can be operated independently over the long term. It points to LUMI-AI, shared by six countries and backed by a €387.8 million contract, which is expected to deliver ten times the AI capacity of today's LUMI. It also cites Alice Recoque, France's first exascale system, which pairs Bull's BXI interconnect with SiPearl's Rhea2 processor from 2027 alongside AMD accelerators. The author concludes that Europe's strength will come from combining performance, governance, sustainability and sovereignty in a repeatable model, and that energy may prove the bottleneck that matters most.

Articles.Title: Europe’s AI Factories Are Switching On – And Raw Power Won’t Decide the Race

stories.Headline: Israel’s AI chief: “Whoever controls it will control the switch of states”; launches national AI impact institute
stories.Summary:
Israel's national AI chief, Brig. Gen. (res.) Erez Askal, told an audience at AI Week at Tel Aviv University that the country is on the threshold of a new sovereign reality in which national infrastructure will run on artificial intelligence within a few years. He warned that whoever controls that technology will control the switch of states.

The remarks were made during the opening lecture of the event, which drew experts, startups and governments to Tel Aviv. Askal leads the National AI Staff in the Prime Minister's Office. To compete, Askal said, Israel must build technological sovereignty across several layers, including energy, computing power, a national model, quantum computing and training of personnel. The targets he presented include an energy infrastructure of 2 gigawatts, 100,000 GPU processors, a sovereign foundation model and an Israeli quantum computer. Beyond infrastructure, he argued the country needs an ecosystem of fair AI that can be trusted, with clear responsibility for how systems operate and what they produce.

He also pointed to AI security, using AI for cyber defense, and defending AI systems themselves. Israel has also launched the National Institute for Impact Oriented AI, known as NIIA, which sits within the National AI Staff. Its purpose is to close the gap between what AI can technically do and how it is used to improve citizens' lives, by linking government ministries, industry, academia, civil society and philanthropy. The institute will focus on nine national challenges, among them the health system, aging population, education, national resilience, environment and climate, equality and economic growth. Askal presented a plan to tackle ten challenges a year over five years, each with a main barrier identified as regulation, data, technology or process.

The initial work plan calls for 10 to 14 missions a year, with a goal of bringing five of the first ten to implementation within one year. The articles say the emphasis is not only on developing technology or running pilots, but on creating measurable change in daily life and handing solutions to bodies that can run them independently over the long term. Examples cited include fourth-grade math, traffic congestion on Highway 6 and the first meeting between a doctor and a patient. The articles do not give further detail on how the missions will be funded or evaluated.

Articles.Title: Israel’s AI chief: “Whoever controls it will control the switch of states”; launches national AI impact institute

stories.Headline: EXCLUSIVE: Democrats Took Congress. But AI's Spending Binge Isn't Going Anywhere, This CEO Says
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections, and Benzinga published an exclusive interview on November 8, 2026, in which Axe Compute CEO Chris Miglino said the shift is unlikely to slow AI spending. The article, written by Surbhi Jain, reports that Miglino shared his comments by email. It frames the election as putting a new political spotlight on the cost of America's AI buildout. The piece names Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet as companies that are unlikely to step back from the spending race.

Miglino told Benzinga that he remains extremely bullish on AI infrastructure spending regardless of the election outcome. He argued that the capital going into AI reflects a structural change in how businesses operate rather than a short political cycle. He said demand is considerably larger than any single political cycle. He also said the companies may become more selective about where they invest, because commercial pressure to secure computing capacity remains too strong to ignore.

Miglino said Washington can still influence the economics of new data center capacity through electricity pricing, permitting and the infrastructure needed for large-scale projects. He suggested these issues could affect project timing and costs without eliminating the need for computing power. He said the largest cloud companies have advantages in existing infrastructure, customer relationships and access to capital, but their returns will depend on how efficiently they turn investment into revenue-generating capacity. He expects more interest in power-secured sites, flexible deployment models and partnerships that give hyperscalers access to outside capacity.

The article presents these as Miglino's views and does not report any response from the named companies. The article's closing section suggests that investors should watch how quickly projects move through permitting, whether power is secured and whether new facilities attract committed customers. It describes these measures as a better guide to the AI trade's next phase than the election result alone. The surrounding page also lists other coverage about midterm effects on AI policy and data center curbs, but the article itself does not detail any specific legislation or timetable.

Articles.Title: EXCLUSIVE: Democrats Took Congress. But AI's Spending Binge Isn't Going Anywhere, This CEO Says

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania Enacts Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania enacted the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act after Governor Josh Shapiro signed Senate Bill 806 on October 22, 2026. The bill became Act 99 of 2026 and sets a disclosure requirement for advertisers who use synthetic content in ways that create a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of advertised goods or services. The law defines synthetic content as images, video, audio clips, or text that AI has significantly modified or generated, and its definition of AI includes generative AI. It does not require disclosure every time an advertiser uses AI, because the duty is tied to content that creates a false impression.

The law takes effect 60 days after enactment, which is December 21, 2026. A disclosure must be clear and conspicuous, appearing in a size, color, contrast, location, duration, and volume that make it noticeable, readable, understandable, and audible. It must be in the language the consumer uses, must not contradict nearby information, and must appear the first time the synthetic content is shown, in the same medium, and, where technically feasible, in a form that is permanent or very hard to remove. The law excludes content that is evidently fictional, parody, satire, commentary, or criticism, and content limited to text.

The Pennsylvania Attorney General or the appropriate district attorney can seek an injunction when a prohibited practice is occurring or about to occur and proceedings would serve the public interest. They can also bring a civil action, and a court may award a civil fine of up to $3,000 plus actual attorney fees and court costs. The statute does not expressly create a private right of action, and it says disclosure of AI use does not limit any other recourse available under law. The articles say businesses should review consumer-facing ads that use AI-generated or significantly AI-modified images, videos, and audio, and should check the controls used by advertising agencies and third-party marketing vendors.

The articles describe the law as narrower than a general AI transparency mandate and as another state-level requirement in the evolving legal framework for generative AI in commercial communications. They say the most immediate concern is not the use of AI itself but the potential for synthetic content to create a misleading impression about a product, service, customer experience, or endorsement. Businesses should not assume that a disclosure buried in fine print or added after the content has already been presented will suffice. The articles say reviewing advertising practices and putting disclosure controls in place before the December 21 effective date would be a prudent compliance measure.

Articles.Title: Pennsylvania Enacts Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act - Inside Global Tech

stories.Headline: Practical workshops on Artificial Intelligence Applied to Legal Research begin today - Universitat de València
stories.Summary:
The Regulation Research Group at the University of Valencia began a series of practical workshops on artificial intelligence applied to legal research today, 9 November 2026. The sessions are taught by Andrés Marzal Varó of the Universitat Jaume I and will run on 9, 16 and 23 November 2026, with a final session on 14 December 2026. Each session runs from 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m.

In-person classes take place in Room 3P12 of Administrative Law at the Faculty of Law, and online attendance is also available. The course is built around four highly practical sessions in which participants work directly on their own laptops. Its theoretical part is limited to a conceptual framework covering how generative AI learns, why it is not deterministic, what hallucinations are and how to reduce them, what an AI agent is, and how these systems connect to external sources such as the internet, databases and personal documents. The main goal is to learn how to carry out common research tasks efficiently and to verify what AI systems produce.

Each session ends with a usable output, such as a configured research assistant, a case-law summary workflow, an AI-assisted thematic wiki, or tools for tracking developments in a research area. Participants must hold an active Claude Pro subscription during November, which the article puts at about €20 for one month. The course itself is free, and the subscription can be cancelled once the training ends. The workshops are organised by the Regulation Research Group, which belongs to the University of Valencia, and the article identifies Andrés Marzal Varó of the Universitat Jaume I as the instructor.

The article presents the programme as a response to the growing role of artificial intelligence in legal research, and it states that this role is likely to become more important in the short and medium term. It does not describe any dispute, incident or regulatory change behind the course. The article is a university announcement, so it gives no information on outcomes or enrolment numbers. It also does not say whether further editions are planned after the series ends.

Articles.Title: Practical workshops on Artificial Intelligence Applied to Legal Research begin today - Universitat de València

stories.Headline: Lawyer builds private AI server with eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs — up to 215 tokens per second to keep legal files offline, costing about $2,400 per four-GPU board
stories.Summary:
A lawyer who posted on Reddit has built a private AI server from eight used 2018-era Nvidia Tesla V100 data center GPUs so that case files never have to leave the office. The system uses two four-card SXM2 NVLink boards, four PEX switches and SlimSAS cables, and the builder has already suffered one burnt power connector along the way. It now runs the open DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model with every expert held in GPU memory, reaching up to 215 tokens per second. The builder bought the four-GPU boards for about $2,400 apiece.

The hardware uses eight V100-SXM2-32GB cards, each with 32GB of HBM2 memory, which plug into Nvidia's SXM2 socket rather than standard PCIe slots. The cards sit on two baseboards, with all four cards on each board linked by NVLink for 128GB per board, while the two boards communicate with each other only over PCIe. Each board connects to the host through two PEX switch cards, and the host includes a Threadripper Pro motherboard, a 12-core 3945WX processor, 256GB of DDR4 memory and two power supplies totaling 2,800 W on separate office circuits. The article notes that used V100 SXM2 32GB cards now sell for about $900 on eBay, more than double the roughly $400 apiece cited in the original post, and that prices appear to be still rising.

The builder, who is a lawyer, says the server is used daily for first-pass work on case files, including pulling out facts, dates and numbers, summarizing records and making a first attempt at routine drafting. The builder stresses that nothing leaves the office without a full human review, and that the setup protects client files that cannot be sent to a cloud or frontier model. The model is compressed to mostly 2 bits, with weights totaling 248.8GB, and about 110GB of lookup tables stay in ordinary system RAM. Code generation is fastest, at up to 215 tokens per second, while legal writing runs at up to 118 tokens per second. The builder estimates that 50% to 60% of their AI work can now skip frontier models, and the server currently handles only one request at a time.

Articles.Title: Lawyer builds private AI server with eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs — up to 215 tokens per second to keep legal files offline, costing about $2,400 per four-GPU board - Tom's Hardware

stories.Headline: QommonsAI utilization training held in Saroma Town, Hokkaido, to learn everything from the basics to practical business use ahead of the first introduction of generative AI
stories.Summary:
On October 14, 2026, Polimill Inc. held a training session on QommonsAI, a generative AI tool built for local governments, for staff of Saroma Town in Hokkaido. The session was part of the "QommonsAI Hokkaido Caravan," a series of training events held across municipalities in the prefecture. It was Saroma Town's first introduction of a generative AI tool in its government. The company's announcement was published on November 4, 2026 through the PR TIMES press release service.

The training covered the basics of generative AI for staff with very different levels of experience. About half of the participants had used generative AI privately, while many others were touching it for the first time. The instructor used live demonstrations, walking through the tool's screens, web search function, prompt writing and business use cases. Most questions focused on generative AI in general rather than on specific features, so the session became a review of fundamentals for future work use. Participants took notes throughout.

Polimill's representatives, Ayame Ito and Nonoka Taniguchi, are named as the company's leaders, but the release does not quote them directly on the event. The company said that staff attending were encouraged to use the tool in daily work while following established rules for safe use. Polimill also said it would keep supporting the town after the introduction. The company runs in-person training programs nationwide for municipalities that adopt QommonsAI, with curricula ranging from beginner to management levels.

The release describes QommonsAI as drawing on tens of millions of items of domestic and foreign legal, policy, academic and municipal case data. As of July 2026, it said, about 1,100 local governments and roughly 600,000 people were using it for tasks such as assembly responses, policy drafting, resident services and public relations. Polimill describes itself as a five-year-old ICT startup founded in February 2021, headquartered in Minato City, Tokyo. The release does not give details of Saroma Town's budget or the tool's cost.

Articles.Title: QommonsAI utilization training held in Saroma Town, Hokkaido, to learn everything from the basics to practical business use ahead of the first introduction of generative AI

stories.Headline: Forum: AI useful in schools, but students need reassurance too
stories.Summary:
A student named Tiffany Ong Rou Ying, aged 13 and in Year 1, wrote a youth forum letter published by The Straits Times on November 8, 2026, about the use of artificial intelligence in schools. She says AI is increasingly used for tasks such as generating learning materials and giving feedback, and that while it can improve education, its use must address students' concerns and keep the human side of learning. She reports that her schoolmates have raised worries about AI's overly positive portrayal and the risk of students relying on it too much. Her letter also points out that AI's environmental impact, including its use of water and electricity, is rarely discussed in schools.

Her letter sets out several specific concerns and proposals. Some students question the value of assignments when feedback is largely AI-generated rather than given directly by teachers, and posters made with AI may feel less meaningful without students' creative input. She writes that some students would feel more reassured if schools made clear that examination scripts are fully marked by teachers and not by AI. She argues that transparency is important, particularly in assessment and feedback, and that schools should explain clearly how and why AI is used. She also notes that many students see AI as a useful supplementary learning tool that can make learning more accessible and let them learn at their own pace.

Ong's central recommendation is that schools introduce AI gradually, explain its purposes and limitations, and ensure it supports rather than replaces teachers' professional judgment. She writes that students should be able to voice their concerns and take part in decisions about how AI is implemented. Her closing position is that AI should enhance education without undermining independent thinking or human connection, and that the aim should be to combine technology with meaningful teacher-student relationships. The article is a letter from a student rather than a policy announcement, so it does not name any school or authority that has adopted these measures. The published text does not say whether schools are planning such changes or what steps might follow.

Articles.Title: Forum: AI useful in schools, but students need reassurance too

stories.Headline: AI demand rises: Telekom expands AI factory in Munich
stories.Summary:
Deutsche Telekom will expand its AI factory at Munich's Tucherpark, CEO Tim Höttges announced at a company press conference in Munich on 9 November 2026. The company is adding NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra (B300) GPUs alongside its existing Blackwell B200 systems, which doubles the number of chips in that class at Telekom. The facility will also keep using NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. Telekom is investing nearly another quarter of a billion euros to lift the AI factory's capacity to 20 megawatts. The company is also exploring a further expansion of its commitment in Bavaria.

The Industrial AI Cloud only went live in February 2026, and its first expansion stage was fully booked within seven months. That stage raised available AI computing capacity in Germany by 50 percent, and Telekom began planning further stages as early as May. The new hardware is aimed at training and running large AI models, complex reasoning tasks and simulations, including physical AI, where companies can test robots and production facilities in virtual environments. Companies can also train their own AI models there. The facility's power usage effectiveness is 1.2, meaning it needs less than 1.2 kilowatt-hours of electricity for each kilowatt-hour of IT consumption, and its waste heat will supply the Tucherpark district.

Customers so far include Siemens, Daimler Truck, Currenta and Soofi, a German language model trained on Telekom infrastructure. Höttges framed the investment as a way to keep Germany and Europe from being mere users of AI, arguing that the country should also create value and prosperity from it. Karsten Wildberger, the federal minister for digital affairs and state modernization, praised the company for moving from idea to operation in a few months and said the federal government would help make further successes possible. Ferri Abolhassan, a member of Telekom's board and CEO of T-Systems, said that industrial AI is an opportunity for customers, industry and the country as a whole. Telekom said a final investment decision on the Bavarian expansion has not been made and depends on sustainable financial conditions, reliable financing and an economically viable model.

Articles.Title: AI demand rises: Telekom expands AI factory in Munich

stories.Headline: Democracy 21 proposes to promote artificial intelligence as a driver of productivity and to anticipate its impact on employment - Demócrata
stories.Summary:
Democracia 21 has proposed placing artificial intelligence at the center of its economic modernization plan, promoting its use across Spain's productive sectors while studying its effects on employment. The party's leader, Miriam González, made the proposal in an interview with Europa Press, which Demócrata reported on 8 November 2026. She said AI should become a productivity factor for the Spanish economy, especially in activities where the country can compete. González also argued that companies and public administrations should share in bringing the technology into the business fabric.

González's plan also calls for mechanisms to track how the technology changes the labor market, so that the party can gather information about shifts in each sector. The aim, she said, is to design measures that soften any negative effects on jobs. She criticized the current political debate, saying attention to the issue is practically nil among parties with seats in parliament. She added that Spain and much of Europe have fallen behind in building large language models, with partial exceptions such as France and Germany.

She proposed studying international experiences, such as Japan's, and pointed to existing observatories in Spain as possible tools for analysis. The proposal extends beyond business to education, where González says technology should again take a central role to prepare society for AI-driven change. Democracia 21 presents this as part of a wider agenda that includes a more agile administration, fewer bureaucratic obstacles, and an economy ready to compete in the current technological setting. Separately, González called for an expedited constitutional reform to remove parliamentary immunity, which she described as a privilege for officeholders.

She also said her party's main proposals for the 29 November general election do not involve other constitutional reforms, and that the monarchy-versus-republic question is not a priority now. González further said her party would support whichever formation agrees to approve its non-negotiable measures during the first 20 days of government. She presented Democracia 21 as a project meant to continue beyond the coming election. The article also records her comments on the amnesty, which she said she would not have pushed without an electoral mandate, and on the Middle East, where she called Israel's government's actions unacceptable while noting the party has no official position on recognizing Palestine.

Articles.Title: Democracy 21 proposes to promote artificial intelligence as a driver of productivity and to anticipate its impact on employment - Demócrata

stories.Headline: Huang allegations, Berkshire earnings, AI regulations - What’s moving markets
stories.Summary:
Investors are heading into a busy week shaped by unverified allegations involving Nvidia's chief executive, a leadership change at Binance, Berkshire Hathaway's latest results, and a possible shift in Washington's approach to artificial intelligence. The Nvidia claim alleges that Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence of links to China, and that the company's board has opened an independent investigation. These allegations have not been independently established, and the article warns they should not be reported as fact without confirmation from credible sources. Nvidia's Frankfurt-listed shares opened 6% lower.

Binance said its chief financial officer, Kaiser Ng, is leaving to pursue another venture, with Justin Yek, a former vice-president of finance at Airwallex, taking over. The departure came days after a breach in which hackers reportedly stole $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency, an attack the exchange said began months earlier and unfolded on October 29. The FBI has attributed the theft to a North Korean hacking group, a claim Pyongyang denies. Binance has said it will fully reimburse affected customers.

Berkshire Hathaway reported a 5.8% decline in third-quarter operating earnings, falling to $12.7 billion from $13.48 billion a year earlier. Its cash holdings climbed to a record $377.4 billion, and it bought back about $9.6 billion of its own stock during the quarter. The article notes that operating earnings are a measure Warren Buffett considers a better guide to underlying performance than net income. Investors will also watch Tuesday's U.S. consumer price index report, along with earnings from CoreWeave, Applied Materials and Cisco Systems.

Democrats are preparing proposals on AI and data centers for when they take control of Congress in January, according to lawmakers, aides and advocates. The measures under consideration would protect consumers from higher electricity costs tied to data-center demand, require independent testing of advanced AI systems, and clarify when AI companies could be held liable for harm. The article notes these proposals could face major obstacles while Donald Trump remains president, since he has repeatedly opposed mandatory federal AI rules. Such rules could add regulatory uncertainty for AI developers and data-center investors.

Articles.Title: Huang allegations, Berkshire earnings, AI regulations - What’s moving markets

stories.Headline: Healthineers Ties Its Future to AI Imaging in China While Footing a €300 Million Breakup Bill - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
Siemens Healthineers has moved on two fronts at once, reaching for growth in medical artificial intelligence while absorbing the cost of separating itself from Siemens. On Friday the company signed a strategic cooperation agreement with the Alibaba DAMO Academy to pair photon-counting CT imaging with medical AI, with the aim of detecting cancer and cardiovascular disease earlier. The announcement followed a day after finance chief Jochen Schmitz put the restructuring at roughly €300 million. That cost covers the carve-out of the in-vitro diagnostics business, the separation from Siemens, and a sharper focus on ultrasound.

To help fund the reshuffle, Healthineers has announced a further savings programme called "Transform4 Future," which is due to begin in 2028. Reuters reports the measures will be rolled out between 2028 and 2030, with at least €300 million of savings targeted at Healthineers and a further €400 million planned at Olyrian Diagnostics. The diagnostics unit, which began its carve-out on Thursday, will be built up step by step as a standalone organisation under the Olyrian name, with management expecting the transition phase to conclude by mid-2028. The group also intends to rename itself simply "Healthineers," subject to shareholder approval at the annual general meeting in February 2027, with the branding change starting after the planned spin-off from Siemens and running for three years.

Governance changes are also in the pipeline. The supervisory board said on Wednesday it will propose Melanie Kreis, Heyo Kroemer, Jonathan Lewin and Pascale Witz as new shareholder representatives at the 2027 AGM, while Roland Busch will step down early and Ralf Thomas and Peter Körte will be put forward for re-election. On the capital side, the company disclosed a buyback of 50,000 of its own shares for the period from 26 October through 1 November, and since the programme began on 1 June it has repurchased around 3.6 million shares in total. Analysts are divided after the annual results: Deutsche Bank Research kept its "Hold" rating with a €39 target, while Barclays raised its target from €47.50 to €51 and reaffirmed "Overweight," with the stock closing at €44.70 on Friday. Healthineers guides for comparable revenue growth of 4.0 to 5.0% in fiscal 2027 and adjusted earnings per share of €2.20 to €2.40.

Articles.Title: Healthineers Ties Its Future to AI Imaging in China While Footing a €300 Million Breakup Bill - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: Environmental activists set to rally outside Schumer's office over AI data center bill
stories.Summary:
Environmental activists planned a rally on Monday, November 9, 2026, outside Senator Chuck Schumer's Midtown office in Manhattan, beginning at 10 a.m. The protesters are urging the New York Democrat to oppose legislation they say would speed up the expansion of unregulated artificial intelligence data centers. The demonstration comes as the Senate is expected to take up a bill that would accelerate approvals for data center projects. That measure has bipartisan support in Congress.

Protesters contend that these projects would increase energy consumption, water use and pollution. Supporters counter that expanded data center capacity is needed to meet growing demand for AI technologies and to keep the United States competitive. The activists' concerns were laid out by Pete Sikora of New York Communities for Change, who described data centers as major energy users that consume large volumes of water and power. He said the facilities create water pollution and air pollution, the latter from gas turbines used to run them. The article does not describe the bill's specific provisions or dates for a Senate vote.

Eyewitness News reached out to Schumer's office for comment but had not received a response when the article was published. The article does not say whether Schumer has taken a position on the measure. It also does not indicate what action the activists will take after the rally. The story is part of a broader national debate over how quickly the country should expand the infrastructure needed for artificial intelligence.

Articles.Title: Environmental activists set to rally outside Schumer's office over AI data center bill

stories.Headline: How will LAUSD respond to Google’s AI mandate? What families should know
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District said it is reviewing how to respond after Google announced last week that schools will lose access to its search engine unless they opt in to artificial intelligence. Google said that in the coming months, products like Gemini and Google Search will be turned off by default for schools until they turn them on. The company said it believes schools should have control over AI in their classrooms. Because Google Search by default includes an AI chatbot and uses AI to summarize results, schools that restrict AI would lose access to Google Search. The district had already placed a moratorium on students using generative AI on district-issued devices earlier this school year.

LAUSD's Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee is scheduled to meet on Friday, Nov. 13, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., with the agenda posted publicly. The board meets in person at 333 S. Beaudry Ave. in downtown Los Angeles, streams its meetings online, and offers American Sign Language and Spanish interpretation. Community members can request interpretation in other languages by contacting the Board Secretariat at secretariat@lausd.net or (213) 241-7002.

For now, students can still use Google to search for information, but the AI mode, where they can converse with the chatbot Gemini, is turned off. Some searches may still show AI-generated summaries, and the district has asked Google to allow those summaries to be turned off. Google's vice president for education, Chris Phillips, told The New York Times that search and AI are deeply integrated. He said that if a school bans AI, students will not have access to search and will see a message from the school saying it is unavailable. Google also said that if a school opts in, it will offer a "guided learning" tool in its chatbot for student accounts to help them work through problems.

Lila Byock, founder of Schools Beyond Screens, which pushed for the AI moratorium, said Google is refusing to accept no for an answer. Her group is calling on district leaders to reclaim their authority from corporate interests and divest from Google. The dispute comes as the district weighs its options under a broader policy debate over AI in classrooms, with the ad hoc committee's next meeting on Nov. 13 expected to add to that discussion. LAUSD's own statement said emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, can enhance teaching and learning when introduced thoughtfully, responsibly and with clear safeguards. The articles do not say what the district will decide or when any change to Google's default settings will take effect.

Articles.Title: How will LAUSD respond to Google’s AI mandate? What families should know

stories.Headline: Bill Gates says billionaires should pay more taxes as AI widens wealth gap | Trending
stories.Summary:
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has argued that governments, not philanthropy, must address the inequality that artificial intelligence could widen. He made the point in an interview for the Financial Times' Tech Tonic podcast, which was reported on November 8, 2026. Gates believes the financial gains from AI could mostly flow to people who already hold significant wealth. He added that tax systems will need to change in an AI-driven economy, including measures that let governments tax people with substantial wealth and billionaires.

Gates said voluntary giving cannot serve as a safety net, and that responsibility for inequality will always rest with governments. He has pledged to give away virtually all of his fortune, estimated at around $100 billion, through the Gates Foundation over the next 20 years. Even so, he holds that large charitable contributions cannot replace public policy. He also said wealthy individuals who want to use their money for social good can complement government support but should not substitute for it.

Gates has further proposed taxing robots and AI tools. In an essay on Gates Notes, he noted that employers pay payroll taxes when they hire people, while buying a robot is often treated as a business expense. He argued that taxing robots and AI use could slow the shift away from human labour and fund worker retraining and stronger social support. Not everyone in the technology industry agrees: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang supports people contributing through taxes but disagrees with taxing robots. In an interview with Fox Business, Huang said he viewed AI's impact differently and saw several ways to address the changes it brings.

Articles.Title: Bill Gates says billionaires should pay more taxes as AI widens wealth gap | Trending

stories.Headline: Congress faces year-end deadline for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence legislation
stories.Summary:
Congress returned to Washington in November 2026 with a tight calendar and a deadline of December 11 for the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, the law that gives companies legal protection when they share threat data with the government. Lawmakers are also weighing the renewal of the Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act and the Technology Modernization Fund. Those provisions are being debated as part of the National Defense Authorization Act, which has run into procedural hurdles in the Senate. The reporting comes from SC Media, which cites Nextgov for the original account.

Beyond infrastructure, Congress is examining artificial intelligence proposals, including the FRONTIER Act and the AI Kill Switch Act. According to the article, these bills would require safety disclosures and emergency shutdown capabilities for advanced AI models. The discussions follow high-profile security incidents involving AI labs. The session may also address Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, an intelligence-gathering authority that lapsed earlier this year.

The article presents the session as a last opportunity before a transition in congressional leadership in January. It frames the current window as the chance to secure existing protections and set regulatory frameworks for emerging technologies. The article does not name individual lawmakers or report specific positions taken by them. It also does not say how or when the pending votes will be resolved.

Articles.Title: Congress faces year-end deadline for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence legislation

stories.Headline: The use of artificial intelligence in regulatory activities – key areas and considerations
stories.Summary:
On 9 November 2026, the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations (IFPMA) published a position paper on the use of artificial intelligence in regulatory activities for medicinal products. The paper presents reflections from the innovative pharmaceutical industry on how regulatory authorities might apply AI in their work. It draws on publicly available initiatives and emerging experience to set out key considerations about opportunities, challenges, and implementation. The aim is to inform dialogue among regulators, industry, and other stakeholders. The paper describes AI as a way to strengthen regulatory capacity, make better use of complex data and evidence, and support more efficient regulatory processes.

Regulatory authorities are considering its use in internal operations, regulatory documentation, medicinal product review, scientific assessment, inspections, and other procedures. According to the paper, such tools could support regulatory activities and inform regulatory decisions. The document does not set binding requirements or new rules, and it presents its points as observations and considerations rather than mandates. IFPMA, which represents the innovative pharmaceutical industry, is the body behind the paper. The federation states that frameworks governing the responsible and ethical use of these technologies must keep pace with innovation while preserving the rigour, trust, and confidence that underpin regulatory decisions.

It also argues that greater alignment on principles, terminology, and strategies among national regulatory authorities could help avoid fragmentation. In its view, such alignment would support shared learning, capacity building, and more efficient global development and regulatory pathways. The paper sits within a wider discussion that IFPMA has been pursuing in 2026. In statements delivered in May and August of that year, the federation addressed harmonizing regulatory approaches and governance for data, digital health, and artificial intelligence at the World Health Assembly, and the regional regulatory strategy for medical products in Africa. The articles provided do not say what follow-up steps regulators or the federation will take after this paper.

Articles.Title: The use of artificial intelligence in regulatory activities – key areas and considerations

stories.Headline: Defeat for AI giants: regulation supporters win in US midterm elections
stories.Summary:
In November 2026, supporters of AI regulation won a string of contests in the US midterm elections, defeating candidates and campaigns backed by major technology companies. The turning point, according to a Politico investigation cited by the article, came in May 2025, when industry players pushed a budget bill provision that would have barred states from enforcing their own AI rules for a decade. The Senate rejected that provision 99-1 in July 2025, but the effort spurred an opposing movement. Later that year, the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI launched Leading the Future, a super PAC with $100 million meant to deter lawmakers from slowing AI rollout.

That industry push backfired as a coalition of technology policy veterans, consumer advocates, antitrust groups and AI engineers organized against it. Among the leaders named were former Rep. Brad Carson, who founded the Public First network, and lawyer Jay Schuster, who gathered Silicon Valley donors. The article describes a rift among AI companies, with OpenAI pressing for faster development and fewer barriers while Anthropic took a pro-regulation stance and channeled about $40 million into Public First-linked groups. Safety-focused groups spent $44.4 million in the midterms, against $27.9 million from industry-backed groups.

Even so, regulation supporter Alex Bores lost the New York Democratic primary in June despite outspending his rivals, $19 million to $8 million. The campaigns succeeded by turning abstract fears about AI into concrete local concerns, especially job losses, child online safety and opposition to energy-hungry data centers in residential areas. The article says no Democratic campaign ad mentioned data centers between 2020 and 2024, while this cycle saw 659 such ads, plus 387 ads attacking technology giants, with combined spending above $103 million. Public alarm after an Anthropic researcher's viral resignation and a September security breach at the Hugging Face platform also helped.

Four Republican-held House districts flipped to Democrats, and exit polls found AI and data centers a decisive or major factor for 56% of voters. The article compares this American fight with other models: the European Union regulates from the top through its AI Act, China's government tightly controls algorithms and infrastructure without resident objections, and Israel still relies on light regulation that favors innovation. It presents the US contest as a warning to technology firms and to those planning energy and data infrastructure in Israel. The article does not say what legislation, if any, these newly elected lawmakers will pursue next.

Articles.Title: Defeat for AI giants: regulation supporters win in US midterm elections

stories.Headline: Congress Could Hand China the AI Race by Trying to Win It - International Policy Digest
stories.Summary:
Congress is preparing the National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027 after the midterm elections, and the defense bill may shape whether the United States keeps its lead in artificial intelligence. The article argues that the bill could instead speed China's technological progress if lawmakers adopt the wrong restrictions. Three measures under consideration, the AI OVERWATCH Act, the Chip Security Act, and the MATCH Act, are the focus of the concern. The author says these proposals risk failing the test of keeping America at the front of AI development and supplying the technology much of the world relies on.

The AI OVERWATCH Act, in the House version, would give Congress a role in certain AI chip export decisions through a 30-day review period in which lawmakers could block a transaction with a joint resolution. The Senate approach differs, so the final language will need close review. The author accepts that Congress has a legitimate oversight role but argues that export licensing needs technical expertise and flexibility that belong mainly to the executive branch. The Chip Security Act would impose location verification and related security mechanisms that the article describes as untested and possibly impractical worldwide. The MATCH Act would extend reach beyond U.S. borders and has drawn objections that the article says could disrupt allied industry and supply chains.

The article points to the Semiconductor Industry Association, which has warned that the chip security mechanisms may not work at global scale, and to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, which has warned that the MATCH Act could disrupt the global memory chip supply chain. The Netherlands has formally objected to the MATCH Act's extraterritorial reach, and Dutch Trade Minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma has raised those concerns directly in Washington. Japan has also reportedly raised objections, while Representative Michael Baumgartner, a leading advocate of the legislation, has continued pressing for its passage. The author urges Congress to reconsider these measures, arguing that the goal should be to slow China's progress rather than to constrain America's own position.

The article frames the debate against China's recent moves, noting that Huawei unveiled its next-generation AI chip roadmap and DeepSeek announced software tools meant to challenge Nvidia's ecosystem in September. It argues that restrictions which limit American firms' access to the Chinese market have encouraged Chinese companies to build alternatives. The author recommends protecting sensitive technology, targeting military end users and illicit procurement networks, funding enforcement agencies, negotiating controls with allies, and testing verification technology before imposing sweeping rules. The article concludes that winning the AI race depends on ensuring the rest of the world still wants to use American technology.

Articles.Title: Congress Could Hand China the AI Race by Trying to Win It - International Policy Digest
