stories.Headline: Controlling AI - Regulation is required now - Part two - Pearls and Irritations
stories.Summary:
Australia is moving to legislate oversight of frontier AI, while the United States has taken a voluntary path, according to an opinion piece by Connie Peck published on Pearls and Irritations on 9 November 2026. The piece argues that advanced AI systems are edging toward recursive self-improvement, where machines write software for the next generation of models. It says that only binding national and international rules can keep such systems under human control. Peck's article is the second in a four-part series.

Peck draws on several voices to make the case for limiting AI's agency. Fareed Zakaria, writing in the Washington Post, warns that a system needs only a goal, enough intelligence and enough access to the world to cause harm. Jakub Pachocki, cited in the piece, says models are becoming superhuman at breaking into computer systems, which widens the scope of risk. Bill Gates is quoted calling AI the most dangerous thing humans have ever approached. The article also reports that executives at some AI companies have privately modeled a public revolt after a catastrophic AI event, such as a cyberattack that shuts down financial services, internet access, or power and water.

The article describes Australia as well ahead of the United States on regulation. On 15 July, Prime Minister Albanese announced a new Office of AI within the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, which is to coordinate across government to create Australian AI Standards by early 2027 after consulting states, territories and the public. Albanese also worked with Finland and Norway on a document, "A Call for Control of Frontier AI Models," which 22 other countries signed, calling for AI to remain under human direction, oversight and control. By contrast, the article says President Trump rejected a global body to oversee AI at the UN General Assembly. After public concern, he invited six AI industry leaders to a White House luncheon to sign a voluntary self-regulation agreement, which he called morally binding, though the article notes such self-regulation has been widely criticized.

Peck's article puts these developments in a wider context. It notes that Anthropic is reportedly preparing a public offering at a valuation of $2 trillion while warning investors that advanced AI could pose catastrophic risks. Jeffrey Sachs, quoted in the piece, argues the offering should be postponed until Congress enacts a licensing and safety evaluation system for frontier AI. David Kruger, a professor at the University of Montreal, calls for an immediate, indefinite international moratorium on frontier AI development. The article ends by saying that wise regulation is needed immediately, and that the views expressed may or may not reflect those of Pearls and Irritations.

Articles.Title: Controlling AI - Regulation is required now - Part two - Pearls and Irritations

stories.Headline: AI Wants “Every Scrap of RAM.” Qualcomm and Arm Just Showed Who Pays the Bill
stories.Summary:
Chip stocks sold off sharply on November 5, 2026, after Qualcomm guided its December-quarter earnings below analyst expectations. Qualcomm fell 9.5 percent and Arm Holdings dropped 13 percent, both hurt by rising memory costs in phones, while Micron Technology fell 17 percent in the same selloff. Both Qualcomm and Arm bounced on Friday, November 6. The selloff came as a broader market slump, with the Magnificent Seven losing over $1 trillion in combined market value across the Thursday session.

Memory makers such as Micron are benefiting from the AI-driven shortage, while phone-chip designers are absorbing the higher costs. Qualcomm's gross margin fell to 50.8 percent from 55.3 percent a year earlier, and it said its price increases will not fully reach its chip unit's gross margin until the second half of fiscal 2027. For the December quarter it guided non-GAAP earnings per share to $2.15 to $2.35, with the top of that range still 33 percent below the $3.50 earned a year earlier. Arm's royalty revenue grew only 8 percent to $670 million in the September quarter, even as its total revenue rose 27 percent to $1.44 billion.

Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said the anxiety about data center spending does not pose a significant threat to the company because data center infrastructure is only one segment of its business. Arm CEO Rene Haas called the postelection fear "very, very short term thinking" and said the United States must keep investing in data center build-out. Arm said memory pricing in smartphones partly offset higher royalty rates and data center growth. Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said the company expects "an even stronger fiscal 2027."

The selloff followed a Democratic sweep of Congress and many governorships in the midterm elections on November 3, which prompted market fears of a slowdown in data center construction. Stocks rallied on Wednesday before falling sharply Thursday, then recovered some losses Friday. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar said the company will keep investing in data centers despite the election results and will focus on community concerns, including electricity costs. Industry analysts expect Qualcomm's next gross margin figure, due with its December-quarter report, to show whether the memory squeeze is easing.

Articles.Title: AI Wants “Every Scrap of RAM.” Qualcomm and Arm Just Showed Who Pays the Bill

stories.Headline: Algorithmic Stewardship Framework Reframes Urban Artificial Intelligence for Climatic Justice
stories.Summary:
Researcher Ehsan Dorostkar has published a qualitative study in City and Built Environment arguing that municipal artificial intelligence in cities should shift from techno-managerial control to what he calls algorithmic stewardship, so that automated systems do not deepen existing social and spatial inequalities. The study was announced on November 8, 2026, and was reported by bioengineer.org. Dorostkar contends that many smart-city platforms reduce complex social and environmental conditions to narrow efficiency measures, treating climate algorithms as neutral tools when they actually shape how value and risk are distributed across a city. He proposes a governance framework that retools automated systems around what he describes as multidimensional justice, prioritizing restorative ethics, transparency, and collective preservation over operational efficiency alone. The research centers on Tehran, a water-scarce megacity facing environmental hazards, seismic risks, and rapid urbanization, and draws on academic literature, municipal policy documents, and analysis of public statements about the city's Smart Tehran agenda.

The article describes the author's definition of urban climatic justice as having three parts: recognitive justice, which values informal adaptation practices and local environmental knowledge; procedural justice, which gives affected communities inclusive participation and formal veto rights in automated decisions; and intergenerational justice, which requires systems to protect long-term ecological viability. Dorostkar argues that the short calculation horizons of conventional algorithms conflict with these goals, since they favor quick, measurable gains such as energy savings while neglecting aquifer stability, cultural heritage, and resilience over decades. In Tehran, he finds that algorithmic water rationing favors industrial users and high-revenue sectors while restricting supply to economically marginalized outlying settlements, and that reservoir management targeting short-term goals accelerates overuse of peripheral groundwater and threatens traditional qanat networks. Heat-vulnerability mapping, he writes, equates adaptive capacity with formal engineering and property value, overlooking customary cooling methods in informal neighborhoods, which steers protective investment toward affluent commercial areas. Air-quality and traffic systems, according to the study, focus restrictions on private vehicle owners while sparing state-affiliated industry, and the article describes his related concept of an algorithmic justice paradox, in which systems reduce citywide risk while concentrating vulnerability among marginalized groups.

To address these problems, the article says Dorostkar proposes three operating principles: a legibility principle requiring that hidden value trade-offs in climate algorithms be open to public scrutiny, an intergenerational proxy that builds future generations' ecological interests into optimization, and a principle of democratic immunity that places certain decisions, such as flood gates and emergency life-safety choices, beyond automation. He also proposes institutional measures, including Algorithmic Courts of Equity where residents can challenge discriminatory computational allocations and Ecological Application Programming Interfaces that would require platforms to incorporate local environmental knowledge. The article is largely a summary of the study and does not report any responses from Tehran officials or the institutions named in the research. Further details on implementation or reactions to the proposals are not included in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Algorithmic Stewardship Framework Reframes Urban Artificial Intelligence for Climatic Justice

stories.Headline: Why Jensen-Gate May Actually Help the AI Boom
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair, and the company's board is investigating whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. According to The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal, US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, was recruited to spy for China. Business Insider has not independently verified that assessment, and the claim is not established fact. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. The episode has shaken Silicon Valley, and Wall Street's reaction on Monday suggested it would have little effect on the AI boom.

The article argues that demand for AI is unlikely to fade because of the scandal. It cites Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello, who wrote that he still expects Nvidia's forecast of $3 trillion to $4 trillion of annual AI infrastructure spending by 2030 to come to fruition. Nvidia's shares fell 4% on Monday, while rival AMD surged 13%, a sign that demand remains strong even if it could shift away from Nvidia. The more uncertain question is the supply of chips, since Huang built Nvidia's position and his departure could disrupt its strategy, relationships and financing.

The article also suggests that scrutiny of Megaspeed, which has been examined over whether its overseas data centers helped Chinese customers reach Nvidia chips despite US export restrictions, could limit Nvidia's China sales and leave more supply for American buyers. Bernstein chip analyst Stacy Rasgon questioned whether any Chinese influence was needed to push Huang's lobbying for wider chip sales to China, since Huang has pursued that for years, though with limited success. Colello kept his $310 fair value estimate for the stock, nearly double its Monday trading price. He also noted that Huang's position as co-founder and only CEO likely gives him more support from the board than most executives get, and that President Donald Trump announced his support when the allegations first arose.

The article says the scandal could also fade without lasting impact on Nvidia's business. The article concludes that the future of AI depends on whether people and businesses keep finding the technology useful and whether companies can build enough infrastructure to meet demand, and that Huang's personal life changes neither. It adds that the affair might leave America with more chips to power its AI ambitions. The articles do not say whether Huang will remain CEO or what the lawmaker probes that could follow will find.

Articles.Title: Why Jensen-Gate May Actually Help the AI Boom

stories.Headline: East Lyme zoning commission withdraws proposed Black Point rezoning after resident pushback
stories.Summary:
The East Lyme Zoning Commission voted unanimously on November 5, 2026, to withdraw its own proposal to rezone a northerly section of Black Point Road. The proposal would have changed the area from CA commercial to R-10 residential. The vote followed a public hearing at which several neighbors spoke. The articles describe the withdrawal as coming after resident pushback. Neighbors who testified raised concerns about property values and traffic safety.

The articles say the commission will revisit alternative approaches, but they do not describe what those alternatives would be. The withdrawal means the rezoning will not proceed in its current form. The article provided does not say whether any timetable has been set for the next steps. The zoning commission, which initiated the proposal itself, took the action on its own motion following the hearing. The articles do not include direct statements from individual commissioners explaining their reasons.

They also do not name the individual residents who spoke at the hearing. The Black Point area has been the subject of zoning discussion, but the articles provided do not offer further background on earlier proposals. More details are expected as the commission considers its alternatives. More to follow.

Articles.Title: East Lyme zoning commission withdraws proposed Black Point rezoning after resident pushback - Citizen Portal AI

stories.Headline: Planning commission deadlocks on rezoning 150-acre Burgetts Cove site; item goes to council with no recommendation
stories.Summary:
The Johnson County planning commission deadlocked on a request to rezone roughly 150 acres at the southeast corner of 175th Street and Lone Elm Road, sending the item to the city council without a recommendation. The application, designated Z26-5, asks to change the site from RR (Rural Residential) to M1 (Light Industrial). The article is dated November 5, 2026, and reports that the commission vote ended in a 3-3 tie. Planning staff presented the request and recommended approval.

Under the M1 designation, the articles say warehousing, limited manufacturing and a range of commercial uses would be allowed, but the district's performance standards require operations to be indoors and restrict outdoor storage. Staff told the commission that data centers were removed from the M1 zoning designation and are not permitted there. The developer's representative, from Opus Development, said the firm plans to market the property for build-to-suit industrial users and is not seeking data centers. Public commenters urged caution and raised concerns about traffic, drainage and property values.

Because the commission split evenly, no recommendation will be forwarded to the city council, which will take up the rezoning request on its own. The articles do not say when the council will consider the item or what vote it may take. The reporting is limited to the commission meeting itself, so the outcome of the council's review remains open. Residents and the applicant will presumably have further opportunities to weigh in before a final decision, though the articles do not specify the schedule.

Articles.Title: Planning commission deadlocks on rezoning 150-acre Burgetts Cove site; item goes to council with no recommendation - citizenportal.ai

stories.Headline: Microsoft Stock Outlook: Azure Growth and New Copilot Features Face a $50 Billion Spending Test
stories.Summary:
Microsoft's stock closed at $516.17 on September 25, up 3.66% from the previous day, as investors weighed strong cloud growth against rising spending on AI infrastructure. The company announced a new version of Copilot on September 25, with Home and Code beginning rollout through its Frontier program over the coming weeks and an Autopilot feature expanding to private preview at the end of September. The new tool is built to handle delegated work, code apps automatically and run tasks through a persistent agent, and it adds usage-based billing as a way to earn money beyond software licenses. Microsoft 365 Copilot has also passed 30 million paid seats, and the company is aiming the new features mainly at enterprise customers.

For the quarter ending June 30, 2026, Microsoft reported revenue of $90.0 billion, up 18% from a year earlier, with operating income rising 18% to $40.6 billion. Azure and other cloud services grew 43%, or 42% under the new fiscal 2027 reporting definitions, and one article put quarterly Azure revenue at $29.4 billion and full-year Azure revenue at about $101.9 billion. GAAP diluted earnings per share were $4.81, while adjusted earnings per share were $4.74, up 23%, and the quarter included a $3.2 billion gain from Microsoft's investment in Anthropic. Unfulfilled commercial performance obligations stand at $678 billion, up 84% from last year, or up 25% excluding OpenAI. Capital spending was $41 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, with about $27 billion going to shorter-lived assets such as CPUs and GPUs, and Microsoft expects it to exceed $50 billion in the first quarter of fiscal 2027.

Microsoft's management attributed a drop in Microsoft Cloud gross margin to 65%, from 68% a year earlier, to a shift in mix toward AI and other cloud infrastructure costs. For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, management guided to revenue of $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion and Azure growth of roughly 44% to 45% in constant currency. For the full fiscal year, it expects double-digit percentage growth in revenue and operating income, with operating margin falling by less than 1 percentage point. The company has also reorganized into two reporting segments, Agents and Infra and Devices and Consumer, which reclassifies revenue across products such as Azure, Microsoft 365, Windows, Xbox and advertising. The articles' author, Arslan Ali of TradingKey, said the main test is whether the heavy spending delivers adequate returns, and that he wants proof that added cloud capacity improves profitability.

On the chart, the stock broke out of a symmetrical triangle, and the author said it stays bullish above $507.41 support. The first major resistance is $519.44, and a break above it would point to a target of $526.37, while a drop below $507.41 would bring $501.26 into focus. An earlier article from September 15 had the stock at $505.41 and watching a resistance zone between $504.20 and $509.82. TradingKey noted that the content is the author's personal opinion and not investment advice.

stories.Headline: Broadcom's Software Moat Meets Its AI Bill: DOCOMO, FedEx and a $63 Billion Financing Bet - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
Broadcom's investment case now depends on whether its long-term software contracts can keep producing value while the company takes on large obligations tied to AI infrastructure. On October 19, Broadcom and NTT DOCOMO agreed a ten-year collaboration to advance DOCOMO's private cloud infrastructure, which Broadcom described as its first comprehensive VMware software agreement of that length in Japan. The company also renewed its infrastructure agreement with FedEx about three weeks before the article's publication, with FedEx continuing to use VMware Cloud Foundation, Avi Load Balancer and Tanzu Platform. The article treats the extension as a positive sign for the existing relationship, though it notes that the benefit depends on Broadcom keeping those products useful. Both contracts run for years, so the article argues that they will be judged by how well Broadcom maintains the software over time.

Broadcom has also released product updates aimed at keeping its software relevant to customers. On October 27, it rolled out extensions to TrueSource Spring Enterprise, including a hub and tools for assessing application attack surfaces and automating security patch deployment, and it said it shipped fixes for 89 new security vulnerabilities. Four days earlier, on October 21, Broadcom introduced Arcot Scam Defense, which is meant to detect and block card-payment fraud driven by social engineering when no physical card is present. The article says that the value of both launches will depend on how easily customers can use them in daily operations. Those launches are presented as evidence that the software business continues to receive attention.

The AI side carries heavier financial commitments, and the article describes a financing structure announced about two weeks earlier. Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley announced a $63 billion arrangement that would let a special-purpose vehicle buy Broadcom AI chips and networking equipment for lease to Anthropic, with shipments expected to begin in 2027. Broadcom judges the probability of a contingent liability from a default on those leases to be low, and the article notes that the protection shrinks as lease payments are made. Powertech Technology also plans to invest $400 million in a joint venture with Broadcom for advanced chip packaging in Singapore, with production possibly starting in 2028, according to remarks by its chairman reported by Reuters. The article therefore suggests that AI growth should be weighed cautiously while those obligations remain open.

The wider market is under pressure, and competition is increasing. Reuters reported a sharp Nasdaq decline on a Thursday after Democratic gains in the midterm elections, with investors worried about tighter AI regulation and slower data-center expansion. Marvell Technology agreed on November 2 to acquire Lumentum Holdings in an all-stock deal valued at $115 billion including debt, which Reuters said strengthens Marvell's position against Broadcom in AI data-center hardware. The article concludes that the investment case rests on two timelines: software relationships that must keep paying off over many years, and an AI build-out whose financing and deliveries extend into 2027 and 2028. It says the business case holds if those long-term customer relationships deliver lasting value and if the AI obligations remain as contained as Broadcom expects.

Articles.Title: Broadcom's Software Moat Meets Its AI Bill: DOCOMO, FedEx and a $63 Billion Financing Bet - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: From Anthropic scare to $12.5 billion valuation: JFrog's AI comeback - CTech
stories.Summary:
JFrog, an Israeli-founded software company, told investors on Friday that AI is now driving demand for its products, and its shares jumped 35% to about $101. The rally came after the stock had lost roughly half its value when Anthropic unveiled an AI model able to find software vulnerabilities. The move lifted the company's market value to about $12.5 billion, just below its all-time high. The article reports the results from the third quarter, which ended in the period covered by the filing.

JFrog reported third-quarter revenue of $179.2 million, up 31% from a year earlier and about $14 million above the midpoint of its August guidance of $164 million to $166 million. Cloud revenue rose 60% to $101.5 million and now makes up 57% of total revenue, compared with 46% a year ago. The company raised its 2026 revenue forecast to a range of $680 million to $682 million, up from $648 million to $652 million. Other measures improved as well, with customers paying more than $1 million a year rising to 112 from 71, and net dollar retention reaching 124%, up from 118%. Free cash flow was $66.5 million, or 37% of revenue, against $28.8 million a year earlier.

CEO Shlomi Ben Haim pointed to a $76 million multiyear agreement with a global telecom company as the clearest evidence of demand. He said the customer's cloud data consumption grew 167% compared with its previous commitment, and that the deal covers tens of thousands of developers working with tens of thousands of agents. CFO Eduard Grabscheid said the company is converting customers' spending above their contractual minimums into larger annual commitments, and that guidance excludes usage beyond those minimums. Asked whether AI labs could build their own tools, Ben Haim argued that what the labs build is complementary to JFrog's system of record, noting that Anthropic and OpenAI are both customers. Grabscheid also acknowledged that the first half of the year brought some hesitation, and that timelines for converting spending into commitments have not necessarily shortened.

The context is that JFrog's shares had fallen sharply on fears that AI tools could displace software vendors, and the quarter was meant to show the reverse. The filing also shows lease assets rising to $109.3 million from $12.1 million at the end of 2025, with leases running to May 2036, and cash and short-term investments reaching $880.9 million. Four insider trading plans were adopted during the quarter, including one for director Frederic Simon covering up to 900,000 shares. The articles do not say how the stock will trade after the rally or what the company plans for those lease commitments beyond the disclosed terms.

Articles.Title: From Anthropic scare to $12.5 billion valuation: JFrog's AI comeback - CTech

stories.Headline: Estevan council considers AI research lab, billboard sites and demolition orders
stories.Summary:
Estevan City Council is set to consider several community and development matters at its regular meeting on Monday, November 9, 2026. The main item is a request for a city letter of support for an application by Southeast College to the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada for up to $200,000 in equipment funding. The college wants to set up an on-premises AI test bed at its Centre of Sustainable Innovation, and the city would not be asked for funding or staff time. The application deadline is November 18.

The proposed facility would let local businesses and organizations test how artificial intelligence could be used without relying on cloud-based services that send their data elsewhere. Equipment would range from entry-level computers to higher-end AI workstations, helping businesses judge what suits their needs and budgets. The project would also give students hands-on experience and support local technology capacity and economic diversification. Council is also weighing three billboard proposals on city-owned land, at Kensington Avenue near Walmart's south entrance, at Souris Avenue and King Street, and near Canadian Tire's north entrance. Administration recommends approval of all three, with conditions requiring sign owners to mow grass within one metre of their billboards where applicable.

Council will also consider demolition orders for two properties, 905 Fourth Street and 1132 Fifth Street, based on a report from Bylaw Enforcement Officer Justin Herod. The city has received numerous complaints about 905 Fourth Street since July 2025, and the building has remained uninhabitable, raising public safety concerns, previous break-ins and squatting. That demolition order is set to take effect after December 4, 2026. For 1132 Fifth Street, administration recommends an exemption if its sale to new owners goes through, while the existing order to remedy would stay registered against the property.

Council will receive the October building permit report, which shows four permits worth $2,565,500 compared with three valued at $871,900 in October 2025. Year to date the city has issued 44 permits worth $13,844,489, against 35 permits worth $8,768,810 at the same point last year. The October water quality report notes no water main breaks and no failures to meet testing regulations, and upgrades to the Smith Street Reservoir are on schedule for completion by the end of December 2026. Council will also consider letters of support for the Estevan Curling Club's bid to host the 2028 Saskatchewan High Schools Athletic Association High School Provincial Doubles Curling Championships, which involves no financial request, and appoint Western Municipal Consulting Ltd. to manage the 2027 Board of Revision process.

Articles.Title: Estevan council considers AI research lab, billboard sites and demolition orders - DiscoverEstevan

stories.Headline: Anthropic Calls for Leaner Harnesses for Agentic AI Development
stories.Summary:
At an AI DevCon event hosted by Tessl, Nicolas Carmont Zaragoza, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, advised DevOps teams to switch to lighter harnesses for agentic engineering workflows. The reason, he said, is that many harnesses now send duplicate instructions to AI models, which drives up token use and cost. As models grow more capable, many instructions that developers once had to write are created by the models themselves, and instructions built into a model always run. He argued that teams should favor lean harnesses that issue high-level prompts, which lowers the chance of instructions clashing with one another.

Carmont Zaragoza told attendees that harnesses have a limited shelf life and should be revisited regularly as models improve. Verification, for example, is now built into the model, so a harness no longer needs to supply explicit verification steps. He urged teams to "unharness" by cutting stale prompts and setting a new baseline for grading outcomes, saying the goal is no longer to build the biggest harness possible. He also said teams should spend more time studying how outcomes were produced, since transcripts often show agents wasting tokens by reasoning across conflicting instructions. Engineers can even ask the model how to improve evaluations, and should keep reviewing those evaluations instead of relying only on traditional test coverage.

The advice comes from Anthropic itself, which previously said it cut the size of its own internal system prompts by 80%. The company is now making a stronger case for others to follow that example. The article's author, Mike Vizard, noted that it is not yet clear how DevOps workflows will change in the AI era, though the general direction is toward software factories that automate them. A debate is also emerging over whether to lean on the model or on a complementary platform where AI skills can be defined and reused.

Separately, Anthropic is moving quickly on its models, according to an analysis released Thursday by the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research, known as METR. The group estimated that Anthropic is improving its models' ability to do "well specified tasks" about twice as fast as a year earlier, and it suggested that much of the speedup comes from using AI itself in development. METR reviewed about 11 weeks of internal data, from mid-August through late October, and interviewed employees. It said Anthropic seems to have made as much benchmark progress in the past year as it did between October 2023 and October 2025.

The finding stands in contrast to a Sept. 12 essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who urged the industry to slow the pace at which it improves model capabilities. Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and it is planning to go public later this month in what could be the biggest initial public offering ever. METR cautioned that its findings could be overstated if the acceleration applies only to tasks that are easy to grade, and it ruled out growth in computing power as the cause. In his essay, Amodei named METR as an appropriate outside evaluator, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he also backed independent evaluators with employee-like access.

Articles.Title: Anthropic CEO Calls for Stronger AI Regulation Measures - RS Web Solutions

stories.Headline: Got $5,000? 2 Growth Stocks Building the Software Backbone of Artificial Intelligence (AI).
stories.Summary:
Microsoft and CrowdStrike are two software companies that a Motley Fool writer, Patrick Sanders, says could benefit from the spread of artificial intelligence, and he suggests an investor with $5,000 might split that money evenly between them. The piece was published on November 8, 2026, and the writer argues that software matters as much as chipmakers because AI chips need programs to do useful work. The more companies rely on AI, the more demand there will be for these services. He frames the two companies as approaching AI from different directions, but both report growing demand for their products.

Microsoft sells familiar programs such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook, which are bundled in its Microsoft 365 suite. Its Azure cloud platform supplies the infrastructure for building and running AI applications, and tools such as Azure AI Foundry and GitHub Copilot help developers. In the fiscal first quarter of 2027, which ended September 30, Azure and other cloud revenue rose 48 percent to $33.16 billion. Daily Copilot users grew nearly 50 percent from the prior quarter and more than fivefold from a year earlier, and commercial remaining performance obligations reached $677 billion, up 73 percent, with OpenAI commitments contributing much of that growth. The writer notes the downside is spending, with capital expenditures of $45.2 billion in the quarter and an expected rise to $50 billion in the second quarter, which pressures margins, though the company still produced $18.6 billion in quarterly free cash flow.

CrowdStrike, according to the article, addresses the security risks that come with AI agents that can access sensitive information and act without constant human supervision, through its Falcon cybersecurity platform. On its fiscal second-quarter earnings call, CEO George Kurtz discussed the emerging market for AI detection and response and suggested that protecting AI agents could eventually become a larger business than traditional endpoint detection and response. In the quarter ended July 31, revenue rose 26 percent to $1.47 billion, annual recurring revenue reached $5.84 billion, and accounts using its Falcon Flex model generated more than $2.29 billion in annual recurring revenue, up 101 percent. The writer concludes that the two companies serve different parts of the AI build-out, so they complement rather than compete with each other, and he presents this as a stronger case for long-term investors than a simple bet on AI growth.

stories.Headline: The AI coverage gap businesses can’t afford to ignore
stories.Summary:
A new report from Avanade, released in early November 2026 and covered by Supply & Demand Chain Executive on November 7, finds that many businesses believe they are further ahead with artificial intelligence than they really are. Three quarters of the organizations surveyed describe themselves as established, advanced, or AI-first, and 72 percent say they are highly confident their teams use AI effectively. Yet only 18 percent say they have fundamentally reshaped how their teams operate around what AI makes possible. The gap between perceived and actual progress is the central finding of the study. The survey also points to weak financial discipline around AI spending.

Sixty-five percent of respondents say AI has not yet delivered financial returns that justify the investment and effort, and 62 percent say their organizations have not formally calculated AI's financial return or had those results reviewed by finance or senior leadership. Most respondents, 75 percent, say too much of their AI money goes toward incremental improvements rather than transformational opportunities. Only 7 percent plan to use AI to build fundamentally new operating models, revenue streams, or businesses over the next 12 months. Eighty-two percent say they need to approve AI initiatives more quickly to stay competitive, and an equal share wants a better way to approve, monitor, and control AI use.

Chris Howarth, chief executive of Avanade, warns that a dangerous gap is opening between AI confidence and AI reality. He argues that the problem is not confidence or ambition but the habit of using AI to improve a business model that AI could instead replace. Ben Beath, Avanade's chief AI officer, says that adding more AI tools does not automatically make a company more competitive. He says the key question is whether those investments change how decisions are made, how work gets done, and how value is created.

Beath also notes that AI-native businesses start without legacy structures, so established firms should check whether they are measuring progress against the right expectations. The findings come as companies across supply chains and other sectors continue adopting AI tools at a rapid pace. The report suggests that without a shift toward transformation, measurement, and faster governance, many organizations will struggle to convert their AI spending into lasting competitive advantage. The article does not describe any further specific actions or timelines for the companies involved.

stories.Headline: Dan Ives Sees A ‘Multiyear Tech Bull Market’ Despite AI Stock Rout — ‘This Was Just A... Scary Moment’
stories.Summary:
Dan Ives, the Wedbush and Yorkville analyst, said on Saturday that technology investors have overreacted to a sharp sell-off in AI-linked stocks. Speaking with Bloomberg, he said semiconductor stocks, hyperscalers and data center companies were hit hard after the U.S. midterm elections, which he called a painful shakeout. He still believes the broader tech bull market is intact. Ives made these comments in an interview published on November 8, 2026.

Ives said Democratic election victories and growing local opposition to data center construction were a major shock to tech investors. He argued that investors reassessed whether political resistance could derail the large infrastructure spending behind the AI boom. He also said concerns grew that tech companies could reach their peak capital spending sooner than expected. He acknowledged the spending trajectory is changing and suggested Big Tech's capital expenditure growth, once expected to peak around 2028 and 2029, could now peak as early as 2027. Ives added that this shift was being taken too far by investors.

Ives said the backlash could make it harder for technology companies to win over ordinary Americans, given fears of white-collar job losses and higher electricity bills. He believes companies will need to show concrete local benefits such as jobs, tax revenue and infrastructure investment. He pointed to projected AI infrastructure spending of $3 trillion to $4 trillion, arguing the investment cycle may last longer rather than end. He said fears of insufficient data center capacity were misplaced because chip demand and orders remained robust. He also said investors were starting to separate likely winners from losers, particularly among neocloud companies facing tougher competition.

Nvidia shares fell nearly 9% last week and AMD dropped over 11% for the week, despite an 11% gain on Friday. Ives said the ripple effects of AI spending reach companies such as Caterpillar, Lockheed Martin, energy firms and financial services providers. He believes political resistance may slow certain projects but will not stop the technology's advance. He described the recent turbulence as a white-knuckle roller-coaster moment. During Friday's after-hours session, the S&P 500, Nasdaq-100 and Dow Jones ETFs were modestly higher, while the Global X AI and Technology ETF rose 1.32% on Friday.

stories.Headline: 'I don't like them' | AI data center backlash fueled election votes as Bottoms plans project pause
stories.Summary:
Voters in several places pushed back against AI data center construction in the recent midterm elections, and the backlash has now reached local government and company policy. The articles describe the backlash as a factor in election votes, with ballot measures meant to limit the construction boom passing widely. On Thursday, November 5, OpenAI said it would change how it deals with communities where it builds its large data centers, which it now calls "compute campuses." Its announcement came two days after those ballot measures drew broad support. Separately, a politician named Bottoms was reported to be planning a pause on projects.

OpenAI described a National Community Compact under which each future campus it owns and operates will have its own local agreement and an annual public report. The company pledged to pay the full cost of the electricity it uses along with the grid upgrades needed to serve it. It also said it would post financial guarantees so local households and businesses would not be stuck paying for grid upgrades if a project were canceled. The company added that it would publish water and power use for each site. It also said it would stop requiring public officials to sign nondisclosure agreements, except in narrow security and trade-secret cases.

OpenAI's Stargate project in Abilene, Texas, is one of the largest data centers under construction in the country, and the company's pledges are a direct response to the local resistance. The company's own statement framed the changes as a commitment to the towns that host its facilities. The articles attribute the policy shift to OpenAI itself, which made the pledges public. Other stories in the same news cycle covered unrelated matters, so the articles do not link those to the data center debate.

The articles do not say whether the pause Bottoms is planning will take effect, what form it would take, or how OpenAI and other developers would respond. They also do not describe how the new compact will be enforced or whether other companies will adopt similar terms. The coverage leaves open how much the local backlash will shape the next round of AI construction. Further details on the pause and on how the compact is implemented would be needed to judge its effects.

stories.Headline: AI infrastructure grows in Texas with new facilities in Dallas, College Station - NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth
stories.Summary:
In Bryan, a 73-megawatt data center is being developed on 25 acres of Texas A&M's RELLIS Campus by Austin-based ThisWay Global, which calls its project the Research and AI Compute Center, or RACC. The facility is focused on sovereign artificial intelligence, a model that lets organizations keep tighter control over their data and the output of AI systems. The center plans an eight-week course for eligible students and community members, extending training beyond Texas A&M's own students. The company expects to begin computing at the Bryan site by June 2027. Students and researchers say that a nearby facility would make it easier to keep their work on campus instead of seeking outside partners for large computing systems.

In Dallas, technology integrator GDT has opened what it calls an "AI factory," a supercomputer lab where businesses can build and test AI applications before investing in their own systems. The lab runs on NVIDIA GPUs, NetApp storage and Cisco networking, and companies can use it to judge whether a given AI use case makes sense for their operations. GDT executives say large enterprises now need to deploy AI at scale, which is far more complex than casual use of a public chatbot. GDT's vice president of advisory and transformation, Chris Kapusta, said the lab is meant to speed companies from exploring AI to confirming real value. He added that the facility gives North Texas businesses local access to the technology and draws national attention to the region.

GDT's CEO, Shawn O'Grady, compared AI to a hammer, arguing that the tool itself is not the problem and that its effect depends on how people use it. Kapusta said bad actors are already using AI to search for security weaknesses, while companies can use the same technology to find and fix vulnerabilities first. ThisWay Global's CEO, Stefan Fable, said AI will become part of everyday systems, including payment systems and points of sale. He also stressed that users keep control over both inputs and outputs in a sovereign setup, which he called important for research, regulated industries and defense. Together, the two projects reflect a push to put computing power within reach of more people as AI spreads through business, research and daily life.

stories.Headline: Stocks extend losing streak to 3rd consecutive session on AI uncertainties
stories.Summary:
Stock markets in South Korea have fallen for a third straight session, with investors pulling back amid uncertainty over artificial intelligence, according to a Yonhap News Agency report published on November 9, 2026. The article's headline captures the main point, though the page itself offers little beyond the headline and a list of related stories. Other coverage on the same site noted sharp gains in Seoul shares on a tech rally and lower oil prices, which suggests the mood swings quickly. Separate reporting from Yahoo Finance and StockTwits, dated November 7, 2026, shows the same kind of pressure on individual names.

That report focuses on Hut 8 Corp., which posted its lowest weekly close in seven months on Friday, extending its losing streak to a seventh straight week. The stock fell roughly 28 percent from Tuesday's close to Thursday's close, then rebounded more than 14 percent on Friday. The company reported third-quarter revenue of nearly $71 million, down from $83.5 million a year earlier, and a loss of $1.23 per share. Hut 8 said it is targeting delivery of the first data hall at its River Bend campus by the second quarter of 2027.

The pressure was tied in part to Texas, where Hut 8 is building its Beacon Point site, and to political uncertainty there. According to an Investing.com report cited by StockTwits, the Democratic governor-elect campaigned on freezing new data center construction, and the existing administration had already halted permitting ahead of a December audit. Several Wall Street firms lowered their price forecasts for the company on Thursday, citing permitting risks at its 1,000-megawatt Nueces County facility. The article also noted that Hut 8 has shifted its focus from Bitcoin mining toward building data centers for artificial intelligence, and that its compute business still drove most of its revenue.

stories.Headline: AI may be helping Anthropic make two years of progress in one, METR estimates
stories.Summary:
METR, an AI evaluation group, has estimated that Anthropic may now be making roughly two years of progress in one on clearly defined AI tasks. According to the assessment, the company's use of AI is helping its researchers build more capable models faster. The estimate draws on 11 weeks of access to Anthropic's internal research data and staff, with the review covering August 12 to October 29. METR judges that by October 2026, progress ran at about twice the company's pace between March 2024 and October 2025. Anthropic's version of the Epoch Capabilities Index showed benchmark performance improving at an estimated 1.9 times its earlier rate.

The report suggests researchers now spend less time writing code and more time testing ideas, with several interviewees saying AI lets them turn ideas into experiments more quickly. METR says most of the gains come from AI helping human researchers rather than working autonomously, though early signs of more independent contributions were noted. About 80 percent of the acceleration is attributed to Anthropic's internal use of its models for research and development, though METR did not find decisive evidence and staff disagreed on the figure. METR also said faster growth in training compute did not explain the acceleration, and it found no clear constraints on algorithms, computing resources or data that would block rapid progress over the next 12 months. Its estimate is uncertain, and it said the true pace could fall anywhere from 1.3 to three times the historical rate.

METR's full report ran to about 100 pages, and Anthropic redacted most of the evidence the assessors found most informative, citing the need to protect confidential information that could help other AI developers. The omitted material includes detailed estimates of algorithmic progress and analysis of specific constraints on future development. METR said it gave Anthropic the longer report before preparing the public version and agreed the withheld material fit that description, though it did not judge whether the redactions were justified overall. The assessors could not freely search Anthropic's internal systems, and METR said the public must rely on its judgment more than it considers ideal. METR received no payment from Anthropic, which supplied devices and free AI tokens, and it disclosed that one assessor held equity in a competitor and had discussed a possible Anthropic role before declining an offer.

The findings bear on concerns about recursive AI self-improvement, in which AI systems help develop later systems. This assessment followed Anthropic's October 15 announcement that six METR employees would gain access to certain internal systems, equipment and office space through its safety review arrangement. Anthropic also canceled a planned examination of how it allocated computing resources between capabilities and safety before METR reached substantive conclusions, saying it wanted to focus on risk assessment and would revisit that work later. The articles do not say whether any further assessment is scheduled.

According to sources cited by the Financial Times, the purchase is the largest known of its kind made by an AI lab. The agreement was reported on November 8, 2026. The deal shows how much electricity the AI industry now needs and how developers are securing it themselves rather than relying only on existing grid supply. The article describes the purchase as a commitment to generators rather than an outright purchase of finished plants. It sits within a wider pattern in which AI companies are signing large contracts for the computing capacity and infrastructure that support their models. The figures reported here cover only the power equipment and capacity named in the deal.

Responsibility for the agreement lies with Anthropic, which made the purchase, and with OnePWR, which supplies the generators. The Financial Times reporting, credited to Martha Muir, relies on sources familiar with the transaction rather than on a public statement from either company. The available reporting does not give a direct quotation from executives at either firm about the deal's terms or timing. Readers should note that the details come from people briefed on the matter.

The wider context is the rapid growth of computing spending by AI developers, which has drawn attention from investors concerned about whether revenues can keep pace. A separate Investing.com analysis, citing Bernstein, estimates that OpenAI's compute commitments could total $614 billion in infrastructure spending through 2030, below some widely cited figures. That analysis assumes every contract proceeds on schedule, which it describes as unlikely, since delays and cancellations could defer payments. The articles do not say what further steps Anthropic or OnePWR will take under the agreement or when the generators will come online.

stories.Headline: 300 media outlets worldwide “Cooperate to bridge AI technology gaps and ensure responsible reporting”… Joint statement announced at the 7th World Media Summit
stories.Summary:
The 7th World Media Summit opened in Beijing on Saturday, the 7th of November, 2026, under the theme of media in the intelligent age. Hosted by Xinhua News Agency and organized with the Beijing municipal government, the summit runs from Thursday to Monday and drew roughly 500 representatives from about 330 mainstream media outlets, think tanks, government bodies and international organizations across 112 countries and regions. Li Shulei, head of the Publicity Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, gave the keynote speech at the opening ceremony. The gathering adopted the Beijing Consensus, a joint statement that calls for working together on the transformation of the global media industry in the AI era.

The statement commits signatories to encouraging the broad and responsible use of AI in media so that its benefits reach outlets at every stage of development and in every country. The summit also released the Global Media Initiative for the Joint Development of AI Application Standards, launched by Xinhua. Its first 22 participants include Russia's TASS, Malaysia's Bernama, South Africa's Independent Media, and China's People's Daily and China Media Group. Over roughly two years, participants plan to draft standards for different media uses of AI, validate them through media outlets, and build a global database of AI applications. The initiative aims to protect the authenticity of information, data security and media ethics so that public trust in the media is maintained.

Speakers at the summit framed the gathering in terms of the wider stakes. Li Shulei said the scientific and technological revolution, especially AI, would bring profound changes to the global media industry, and he proposed improving content quality, advancing digital transformation together, addressing imbalances in data and algorithms, and expanding cross-border media exchanges. Xinhua president Fu Hua presented an AI assistant called Xinhua Style and urged active adoption of AI alongside international cooperation. At the afternoon thematic discussions, participants raised concerns that infrastructure gaps and the lack of large language models for non-English and minority languages could lead to biased information. The UN Office at Geneva's director-general, Tatiana Valovaya, said developing countries need access to digital infrastructure and computing resources.

The summit began in 2009 at Xinhua's proposal and has become a major global platform for media exchange, with the last edition held in Urumqi in 2024. Korean coverage noted that Park Jong-Seong, president of the Kyunghyang Shinmun, was the only Korean media executive reported as attending, and that South Korea's ambassador to China, Noh Jae-Heon, also attended the opening ceremony. Reuters president Paul Bascobert argued that the tools have changed but journalistic principles have not, and Park said journalists would survive the AI era but that those who use AI well would thrive while those who do not would be weeded out. Coverage also reported that a session on the right to know and efforts to police misinformation did not go into depth that day.

stories.Headline: Machine Learning Meets EMS Stroke Triage
stories.Summary:
The articles describe how PubMed, run by the U.S. National Library of Medicine, uses machine learning. Since April 2022, all journals indexed for MEDLINE have their MeSH (Medical Subject Headings) terms applied by an automated system called MTIX, which the National Library of Medicine describes as a neural network, a type of AI. MTIX replaced the earlier MTIA algorithm and was trained on millions of MEDLINE citations published between 2007 and 2022. It works from the title, abstract, publication year, indexing year and journal name, not the full text.

The change applies many more MeSH terms than before, with similar precision and about 50% more terms per article, according to the library's March-April 2024 Technical Bulletin. About one-third of automatically indexed articles also receive human curation, focused on publication types such as systematic reviews and trials, and on gene and protein citations. Separately, PubMed's default Best Match sort re-ranks the top results using a machine-learning algorithm, weighting by matched terms and fields and giving recent articles somewhat more weight. Other sort options include Most Recent, Publication Date, First Author and Journal.

The library itself is responsible for these systems, and the PubMed User Guide and the MeSH indexing FAQ are its stated descriptions of them. The articles also note that people searching for "PubMed AI" often want papers about artificial intelligence, which PubMed covers through the MeSH heading Artificial Intelligence and its narrower terms. Because MeSH indexing lags new terminology and automated indexing uses only titles and abstracts, the articles suggest pairing MeSH terms with title and abstract text words, such as "machine learning" or "large language model," and checking Search Details to see how a query was translated. They also say the PubMed User Guide does not describe any generative-AI or chatbot feature in PubMed.

stories.Headline: [New feature] HIX AI releases simultaneous multi-model comparison chat! Compare answers from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and more side by side on one screen
stories.Summary:
HIX AI, an AI agent service run by Singapore-based INNOVATE AI PTE. LTD., released a new "multi-model comparison chat" feature on Monday, November 9. The feature lives inside its main AI chat tool and lets users see answers from several AI models on the same screen. Until now, the company says, people looking for the best answer had to open ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and other platforms one by one and paste the same question into each. The new tool is meant to remove that repeated work and speed up research and decision making.

Users can pick up to four models at once, either from a recommended list or from the brand list, and a single question is sent in parallel to all of them. The answers appear side by side on one page in a fixed order, so users can compare how complete, logical and nuanced each response is. Each model keeps its own separate conversation context, which means follow-up questions to one model do not affect the others, and an error in one model does not disrupt the rest. Once the first message is sent, the combination of models in that conversation is locked, and choosing different models starts a new chat session automatically. To use it, a person selects the AI chat agent from the HIX AI home page, clicks the model name under the input box, and chooses between one and four models.

The company points to several uses. Content creators and marketers can have multiple models draft slogans or copy on the same theme and pick the strongest angle. Researchers and analysts can cross-check answers to reduce the risk of hallucinations, and engineers can compare the code and technical approaches each model suggests. HIX AI chat also includes web search and PDF analysis as standard features. The press release was issued by INNOVATE AI, whose representative is listed as Kaya Huang, and the company can be reached at social@hix.ai.

The launch comes as interest in using several AI tools together is growing, at least in Korea. A report from Seoul Economic Daily says ChatGPT had 18,762,276 monthly mobile users there last month, up 43.8% from a year earlier, and held 91% of users of the AI apps surveyed, up from 84%. Claude's monthly users jumped 15-fold to 2.1 million from 140,000, moving it to second place from seventh. The paper noted that this makes the ability to work with more than one AI tool increasingly important for job seekers. The articles do not say whether HIX AI plans further updates to the feature.

stories.Headline: Microsoft Patent Describes Paying PC Owners to Train AI on Idle GPUs
stories.Summary:
In early November 2026, Microsoft's patent application US-20260349820-A1, titled "Opportunistic Micro-training on Edge Devices Using Spare GPU Utilization," became public on November 5, after being filed in April 2025. The filing describes splitting large AI training jobs into small pieces sized for individual devices, such as phones, laptops, and gaming PCs, and sending those pieces whenever a device has spare capacity. Owners would have to opt in, and the system would track their contributions and credit their accounts with free software, access to the trained model, or money. The system would monitor GPU and CPU load, memory use, temperature, and power draw, checking less often when a device is busy or hot, and it could pause tasks when limits are exceeded. Results would be cross-checked across devices to catch faulty or tampered work.

The filing does not give a payout rate or list which hardware would be supported, so it is unclear whether rewards would offset the added electricity cost. Microsoft has not announced any Windows or Xbox service based on the idea, and the document is only an application, which is not a guarantee of a product. One commentator pointed to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's argument that DRAM in home PCs, used about 5% of the time, is a poor use of limited memory supply. A separate Microsoft patent filing described in the same period concerns AI that alters livestreams in real time, though that report comes from a different source and is not part of this proposal.

Microsoft is named as the applicant, and the filing itself is the only source describing the plan, so no statement from the company about its intentions is available in the articles. Readers have raised concerns about hardware wear, storage use, and fine print that could disclaim responsibility for damage or failures. Some have compared the scheme to earlier GPU cryptomining and volunteer computing projects like SETI@home. The articles say that patents often never become products, so whether this idea reaches users remains open, and any opt-in service would still need to be proven worthwhile for owners.

stories.Headline: AI Should Speed Veterans’ Benefits, Not Decide Them
stories.Summary:
Earlier this month, President Trump signed an executive order aimed at speeding up veterans' benefits, directing the Department of War and the Department of Veterans Affairs to modernize how records are shared, build and use new digital tools, and improve transition assistance. Veterans can wait months or years for a benefits decision, which can delay plans for housing, school, and supporting a family. Rob Schroder, a Marine Corps veteran and founder and CEO of SteerBridge, wrote about the order in an opinion piece published on November 7, 2026. Separately, a Calvert County, Maryland, military spouse named Tracy Contrino described a nonprofit she founded to make the process easier.

Schroder argues that artificial intelligence should help officials work faster but should not decide whether a veteran qualifies for a benefit, which he says remains a job for qualified VA personnel. He points to tasks where AI could help, such as organizing thousands of pages of records, summarizing evidence, identifying missing information, and handling administrative work. He also says government technology should be judged by measurable results rather than by spending, using questions about whether it reduces delays and improves the veteran's experience. He notes that the VA's electronic health record modernization program drew congressional questions about cost and accountability, and he says that the test for any tool is whether it works for the people who rely on it. He adds that his company has helped government agencies cut processing times, though he gives no further details here.

Contrino, whose husband served 18 years in the Army and National Guard and is rated 100% P&T disabled, founded TheClusterFix, an independent nonprofit that is not part of the VA. Its AI assistant, named Frank, helps veterans find and understand publicly available information from the VA and other federal sources, but it does not offer legal or medical advice. Contrino said getting a disability rating can take months or even years, and that many veterans give up when denials leave them confused. Hope Bald, the nonprofit's board president, said Frank helped her with her own claim by surfacing information that a service officer had not mentioned. The group is seeking grants and donations, and it plans to expand Frank's guidance on education benefits and build partnerships with other organizations.

Taken together, the two pieces describe a shared aim of making the path to earned benefits shorter and clearer, though they approach it from different sides. Schroder focuses on what government agencies should do and how they should be judged, while Contrino describes a free tool built outside government to help veterans find their way through it. Neither article reports on how well AI tools perform in actual VA claims decisions or on how the executive order will be carried out. Both leave open how the next steps will unfold, with Schroder calling on Congress and others to ensure modernization delivers measurable results.

stories.Headline: Wall Street's Biggest Bubble Looks Ready to Burst, and I Don't Mean AI or Quantum Computing
stories.Summary:
Outstanding margin debt on Wall Street hit an all-time high of $1.502 trillion in June 2026, according to FINRA, the industry regulator. Margin is money an investor borrows from a broker, with interest, to buy securities or bet against them, so it amplifies both gains and losses. The Motley Fool's Sean Williams argued on November 8, 2026, that this surge, rather than any bursting of an AI or quantum computing bubble, may be what ends the stock market's four-year rally. The piece appeared as the S&P 500 stood at 7,376.86, the Nasdaq Composite at 24,579.42 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average at 51,285.73.

The article points to a pattern over roughly three decades in which margin debt climbed by at least 65% over a fairly short span of 12 to 19 months. The first three such surges all came before major bear markets. From March 1999 to March 2000, margin debt rose 80% to nearly $300 billion, and after the dot-com bubble burst, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq lost 49% and 78% of their value by October 2002. From June 2006 to July 2007, it jumped 66% to more than $416 billion, and the S&P 500 later fell 57% during the financial crisis. From March 2020 to October 2021, it grew 95% to almost $936 billion, and the 2022 bear market that followed wiped out about a fifth of the Dow, a quarter of the S&P 500 and a third of the Nasdaq.

The fourth instance is the current one. Between April 2025 and June 2026, a stretch of 14 months, margin debt rose 77% to the $1.502 trillion record, which the author links to the growth of artificial intelligence and the arrival of quantum computing. Williams says the measure cannot show when the market will turn or what will trigger a decline, but it does show that heavy risk-taking is unsustainable, especially when stocks are historically expensive. He adds that if history repeats, a sharp bear market could come in the not-too-distant future.

For context, the article notes that the current bull market began on October 12, 2022, and is now the ninth longest in S&P 500 history, according to Bespoke Investment Group. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq have more than doubled from their 2022 lows, while the Dow has risen as much as 90%. Bespoke's review of bull and bear markets since September 1929 found the average bear market took about 286 days, or roughly 9.5 months, to hit bottom, while the average bull market lasted 1,023 days. Crestmont Research data covering 107 rolling 20-year periods from 1900 to 2025 showed a positive average annual total return, dividends included, in every one. Williams concludes that patient investors should treat any bursting of the margin debt bubble as a buying opportunity.

stories.Headline: Apple, Samsung turn to Chinese AI rivals to stay competitive
stories.Summary:
Apple and Samsung are leaning harder on Chinese technology companies to run their artificial intelligence features in China, according to a Korea Herald report published on November 9, 2026. Apple announced on October 31 that Alibaba's Qwen model will be built into Apple Intelligence in China, with developer testing starting that week and a public rollout planned for December through iOS 27.3. Samsung has worked with Baidu since January 2024 to localize Galaxy AI, and its Chinese version of Circle to Search relies on Baidu's Ernie model instead of Google's technology. The Korea Herald also reported that Chinese media said in July that the Baidu collaboration had expanded to the Galaxy S26 series.

The Qwen integration will support Siri, Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence, letting users generate text and ask questions about photos and documents. Apple's own models will still handle features such as live translation and photo editing, and its next-generation Siri AI is not part of the initial rollout. Samsung and Baidu have also worked on Chinese-language input, document summarization, Bixby and an AI call assistant that can handle courier and food-delivery calls when users set it up. The report notes that Alibaba reportedly built technology to filter Apple's AI output under Chinese content rules, though neither company has publicly explained how it works. Under China's rules, public-facing generative AI services must meet content and security standards and be registered with regulators, and in July the cyberspace regulator listed Apple Intelligence and Galaxy AI among seven registered smartphone AI services.

The experts quoted in the report say these partnerships are less a free choice than a practical requirement for entering the Chinese market, though Chinese law does not explicitly force foreign phone makers to use domestic AI providers. Park Seung-chan, a Chinese studies professor at Yongin University, said the arrangements are "less a matter of choice than something they have to do." Lee Sang-woo, an adjunct professor at Inha University, said local partners give foreign companies infrastructure already adapted to China's regulatory environment. The report also says that Chinese platforms such as Alibaba's Taobao and Alipay and Baidu's search and mapping could make these assistants more useful, though neither Apple nor Samsung has confirmed plans to connect them to those services.

The stakes differ for the two companies. According to Counterpoint Research, China's smartphone shipments fell 10 percent on the year in the third quarter, with Huawei leading at a 21.3 percent share and Apple second at 19.5 percent, while Samsung stayed outside the top six. Park said the tie-up is a necessary tool for Apple to defend its share, while for Samsung, staying close to China's supply chain may matter more than an immediate sales recovery. The report warns that relying on Chinese AI providers brings risks, including fragmented user experiences across markets, regulatory uncertainty and less control over technology and data, and Park cautioned that these firms "could become competitors in AI services." Park also expects that the partnerships will not change market shares much, since the market remains dominated by Apple and domestic Chinese brands.

stories.Headline: AI Framework Detects Hidden Grouting Defects and Maps 3D Porosity in Prefabricated Building Sleeves
stories.Summary:
A new study describes an artificial intelligence framework that can spot hidden grouting defects inside prefabricated building sleeves and estimate the porosity of those voids in three dimensions. The work, published in Discover Applied Sciences by Wang and Wu, targets grouted splice sleeves, which are key load-bearing connections in precast concrete construction. Defects in these connections are hard to detect because incomplete grout filling is concealed inside the sleeve, where external inspection cannot see it. The authors built a dual-pathway system called Swin-MFF-BUQ to address this gap.

The system has two pathways that share a common design. The first works in two dimensions, processing time-frequency maps from impact-echo and ultrasonic array measurements to predict an anomaly-support mask and a five-class fullness grade. The researchers stress that this mask reflects anomaly support in the signal domain rather than a physical map of voids in space. The second pathway processes industrial computed tomography volumes to estimate void geometry and porosity descriptors. Both pathways use deformable-window Swin encoders, bidirectional cross-scale weighted fusion, and uncertainty-aware prediction heads.

The team assembled 240 sleeve specimens across five fullness levels, producing 12,000 records for each sensing modality, and used a separate development collection of 36 CT volumes for the three-dimensional pathway. They held out entire specimens during evaluation so the model could not simply memorize patterns tied to particular specimens. On the held-out signal test split, the 2D pathway reached a mean intersection-over-union of 91.4 plus or minus 0.3 percent and an image-wise Dice score of 95.1 plus or minus 0.2 percent, a 2.8-point gain over the strongest of eight baseline architectures. Fullness grading reached 96.8 plus or minus 0.4 percent accuracy with a macro-F1 of 96.5 percent. The 3D pathway, tested on held-out CT volumes, gave a mean absolute porosity error of 0.62 plus or minus 0.05 percentage points, a root mean square error of 0.84 percentage points, and a coefficient of determination of 0.976.

The researchers applied temperature scaling, which reduced expected calibration error from 0.034 to 0.021, and reported a Spearman correlation of 0.81 between predicted uncertainty and segmentation error. When the most uncertain 10 percent of cases were deferred to human review, mean intersection-over-union on the retained cases rose to 93.6 percent. Standard 2D inference took 38 milliseconds per 512-by-512 map, which the authors describe as fast enough for near-real-time screening on construction sites. They frame the design as a two-step workflow, with rapid signal screening first and CT-based volumetric characterization when detailed geometry is needed.

The authors, Q. Wang and D. Wu, acknowledge the limits of the evidence. The CT results come from a developmental collection of 36 volumes, and they state that independent sleeve-level validation is still needed before those figures can be treated as generalizable. The paper is open access with a permanent DOI and is subject to further editorial refinement before the final Version of Record is issued. The articles do not describe any planned deployment timeline or next steps beyond that validation.

stories.Headline: Northern Trust and Microsoft Frontier Company collaborate to transform client onboarding through AI
stories.Summary:
On November 9, 2026, Northern Trust and Microsoft announced an expanded collaboration to accelerate AI transformation across Northern Trust, beginning with a new AI-powered client onboarding agent. The agent is being deployed for clients on Northern Trust Asset Servicing's Front Office Solutions platform, which provides performance and analytics for institutional investors such as foundations, endowments, pension schemes and large family offices. It was developed jointly by Northern Trust and the Forward Deployed Engineering teams of Microsoft Frontier Company. The announcement was made in Chicago and Redmond, Washington.

The agent addresses a difficult stage of onboarding, in which years of investment and transaction history from multiple sources must be converted into a standardized format that fits Northern Trust's reporting environment. According to the companies, it cut data preparation time by 83 percent, from about two and a half weeks to three days, and achieved a 96.5 percent F1 first-pass quality score, a standard AI measure combining precision and recall. Northern Trust said 57 percent of asset owners it surveyed named consolidating data from disparate sources as their biggest challenge. The agent is built on Microsoft Azure and Microsoft Foundry, works with Excel and SharePoint, and keeps human analysts in the review loop, with Microsoft tuning the system using only anonymized data so client data stays under Northern Trust's control.

Northern Trust's Chief Operating Officer, Pete Cherecwich, said the agent pairs the firm's asset servicing expertise with Microsoft's AI capabilities to get clients running faster while keeping the oversight clients expect. Bill Borden, Corporate Vice President, Worldwide Financial Services at Microsoft, said the collaboration shows AI amplifying human expertise, with governance and human oversight built in, and that the approach points to opportunities across regulated industries. The companies present the work as a model for how highly regulated institutions can adopt frontier AI while retaining ownership of their data and expertise. The articles do not describe any rollout beyond the Front Office Solutions clients or set a timetable for wider use.

stories.Headline: "By 2027 we could witness a Chernobyl of artificial intelligence": the warning of Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton
stories.Summary:
Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel Prize winner and one of the founders of artificial intelligence, has warned that AI could cause a large-scale accident within the next year or so. In an interview with the Guardian, published in early November 2026, the British computer scientist said such an event might hit financial systems or electricity grids. He compared it to the Chernobyl disaster, though he did not predict a nuclear accident. Hinton, who is 78, said that humanity might have been better off never developing the technology. Coverage from thevermilion.com and ukrmedia.news reported his remarks in the same period.

Hinton said that within a decade, if not sooner, society will learn whether it can manage the risks of AI. He warned of a widening gap between rich and poor, serious cultural problems, mass unemployment and, ultimately, the breakdown of social order. He also said that AI could have a positive future if its dangers are handled well. The articles present these as his own assessments rather than established facts. Ukrmedia.news noted that he had repeatedly raised similar concerns since leaving Google in 2023.

Hinton criticized the leaders of major AI companies, naming Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Sam Altman. He said he believed they understood the risks but were more concerned with money than with safety. Ukrmedia.news described this as his personal view about their motives, not a proven fact. Hinton also pointed to recent cybersecurity incidents triggered autonomously by AI agents as a warning sign. He likened them to the 1979 Three Mile Island partial meltdown, while the articles treat the Chernobyl comparison as a metaphor for a large event.

The articles say Hinton wants independent testing of powerful AI models before they are released, similar to the approval process for medicines. He argued that voluntary commitments by companies are insufficient and called for common standards and international cooperation. He also said he does not think losing control of AI is inevitable if more resources go into safety research. The articles note that the feared disaster has not yet happened, so his warning remains a judgment about potential risks.
