Arrow expects fourth-quarter sales between $11.55 billion and $12.15 billion, and it also announced leadership changes, including the retirement of Enterprise Computing Solutions president Eric Nowak and the arrival of Rodney Clark and Anuj Gore.

Articles.Title: Arrow Electronics Expands AI Infrastructure Business as Quarterly Sales Jump 39%

stories.Headline: Doximity expands clinical AI footprint to more than 190 health systems
stories.Summary:
Doximity said on Thursday, November 5, 2026 in its fiscal 2027 second-quarter earnings call that more than 190 health systems have now bought its AI suite, up from 165 last quarter. The customers include 10 of the nation's top 20 hospitals. NewYork-Presbyterian has built Doximity's AI tools into its electronic health record workflow for clinicians across NewYork-Presbyterian, Columbia University Irving Medical Center and Weill Cornell Medicine. UCSD Health is among the first hospitals to adopt the company's new patient context feature, which lets the AI read charts, labs and patient history. The company is also opening API access to its clinical intelligence layer.

The company's CEO, Jeff Tangney, said the patient context feature is now available to thousands of doctors and cuts the length of their prompts from an average of 24 words to 12. Tangney described Doximity's offering as a full suite covering telehealth, AI documentation, scheduling, clinical questions, patient context and clinical evidence. He argued that larger health systems are tightening AI governance over concerns about patient data, liability and security, which he believes favors approved platforms with enterprise privacy and security controls. He said the company has more than 300 enterprise clients, which together reach nearly half of all U.S. physicians.

Tangney also said accuracy is the top concern doctors have about AI, and he pointed to Doximity's recently launched DoseCheck medication safety verifier. Through a partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health, UpToDate's evidence-based content is now embedded in Doximity Ask, and Tangney said he expects the partnership to grow over time. Physician engagement is rising as well, with quarterly active workflow prescribers up 34% year over year and about 900,000 of the 1.8 million U.S. prescribers using its workflow products during the quarter. Chief financial officer Matt Sonefeldt said that engagement lays the groundwork for future monetization.

Doximity reported $174.5 million in revenue for the quarter ending September 30, up 4% year over year and above guidance, with adjusted EBITDA of $89 million. It raised its full-year revenue outlook to $678 million to $683 million. Its AI Search product for pharmaceutical companies, launched in late April, has been bought by 16 of the top 20 drugmakers, with three more in contracting. Shares fell after the report over margin compression, and the stock is down nearly 25% this year. The company plans to pursue pharma paid search spending, which Tangney estimated at $14 billion a year in the U.S.

Articles.Title: Doximity expands clinical AI footprint to more than 190 health systems

stories.Headline: Systematic Review Examines AI Risks and Accountability in High-Stakes Decision-Making
stories.Summary:
A systematic literature review published in Artificial Intelligence Review examined the operational impact of artificial intelligence systems used in high-stakes environments where human lives are at risk. Researchers Nataly R. Panczyk and Majdi I. Radaideh evaluated safety risks, protective mitigations, and governance structures surrounding automated and assisted decision-making across safety-critical domains. The study was released on November 9, 2026, as an open-access work with a permanent digital object identifier, ahead of its final version of record. The authors described the work as addressing a gap in which technological advances outpace the regulatory frameworks meant to protect the public.

The authors said that earlier reviews had examined related computational questions but had not synthesized literature focused specifically on safety-critical industries and the relationships among technology developers, operational end-users, and regulatory authorities. To find relevant research, the investigators searched Web of Science and Scopus on December 15, 2025, and retrieved an initial pool of 1,135 candidate papers. Screening criteria covering each system's operational sensitivity, decision-making framework, and risk profile narrowed that collection to a final corpus of 72 reports. Each of those reports was subjected to formal quality assessment and risk of bias evaluation to check methodological rigor.

The reviewers organized their findings into three areas: the safety risks of using artificial intelligence in critical choices, practical mechanisms for mitigating those hazards, and procedures for assigning accountability for computer-generated decisions. They also extracted variables covering the types of artificial intelligence implemented, the technical expertise of operational end-users, and the decision-making time windows allotted to human operators. Industry-level qualitative assessments of operational trends complemented these quantitative patterns. The article does not, however, report specific findings on each of these points in the material provided.

The study was authored by Panczyk and Radaideh and carries the citation Artificial Intelligence Review, 2026, with the digital object identifier 10.1007/s10462-026-11734-z. The article's title is "When computers call the shots: a systematic review exploring the impact of AI in high-stakes decision-making." The coverage was published by Scienmag and written by Blake Davidson. The available material does not describe any regulatory changes or further steps that follow from the review.

Articles.Title: Systematic Review Examines AI Risks and Accountability in High-Stakes Decision-Making

stories.Headline: InsureThink What to weigh before putting AI agents on legacy claims tech
stories.Summary:
The articles are an opinion-and-analysis piece rather than a breaking news story, and they describe no single event with a date, actor or action beyond general industry trends. Writing the requested format requires at least three paragraphs of four to five sentences each, and the material here does not support a full news story of that length without inventing facts. The sources give no specific numbers, dates or named decisions, so I have kept to what they say. The core argument, from a piece on the InsureThink channel of Digital Insurance, is that insurers are eager to place AI agents on top of existing claims systems instead of replacing them.

The writer sees value in agents that help claims examiners move through those systems and find information faster. The article is framed as a set of questions for carriers weighing that approach before committing to it. It is part of a wider set of reports on AI in insurance. Other pieces in the same collection touch on related concerns.

One describes submission intake as an early place where carriers and MGAs use AI, with a warning that tools may read poor documents incorrectly without signaling the error. Another covers a rise in cyber risk aimed at small and medium-sized businesses, with Travelers, Beazley and Coalition named as addressing it. A third reports that consumer groups, including the Consumer Federation of America and the Greenlining Institute, object to opaque AI claims denials and urge more oversight and a slower pace of adoption. More to follow.

Articles.Title: InsureThink What to weigh before putting AI agents on legacy claims tech

stories.Headline: KAIST vs. MIT: Which University Is Harder to Get Into, More Prestigious, and Better for Artificial Intelligence?
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story, so I cannot end it with "More to follow." The article is an opinion-style comparison piece, not a report of a recent event, so the required structure of what happened, what it changes, who is responsible, and what comes next does not map onto it cleanly. Below is a faithful account of what the article says, in three paragraphs of five sentences each. The article, published by Rebellion Research on November 9, 2026, compares the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology on admissions difficulty, prestige, and strength in artificial intelligence. It describes MIT as a long-established engineering and computer science powerhouse and KAIST as South Korea's leading science and technology institution.

The piece argues that both schools attract highly talented students but differ in admissions standards, reputation, resources, and career opportunities. It frames the central question as which university offers the better education for students interested in AI or advanced engineering. On admissions, the article says MIT admits roughly 4% to 5% of undergraduate applicants in recent cycles and concludes it is generally the harder school to enter. It cites a KAIST domestic early-admissions competition ratio of about 8.47 applicants per place for the 2026 academic year, while cautioning that this does not translate directly into a comparable acceptance rate. On prestige, the article holds that MIT has far greater recognition among American employers, investors, and the general public, while KAIST is well respected in specialized scientific circles.

For AI, it describes MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and KAIST's Kim Jaechul Graduate School of AI, established in 2019, and says MIT offers the stronger startup and American industry ecosystem while KAIST suits those interested in robotics, semiconductors, and South Korea's technology sector. The article's final verdict is that MIT is the stronger overall choice for global prestige and opportunity, but that KAIST is a formidable technical university deserving more recognition in the United States. It notes that both schools offer financial aid and scholarships, so students should compare net costs rather than published tuition. The piece makes no predictions about future rankings or policy changes, and it does not name a specific author or cite outside sources for its claims.

Articles.Title: KAIST vs. MIT: Which University Is Harder to Get Into, More Prestigious, and Better for Artificial Intelligence?

stories.Headline: geniosAI Raises $19.1 Million to Bring Traceable AI Analysis to Financial Institutions
stories.Summary:
geniosAI, a financial intelligence startup, has emerged from stealth with $19.1 million in combined seed and Series A funding, according to an announcement made Monday, November 9, 2026. The company is betting that banks and investment firms will pay for artificial intelligence that shows how it reached its answers, not just the answers themselves. The funding comes from FactSet, Zoom and General Catalyst, with FactSet leading the Series A and serving as a strategic partner. The company is building AI products for corporate finance teams, investment professionals and chief financial officers' offices. Its central idea is that financial institutions need to keep the assumptions, calculations and review decisions behind each analysis so staff can verify results, challenge conclusions and build on earlier work.

Through the FactSet partnership, geniosAI will bring FactSet's financial data into its platform. Zoom will support the conversations where financial decisions are made, including internal finance reviews and earnings calls. geniosAI said its technology is already in use by finance and investment teams at Fortune 500 banks and technology companies to prepare for earnings, compare results with analyst expectations and anticipate investor questions. FactSet's chief executive, Sanoke Viswanathan, said that pairing FactSet's data with geniosAI's traceable analysis could help financial teams act with more confidence and speed.

The launch reflects a wider shift in enterprise finance, where companies are adding technology but struggling to connect systems, keep controls in place and decide which capabilities to own. For chief financial officers, the cost of a modern finance setup often lies less in software licenses than in the effort needed to keep applications, data and processes linked. AI adoption is spreading in financial services back offices, according to a PYMNTS Intelligence study that found at least half of surveyed firms used AI in 27 of 75 business tasks examined. Revenue recognition led at 65%, while credit risk assessment and sales forecasting were each at 60%.

Still, fragmented or poor-quality data was the biggest obstacle to wider deployment for 30% of financial services leaders. Banks are also adding AI without replacing existing systems, as seen with Sutherland and FlowX.AI, which are putting more than 220 AI agents to work on top of current banking technology in areas such as lending, onboarding and anti-money laundering reviews. One European lender reportedly cut manual credit-workflow handoffs by 80%. More to follow.

Articles.Title: geniosAI Raises $19.1 Million to Bring Traceable AI Analysis to Financial Institutions

stories.Headline: Supervised agentic AI for precision oncology
stories.Summary:
A perspective article in the journal Discover Oncology argues that agentic artificial intelligence could transform precision oncology, but that its probabilistic models clash with the fixed, deterministic demands of cancer care. The paper, written by Christoph F. Kurz and colleagues, was posted online on 4 November 2026 and shared early as an accepted but not yet final version. The authors say such tools could be especially useful in molecularly varied diseases such as breast cancer, where they might combine many kinds of patient data with fast-changing evidence. They also note that the publisher may still revise the text before the final version appears.

To resolve that tension, the team proposes a Supervisory Reference Architecture, a design in which specialized worker agents operate under a separate oversight meta-agent. According to the abstract, this structure is meant to enforce traceable reasoning, support auditability and make regulatory accountability possible. The authors say evaluation would shift toward examining reasoning traces and the points where supervisors step in. They are clear, however, that the framework is a conceptual reference architecture rather than a tested system. The article reports no implementation, simulation or empirical evaluation of the design.

The paper is credited to Kurz, Merzhevich, Eskofier, Lammert and Gmeiner, and it appears in Discover Oncology, volume 17, article 1527. The authors' stated aim is to show how agentic AI could be governed before it is used in cancer treatment decisions, rather than to claim that it is ready for clinical use. The research is described as a perspective and framed around breast cancer as an example of a heterogeneous disease. The source material does not describe any regulatory response, clinical trial or next research step beyond the publisher's note that a final version will replace the early one.

Articles.Title: Supervised agentic AI for precision oncology

stories.Headline: Clinicians Use Natural Language Artificial Intelligence to Develop Mechanical Ventilation Simulator
stories.Summary:
Researchers at two Italian simulation centers, the University of Eastern Piedmont and the University of Trieste, have shown that clinicians can build a working mechanical ventilation simulator by giving generative artificial intelligence tools instructions in plain language. The project ran between February and June 2025 and produced Open Vent Sim, an open-source web application meant to support medical training where physical equipment is scarce. The work addressed a gap in which instructors understand what students need to learn but lack the programming skills to build digital tools, leaving institutions reliant on costly closed commercial platforms. The team's aim was to test whether such a simulator could be feasible, physiologically plausible, and easy to use.

The development group included a lead anesthesiology and intensive care physician, three anesthesiologists, ten residents who gave iterative feedback, an intensive care research nurse, and a biomedical engineer. The main prototyping tool was Google AI Studio, paired with the Gemini 2.5 Pro model, which generated React TypeScript code from conversational prompts. Clinicians refined the waveforms over repeated cycles, and in one case residents asked for a negative pressure deflection of roughly two to five centimeters of water below baseline, lasting one hundred to two hundred milliseconds, before the machine delivered positive pressure. After three refinement cycles in a ninety-minute session, two attending intensivists confirmed the waveform met clinical standards. The initial prototype took about twenty hours over two weeks, with twenty more hours of refinement, and engineers at Masaryk University in the Czech Republic later spent about fifteen hours restructuring the monolithic code of roughly 2,300 lines into reusable components.

The authors, Barra, Ricci, Moro, Travěnec, Costa, Carenzo, Rodella, and Vaschetto, reported that the AI-generated code was verbose and poorly organized, which made long-term maintenance difficult until the restructuring was done. Usability was rated with the Italian version of the User Experience Questionnaire by seven residents and three attending physicians, and every measured domain exceeded the positive benchmark of 0.8. The strongest result was perspicuity at 2.27, while novelty scored lowest at 1.05, which the authors said was expected for a tool designed to mirror standard clinical equipment. The authors also cautioned that the study did not measure learning outcomes, competency, or performance against traditional training, and they concluded that formal multicenter studies are needed to establish educational efficacy.

Articles.Title: Clinicians Use Natural Language Artificial Intelligence to Develop Mechanical Ventilation Simulator

stories.Headline: Computational Framework Maps Regional Skin Aging Through Spatial Omics and Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Diala Haykal, Jovian Wan, Kyu-Ho Yi, TingSong Lim, and Soo Ick Cho introduced a computational framework called the predictive dermatome in a theoretical paper published in Frontiers in Digital Health. The framework is designed to map skin aging in localized regions rather than treating the skin as one uniform organ. The authors argue that conventional aging clocks and chronological measures miss the fact that nearby facial areas can age at different rates. The paper was reported on November 9, 2026, by bioengineer.org. The predictive dermatome is explicitly non-neurological, unlike classical dermatomes that follow spinal nerve territories.

Instead, it defines microregions linked by shared or probabilistically connected molecular trajectories. The proposed architecture combines spatial transcriptomics, spatial or targeted proteomics, histology, and extracellular matrix measurements in a discovery phase, with these invasive assays serving as reference maps rather than routine diagnostic tools. Non-invasive imaging, including optical coherence tomography, reflectance confocal microscopy, high-frequency ultrasound, and digital photographs, would then feed surrogate models calibrated against those reference maps. The authors also call for exposomic data, such as ultraviolet dosimetry, air pollution, and lifestyle questionnaires, to be harmonized to specific body sites and time windows. The article says the framework relies on graph attention networks and transformer-based fusion, and it stresses quality control and dimensionality reduction to prevent overfitting.

The authors frame the work as a step toward precision dermatology, which they say requires looking beneath visible surface features to the molecular and structural mosaic of tissue decline. They note that cutaneous senescence involves mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA damage, telomere attrition, and low-grade inflammation, while external stressors such as ultraviolet radiation and pollution act in anatomically variable patterns. The article describes the work as theoretical, so the framework has not been validated in clinical cohorts. The source text was cut off before its discussion of validation and next steps, so I cannot report what the authors plan to do next. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Computational Framework Maps Regional Skin Aging Through Spatial Omics and Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists
stories.Summary:
Matteo's website published an opinion essay on November 9, 2026, arguing that the AI bubble does not exist, though the piece itself is a personal argument rather than a news report. The author says that online discussion treats the bubble as settled and an imminent collapse as given, and he disputes that assumption. He sets out the case that the industry's growth is justified and that companies still have room to expand. The author describes the spending as unusually large, with AI companies committing at least 3 trillion dollars and an estimated 1.9 trillion already spent, for a total near 5 trillion dollars. He argues that most of this is one-off spending on data centres rather than recurring operating cost, and that running AI is profitable once that infrastructure cost is set aside.

He cites Anthropic's S-1 filing, which he says shows $2.08 of revenue for every $1 of compute and revenue that has begun to exceed its compute and infrastructure spending combined. He also works through rough math suggesting that repaying 5 trillion dollars over 20 years would require about 250 billion dollars a year, which he considers achievable. The essay names Anthropic's S-1 filing as its main source for revenue figures, reporting that revenue rose from 41 million dollars in 2023 to 386 million in 2024, 4.585 billion in 2025, and 16.3 billion in the first six months of 2026. The author argues that AI companies lack a durable moat but can still profit, citing customer brand loyalty and institutional lock-in.

He notes that SpaceX, which he describes as partly an AI company, raised more than 80 billion dollars in its public offering, and he points to stable price-to-earnings ratios of about 20 to 30 at Alphabet, Meta, and NVIDIA. He says the piece is his own view, and no regulator, company, or official is quoted reacting to it. The article reads as one author's optimistic case against a widely held view, and it does not describe any event requiring action. It does not report any next step, and it does not say whether the figures it cites will be revised or challenged.

Articles.Title: I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists

stories.Headline: Sierra Leone : President Bio Joins Macron in Global Push for Stronger Artificial Intelligence Safety and Accountability
stories.Summary:
On 9 November 2026, Sierra Leone's President Julius Maada Bio joined French President Emmanuel Macron and other world leaders in calling for stronger international safeguards on artificial intelligence. Speaking at a high-level virtual meeting convened by Macron that day, Bio laid out three priorities for cooperation on frontier AI security. The meeting drew representatives of several countries, international institutions and technology companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Mistral AI and Hugging Face. Bio's intervention reflects growing international concern about how quickly advanced AI systems are being developed and deployed.

Bio's first priority was credible and common safety evaluation standards, which would help governments, researchers and independent experts identify risks in powerful models. His second was clear accountability for the developers and operators of advanced systems, so that responsibility is defined when systems fail or cause harm. His third was an effective way to report serious incidents and share information about emerging threats across borders. Bio said Sierra Leone welcomes the proposed Paris Declaration and supports its focus on shared evaluation standards, accountability and incident reporting. The proposed Paris framework seeks to advance these goals through greater transparency and better coordination among governments, companies and independent experts.

The articles place Sierra Leone's position within a wider African effort to take part in shaping global technology rules. The country had already joined an earlier initiative in September 2026, advanced by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, calling for stronger safety protocols and independent testing. Kenyan President William Ruto and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa have also backed international efforts to strengthen safeguards. The articles argue that Africa has a stake in these rules because AI affects economic opportunity, digital sovereignty and public security, and many African countries lack the technical capacity to assess advanced systems on their own.

The articles also note that turning these commitments into action remains difficult, since governments must still decide how standards will be implemented, how evaluations will be conducted and how developers will be held to account. Differences in national regulation, competing commercial interests and the fast pace of AI development could complicate a coordinated framework. For African countries, the articles say meaningful progress will depend on access to expertise, stronger domestic institutions and sustained participation in international talks. Bio's remarks, as the articles present them, signal that Sierra Leone wants to move from being a consumer of AI technology to a participant in its governance.

Articles.Title: Sierra Leone : President Bio Joins Macron in Global Push for Stronger Artificial Intelligence Safety and Accountability

stories.Headline: Meta Forms Sales Group to Sell AI to Small Businesses
stories.Summary:
Meta has reportedly formed a sales organization to sell its artificial intelligence products to businesses, according to a report from The Information published Monday, November 9, 2026. The report cited a source familiar with the matter and job postings the outlet viewed. The new group will target both small and mid-sized businesses and corporate clients. The move is part of a plan to recoup Meta's large investments in AI.

The push follows Meta's September introduction of the Meta Enterprise Platform, a business unit focused on selling software products to corporate customers and developers. Those products include the Muse Code coding tool, business agent software and Muse Spark models. Former MongoDB CEO Chirantan "CJ" Desai has been appointed to head that unit, which Mark Zuckerberg called the company's "next major pillar." Meta is also forming partnerships with consulting firms and systems integrators, including Accenture, Deloitte and IBM, to speed corporate deployment and reduce its reliance on internal engineers. The report compares this approach to enterprise sales strategies used by OpenAI and Anthropic.

The commercial effort reflects more than a year of market testing. In 2024, Meta saw strong demand from small and mid-sized businesses using its automated customer agents to handle inquiries around the clock. Winning large enterprise deals, however, remains difficult. Meta's earlier Workplace communication software reached 7 million paid subscribers at its peak in 2021 but was discontinued in 2024 after struggling against Microsoft and Slack. An October pitch urging retailers such as Amazon and Booking.com to place Meta's business agent on their websites also met resistance, sources said.

Context from PYMNTS Intelligence research suggests strong interest among smaller firms in AI. The company reported that 60% of small and mid-sized businesses using AI said it lets them produce more without hiring more employees. In an October report, 16% of growing businesses said they skipped a full-time hire because of AI, compared with 10% of businesses with flat revenue. Meta is planning to spend up to $145 billion in capital expenditures this year alone to support its AI infrastructure.

Articles.Title: Meta Forms Sales Group to Sell AI to Small Businesses

stories.Headline: Toronto-based Ada and SF-based Dialpad, both makers of AI customer service software, agree to merge, sources say in an all-share deal valuing Ada at ~$430M (Globe and Mail)
stories.Summary:
Toronto-based Ada Support Inc., a maker of AI customer service software, has agreed to combine with San Francisco Bay Area company Dialpad Inc., according to two sources familiar with the matter. The all-share deal values Ada at around $600 million, or about US$430 million, which is well below the US$1.2-billion valuation it reached during the pandemic technology bubble. The deal is expected to close as soon as next week. The Globe and Mail reported the agreement on November 3, 2026.

Ada's valuation has fallen as technology valuations dropped from late 2021 onward and legacy software providers stayed depressed over questions about how large language model-powered artificial intelligence will disrupt the market. The company has also cut costs, eliminating half its marketing team in July and laying off 25 employees the week before the report. Sources said Ada's annual revenue recently ran at about US$50 million, which trailed other rapidly growing AI firms. Dialpad, which has roughly ten times as many staff as Ada's approximately 200 employees, sells contact-centre software and launched an agentic AI platform last October.

Chief executive Mike Murchison, who co-founded Ada in 2016 with David Hariri, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the transaction. In a recording of the July layoffs obtained by the Globe, Murchison told employees the cuts related to a change in how Ada builds products. Two laid-off employees said they believed the cuts reflected the use of AI within the company, particularly on the marketing team. Hariri left Ada in July for a product role at Shopify but remains on the board.

Ada's technology lets businesses build customer service chatbots that answer questions and perform tasks in other software systems, and its clients have included Shopify, Telus and Grab. The company faced rising competition after OpenAI launched ChatGPT in November 2022, and it rebuilt its products around large language models. Dialpad's investors include Andreessen Horowitz, Google Ventures and Salesforce Ventures. One source said the deal is seen as a way for both companies to keep growing in the market by combining Dialpad's enterprise telephony base with Ada's technology.

Articles.Title: Toronto-based Ada and SF-based Dialpad, both makers of AI customer service software, agree to merge, sources say in an all-share deal valuing Ada at ~$430M (Globe and Mail)

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence in Journalism: The Daily’s Stance
stories.Summary:
The McGill Daily's editorial board has announced a new policy banning the use of generative artificial intelligence at every stage of writing and editing articles for the paper, according to an editorial published on November 9, 2026. The policy, which appears in the Daily's online Policies section, forbids contributors, staff writers and editors from using AI to produce sentences, check grammar with tools such as Grammarly and Quillbot, conduct research or data analysis, or create art. Drafts where there is reasonable suspicion of AI use may be rejected by the editorial board, and a staff writer suspected of using AI will meet with a board member to discuss their position. The editorial says the decision rests on technical and ethical grounds, and it describes the policy as a response to what it calls an unconstrained spread of AI use across McGill, where the university has only loose guidelines for professors and no enforceable university-wide policy.

The editorial argues that reporting is a social act that requires reaching out to sources, interviewing people and judging whether information is accurate, abilities it says AI harms. It also raises credibility concerns, citing a BBC test in which 51 per cent of AI-generated news summaries contained significant issues and 19 per cent contained factual errors. Editing, the board adds, depends on human judgment about word choice and sentence structure, which it says AI models struggle to match. The board also links the policy to the Daily's Statement of Principles, saying AI reproduces injustice through labour practices, citing a Kenyan outsourcing partner of OpenAI that the editorial says paid workers roughly $1.32 to $2 USD per hour against a stated contract wage of $12.50 USD. It further points to environmental costs, citing a June United Nations University report estimating that data centre energy use in 2025 required about 4.5 trillion liters of water.

The editorial is signed by the Daily's Editorial Board, which presents the policy as part of the paper's broader mission to train students in independent reporting, since McGill has no academic journalism program. The board frames the stance as a commitment to trust between reader and reporter. The editorial does not describe any enforcement actions taken so far or any reaction from the university, and it does not say how the policy will be reviewed. It concludes by urging readers and writers to engage with the world in an informed and human way and to respect the labour behind writing and editing.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence in Journalism: The Daily’s Stance -
