stories.Headline: Surging AI demand turns CoWoS into a headache; securing packaging capacity becomes top priority, says MediaTek deputy GM
stories.Summary:
Demand for advanced chip packaging, driven by artificial intelligence, has turned chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) into a difficult problem, according to a deputy general manager at MediaTek. The article reports that the technology, once viewed as interesting, has become an urgent matter for the company. The main point is that securing packaging capacity has moved to the top of MediaTek's priorities. The article was published on November 9, 2026, by DIGITIMES. The article describes what the company now needs to do: secure wafer, packaging, and substrate supply.

Because the surge in AI demand is pushing capacity tight, the company must treat these inputs as a priority rather than a routine purchase. The article gives no specific figures, dates, or capacity targets for this effort. It also does not say how the company plans to achieve these goals. The deputy general manager is the source of the assessment, and the article attributes the view to MediaTek's deputy general manager.

The article makes clear that the executive described the packaging constraint as a headache for the company. The article does not provide a direct quotation beyond that summary, and it does not name the deputy general manager in the portion available. The surrounding context in the article concerns a broader competition for AI computing resources across the industry. The article is a paywalled piece, and the visible text does not include further details about the timeline, the suppliers involved, or any next steps the company intends to take.

Articles.Title: Surging AI demand turns CoWoS into a headache; securing packaging capacity becomes top priority, says MediaTek deputy GM - digitimes

stories.Headline: Custom HBM Era: SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics Deploy Tech Experts to Front Lines in the Americas
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, the two South Korean memory makers, have each moved technology experts into top leadership roles covering the Americas, as the market for customized high-bandwidth memory takes shape. SK Hynix created a president-level post called the Americas Chief on the 30th of last month and gave it to Ahn Hyun, the president who has led its development work. The company plans further personnel moves and organizational changes around the 3rd of next month. Samsung had already placed Cho Sang-yeon, a vice president who oversaw solution development in its memory business, in charge of the Americas for its chip division in December 2024.

The shift reflects a change in how HBM orders are won. Standard HBM has been sold as products that meet set performance targets, but from next year the market is expected to move toward custom HBM, where the memory design is adjusted to fit each customer's AI chip architecture and workload. Nvidia's NVHBM, unveiled in August, is cited as an example, since it moves memory control circuitry into the base die, which brings the accelerator maker into the memory design itself. Under these conditions, the articles say, being able to understand customer needs locally and coordinate design changes, sample production and verification with headquarters teams has become a competitive advantage.

Ahn Hyun said at a TSMC symposium in the United States in April, while he was still head of development, that memory makers are evolving from simple suppliers into creators who think through the needed solutions from the architecture stage. In its third-quarter earnings call, SK Hynix said it was working closely with major customers on projects tied to custom HBM for their systems and workloads. Samsung is expected to announce its presidential and executive appointments as early as mid-to-late this month, with its evaluations reportedly complete. The company has moved its year-end appointments up to late November in recent years, and some observers say it could move them earlier again this year.

Industry observers quoted in the articles see the reshuffles as more than routine organizational changes, since the center of AI chip competition has moved to U.S. Big Tech companies such as Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom. Samsung is also expanding HBM supply cooperation with those firms while building local production around its Taylor Foundry plant. Analysts say local organizations led by technologists could shape the terms and pace of future supply contracts. The articles also note that the key open question is how quickly the companies can change a culture built around supplying standard products.

Articles.Title: Custom HBM Era: SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics Deploy Tech Experts to Front Lines in the Americas - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: The AI-Resistant Pedagogy Studio: Redesigning Assignments for an AI-Augmented Classroom
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion and professional-development piece by Stacy Ybarra Evans, EdD, published on Faculty Focus on November 8, 2026, describing a free, openly licensed toolkit called the AI-Resistant Pedagogy Studio. The Studio is hosted online and was first published in 2025, and it is organized into eight sections, including an interactive toolkit for redesigning assignments. Evans says it grew out of faculty asking how to stop students from using AI, and she reframed that question around designing learning that cannot be outsourced. The article reports that the Studio has been adopted for faculty development at institutions including Clemson University, South Dakota University, Washington University, Hood College, the University of Houston-Downtown, Loyola-Notre Dame, and Roman University. It also says the resource appeared on page 7 of the American Art Therapy Association's undergraduate educators newsletter in 2026.

The Studio centers a shift from product-based assessment toward process-based assessment, where the research process, collaboration, reflection and iterative thinking are graded alongside or instead of the final artifact. The article lists practices such as multi-stage assignments, oral defenses or one-on-one conferences, critique tasks in which students analyze AI output for flaws and bias, and community-based projects. It frames three strategies for designing AI-resistant work: collaborative inquiry, authentic engagement with real-world contexts, and metacognitive reflection. Evans also argues that equity must shape these designs, since premium AI tools and reliable internet access are not available to every student, and AI models can reproduce bias in their training data. On academic integrity, she writes that the focus is moving from detection and bans toward disclosure, with students documenting how they used AI tools.

Evans, who leads the Center for Teaching Excellence at Our Lady of the Lake University, presents the Studio at conferences and is credited with the approach, which she says is designed for incremental adoption. She suggests three starting steps: adding a prompt history or reflection log to an existing assignment, introducing one locally grounded activity per unit, and shifting from detection-focused policies to disclosure-focused ones. The article ends by pointing readers to the free online toolkit. It does not report any independent evaluation of the Studio's outcomes, so claims about its effectiveness rest on the author's own account and the institutions she names.

Articles.Title: The AI-Resistant Pedagogy Studio: Redesigning Assignments for an AI-Augmented Classroom

stories.Headline: 'Should I replace my glasses?' Fears of AI cheating accusations grip college admissions test-takers.
stories.Summary:
Ten days before Korea's College Scholastic Ability Test, known as suneung, students who wear glasses are worried that their frames could be mistaken for AI-powered smart glasses. On Monday, the Busan Metropolitan City Office of Education received dozens of calls from test-takers asking whether they should replace their thick-framed glasses. Some also asked what would happen if a supervisor told them to take their glasses off during the exam. The concern follows a wider rise in smart-glasses misuse in schools, and the article reports that the nation's education authorities are preparing for it. Under the rules described, simply wearing smart glasses at an exam center will be treated as cheating, even if the device is not used.

Students who break the rule will have their results voided and be barred from taking the exam the following year. The same penalty applies to students who hide undeclared smart glasses or refuse to let staff check their eyewear. The Education Ministry has also said it will refer students who cheat with smart glasses to law enforcement for investigation. If a proctor suspects a student, the student may finish the session before the proctor collects the papers and asks to examine the glasses. At least one official trained to identify smart glasses will be stationed at each of the 1,312 exam centers nationwide, and the exam will be given in more than 20,000 rooms.

Education officials, including Park In-jeong, an education supervisor at the Busan education office, say that preventing disruption to the exam takes priority over immediate inspections. Park said the guidance is that the exam must not be interrupted. Teachers who will act as proctors, however, say most have little firsthand experience with these devices and that the many models are hard to identify by sight. Lee Bun-yeo, a teacher at Busan Computer Science High School, warned that close scrutiny could distract students or provoke protests, while proctors could still be held accountable for any cheating they miss. The Education Ministry's nationwide survey found that students at four schools were caught cheating with smart glasses this year.

The article gives the penalties some schools imposed on those students, including zero scores in the affected subjects, three days of special education, four hours of community service, and a five-day suspension. A separate case involved about 170 students at a high school in western Seoul who were suspected of using AI on a performance-based assessment, and the school has decided to administer the assessment again. Leem Hyun-sung, a professor of optometry at Eulji University, said trained proctors should be able to spot common signs of smart-glass use, such as fiddling with the frames. He also called for longer-term changes, including better tools to detect cheating and tests that measure creative problem solving rather than memorization.

Articles.Title: 'Should I replace my glasses?' Fears of AI cheating accusations grip college admissions test-takers.

stories.Headline: The bittersweet dream of AI smarter than us
stories.Summary:
A Korean professor at KAIST, Kim Dae-shik, argues in an opinion column published by the JoongAng Ilbo on November 10, 2026, that the dream of artificial intelligence smarter than humans carries a bitter side. Kim frames the idea through the ancient Greek poet Sappho, who described love as glukupikron, meaning both sweet and bitter at once. He suggests that the pursuit of artificial general intelligence, or AGI, could fulfill humanity's wishes while removing the purpose humans get from solving problems themselves. The column appeared with a photo of a technician at an Amazon Web Services data center in Indiana.

Kim lists the hopes attached to AGI, including curing cancer, preventing wars and freeing people from work. He warns that granting such wishes literally could backfire, since an AI asked to end tedious meetings might eliminate the company, and one asked to stop a missed flight might shut down Incheon International Airport. He also raises the question of how to define happiness, freedom or justice for machines when people cannot agree on those terms themselves. Kim proposes treating AI as a colleague rather than a servant, and he describes working with a chatbot on the column itself.

Kim does not claim that any specific party has caused a harm, and the column is a commentary rather than a report of an event. He is a professor at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, and the piece was originally written in Korean, then translated with generative AI tools and edited by a native English speaker. Kim's central warning is that the greater danger lies not in machines outperforming people but in people losing the ability to judge whether a machine's recommendations make sense. The column does not set out specific policy steps or a timetable, and it ends by asking whether people want intelligence greater than their own or a future in which humans still have a reason to exist.

Articles.Title: The bittersweet dream of AI smarter than us

stories.Headline: Korean AI semiconductors join Nvidia’s ecosystem···SKT and Rebellions in three-way collaboration
stories.Summary:
On November 9, the Ministry of Science and ICT announced at COEX in Seoul, during Nvidia AI Day, that Nvidia, SK Telecom and the Korean startup Rebellions had signed a three-way memorandum of understanding. The three companies will build and test a data center system for SK Telecom that pairs Nvidia's graphics processing units with Rebellions' neural processing units, which are designed specifically for AI computation. The arrangement relies on Nvidia's NVLink Fusion technology, which extends the high-speed link Nvidia GPUs use to exchange data so that it can also work with other companies' AI chips. Rebellions plans to connect its in-development chip, the Rebel R200, to this link. The agreement also covers a split of work during the inference stage, when an AI model produces answers, with GPUs handling the analysis of questions and the more power-efficient NPUs generating the response word by word.

The goal is to speed up responses and reduce power consumption by assigning each task to the chip best suited to it. SK Telecom is also considering using this approach for its own AI models and services. The articles say that as demand for AI inference grows, combining GPUs and NPUs is becoming a major trend in next-generation AI infrastructure. If a domestically developed NPU is built into Nvidia's infrastructure, Korean companies could gain wider opportunities to enter overseas data center markets. The deal is part of broader cooperation between the ministry and Nvidia on domestic NPUs, which follows an earlier collaboration the ministry pursued with AMD.

Nvidia also signed a separate agreement the same day with Kakao Mobility to co-develop Level 4 autonomous driving technology, to be applied first to Kia's purpose-built vehicles. At a partnership forum hosted by the ministry and Nvidia, 22 domestic startups, including Upstage, RealWorld, Twelve Labs and FuriosaAI, took part. Lee Do-gyu, the ministry's Director-General of ICT Policy, said he hoped the companies would find technical and business opportunities to work with Nvidia and jointly enter the global market. The articles do not say when the system will be deployed or how its performance will be verified.

Articles.Title: Korean AI semiconductors join Nvidia’s ecosystem···SKT and Rebellions in three-way collaboration

stories.Headline: How Are Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq Futures Trading After Last Week’s AI Bloodbath?
stories.Summary:
U.S. stock futures rose overnight on Sunday, November 8, 2026, after a sharp selloff in AI-related shares the previous week. As of 10:11 p.m. Eastern, Dow futures were up 0.71 percent, S&P 500 futures gained 0.61 percent, and Nasdaq-100 futures rose 0.62 percent. The rebound followed a session in which markets lost about $3 trillion in total value on Thursday, November 5, as investors sold off AI-linked names. The article notes that the three benchmark indexes ended the week lower amid pressure on AI and technology stocks.

The selloff came after the November midterm elections, in which Democrats swept both the Senate and the House. After an initial climb, stock markets crashed on November 5 as concerns grew over a pullback in AI policy and stronger regulations, which stoked fears of a slowdown in the AI trade. Markets have also been watching the geopolitical picture, including the U.S.-Iran conflict, which has not reached a conclusion. Oil prices were trading slightly higher, with Brent crude at $98.41 a barrel and WTI at $91.38 per barrel at the time of writing.

Nvidia drew particular attention because its board said it would launch an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, raising concerns about a foreign intelligence effort targeting the company. Gary Black, managing partner at The Future Fund, said the matter could lead Huang to step down, which could pressure the stock in the short term because the company has no natural successor. Nvidia shares fell 3.5 percent in the overnight session, while Advanced Micro Devices gained about 1.66 percent as investors rotated out of Nvidia. President Donald Trump is also set to meet Qatar's prime minister at the White House on Monday, a meeting likely to cover the Iran war.

The article describes the broader context as a period of uncertainty, with the Iran conflict unresolved and Trump, according to a CNBC interview, saying he is highly unlikely to restart a full-scale war if talks on Tehran's nuclear program and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz progress. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, called Iran's demands unacceptable. Markets will also await October's consumer price index and producer price index data next week, while more companies report quarterly results. The article adds that Asian markets opened higher on Monday.

Articles.Title: How Are Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq Futures Trading After Last Week’s AI Bloodbath?

stories.Headline: Book Review: The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results by Gleb Tsipursky
stories.Summary:
This is a book review, not a news event, so the articles carry no breaking news. Unite.AI published a review on November 8, 2026, of "The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results" by Gleb Tsipursky, published by Georgetown University Press. The reviewer, who is one of the site's founding partners, says he came to the book after his own news website met internal resistance to adopting agentic AI, the kind of research agents that discover and report news autonomously. He pushed ahead anyway while working to ease staff concerns, and that experience drew him to the book.

The review says the book is aimed at executives who need to persuade their staff to adopt AI before a competitor does, and that it draws on various studies and reports to show AI's potential for productivity and business growth. It describes the psychological barriers the book covers, including automation anxiety, status quo bias, confirmation bias, and reluctance to trust "black box" models whose reasoning is hard to explain. The book also sorts middle managers into five profiles, from skeptics and wait-and-see traditionalists to enthusiastic experimenters and AI catalysts, and then describes eight psychographic profiles of employees. The reviewer notes that the book's main job is to teach leaders how to acknowledge concerns, mitigate risks, and reshape corporate culture for adoption.

The reviewer's verdict is favorable. He says the book helps founders and executives understand resistance that can seem puzzling when the benefits of AI already look obvious to them. He adds that he already believes in AI's transformative potential, so for him the value lies in learning how to bring more of a team along. He recommends the book to business owners and leaders who are ready to move ahead with AI and want to build a culture that can move with them. The article does not report any sales figures, edition details beyond the publisher, or other developments, and it does not indicate any follow-up.

Articles.Title: Book Review: The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results by Gleb Tsipursky

stories.Headline: AI Shopping Statistics 2026 Across Buyers and Brands
stories.Summary:
AI shopping tools are now part of how many consumers research products, compare offers and sometimes buy, according to a set of 2026 surveys and data reports compiled by Memeburn. Adoption figures depend heavily on the question asked and the group surveyed. YouGov found that 18% of US adults had used AI to help them shop in its July to August survey, while Attentive reported that 68% of recently active US shoppers had used a general chatbot for shopping within three months. Adobe separately observed that retail visits referred by AI converted at a rate 90% higher than visits from other sources in September, a comparison the report describes as observational rather than causal.

The report stresses that its figures measure different things, so they should not be combined into one adoption rate. A survey response, an AI referral, a brand mention and an autonomous purchase are treated as separate units. Within the surveys, the most common tasks consumers say they would hand to AI are price-related, with 43% of likely US Black Friday and Cyber Monday shoppers comfortable having it find the best price. Only 4% said they would let AI complete a purchase without asking first, while 43% of US consumers said they would be comfortable letting AI buy within a preset limit, according to a May survey by Synchrony and Oxford Economics. Generational differences are also visible, with 83% of Gen Z and 45% of baby boomers reporting chatbot use for shopping in Attentive's August sample.

Memeburn's own recommendation is that brands track AI visibility, referred visits and orders as distinct measures, and evaluate autonomous checkout only under explicit purchase controls. The report notes that brand visibility in AI answers varies widely, with Yarnit finding a median visibility of 1.9% across selected category lists and sharp differences between ChatGPT and Gemini in how often they linked to brand websites. The data sources are a mix of consumer surveys, vendor research and forecasts, and the report flags that several come from unweighted samples or narrow subgroups. Further detail on sample definitions, fieldwork dates and forecasts is set out in the sections that follow the summary tables.

Articles.Title: AI Shopping Statistics 2026 Across Buyers and Brands

stories.Headline: Hut 8 Expands AI Campus Commitments While Funding Buybacks With Bitcoin Sales
stories.Summary:
Hut 8 said on November 4, 2026, that a second 352-megawatt IT lease at its Beacon Point AI campus had fully commercialised the site, as reported in its third-quarter update. The same update put expected aggregate base-term contract value across its AI data-centre portfolio at about $26.6 billion and reported 1,330 MW of utility capacity under construction. The company also said it sold Bitcoin to fund share buybacks during the quarter. Because the articles describe the update in a single TradingView summary, the details below rest on that one source.

The figures describe multi-year commitments rather than cash already in hand. Hut 8's timetable sets an initial River Bend data-hall delivery target in the second quarter of 2027, followed by Beacon Point Phase 1 in the third quarter of 2027 and Phase 2 in the second quarter of 2028. The company also reported 1,300 MW of additional energy capacity entering exclusivity, bringing that category to 3,180 MW. The articles say buybacks of $74.7 million were funded by selling about 954 Bitcoin, and a later $175.3 million repurchase was funded by selling roughly 2,148 more. The repurchase authorisation was then raised to $1 billion, and the company closed a $1.07 billion senior secured revolving credit facility.

Hut 8 is the company making these statements, and its results were presented in its own third-quarter update. The article notes that execution still depends on power availability, construction, testing, financing and customer readiness, and it treats exclusivity as a development milestone rather than an operating facility or guaranteed utility connection. The writer frames the share-buyback decision as a capital-allocation choice whose value depends on the repurchase price and the business's long-term performance. The article also says the credit facility is committed borrowing capacity, not revenue or money already drawn.

The article places the update within a wider shift among listed Bitcoin infrastructure businesses, whose market stories increasingly revolve around electricity access and long-term AI customers rather than Bitcoin holdings. It refers to earlier coverage of the financing pressure miners face from AI expansion. The articles state that the crucial tests are whether the named delivery targets are met, whether project-level financing stays on acceptable terms, and how much profit flows through once sites become operational. Beyond those dated milestones, the articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Hut 8 Expands AI Campus Commitments While Funding Buybacks With Bitcoin Sales

stories.Headline: Korea’s AI-driven export boom fuels growth, but household gains still lag
stories.Summary:
The Korean economy appears to be growing at a solid pace, driven by global investment in AI infrastructure, according to a monthly assessment released on Monday by the Korea Development Institute (KDI), a state-run think tank. The KDI said semiconductor production and investment continue to grow strongly, supported by robust external demand, and that other sectors tied to AI infrastructure investment also appear to be improving. In October, Korea's outbound shipments rose 93.7 percent from a year earlier to $115.3 billion, the second-highest monthly figure on record. Exports of products closely linked to AI data center construction, including steel products, nonferrous metals and electronic devices, rose sharply, and equipment investment in machinery also grew at a solid pace overall.

The think tank cautioned that the gains are spreading only gradually across households, with consumption improving at only a modest pace. It said private consumption growth was relatively low in the third quarter because income gains from the semiconductor boom had not clearly spread broadly across households. High oil prices continued to weigh on household finances, and higher market interest rates constrained households' spending capacity. Consumer prices rose 2.8 percent on the year in October, down from 2.9 percent in September and 3.1 percent in August, though inflation remained high amid volatility in global oil prices.

The KDI's assessment, as reported, points to a split between an export-led expansion and a household sector that has not yet felt the same benefit. The KDI, which issued the monthly economic assessment, attributed the strength in exports and investment to robust external demand for semiconductors and continued AI infrastructure spending by major technology companies. It also pointed to the price pressures and interest rate conditions that are weighing on households. The think tank warned of continued conflict in the Middle East and escalating policy uncertainties in major economies, which it presented as risks to the outlook.

The report does not say what policy steps the KDI recommends in response to the uneven recovery. The articles do not say how long the export boom is expected to last or when household consumption is likely to pick up. They also do not provide a full-year growth forecast from the KDI. The next monthly assessment would be the natural point to see whether household spending begins to follow the export gains.

Articles.Title: Korea’s AI-driven export boom fuels growth, but household gains still lag

stories.Headline: Asia stocks roar back as Taiwan jumps 6%, Nvidia probe rattles AI trade
stories.Summary:
Asian stock markets rebounded sharply on Monday after a turbulent week, with the MSCI Asia Pacific index rising 2.3%, Japan's Nikkei 225 gaining 3.5% and South Korea's KOSPI climbing 1.6%. Taiwan's Taiex led the recovery, jumping as much as 6.4%, its biggest advance since July. The rally followed a week in which Japanese and Taiwanese equities entered bear-market territory and Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each lost more than 16%. The rebound also came as Nvidia futures initially slipped as much as 1% after the company's board announced an independent investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence operation.

Taiwan's market regulator and finance ministry moved to steady investors after the Taiex endured a seven-session losing streak, its longest since 2022. The Financial Supervisory Commission cut the permitted volume of intraday short-selling orders using borrowed securities to 3% of a stock's average daily trading volume over the previous 30 sessions, down from 30%. It also raised the minimum margin requirement for short-selling to 130% from 90%. Authorities said the NT$500 billion ($15.2 billion) national stock stabilization fund remained available. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and MediaTek each rose at least 6% in the rebound.

The Nvidia board said it had no reason to believe its secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised, and Huang had acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife. Earlier in the week, U.S. chip stocks had rallied as investors bought beaten-down shares, easing worries that a Democratic-controlled Congress would tighten restrictions on the AI industry after the party's midterm gains. Still, the S&P 500 posted its steepest weekly decline since April 2025, and the Nasdaq 100 lost $2.3 trillion in market value on Thursday alone. Investors were also weighing inflation data due Tuesday, with markets pricing in nearly an 80% chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase by year-end.

Elsewhere in the region, mainland China's CSI 300 rose 0.3% and the Shanghai Composite gained 0.5%, while India's Nifty 50 fell 0.2%. Chinese October inflation showed higher factory-gate prices from energy and commodity costs, but weak domestic demand left many manufacturers unable to pass those costs on. Australia's ANZ Group shares fell 4.5% despite a full-year cash profit of A$7.59 billion that narrowly beat expectations, as the bank raised provisions. Analysts and investors remain cautious about AI valuations, regulatory risks and infrastructure spending, with attention now turning to the U.S. inflation report.

Articles.Title: Asia stocks roar back as Taiwan jumps 6%, Nvidia probe rattles AI trade

stories.Headline: Generative AI use in Japan nearly doubles as mobile habits shift - NTT Docomo
stories.Summary:
Generative AI use in Japan has nearly doubled in a year, according to research by NTT Docomo's Mobile Society Research Institute. The survey found that 51 percent of respondents now use the technology, up from 27 percent in February 2025. Use is spreading beyond younger people and beyond searching and writing, reaching business tasks and personal advice as well. The change comes as mobile habits shift among users in Japan. In the institute's 2025 survey, 54 percent of users said generative AI quickly resolves their questions or concerns.

Another 51 percent said consulting the tool was easier than talking to a person. The article notes that trust in the technology still lags behind its use. The figures point to a wider role for the tools in everyday decisions and problem solving. The research was carried out by NTT Docomo's Mobile Society Research Institute, which published the findings. The article attributes the survey results to the institute and does not describe any additional statements from company officials.

It also does not identify any regulatory or policy requirements arising from the data. The findings add to a picture of rapid adoption of generative AI in Japan over a short period. The article does not say what the institute expects next or whether usage will continue to climb. It also does not describe any planned changes to services or products. More detail on future trends was not included in the reporting.

Articles.Title: Generative AI use in Japan nearly doubles as mobile habits shift - NTT Docomo

stories.Headline: Masahiro Sakurai doesn’t use AI for his games, but believes that avoiding it entirely could cause devs to fall behind in the “far-too-demanding” industry climate
stories.Summary:
Masahiro Sakurai, the game designer behind the Kirby and Super Smash Bros. series, spoke at a stage event held on November 7 in Akihabara, Tokyo, as part of Famitsu's 40th Anniversary Festival. The talk was tied to the release of Thoughts on Games: Final, a compilation of columns Sakurai wrote for Famitsu that was published on November 6, and a portion of the festival was livestreamed on Famitsu's YouTube channel. During the event he addressed generative AI and current industry conditions, which the article reports as the main focus of his remarks.

Sakurai said he does not use generative AI in his own work, including for brainstorming ideas, and that he did not use it for recent projects such as Kirby Air Riders. He argued that game design involves many factors beyond raw ideas, such as whether a team can meet a fixed deadline and whether the work fits the budget, and that prompts alone cannot capture all of that. He also said AI may improve to the point where it becomes useful for such tasks, but he does not believe it has reached that stage yet. On graphics, he said the technology has not yet earned developers' trust, that it must not become a tool for exploitation, and that creating assets by hand is still quicker for now.

At the same time, Sakurai described the games industry as being in a very tight position, calling the current climate "far too demanding." He said Kirby Air Riders required ten times the workload of Kirby Air Ride, and the article notes that several recent titles have left developers operating at a loss even after selling millions of copies. He warned that refusing AI entirely could leave developers falling further behind, and that those who adopt it without hesitation may be able to produce many more games, so doing nothing could also be a poor choice. Because the question of where and how to use AI is complex, he said he is taking a cautious approach and did not commit to whether he will adopt the technology in the future.

Articles.Title: Masahiro Sakurai doesn’t use AI for his games, but believes that avoiding it entirely could cause devs to fall behind in the “far-too-demanding” industry climate

stories.Headline: Holding data centers accountable at COP31…“Korea must join the Antalya AI Pledge”
stories.Summary:
On November 9, 2026, civil society groups in Korea, including the Green Transition Institute, People's Solidarity for Participatory Democracy, and Environmental Justice, called on the Korean government to join the Antalya AI Pledge. The pledge was launched at the opening of the 31st UN climate conference, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, and is promoted internationally to manage the environmental impacts of AI data centers. The groups made the call as the conference opened that day. The pledge is led by Turkey, which holds the COP31 presidency.

The Antalya AI Pledge is a voluntary international commitment and is not legally binding. It calls for data centers to be powered by low-carbon energy and for disclosure of information about the energy and environmental effects of AI systems. The push comes from rapid growth in data center electricity use as AI spreads. The International Energy Agency projects that under a high AI growth scenario, data centers could consume more than 1,700 terawatt-hours by 2035, with their share of global electricity demand rising from about 1.5 percent to as much as 4.4 percent. Data centers also use large amounts of water for cooling, and about 25 percent of them sit in regions facing year-round water shortages.

Rising electricity demand also raises greenhouse gas emissions, since the extra power is often generated from coal and gas. The IEA expects data center emissions to double by 2035 compared with today. Other major economies are moving to tighten rules. The European Union requires large data centers to disclose energy use, efficiency, renewable energy use, water consumption, and waste heat recycling. China is lowering the power usage effectiveness target for data centers to below 1.5 and requires more than 80 percent of power for new facilities in national hubs to come from green sources.

Korea is moving in the opposite direction, according to the groups. Through its "three mega projects," the government plans to expand AI data center capacity to 18.4 gigawatts by 2035 and streamline permitting, but it has not set specific systems to manage the electricity, water, or emissions of data centers. The Board of Audit and Inspection flagged gaps last year in how data on domestic data centers is managed and asked the Ministry of Science and ICT to improve, yet no follow-up has been reported. The groups said the government must move beyond deregulation and the race to expand data centers and take concrete steps toward sustainable AI.

Articles.Title: Holding data centers accountable at COP31…“Korea must join the Antalya AI Pledge”

stories.Headline: Raycast’s new Dictate to AI reads your Mac screen as you talk, for $10 a month
stories.Summary:
Raycast released version 2.11 of its Mac launcher on November 4, adding a command called Dictate to AI. The feature lets a user speak a request while the AI receives context from whichever app is in focus, so a spoken instruction such as turning an email into a polite reply can be handled without copying and pasting text first. Raycast suggests assigning a shortcut like Control and A so the command is always one press away. The company describes the change in its official changelog as a way to go from talking to responses in seconds. The command builds on Raycast's existing Screen Awareness feature, which already let its AI Chat pull in content from the active app or window.

Users can switch off the app context in the command's settings when they only want a plain dictated question. The article advises deciding that setting in advance, since an open banking site, private message or work document would otherwise be sent as context by default. The update also adds an AI usage meter in the menu bar, a Dictation AI extension, a Contacts AI extension, better dictation quality and speed, and smoother handling of chat renaming and unavailable models. Raycast itself is free, but its AI features and dictation require a paid plan. The Pro plan costs $10 a month or $96 a year and includes 500 AI credits a month along with dictation, while Plus costs $20 a month or $192 a year with 3,000 credits and Max costs $50 a month or $480 a year with 7,500 credits.

Plus and Max add access to top-tier AI models. Verified students receive 50 percent off the Pro plans, and new accounts can start a free Pro trial whose credits expire after seven days. The article compares Raycast with the free Dictation already built into macOS and with the Siri AI features Apple continues to add. Its distinction is that Raycast connects voice input to the AI model a user chooses, works across any focused app, and keeps everything within the launcher many people already use. The article concludes that existing Raycast Pro subscribers can update and assign a hotkey at no extra cost, while others may find Apple's free tools sufficient unless they use AI on their Mac every day.

Articles.Title: Raycast’s new Dictate to AI reads your Mac screen as you talk, for $10 a month

stories.Headline: China may have just solved AI's biggest bottleneck
stories.Summary:
China's Envision says it has put an integrated 800-volt direct-current power system into commercial operation at an AI facility in Inner Mongolia. The installation is at the Galaxy AI campus in Ulanqab, where trials of its Dubhe controller and supporting energy model began in August 2026. The company describes this as the first commercial use of this configuration, though independent performance figures have not been published. Conventional facilities usually convert incoming electricity through several stages before it reaches servers and accelerators, which adds equipment and possible conversion losses.

Envision's design uses a solid-state transformer to convert 10-kilovolt medium-voltage alternating current directly into an 800-volt direct-current distribution line. The company says this cuts the number of conversion steps, improves electrical efficiency and lets power equipment take up much less space in data centers. A higher-voltage network could also reduce the copper needed for cabling as computing installations expand. The architecture adds battery storage that responds quickly when processor demand changes and provides temporary backup during unexpected interruptions. Envision says the storage can give immediate support over seconds and sustain backup across periods of several minutes.

The controller coordinates the transformer and batteries within milliseconds to manage sudden shifts in electricity use from GPUs. This matters because AI workloads can cause large swings in demand that strain electrical systems supplying densely packed equipment. The company also says the arrangement can support higher-density server racks, letting operators fit more computing capacity into a given floor area. The Galaxy facility is expected to grow to 3 gigawatts, and Envision says its eventual capacity could serve one million AI accelerators. The company also plans to bring the technology to Mission Gobi, an initiative seeking 5 gigawatts of renewable-powered computing capacity by 2030 in desert locations.

The system is designed to work alongside renewable generation, with batteries intended to balance supply against changing computing needs. However, the company has not provided independently verified measurements of efficiency gains, installation costs or savings compared with conventional systems. The announcement also does not establish how the architecture performs under sustained full-load conditions or across facilities with different hardware setups. The deployment therefore marks a commercial milestone for Envision, while the scale of its claimed advantages awaits detailed independent evidence.

Articles.Title: China may have just solved AI's biggest bottleneck

stories.Headline: Innodisk says AI applications now generate more than 40% of revenue as 3Q26 profit jumps
stories.Summary:
Taiwanese memory and storage maker Innodisk said that AI-related applications now generate more than 40% of its revenue, a shift that helped lift its third-quarter 2026 profit. The company reported the results in a report published on November 8, 2026, according to Digitimes. Demand for high-end memory and storage used in AI servers drove the gains in its third-quarter numbers. The company's figures show that the AI business has grown into a major share of its overall sales.

The article gives no further figures for the size of the profit increase, the exact revenue totals, or the quarter-on-quarter and year-on-year comparisons. It does not describe any new product requirement, regulatory change or business restructuring tied to the results. The reported change is therefore limited to the share of revenue coming from AI applications and the stronger earnings that followed from demand for AI server memory and storage. Readers can see the trend in the company's revenue mix, but the article does not say how the company expects that mix to change next.

The article does not name a specific executive or statement beyond the company's own disclosure of these results. It also gives no comment from analysts, customers or rivals on what the figures mean for the wider market. Digitimes' page carries unrelated headlines and subscription notices, but none of them adds details about Innodisk's results. What happens next, including any guidance for the fourth quarter or later years, is not stated in the material provided. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Innodisk says AI applications now generate more than 40% of revenue as 3Q26 profit jumps

stories.Headline: An interview with Cognition CISO Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity, AI-powered red teaming, vulnerabilities in legacy codebases, and more (Nilay Patel/The Verge)
stories.Summary:
AI tools have made cyberattacks faster and more widespread, and the industry is struggling to keep pace. According to the interview with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition, a series of breaches in October 2026 hit AI-related companies in rapid succession. Stamos described a chain in which attackers breached Fireworks, a provider of AI services, and used stolen API keys to get into Cursor, then pushed a bad plugin that reached about 5,000 companies. He also cited the Binance hack, which he called the largest heist in human history.

The attackers include a range of actors, from private groups to state actors such as Russia and North Korea. Stamos said AI has changed the basic attack sequence, so that systems can now find vulnerabilities and write exploits in real time rather than doing that work in advance. He pointed to ARTEX, an open-source Chinese tool that anyone can download, which when run on an altered open-weight model can break into many organizations. The tool began with three South Korean banks, and Stamos said about 200 more companies had been hit in the week of the interview. He compared the moment to the late 1990s, when security weaknesses were widespread and attackers had few barriers.

Stamos framed the change in terms of the culture and economics that once governed security work. For roughly two decades, after Microsoft's 2002 "trustworthy computing" memo, companies hired former hackers to find flaws, and the industry built norms for responsible disclosure and bug bounties. Stamos argued that open-weight models and inexpensive hardware now let people act outside that culture, without the protections or logging that frontier models carry. He said he expects a difficult transition, which he described as a dark age, while defenders work out how to adapt. The article does not say what specific regulatory or industry steps will follow.

Articles.Title: An interview with Cognition CISO Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity, AI-powered red teaming, vulnerabilities in legacy codebases, and more (Nilay Patel/The Verge)

stories.Headline: ‘2026 Art Korea Lab AI-Convergence Festival’ Concludes Its Five-Day Journey
stories.Summary:
The 2026 Art Korea Lab AI-Convergence Festival, titled "SENSE THE M.O.M.: Reexamining the Senses of the Body in the AI Era," wrapped up its five-day run on the 8th. The event was hosted by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Arts Management Support Center and was held at Space S-50 in Seongsu-dong, Seoul, and at the Gwanghwamun Art Korea Lab. Its programs included conferences, exhibitions, performances, an art hackathon, and an IR Demo Day. The festival used the theme "Moment Opens Memory" to examine how bodily senses and memory can expand into new artistic experiences when they meet AI.

The conferences, held from the 4th to the 6th, covered human-robot interaction, the commercialization of creative work in the AI era, and the role of human senses. Robot interaction designer Madeline Gannon gave the opening keynote on robots and human interaction. KAIST professor Lee Jin-Jun, who led overall planning, focused on how humans and AI perceive the world differently. On the second day, Naoki Ito of PARTY described how creative ideas can link to business and social value through projects such as SF Prototyping and The Chain Museum. On the third day, KAIST professor Jung Jae-Seung and Carly Whitefield of the LAS Art Foundation discussed art, the senses, and creativity, with Jung arguing that connecting distant concepts remains a human strength.

A total of 32 exhibitions and performances combining AI and other technologies were presented during the festival, including invited works from Korea and abroad. Highlights included Jo Young-Gak's "Studio After Emptiness: Prototype," in which robots perform electronic music without human players, and Park Seung-Soon's audiovisual performance "Cosmoscape." The closing performance by Moritz Simon Geist used sounds from droplets and mechanical devices. At the Gwanghwamun site, more than 40 artists, producers, and researchers took part in an art hackathon themed "Human in the Loop," while twenty resident companies held open studios and an IR Demo Day for investors. Kim Jang-Ho, president of the Arts Management Support Center, said the festival showed how new technologies expand artistic methods and that the center would keep supporting such experiments through Art Korea Lab.

Articles.Title: ‘2026 Art Korea Lab AI-Convergence Festival’ Concludes Its Five-Day Journey

stories.Headline: LG Energy Solution's AI cuts battery testing time to 10 minutes
stories.Summary:
LG Energy Solution said on Monday, November 10, 2026, that its AI-powered battery diagnostic software, Re.Pulse, has won a CES 2027 Innovation Award. The company says the software cuts the time needed to assess used batteries from more than seven hours to under 10 minutes. The award was given in the Vehicle Tech & Advanced Mobility category. The recognition comes as the company promotes the tool for evaluating used batteries.

The software uses artificial intelligence to analyze how battery voltage changes in response to controlled electrical pulses. These readings can indicate battery health and remaining capacity. The results help decide whether a used battery can be reused, remanufactured or recycled. Conventional testing requires removing battery packs and repeatedly charging and discharging them, a process that takes more than seven hours. Re.Pulse works with existing testing equipment and EV chargers and can assess batteries without removing them from vehicles.

Unlike conventional methods that measure the overall condition of a whole pack, the software can detect deterioration in individual cells. This allows operators to repair or replace only the faulty components rather than discarding the entire pack. The company plans to make diagnostic results available through web and mobile platforms. Potential users named in the report include EV maintenance centers, fleet operators and energy storage facilities. The company says the tool is part of its Battery-as-a-Service business.

Lee Sang-hoon, head of pack and battery management system development and service solutions at LG Energy Solution, said the award recognizes the competitiveness of the company's battery diagnostic technology and software capabilities. The award is the company's second consecutive CES Innovation Award for software, following its Better.Re battery life extension solution last year. The company is expanding its services for batteries at the end of their useful life. The articles do not say whether Re.Pulse is commercially available or when it will reach customers.

Articles.Title: LG Energy Solution's AI cuts battery testing time to 10 minutes

stories.Headline: KT Q3 operating profit down amid data breach fallout, AI expenditures
stories.Summary:
KT Corp., South Korea's major mobile carrier, reported on Tuesday that its operating profit for the July-September period fell 6.1 percent from a year earlier. The company said continued spending on compensation for a data breach and investments in its artificial intelligence businesses weighed on results. According to its regulatory filing, operating profit came to 505.3 billion won, or US$375.9 million. Sales dropped 1.8 percent on the year to 6.99 trillion won, while net income fell 17.5 percent to 367.3 billion won.

KT tied the third-quarter results to customer compensation programs after a data breach reported in September last year that led to a series of unauthorized micropayments. Its core mobile business has shown signs of recovery since July, which the company credited to its premium mobile plans. Orders received from its business-to-business and AI transformation division, which provides AI-related infrastructure, rose 20 percent from the same period last year. KT expects that infrastructure business to begin generating revenue in the fourth quarter.

KT plans to bring its six newly built data centers into operation in phases next year and aims to expand its AI data center capacity to more than 1 gigawatt by 2031. On shareholder returns, the company carried out a 250 billion-won stock buyback in September. It also plans to pay a cash dividend of 600 won per share on Thursday. The company's headquarters are in central Seoul.

Articles.Title: KT Q3 operating profit down amid data breach fallout, AI expenditures

stories.Headline: Political parties across Asia adopt ‘Seoul Declaration’ on geopolitical stability, AI
stories.Summary:
Political parties from across Asia adopted the "Seoul Declaration" on Friday at the 13th General Assembly of the International Conference of Asian Political Parties (ICAPP) in Seoul. The gathering ran from Wednesday to Saturday at The Shilla Seoul and drew around 200 party representatives from 83 political parties in 36 Asian countries, along with 30 Korean lawmakers. The ruling Democratic Party and the main opposition People Power Party jointly hosted the event, which carried the theme "Rebuilding Trust in a Transforming World." It was the first time in 20 years that Seoul had hosted the assembly, the previous one being the fourth gathering in 2006.

The declaration committed the participants to cooperation on geopolitical stability, democratic governance, climate change and AI. The declaration sets out specific steps for each area. It urges countries to keep diplomatic channels open during periods of heightened tension and to make government decision-making more transparent and accountable. It also calls for investment in climate monitoring and early warning systems, as well as cooperation on safeguards for high-risk AI technologies.

A separate media forum on Friday, the eighth ICAPP Media Forum, involved representatives of 35 parties and 19 journalists from 18 outlets in 14 countries. Those participants unanimously adopted the "Seoul Statement," which calls for transparency, verification and human oversight in AI-assisted journalism. It also urges governments to protect press freedom and technology companies to address the misuse of AI, including deepfakes and disinformation. At the opening ceremony on Thursday, National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik stressed that complex crises threaten humanity's shared future and that no single country can resolve them alone.

President Lee Jae Myung sent a video message encouraging parties to strengthen dialogue and cooperation amid ongoing geopolitical tensions. At the closing press conference, ICAPP Standing Committee chairperson Chung Eui-yong said the declaration showed that parties with different ideological views can find common ground. He added that trust must be rebuilt through sustained dialogue, mutual respect and concrete action rather than declarations alone. Vietnam will host the 14th ICAPP General Assembly in 2028, and the organization plans a second Inter-Continental Dialogue among Political Parties in Istanbul in March 2027 to extend cooperation beyond Asia.

Articles.Title: Political parties across Asia adopt ‘Seoul Declaration’ on geopolitical stability, AI

stories.Headline: 81-year-old ‘SF master’ wins the Booker Prize with a story portraying an ‘AI-era apocalypse’
stories.Summary:
Britain's most prestigious literary award, the Booker Prize, has gone to M John Harrison, an 81-year-old British writer known as a master of fantasy and science fiction. The Booker Prize Foundation announced the winner on the 9th, local time, in London, where Harrison received the trophy at the awards ceremony. His winning book, The End of Everything, is set after British society collapses because of an unexplained catastrophe. The story follows Philip and his aunt Marnie as they try to survive under the threat of extraterrestrial beings.

Harrison has described the novel as a story about the effort to keep living as if nothing were wrong. He said that although the book deals with catastrophe, here catastrophe means being unable to make sense of what is happening. He also explained that he deliberately kept the background of events sparse so readers would share the characters' bewilderment and confusion. The judges chose the book from six shortlisted works after intense debate, and the chair of the panel, classicist Mary Beard, said the judges were unanimous in choosing Harrison. She described the book as not an easy read, yet one that shakes the reader and leaves a faint, unexpected trace of optimism.

Harrison, born in 1945, has been writing for more than six decades since publishing his first short story in 1965. He is the first traditional science fiction author to win the Booker Prize, and at 81 he is the oldest winner in the prize's history. The previous oldest winner was Margaret Atwood, who won in 2019 at the age of 79. The Guardian said the award shows that an author who had stayed on the margins of the literary world has now been recognized by the mainstream. The newspaper also noted that the extraterrestrial beings in the novel, called Igeti, evoke artificial intelligence, and it called the award timely for the age of AI.

Articles.Title: 81-year-old ‘SF master’ wins the Booker Prize with a story portraying an ‘AI-era apocalypse’

stories.Headline: The Teacher in the World of Artificial Intelligence: Illuminating Literature, Awakening Emotions
stories.Summary:
Vietnam.vn and the education newspaper Giáo dục và Thời đại published a commentary on November 9, 2026, by a literature teacher, Ms. Duong Thi Huyen, under the headline about teachers in the age of artificial intelligence. The piece describes a ninth-grade lesson on the excerpt "Kim Kieu's Encounter" from the Vietnamese Literature textbook, in which the author noticed that student homework read unusually polished, as though produced by a tool. The article does not state a specific date for that lesson beyond saying it took place one October morning. It frames the story as a question for colleagues about where a teacher's intellectual guidance and literary passion now stand, given that AI tools can produce strong essays in seconds.

The author reports that she tested AI assistance in class by asking students to have an AI write a diary entry in the voice of Thuy Kieu after her meeting with Kim Trong. Students found the generated passages too rational and lacking the shyness and subtle psychological shifts in Nguyen Du's lines. In a separate lesson on Ho Chi Minh's 1951 essay "The Patriotic Spirit of Our People," from the Grade 8 textbook, she had students compare an AI-written essay on patriotism with the original. The students concluded that the machine could write fluently in general terms but could not reproduce the historical grounding and the forceful tone of the original. She also argues that students should learn to question AI output, for example by having them replace generic evidence about youth apathy with real examples from their own experience.

The article recommends that literature teaching shift toward dialogue, debate and multimedia projects, with students using AI as a tool but drawing their emotional content from their own experience. The author closes by arguing that AI can process language but cannot share the emotional response that literature is meant to awaken. The article offers no institutional policy, no official response and no data on how widely these methods are used. It is a first-person opinion piece, and its claims rest on the author's own classroom experiments rather than on any broader study.

Articles.Title: The Teacher in the World of Artificial Intelligence: Illuminating Literature, Awakening Emotions

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang’s journey: From Taiwan to washing dishes at Denny's to founding AI chip giant Nvidia
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, has risen from a difficult childhood in Taiwan and a dishwashing job at a Denny's diner to become one of the most influential figures in technology. The profile, published by Hindustan Times on November 9, 2026, traces his path from a boy born in Tainan in 1963 to the leader of a company whose chips power modern artificial intelligence. His family first moved to Thailand, and later he was sent to live with an uncle in Tacoma, Washington, in 1972 while his parents prepared their own paperwork. Huang struggled with limited English and bullying at a boarding school in Kentucky, but he focused on his studies. He later attended Oregon State University, where he earned an electrical engineering degree.

After graduating, Huang worked at Advanced Micro Devices and then LSI Logic, where he held engineering, marketing and management roles between 1985 and 1993. He also earned a master's degree in electrical engineering from Stanford University in 1992 while working at LSI. In 1993 he co-founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, starting with $40,000 in capital after discussing the idea at a Denny's restaurant in San Jose. The company first concentrated on graphics technology for video games, and its RIVA 128 processor sold about one million units within four months, helping it survive a difficult early period. Over the following decades, its graphics processing units became essential for artificial intelligence development because they can handle large volumes of data at once.

Huang has credited his early restaurant work with teaching him discipline, resilience and how to perform under pressure, according to Quartr as cited in the article. He has also described his rise in the article's account as the product of long, hard work rather than luck, saying in a CBS 60 Minutes interview that there is no magic involved. Fortune named him Businessperson of the Year in 2017, and Harvard Business Review ranked him first on its list of the world's 100 best-performing CEOs over the lifetime of their tenure in 2019. The article also notes that Huang has been the subject of recent news items, including a remark by US President Donald Trump calling him honorable and a report about a US memo that mentioned his alleged ties to a Chinese spy, though it does not detail either matter further.

Articles.Title: Jensen Huang’s journey: From Taiwan to washing dishes at Denny's to founding AI chip giant Nvidia

stories.Headline: Palantir vs. Snowflake: The AI Sell-Off Is Exposing a Critical Difference for 2027
stories.Summary:
Palantir Technologies and Snowflake are both enterprise AI companies, and an article by RJ Fulton on Fool.com, updated November 8, 2026, compares the two as a sell-off in technology stocks prompts investors to reassess them for 2027. The author argues that the pullback gives investors a chance to look again at how each company is valued. The piece is an opinion and analysis piece rather than a report on a discrete event, so it does not describe a single announcement or decision. The core of the comparison is that Palantir has shown stronger profitability while Snowflake still posts losses. Palantir's software, including its Gotham, Foundry, and Artificial Intelligence Platform products, serves government and commercial customers.

The article reports that its fiscal 2025 revenue was $4.5 billion, up 56 percent, with net income of about $1.6 billion, and that its third-quarter 2026 revenue rose 96 percent to $2.3 billion. Snowflake's cloud data platform generated about $4.7 billion in fiscal 2026 revenue, up 29 percent, but recorded a net loss of $1.3 billion. The author notes that Snowflake's second-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue grew 35 percent to $1.55 billion, and that its stock-based compensation exceeded its operating cash flow. The article identifies risks for each company, including Palantir's reliance on large government and enterprise contracts and its exposure to sensitive defense work, and Snowflake's intense competition and consumption-based revenue model. The author says neither stock is cheap, with Palantir trading at 103 times forward earnings and Snowflake at 131 times.

On price-to-sales, Snowflake is cheaper at 18.9 times sales compared with Palantir's 54.5 times. The author states a personal preference for Palantir for 2027, while cautioning that its valuation leaves little room for disappointment. The article does not describe any upcoming decisions, deadlines, or regulatory changes, and it does not say what will happen to either stock next. It offers a view on the two companies' prospects but presents no forecast beyond the author's stated preference. Readers should weigh that preference as the opinion of one writer.

stories.Headline: Musk Announces Two More Data Centers for Mid-South AI Expansion
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk has announced that two more data centers tied to SpaceXAI's expanding artificial intelligence operation in the Memphis area are expected to begin running before the end of the year. The announcement comes as the rapid growth of the facilities draws increasing scrutiny from residents and city officials worried about the effects of large-scale data center development. The two sites, known as Gun Range and Spam, are part of the company's Colossus 2 computing complex. Both are located in Southaven, Mississippi, just across the state line from Memphis.

Musk said Gun Range is expected to become operational by the end of November, with Spam following in December. These dates are his projections and have not been independently confirmed. Together the facilities are expected to house roughly 420,000 Nvidia GB300 graphics processing units. About 220,000 of those chips at Gun Range would be set up to train AI models, while about 200,000 at Spam would handle inference, which means responding to user requests with already-trained systems. The buildings will add to existing sites within Colossus 2, and Musk has said the full complex is expected to contain about 1.2 million Nvidia Blackwell chips by the end of 2026.

The company runs this computing infrastructure to support its Grok AI platform, and Musk has said he has been spending several days a week in Memphis overseeing construction. Gun Range was once a police and fire training facility, and Spam was a warehouse that stored Hormel Foods products, which is where the names come from. The projects have drawn opposition from nearby residents concerned about pollution, noise, electricity demand and water use. In April the NAACP filed a federal lawsuit against xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech, alleging that methane gas turbines were run at the Southaven site without required permits. A federal judge recently refused to dismiss that lawsuit, so the case will proceed.

Separately, the Memphis City Council approved a 135-day pause on new data center permits after rejecting a proposed yearlong moratorium. The pause gives city officials time to write land-use and siting rules covering neighborhood protections, infrastructure and environmental concerns. It does not shut down existing facilities or automatically halt projects that already hold protected approvals. The latest expansion highlights the challenge facing Mid-South communities as technology companies move quickly to build AI infrastructure while residents and local governments push for greater oversight.

Articles.Title: Musk Announces Two More Data Centers for Mid-South AI Expansion - The Tennessee Tribune

stories.Headline: When China laughs at the US’ AI boom, the joke cuts both ways
stories.Summary:
Chinese social media users have spent the days after the November 3, 2026 US midterm elections mocking President Donald Trump's push for artificial intelligence, using spoof news reports and Mao-style propaganda posters. The most circulated fake was a purported Associated Press report, shared on WeChat, in which the Democrats urged a crackdown on the AI boom, but its ponderous wording copied the officialese of the Communist Party of China. Another poster, first seen in October and revived after the vote, denounces a "Great AI Bubble" and blames Trump and a "Gang of Four" made up of Nvidia's Jensen Huang, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman and Tesla's Elon Musk. The jokes also compare Trump's AI drive to Mao's Great Leap Forward, with one commentator swapping a famous agricultural slogan for one about GPU output.

The article reports that the mockery draws on a real American backlash against energy-hungry data centres, which helped fuel a historic Democratic win. Voters opposed data-centre development in 44 of 45 local ballot measures with complete counts held alongside the midterms, according to the consulting firm Redbud. Democrats are preparing legislation to shield consumers from electricity price increases linked to data centres and to impose tougher AI oversight when they take control of Congress in January. The article notes that a sustained slowdown in US computing expansion could give China more room to catch up, since Beijing regards AI as critical to national strength.

The article also points to a separate scandal involving Huang. On November 8, Nvidia announced an investigation into Huang's relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence suspects of spying for Beijing, though the company said it had found no evidence of a security breach. Beijing has previously dismissed the espionage allegations. Trump said on November 8 that he would still take Huang to the APEC summit in Shenzhen the following week. The article says the affair could complicate the AI rivalry, since Huang has been a vocal advocate for selling US AI chips to China and Beijing could lose an important ally if his influence in Washington weakens.

The article argues the jokes carry an irony for China itself, which had a frenzy of data-centre construction that left less than 40 per cent of its computing capacity in use in 2025. Chinese residents have fewer ways than Americans to challenge data centres in their neighbourhoods, and mocking the US gives people a safer outlet for criticising familiar political excesses. The Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution remain sensitive subjects in China, so the satire also lets readers revisit those upheavals indirectly. The article does not say what further action, if any, Beijing or Washington will take on these matters.

Articles.Title: When China laughs at the US’ AI boom, the joke cuts both ways

stories.Headline: China’s AI datacenter buildout reveals scale, speed
stories.Summary:
China is building gigawatt-scale AI datacenter campuses, and an analysis published by TechGig, citing SemiAnalysis, points to one in Inner Mongolia as an example. The Galaxy campus in Ulanqab is planned for up to 800MW of IT capacity, and its first 120MW phase was reportedly delivered within a year. The buildout is described as notably fast, large, cheap and tightly integrated, with construction costs about a fifth of those in the United States. Envision Group, a renewable systems integrator, owns the facility.

Envision builds its own wind farms and a dedicated power line to supply the campus, and it plans to meet over 60 per cent of power use in the first two phases from its own wind farms. The article says this is made possible by siting, a total of 420MW of installed capacity for a 240MW load, and a 4-hour battery storage system. A pilot 5MW hall uses an 800V DC system, with solid-state transformers converting 10kV AC directly to 800V DC for the racks, a technology the article says is still on the US roadmap. Cooling uses a shared water loop for both liquid- and air-cooled servers, with no central chiller plant, a design the article calls common in northern China.

Envision is highly vertically integrated, manufacturing its own wind turbines, battery energy storage systems and power electronics, and it co-designed the prefabricated substation. The article does not attribute any specific statements to company executives. It notes that China's datacenter market is highly competitive, with rents roughly halved and capital expenditure down about 25 per cent over the past five years. SemiAnalysis's China Datacenter Model tracks over 1,000 facilities across more than 70 operators, including projects like Galaxy. The article does not say what comes next for the campus beyond the planned capacity.

Articles.Title: China’s AI datacenter buildout reveals scale, speed

stories.Headline: Zeta CEO Bhavin Turakhia says coding is overrated in AI era
stories.Summary:
Zeta CEO Bhavin Turakhia has said that coding is becoming overrated as artificial intelligence takes over more software development work. He made the remarks in a YouTube conversation with Vidit Jain, SVP and Head of Scaler Schools at Scaler Campus, published on November 8, 2026. The article was published by TechGig on November 9, 2026, at 4:40 AM IST. It reports that the comments were part of a discussion about how technology careers are changing. Turakhia argues that professionals often focus too much on execution without first considering the outcomes they want.

As AI handles more execution-heavy tasks, he believes skills such as high-level abstraction, clear problem definition, and quick communication of outcomes will matter more. He still stressed that mathematics, data structures, and algorithms remain core fundamentals for aspiring tech professionals. On entrepreneurship, he said execution adds more value than ideas, which he sees as increasingly commoditised. Turakhia, who began coding at age 10, founded Directi, Radix, and Zeta, and his current venture, NEO, focuses on AI. He also advocated building businesses with a co-founder to foster debate and diverse perspectives, which he said improves decision-making.

On hiring, he questioned how reliable resumes are now that AI tools make applications easy to produce. He expects employers to rely more on assessments, case studies, interviews, and proof of work to judge candidates' real abilities. The views come as AI-assisted coding tools reshape software development workflows, and the article frames Turakhia's comments within that shift. The article does not report any formal policy, company decision, or measurable change tied to his remarks. It does not say how other industry figures have responded.

Articles.Title: Zeta CEO Bhavin Turakhia says coding is overrated in AI era

stories.Headline: Entire Git forge rethinks AI agent collaboration with trails
stories.Summary:
Entire, a company led by CEO Thomas Dohmke, has launched a Git forge built for human developers and AI coding agents to work together. The platform was reported on November 9, 2026, and it is meant to address the limits of the traditional pull request model when AI agents generate and revise code at high speed. Its core features are called "trails" and "continuous memory," both aimed at keeping agent-driven development organized. The articles describe these as new tools for a workflow that existing forges were not built to handle.

Dohmke, a former GitHub CEO, argues that GitHub and GitLab were designed around asynchronous code review and version control between people. He says a multi-agent forge instead centers on asynchronous orchestration, versioning, and auditing of AI agents working alongside humans. The trails feature attaches evaluation scores to every code push so developers can judge whether a pull request is stable or needs another round of agent work. A merge should happen only when confidence is high, risk is low, and findings have been cleared. Trails can start from a bug report, a feature request, or manually, and they can span several repositories.

When new code is pushed, a review agent running in a cloud sandbox scores the changes and explains the score based on code quality, security, and "slop." Developers can then tell their coding agent to improve the code, which starts a new iteration, and review agents can suggest fixes that stay visible until resolved or closed. Evaluation agents can be configured through Entire's interface or through repository-level JSON, and developers can set repository-level Gates that define approval conditions. The platform also connects with continuous integration services such as Buildkite and Depot. The articles do not report pricing, availability dates beyond launch, or independent assessments of how the platform performs in practice.

The second concept, continuous memory, is meant to keep knowledge that agents build up available for reuse across sessions. Entire implements it with two open-source tools, entire-graph, which maps the Git repository, and entire-brain, which combines that map with earlier agent sessions and Git history to form a persistent memory layer. The stated purpose is to give agents the context behind code changes, including the reasons for them. The articles do not say what comes next for the platform, such as adoption figures or planned expansions.

Articles.Title: Entire Git forge rethinks AI agent collaboration with trails

stories.Headline: Beyond LLMs? China forges new path for AI with focus on industrial systems
stories.Summary:
China's artificial intelligence sector is moving past general large language models toward a new generation of specialised systems built to tackle real industrial problems, according to a leading computer science researcher. Cui Peng, an associate professor at Tsinghua University in Beijing, said these specialist systems could analyse industrial data such as factory sensor readings and financial records, and could become a key part of AI's next phase in China. He made the remarks at the Hong Kong International Computer Conference on Monday, November 9, 2026. He argued that general models are hard to apply in industry, and that they often struggle to pick up patterns in structured numerical data. The shift is tied to China's "AI plus" strategy, which the reporting says is steering industry in a new direction.

The emphasis falls on collectively developed systems designed around what industry needs, rather than broad tools adapted after the fact. The articles frame this as a change in priorities, with specialised models meant to handle numerical and operational tasks that general chatbots handle poorly. The reporting does not give figures on investment, deployment scale or timelines for these systems. Cui Peng, speaking as a researcher at a university, is the main source for the argument, and he put the case in terms of the technical limits of current models. He said that when it comes to industrial applications, LLMs are very difficult to use, pointing to their weakness with structured data as the core problem.

The articles present his view as his own assessment rather than an official government position. They do not report any response from companies or regulators. The coverage places this within a broader debate over where AI development should go after the rise of general models. The articles do not say what comes next, such as specific products, pilot projects or policy steps. The story was first published on November 9, 2026 and updated on November 10, 2026, and the articles do not describe any follow-up events.
