The move comes as the company has described securing advanced packaging capacity as a top priority, since surging AI demand has made CoWoS packaging difficult to obtain. The roundup frames the appointment as part of a wider race across AI infrastructure, semiconductor manufacturing and advanced memory. Other items in the same digest, including the Panasonic plant explosion, the Terafab talks and the CXMT earnings, are separate stories and are not covered here.

Shahriari's appointment is presented by MediaTek as a step toward stronger process and packaging capability for its AI and high-performance computing business. The articles do not say how his role will change the company's existing supplier relationships or what capacity targets it has set. They also do not describe any statement from Shahriari himself beyond his background and responsibilities. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Weekly news roundup: AI compute race intensifies as DRAM rivals diverge and chipmakers expand investments - digitimes

stories.Headline: Exclusive / Anti-Waymo campaign relied on op-eds written with AI
stories.Summary:
Opponents of Waymo, the autonomous taxi company, ran a campaign of op-eds in local news outlets that used artificial intelligence to draft much of the text, according to a Semafor exclusive published November 8, 2026. The pieces argued that Waymo could cost jobs, endanger riders, deprive the government of information, and block fire trucks. The AI detection service Pangram found significant AI input in many of the articles, yet none carried a label disclosing AI use. Several were drafted by public relations firms, and the outlets involved include the New York Daily News, the Dallas Morning News, the San Francisco Chronicle, the San Diego Union-Tribune, and the Times of San Diego.

The op-eds were tied to specific claims, including one by lawyer Amy Witherite on autonomous vehicle accidents that Pangram rated as 95 percent and 71 percent AI-written in two separate pieces. A Chronicle piece warning that autonomous vehicles could go dormant during power outages was rated 88 percent AI-generated. A San Diego Union-Tribune piece on job displacement scored 95 percent, and a Times of San Diego piece on tracking Waymo's rollout was rated 87 percent likely AI-assisted. Pangram's scores are estimates from a detection tool rather than proof of authorship. The Chronicle's policy asks opinion writers to disclose AI use, and the Dallas Morning News said limited AI use for research or polishing does not disqualify a submission while fully AI-generated pieces are not accepted.

The authors and their representatives gave varied accounts of their roles. Ira Goldstein, former head of New York's Black Car Fund, said his PR firm prepared a first draft that he then edited, and he stood by the piece's content. Michael Redmond, the Chronicle author, said he uses AI tools for research and to test and clarify his arguments. A spokesperson for Witherite said her communications firm uses AI for drafting and press lists, with staff editing and fact-checking before she approves each piece, and called AI a distraction from the substance. The Daily News executive editor said the paper wants stricter guardrails, citing its lawsuit against Microsoft and OpenAI.

The campaign sits within a larger fight over whether Waymo can operate commercially in several major cities, a fight involving labor unions, ride-hailing companies, and safety advocates. The Washington Post reported that the Coalition for Accountability and Road Safety spent more than $2.6 million on Washington-area ads in 2026, and Waymo operates commercially in 15 US cities. Semafor's media editor argues that ghostwriting in op-eds predates AI, but that outlets risk diluting their value if AI-written work is passed off as human perspective. Other journalists contend that disclosure matters less now that AI is widely used for research and drafting, and the Wall Street Journal's opinion editor has said newsworthy, well-argued AI submissions need no disclosure.

Articles.Title: Exclusive / Anti-Waymo campaign relied on op-eds written with AI

stories.Headline: 3 US Chip Stocks for AI Exposure With Lower China Risk
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's internal probe into CEO Jensen Huang and possible foreign intelligence targeting has drawn attention to governance and national security risk across the AI chip sector. An article published by Yahoo Finance on November 8, 2026, by Bailey Pemberton, presents this as the backdrop for three U.S.-listed semiconductor and chip equipment stocks that the author says carry lower China exposure. The piece is a screened list drawn from a low China exposure screener, and it describes the three names as possible alternatives for investors who want AI-related exposure without relying heavily on China. The article notes that the same screen identified 59 other companies that are not discussed.

The three companies profiled are Skyworks Solutions (SWKS), FormFactor (FORM) and MACOM Technology Solutions Holdings (MTSI). Skyworks is described as an analog and mixed signal chip maker whose revenue, about US$4.0 billion, comes from products tied to wireless connectivity and handset demand, and the article cites a multigenerational Android design win expected to exceed US$1 billion in revenue through 2030. FormFactor, valued at roughly US$6.4 billion, makes semiconductor test hardware, with about US$802 million from probe cards and US$178 million from systems, and the article points to a record US$48.5 million systems quarter and co-packaged optics revenue expected to significantly exceed US$20 million in 2026. MACOM, valued at about US$16.1 billion on roughly US$1.3 billion of semiconductor and module revenue, is presented as a supplier of optical chipsets for data center and AI-related connectivity.

The article is written by an AI-assisted content team drawing on data from Simply Wall St., and the piece itself says it is general in nature and not financial advice. It includes no statement from Nvidia, the three companies or any regulator, and it does not say how the Nvidia probe will develop. The surrounding page carries promotional links to other screens and a range of unrelated market headlines, which the article does not tie to its main point. Beyond the author's general suggestion that the Nvidia news could shift investor attention, the article does not describe a specific next step.

Articles.Title: 3 US Chip Stocks for AI Exposure With Lower China Risk

stories.Headline: AI is an 'existential competition' between China and the U.S., so AI buildout will continue: PM
stories.Summary:
The only substantive article here is a CNBC Squawk Box segment, published November 8, 2026, in which Martin Schulz, head of the International Equity Group at Federated Hermes, argued that artificial intelligence has become an existential competition between China and the United States. He said AI spending may be deferred but that the broader AI buildout will not be derailed, despite the mid-term election results and a massive market sell-off the previous week. The rest of the page consists of unrelated video teasers and navigation text, so the article carries no figures, dollar amounts, dates for specific deals, or policy requirements beyond what is described here. Because the source is a short interview summary, the specifics of his reasoning are limited to the points named in the segment description.

Schulz's view, as summarized, is that the competitive pressure between the two countries makes continued investment in AI infrastructure likely even when near-term spending slows. The segment also said he would share views on Japan, India and China markets, though the article text does not reveal what those views were. The page's surrounding material mentions Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang being named as a target of a Chinese spy plot, according to the New York Times, and a $8.8 billion investment by Resonac in the AI chip boom, but those items are separate videos and the article does not connect them to Schulz's argument. It also references a tech stock sell-off, which the segment cites as context for his comments without giving details.

Schulz is the only person the article attributes a position to, and the article does not describe any formal policy, government action, or company commitment that would follow from his remarks. The article gives no timeline for when the buildout would resume or how long spending might be deferred. Beyond the interview itself, the articles provide no further developments or next steps. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI is an 'existential competition' between China and the U.S., so AI buildout will continue: PM

stories.Headline: RBA’s Hunter sees limited AI productivity gains so far
stories.Summary:
On Monday, November 8, 2026, Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter told a UBS conference in Sydney that artificial intelligence has not yet clearly lifted productivity or caused major job losses. She also warned that the technology could create financial stability risks. Her remarks were reported by Investing.com. The article does not report any other official's comments on the matter. Hunter said the evidence that AI has materially improved productivity or significantly changed employment levels remains limited.

She pointed to tentative signs of adjustment, including weaker job ad postings and employment outcomes in more AI-exposed occupations. She also noted stronger growth in areas less affected by the technology, particularly for younger workers. The article does not say what policy changes, if any, the central bank is considering in response. Hunter said AI is currently adding to demand and price pressures while the economy faces supply constraints, and that its effect on inflation will likely shift over time. She said supply will eventually catch up as data centre capacity and related sectors expand, and that if AI delivers broader productivity gains, the initial inflationary pressures from AI investment are likely to fade.

The article notes that domestic data centre investment has contributed to demand pressures in Australia. It also reports that the Reserve Bank has raised interest rates five times this year, to 4.85%, an 18-year high, to combat inflation. The article does not say how the Reserve Bank responded to Hunter's remarks or what its next steps will be. The Investing.com report was generated with AI support and reviewed by an editor. More to follow.

Articles.Title: RBA’s Hunter sees limited AI productivity gains so far

stories.Headline: AI Transforms Bioprospecting for Natural Product Drug Discovery
stories.Summary:
AI is changing bioprospecting, the search for drug candidates in natural compounds, which has long depended on slow extraction and screening. A review published in BMC Artificial Intelligence in July 2025 examines how machine learning and deep learning are making that search faster, more efficient, and more accurate. The authors note that traditional methods struggle with the vast chemical complexity of natural ecosystems and the time needed to isolate active compounds from mixtures. By working through these complex chemical spaces, researchers can identify promising candidates that might otherwise stay hidden in unexplored biological sources.

The review describes several tools now in use. Algorithms such as support vector machines and random forests analyze how chemical structure relates to biological activity, helping flag anticancer or antimicrobial scaffolds early. Deep learning goes further by pulling useful features from raw data, and the review cites halicin, a broad-spectrum antibiotic found through models trained on millions of chemical-activity pairs. AI also supports cheminformatics, metabolomics, genomic mining, and literature extraction, with examples including the compounds monazomycin and oasomycin A, which showed cytotoxicity against human tumor cell lines. Together these methods let scientists focus laboratory work on the most promising leads.

The review's authors stress that AI predictions must still pass through conventional preclinical and clinical testing. Regulators such as the U.S. FDA and the European Medicines Agency require the same pharmacology, toxicology, and efficacy evidence for AI-discovered compounds as for traditional drugs. The FDA's 2024 draft guidance treats AI outputs as supporting evidence and calls for a credibility assessment before such models can shape regulatory decisions. The review also identifies problems with incomplete natural product data and with deep learning models that are hard to interpret, and it points to explainable AI techniques as a partial remedy.

The review raises ethical and environmental concerns as well. Faster compound identification could increase pressure on rare or endangered species and fragile ecosystems, making fair benefit-sharing with biodiversity-rich regions important. The Nagoya Protocol offers a framework for this, though enforcement remains difficult. The review also points to synthetic biology as a route to sustainable production, citing AI-guided work that optimized artemisinin output in yeast. It concludes that continued collaboration among scientists, technologists, and ethicists will be needed to address data quality, interpretability, and sustainability.

Articles.Title: AI Transforms Bioprospecting for Natural Product Drug Discovery

stories.Headline: ETIH Judge Tina Austin launches research consortium to investigate whether AI delivers lasting learning
stories.Summary:
Tina Austin, an ETIH Innovation Awards judge, has launched an international research consortium to test whether AI-supported learning produces lasting gains in critical thinking, metacognition and independent judgment. The initiative, called the UnBlooms Longitudinal Research Consortium, was publicly launched at the Cambridge AI in Education Summit in October 2026. According to Austin, it has drawn interest from more than 40 institutions around the world. The work responds to a growing question for educators as generative AI becomes part of teaching and assessment.

Austin is Project Director of Public Interest Technology Pathways at the University of California, Los Angeles, and specializes in responsible AI and assessment redesign. Her research centers on whether students can apply what they learn independently, beyond the work they produce with AI help. In an analysis published on Substack, she argues that studies of AI's effects are often hard to interpret. Many measure performance while students still have AI tutors or shortly afterward, leaving open whether gains last once support is removed. Differences in how AI scaffolding is designed and delivered, along with inconsistent definitions and weak comparison groups, can also make findings difficult to reproduce.

The consortium builds on Austin's UnBlooms framework, which she presented at OpenAI in 2025 and which centers on students' reasoning before, during and after AI use. As part of that work, she developed the Metacognitive Awareness Scale, described in a peer-reviewed workshop paper, to examine how students verify information, explain decisions and revise AI-assisted outputs. The paper reports preliminary shifts from accepting AI outputs with little scrutiny toward more active checking and self-critique. Austin acknowledges that further validation and longer-term evidence are still needed. The consortium will study how these capabilities develop across subjects and settings, and what remains once the technology is taken away.

Austin also leads an Assessment Redesign team within IEEE's responsible AI in education initiative. Educators and institutional leaders could use the findings to decide which AI-supported teaching strategies produce durable learning and how assessment should change. Interested institutions can find more through the consortium website or contact Austin at tinaaustin@ucla.edu. The article does not report a timetable for the consortium's first results.

Articles.Title: ETIH Judge Tina Austin launches research consortium to investigate whether AI delivers lasting learning

stories.Headline: SpaceX Wants To Turn AI Compute Into A $500B Business Next Year – And Elon Musk Says NASA’s Annual Budget Is No Match
stories.Summary:
SpaceX, the rocket and satellite company led by Elon Musk, said on Friday at the Baron Investment Conference that it could turn AI computing into a business worth $500 billion in annualized revenue by December 2027. Musk projected annualized revenue above $100 billion by this December, and he called the $500 billion figure his "best guess" rather than a promise. SpaceX acquired xAI in February, bringing the Grok chatbot into the company. SPCX shares rose about 2% overnight after the remarks, following a nearly 9% gain on Friday to $134.27.

Musk said that revenue from SpaceX this quarter alone would be substantially higher than NASA's entire annual budget. He pointed to NASA's $18.8 billion fiscal 2027 budget request, while the Congressional Budget Office put the agency's fiscal 2026 appropriations at about $24.4 billion. He also described renting data centers to other companies before their capacity is needed for Grok, citing $50 billion a year against $35 billion in investment. His Terafab plan targets a terawatt of AI chips annually, and he said costs could exceed $1 trillion but would be spent in phases. Musk expects StarMind computers co-designed with Nvidia to begin launching in the third quarter of 2027.

Investor Chamath Palihapitiya argued on the All-In Podcast that a squeeze in data-center supply could let SpaceX charge Anthropic two to three times its current compute price, since either side can terminate on 90 days' notice. Musk acknowledged that the dynamic cuts both ways, warning that if compute becomes plentiful and cheap, SpaceX revenue would drop. Separately, NASA named SpaceX among eight companies eligible to compete for lunar deliveries under the 10-year CLPS 2 program, which has a shared $10 billion contract ceiling. The agency also selected SpaceX to launch communications satellites aboard Starship toward the Earth-Moon region in 2028.

Musk's longer-term claims include a constellation of more than 100,000 satellites and a hypothetical $1 trillion in annual revenue from 100 gigawatts of orbital AI computing, though he noted pricing would determine the outcome. His next Starship flight will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage, which he called the critical step toward full reusability. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits turned bullish from bearish a week earlier, though SPCX stock is still down 17% for the year. The articles do not say what the next Starship flight date is or whether the lunar and satellite contracts will produce revenue before 2028.

Articles.Title: SpaceX Wants To Turn AI Compute Into A $500B Business Next Year – And Elon Musk Says NASA’s Annual Budget Is No Match

stories.Headline: New study finds AI adoption surging across go-to-market teams, but revenue gains lag behind
stories.Summary:
A Harvard Business Review Analytic Services report, sponsored by the go-to-market company Seismic, found that AI adoption is climbing fast across revenue-generating teams but has not yet produced much revenue. Seismic announced the findings from San Diego on November 4, 2026, and CustomerThink published the item on November 8, 2026. According to the study, 75% of respondents said their organization had increased its use of AI for revenue-generating activities over the past year, yet only 11% reported increased revenue or new revenue streams from AI. The survey of 208 members of the Harvard Business Review audience was fielded online in June 2026, and most respondents worked in senior or executive roles at organizations with 1,000 or more employees.

The report points to several gaps between using AI and getting value from it. Among AI adopters, 45% named the lack of a clear AI strategy as the top barrier to using it more effectively, and 88% said a strong governance framework is necessary for safe and effective use, but only 32% said their organization was building one over the coming year. Revenue enablement stood out as an underused area: 39% of respondents said their organization applies AI there, compared with 54% for marketing and 44% each for sales and customer support, yet 71% of those using it for revenue enablement reported significant or moderate value, the highest share of the four functions measured. Real-time execution also lags, with 54% using AI to prepare meeting materials and 50% using it for post-call summaries, while only 19% use it to recommend next-best actions in the moment and 18% use AI agents to assist staff in real time. Just 12% of adopters described their revenue teams as highly confident in using AI effectively.

The study's director of research, Beth Tracton-Bishop, Ph.D., said critical thinking and AI literacy are key skills, since employees need to know when to trust AI output and when to challenge it. Seismic's chief marketing officer, Rob Pinkerton, said closing the gap requires a clear strategy, strong governance and revenue teams able to combine their judgment with AI insights. Timothy Dickson, chief digital and information officer at Regal Rexnord, described his company's experience in the report: AI-powered assistants cut response time for quote requests from nearly four hours to seconds, and sales teams close deals in a quarter of the earlier time, supported by a cross-functional governance process. The full report is available for download on Seismic's website.

Articles.Title: New study finds AI adoption surging across go-to-market teams, but revenue gains lag behind

stories.Headline: INTERVIEW SERIES: AI’s Power Crunch Echoes Bitcoin Mining’s Efficiency Push
stories.Summary:
Bitcoin miners have long tuned chip firmware to squeeze more computing output from limited electricity, and a similar problem now faces AI infrastructure operators, according to an interview series published by TheEnergyMag on November 8, 2026. For miners, the key measure is hashrate, while AI operators often track token throughput, the rate at which models process or generate data. In both cases, the setting that yields the most from a single machine may not yield the most across an entire power-limited facility. Braiins, a bitcoin mining software supplier, describes autotuning that calibrates chip frequencies and voltages to improve efficiency at a chosen power target. The article frames that practice as an established precedent for the AI calculation.

Sherman Ikemoto, group director at Cadence, which supplies chip design and data center simulation software, said operators need to know how much electricity it takes to produce computing output and how that output turns into revenue. He described how GPU performance gains taper as power use nears its maximum, so reducing a processor's power setting can cost relatively little performance while freeing electricity for more GPUs. He contrasted maximum-power operation, called Max-P, with Max-Q, which targets greater performance per watt, and noted that NVIDIA's documentation draws a similar distinction. In an illustrative example, he described running GPUs at 80% of maximum power, while stressing that the right setting depends on the hardware. He summed up the appeal: "within the same power envelope, we can now generate a lot more tokens."

Dipan Patel, chief operating officer of Duos Technologies Group, which develops and operates modular edge data centers, argued that many sites are marketed on headline megawatts even though service agreements often show that much of that capacity is interruptible or depends on a future upgrade. He said AI customers need firm power on a committed date, and that utility studies and infrastructure upgrades can push energization out by several years. Improving output from existing capacity, in his framing, addresses a different part of the problem than waiting for new utility service. Ikemoto added that capturing these gains requires coordinating the chip-to-chiller chain of processors, servers, electrical distribution and cooling. Cadence uses digital twins, virtual models of physical facilities, to test those interactions before equipment is installed or settings are changed.

Ikemoto said the simulations can flag areas with inadequate cooling or power, letting engineers adjust layouts, controls and GPU settings to raise computing output within the facility's limits. He compared an AI facility to a manufacturing plant whose business depends on the efficiency and uptime of its production line. He also noted that additional GPUs still require capital, so the added throughput must generate enough value to justify the hardware and supporting infrastructure, though the interview did not establish a payback calculation for any specific deployment. He acknowledged that the simulations have their own dependencies, citing the ongoing work of maintaining Cadence's equipment model library and obtaining detailed specifications from manufacturers. The article's overall point is that available megawatts set the limit, while equipment and configuration determine what can be produced within it.

Articles.Title: INTERVIEW SERIES: AI’s Power Crunch Echoes Bitcoin Mining’s Efficiency Push

stories.Headline: AI Model Classifies Arrhythmia Risk in Three Clinical Levels
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers including Hua Zhang, Jing Li, and Haiyan Wang has developed a deep learning algorithm that sorts cardiac arrhythmias into three risk levels: normal, not life-threatening, and life-threatening. The study was published in the journal BioData Mining in July 2026, and it introduces a model called PaliConvLSTM. That model combines convolutional neural network and long short-term memory layers, arranged in a palindromic pattern, to analyze electrocardiogram signals. The aim is to help clinicians with limited resources direct urgent care to patients whose arrhythmias are critical while monitoring those with milder conditions appropriately.

The researchers point out that cardiovascular diseases often start suddenly, carry high mortality, and recur frequently, so early screening matters. Because of limited medical resources, monitoring every patient in real time is difficult, which can delay responses to critical cases. Earlier artificial intelligence methods tended to detect specific arrhythmia types or sort cases into only two groups, critical and non-critical. The new scheme instead covers the full range of severity, from mild rhythm abnormalities to life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias. The first level includes normal sinus rhythm, which needs no specific monitoring.

The second level covers arrhythmias such as atrial bigeminy, ventricular bigeminy, and second-degree heart block, which are not immediately dangerous but still need close attention. The third level includes malignant ventricular arrhythmias such as ventricular flutter, ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular fibrillation, which can cause severe changes in blood flow and sudden cardiac death. The model is built to capture both the local shape details and the timing patterns within these signals. The study used three public ECG databases, the MIT-BIH Malignant Ventricular Arrhythmia Database, the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, and the Creighton University Ventricular Tachyarrhythmia Database, with segments of 2, 3, 5, 8, and 10 seconds.

On the 2-second segments from the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, the model reached an accuracy of 99.68% and a specificity of 99.65%. Across all tested conditions, accuracy ranged from 89.95% to 99.69%, and the model outperformed standalone and hybrid neural networks as well as several classical machine learning methods. When tested on new patients, accuracy stayed above 95%, with the 10-second segments reaching 96.50%. The authors acknowledge limitations, including that life-threatening cases are relatively rare in the datasets and that performance on the Creighton database was lower, at 90.56% on 2-second segments. They plan future work on data augmentation and on adding other medical data, such as blood pressure and blood oxygen readings.

Articles.Title: AI Model Classifies Arrhythmia Risk in Three Clinical Levels

stories.Headline: AI Models Show Promise in Pancreatic Cancer Diagnosis and Biomarker Discovery
stories.Summary:
A review published in the journal Cell Division on June 17, 2025, examines how artificial intelligence and machine learning are being applied to pancreatic cancer histopathology, diagnostics, and biomarker discovery. The study was led by Petra Weselá and colleagues, who assessed computational models built to support diagnosis, guide therapy, and enable early detection of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common and aggressive form of the disease. The authors reviewed studies published from 2018 through April 2025 that used histopathological data and involved at least 30 patients. The article itself is listed as published in 2025, while the news reports carrying it are dated later.

The review explains why better tools are needed. Pancreatic cancer often shows no early symptoms, so it is frequently found at an advanced stage, and the median survival for the form studied is about 11.7 months. Surgery, the main potentially curative option, is available to only 15 to 20 percent of patients. The disease also varies widely between patients and within single tumors, which complicates treatment. The authors say these challenges call for computational methods and biomarkers that can predict progression or reveal early cases during screening.

According to the review, convolutional neural networks are especially well suited to analyzing whole slide images because they learn patterns directly from raw pixels. Several studies cited in the article report strong results, including a model that detected pancreatic lesions on non-contrast computed tomography with an area under the curve of 0.986 to 0.996, comparable to human radiologists. In histopathology, some models distinguished the cancer from benign tissue with reliability often above 90 percent, and others classified molecular subtypes with balanced accuracy of 96.19 percent for the classical subtype and 83.03 percent for the basal subtype. The authors caution that direct comparisons are limited by differences in cohort size, data sources, and scanners, and that combining multiple data types does not always improve accuracy.

The authors also identify significant obstacles to clinical use. Training requires large volumes of precisely annotated data validated by expert pathologists, and models often generalize poorly to data from other sources, with one study showing accuracy falling from 99.04 percent to 67.20 percent on a different dataset. The review notes that the absence of legal standards for responsibility when ML tools misdiagnose a patient remains a barrier, along with concerns about patient privacy and bias against underrepresented groups. The authors propose a phased path that begins with validation, moves through prospective clinical trials, and continues with refinement before routine adoption. The news reports do not say when or whether that path will be followed in practice.

Articles.Title: AI Models Show Promise in Pancreatic Cancer Diagnosis and Biomarker Discovery

stories.Headline: OPINION Lotz: What is AI saying about you?
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion column by Dave Lotz, a U.S. Navy veteran and longtime Guam advocate, published on guampdn.com on November 8, 2026. Its subject is artificial intelligence and what AI systems say about individuals. Lotz recounts searching his own name online and finding claims that were false, including that he enlisted in the Navy in 1960 as an electronic technician, that he later enlisted in 1969 as a radioman, and that he once ran a sewage treatment plant in Missouri. He also notes that an AI search on a subject he had written about returned text that read like a quotation from his own article, presented as settled fact.

Lotz urges readers to search for information about friends, co-workers, bosses, politicians and others, while warning that AI results may be wrong, misleading, fake or simply absurd, and that acting on them could backfire. He questions whether AI tools evaluate their own accuracy and suggests readers learn what the internet and AI say about them. The column also refers to large windowless buildings on Guam that he believes are data centers, jokes about AI-driven cars, and suggests the new Guam Legislature hold an oversight hearing on AI and the divergent pre-election polls on the island. These points are presented as humor and speculation rather than verified findings.

The column does not name any company, agency or official responsible for the errors he describes, and it does not report any response from AI developers or regulators. It does not describe any new law, rule or requirement. Its stated aim is to encourage readers to check what AI and online sources say about them. The column is an opinion piece, so its claims about AI reliability rest on Lotz's own experience rather than on data or investigation presented in the article. The article does not indicate any follow-up beyond readers' comments.

Articles.Title: OPINION Lotz: What is AI saying about you?

stories.Headline: Agoda's AI Assistant Brings Travel Planning and Booking into One Conversation
stories.Summary:
Agoda, the digital travel platform, has introduced an AI Assistant that lets users discover, plan and book trips within its mobile app. The tool began as a limited test in September and has now expanded to users in 21 markets. The company describes it as the first new booking experience it has offered in its more than 20-year history. The assistant combines conversational trip planning with Agoda's live inventory of more than 6 million accommodations, flights, tours, attractions and travel add-ons. Travelers can compare options, check prices and availability, and continue to book without starting over at each step.

The assistant keeps track of preferences and trip context as a plan develops, and it places bookings, places to visit and unfinished plans on a trip planner canvas. Early beta results suggest that users are more likely to book a "connected trip" that combines several types of travel product. Agoda has also added web search so the assistant can draw on current information beyond its own inventory. Agoda's chief executive, Omri Morgenshtern, said that travel planning is fragmented because people move between apps, tabs and messages to organize a single trip. He said the company wants its assistant to act as a companion that understands preferences and trip context, reducing repetitive work so travelers can decide with more confidence.

The assistant's core conversational features run on OpenAI models. For restaurants and points of interest, it uses Gemini with Google Maps Grounding to show current ratings, photos, opening hours and locations. The articles describe the launch as a step in Agoda's push into AI-driven travel tools, though they give no further details on future expansion. The company says its mobile app offers access to more than 6 million holiday properties, over 130,000 flight routes and more than 300,000 activities. Travelers can explore these options on Agoda.com or through the Agoda app on the App Store or Google Play.

Articles.Title: Agoda's AI Assistant Brings Travel Planning and Booking into One Conversation

stories.Headline: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records
stories.Summary:
Palantir, the US data analytics company co-founded by the billionaire Peter Thiel, lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI software into NHS GP records, according to messages obtained by Foxglove, a tech equity campaign group, under the Freedom of Information Act and shared with the Guardian. The exchanges, which span July 2025 to March 2026, appear to be between Palantir's UK boss, Louis Mosley, and the former health minister Zubir Ahmed, with the push in February this year. The company argued via a direct WhatsApp channel that joining up primary and secondary care data was "unarguable" and that its software was "ideal" for the job. This came despite GP data being expressly ruled out of the scope of Palantir's existing £330m contract with NHS England to run its federated data platform.

The lobbying matters because it would stretch the company's reach into patient records that doctors and campaigners say should stay out of its hands. The British Medical Association and other groups have argued that bringing GP data into the platform would undermine patient trust and the doctor-patient relationship. When the previous Conservative government announced the deal three years ago, it stated that GP data would not be part of the national platform. Palantir's messages suggested the minister should "get out ahead of" likely political opposition from doctors and critics such as the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, and the Your Party led by Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana. The firm also told Ahmed that its software could bring faster GP access and more targeted management of frail patients, while keeping control of data local.

Foxglove's director of advocacy, Donald Campbell, said the messages showed Palantir lobbying to take in more sensitive personal data and that the company knew how sensitive the request was. The BMA council chair, Dr Tom Dolphin, warned of "scope creep" and of patients worrying about who could access their information. Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytical Officer Network, said Palantir appeared to be bidding to widen its work beyond what ministers and NHS leaders had said, which would require legislative change. Palantir responded that it has long argued data sharing can improve the NHS, that it is for government to decide how the software is rolled out, and that the exchanges reflect those points. The Department of Health and Social Care declined to comment.

The disclosure comes as ministers reportedly stopped short of ending the Palantir contract soon, despite campaigners and two House of Commons committees calling for it to end as early as spring. Health secretary Yvette Cooper told parliament that a review was ongoing and spoke of the long-term benefit of developing UK sovereign AI, which suggests a British replacement may be sought when the contract reaches its next end point in 2029. The articles also report that Tom Watson, a Labour peer hired by Palantir as a full-time lobbyist in September, wrote to Cooper urging her to keep the contract going. The articles do not say whether the lobbying changed any policy, and the status of GP data in the platform remains unresolved.

Articles.Title: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records

stories.Headline: Core Scientific’s AI Colocation Revenue Jumps to $215M as Mining Role Shrinks
stories.Summary:
Core Scientific reported on November 5, 2026, that its colocation revenue reached $215.4 million in the third quarter, up from $136.7 million in the second quarter and $15 million a year earlier. The company said it was billing for 485 megawatts of capacity as of September 30, and total quarterly revenue came to $232.9 million. The results show the Bitcoin miner's shift toward hosting contracted AI infrastructure for tenants. The figures were disclosed in the company's earnings release, as reported by TradingView.

The company said it was billing for 485 megawatts of capacity, which it said represents more than $700 million in average annualized colocation GAAP revenue. Core Scientific described this as a measure of contracted power and computing infrastructure delivered to tenants, not a measure of hashrate or Bitcoin produced. It said it is nearing full delivery under its first colocation agreement and is building capacity under a second agreement across five campuses. The article notes that remaining construction and billing ramps still affect the final financial result.

The company reported about $1.18 billion in quarterly net income, but said that figure was helped by a non-cash change in the fair value of warrants, so it does not reflect recurring cash from operations. Adjusted EBITDA was $133.6 million, compared with $41.1 million in the prior quarter, while capital expenditure reached $985.1 million. The article points out that a fast-growing operating business can still spend heavily as it adds the facilities needed for future contracted revenue. TradingView's article was written by its News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

The article argues that Core Scientific's results show the AI opportunity is becoming measurable, but that revenue alone without spending, financing and delivery schedules would overstate how easy the transition is. It suggests investors watch megawatts actually billing, customer diversification, operating margins, remaining capital needs and changes to lease terms. It also says the company is no longer an identical bet on Bitcoin's price, since its fortunes may increasingly depend on demand for AI compute and on construction execution. The company's mining history remains part of its story, the article says, but its metrics are changing.

Articles.Title: Core Scientific’s AI Colocation Revenue Jumps to $215M as Mining Role Shrinks

stories.Headline: AI Content Festival 2026 to take place in Seoul this week
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Creative Content Agency (Kocca) are set to host AI Content Festival 2026, a three-day event at Coex The Platz in Gangnam District, southern Seoul, running from Thursday to Saturday. Now in its third year, the festival is meant to let the public try AI-powered content firsthand while giving creators and companies a place to network and collaborate. Visitors can explore four themed zones, called Story, Play, Make and Cross, that show how AI is changing the way content is made and enjoyed. Admission to the exhibitions and hands-on activities is free, though people who want to attend must register in advance through the festival's official website by Wednesday.

The festival also adds a new business development program, which runs from Thursday to Friday, to help companies find investment and partners, particularly those that have trouble locating collaborators or gauging market demand. Other elements include AI content production support programs and displays of work from talent development programs run by the ministry and Kocca. Thursday brings a lecture by Kim Rando, an emeritus professor at Seoul National University who heads the Consumer Trend Center, on how AI is changing content consumption. On Friday, a session for creators will cover the production process of CJ 4DPlex's ScreenX, a panoramic cinema format, and how the company uses AI in its work. On Saturday, science content creator Gwedo and criminal profiler Pyo Chang-won will speak about future careers in the AI era and the responsible use of technology.

Kim Kyung-hwa, an official at the ministry's Cultural Industry and Media Policy Bureau, said that in the age of AI the competitiveness of the content industry depends not only on technological advances but on turning them into new creative works and commercial value. The ministry said it will actively support creators who combine imagination with technological innovation to develop new content and open new markets. The articles frame the event as a way to widen opportunities for AI creators while showing the public how the technology is reshaping the industry. Beyond the festival itself, the articles do not describe any further plans or outcomes.

Articles.Title: AI Content Festival 2026 to take place in Seoul this week

stories.Headline: Shanghai to create AI test base for shipping and logistics
stories.Summary:
Shanghai has begun building an artificial intelligence test base for shipping and logistics, according to a Smart Maritime Network report by Rob O'Dwyer dated November 10, 2026. The facility is being developed by Shanghai International Port Group, known as SIPG, together with academic and industry partners. It is meant to support testing of AI applications across port handling, cargo transport and multimodal logistics. Work on the infrastructure is already underway, and 54 business AI agents have been registered for testing and deployment.

The base will supply computing, data storage and security infrastructure, along with industry-specific datasets, AI models and an agent management platform. Its work will focus on three operational areas: port cargo handling, port hinterland transport and multimodal transport. The aim is to give AI applications a route from development into day-to-day use in shipping and port operations. The article describes this as the purpose of the initiative rather than setting out any separate legal or regulatory requirement.

The facility was announced alongside a new action plan from the Shanghai Municipal Transport Commission for integrating AI into the transport sector. The plan covers ports and shipping, aviation, rail and road transport, autonomous driving, postal services and logistics. It names three core development areas: transport large language models and AI agents, high-quality industry datasets, and computing infrastructure. Planned applications include autonomous port hinterland transport and AI-based government transport services, and the city also intends to set up a trusted data space for transport and mechanisms for data sharing.

The same event saw the establishment of a Yangtze River Delta regional centre for the Transport Large Model Innovation and Industry Alliance, with its secretariat in Shanghai. The centre will coordinate technical development and applications across Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Anhui, including sharing operational environments for testing transport AI. The article does not describe any further timetable or next steps beyond these announcements. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Shanghai to create AI test base for shipping and logistics

stories.Headline: AI technology helps enhance nation's logistics, supply chains
stories.Summary:
Chinese delivery companies are putting artificial intelligence into frontline work during this year's Singles' Day shopping rush, which is held on Nov 11. Drones now deliver packages to smart lockers, and couriers use AI tools to sort parcels and plan routes. STO Express has deployed AI "digital employees" through its SClaw intelligent-agent platform, which handles customer inquiries, flags abnormal shipments and helps plan trunk-line routes. The platform also includes a digital quality-control system that flags risks for fresh produce and other sensitive parcels.

Other companies are extending AI into decision-making and warehouse operations. JD Logistics has rolled out its Super Brain 3.0 large model to forecast order volumes by region and adjust logistics capacity in real time, and says AI-recommended routes have an adoption rate above 90.2 percent. The company is also deploying robotic arms in sorting centers that have reached a parcel tracking accuracy of 99.9 percent. Drones are reaching remote villages in Southwest China, where mountains and river crossings have made last-mile delivery hard.

Executives from the companies described the changes in their own terms. Luo Jian, who oversees Double 11 operations at STO Express, said the company is using AI computing power to take on part of the physical workload while proactive services absorb peak pressure, and that efficiency is rising without a loss of safety. SF Express is using sales forecasts and digital supply-chain tools to move inventory closer to consumers, and YTO Express has put more than 100 intelligent agents and 28 digital employees to work in routing and customer service. Zhang Yi, vice-president of the Guangdong Internet Society, said AI now runs across the whole e-commerce cycle, while Hu Dajian of the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing said AI is moving from isolated uses toward coordination across entire industrial chains.

The shift is part of a wider national push. A recent report from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing found that AI adoption in China's logistics and supply chains exceeded 37 percent, with transport at 78 percent, safety and compliance at 52.73 percent and smart warehousing at 47.27 percent. The State Post Bureau reported that express delivery handled 151.3 billion parcels in the first nine months of 2026, up 4.3 percent from a year earlier. China released a policy document in 2025 to advance its "AI Plus" initiative, which sets goals for integrating AI across the economy and society.

Articles.Title: AI technology helps enhance nation's logistics, supply chains

stories.Headline: Return Of The Living Dead Cast Horrified By AI-Made Sequel They Were Originally Set To Star In
stories.Summary:
Last Halloween night, Richard Driscoll published The Return of the Living Dead: Aftermath on his website, a film largely generated by AI. The sequel was meant to be made by the original cast of the 1985 punk zombie classic Return of the Living Dead, who had been attached to star in the follow-up. Driscoll had launched an Indiegogo campaign in 2024 for a project called TRASH's REVENGE Return of the Living Dead Universe, which featured several original cast members as producers. Instead of the planned film, fans and alumni were presented with a production that the articles describe as robotic in its line delivery and confused in its sequence of events. The likenesses of cast members appear throughout the footage, though they did not film any of it.

The cast members say they were not told about the direction the project took. Beverly Randolph said on the Caffeinated Horror Dude podcast that the outcome was not what they had signed up for and that the cast needed to put something out because of the criticism now aimed at them. Linnea Quigley, who had described the planned movie as a blend of Sunset Boulevard and Rocky Horror, said the project became a fiasco and that she had warned Driscoll against using AI. The articles say the cast's main concern is the continued use of their likenesses, since Driscoll appears to have turned the TRASH's REVENGE project into an additional production. Randolph has urged anyone who contributed funding to seek a refund through their credit card company, and she has encouraged Amazon, which bought MGM in 2022, to take legal action.

The original Return of the Living Dead was not released into the public domain, unlike George A. Romero's Night of the Living Dead, which entered the public domain in 1968 through an erroneous paperwork error. That status allowed others to make sequels to Romero's film, but it does not extend to Return. The articles place the controversy within a wider debate over AI, noting that Itch.io has deleted large amounts of AI-generated content and tightened its disclosure policies to counter a rise in spam game uploads. The articles do not say whether Driscoll has responded to the criticism, whether any legal action has been filed, or what steps Amazon or any refund processor has taken.

Articles.Title: Return Of The Living Dead Cast Horrified By AI-Made Sequel They Were Originally Set To Star In

stories.Headline: Apple Makes Major AI Pricing Move as New Revenue Opportunity Emerges
stories.Summary:
Apple has introduced paid usage packs for subscribers who go past their monthly AI limits in its Creator Studio applications. The company, which is based in the United States and makes the iPhone, is trying to turn artificial intelligence into a direct source of revenue. The move was reported on November 9, 2026, by GuruFocus and republished by Yahoo Finance. It marks one of Apple's earliest attempts to charge directly for AI use inside its software.

The AI features cover several creative and productivity apps, including Keynote, Pages, Numbers, Pixelmator Pro, Freeform and Logic Pro. They include image and shape generation, presentation creation, image enhancement and AI help for music production. Subscribers on the entry-level allowance can generate 50 images, 250 shapes and 50 presentations each month, along with presenter notes covering 700 slides. Customers who go beyond those limits can buy additional intelligence usage packs for $49.99. Apple said the feature is available to active Creator Studio subscribers in eight countries, including the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Germany and India.

Apple confirmed the change itself, and the article describes it as part of the company's broader AI strategy. The article also notes that Apple works with outside AI providers, including OpenAI and Google, to support some of these capabilities. Apple has not said how much revenue it expects from the packs or how many subscribers are likely to exceed their monthly allowances. The article links the change to the company's Services segment, which brought in $31.57 billion in its latest reported quarter.

The article presents the move as a test of whether customers will pay extra for AI features that competing software platforms increasingly offer. It says AI features carry computing and infrastructure costs, so the new revenue will only improve profitability if pricing covers those expenses. Investors are advised to watch Creator Studio subscriber growth, uptake of the usage packs and their contribution to Services revenue. The article does not say what Apple will do next beyond these existing plans.

Articles.Title: Apple Makes Major AI Pricing Move as New Revenue Opportunity Emerges

stories.Headline: FedEx adds four weekly China-US freighter flights as AI hardware demand keeps cargo busy
stories.Summary:
FedEx said on November 9 that it is adding four weekly Boeing 777 freighter flights between China and the United States. Three of the flights will leave Shanghai, stop in Osaka, and continue to Anchorage and Memphis, while the fourth will run from Guangzhou to the same two hubs. The carrier said the extra capacity is aimed at advanced industrial manufacturing, semiconductor production, AI infrastructure and high-end e-commerce. The added service is a small move, but it offers a view of where US-China trade demand is concentrated.

The sectors FedEx named matter because air freight is the preferred route for high-value, time-sensitive goods such as chips, servers and networking equipment. Economists expect China's October trade data, due on Tuesday, to show exports up about a third from a year earlier in dollar terms, with demand for AI hardware a central driver. The Osaka routing also points to close links in Asian supply chains for AI components, with Japan a key source of semiconductor materials and production equipment. Trade is likely to come up when US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in mid-November.

The backdrop is mixed. US AI stocks sold off sharply last week on concerns that Democratic gains in the midterm elections could bring new limits on data centre construction, raising questions about how fast the build-out will proceed. A logistics company adding capacity aimed at AI infrastructure suggests that, for now, demand for that hardware is still moving. The article describes the announcement as a modest but real-world signal that the Asia-to-US AI supply chain remains busy, even as investors debate how long the spending boom can last.

Articles.Title: FedEx adds four weekly China-US freighter flights as AI hardware demand keeps cargo busy

stories.Headline: MediaTek, Qualcomm shift focus to cloud AI as smartphones stall
stories.Summary:
Qualcomm and MediaTek, the two leading smartphone chip designers, are moving their attention toward cloud AI application-specific integrated circuits, according to a Digitimes report published on November 8, 2026. The shift comes as the global smartphone market faces what could be its sharpest decline on record in 2026. The article frames the move as a response to weakening demand in handsets, which has pushed the companies to look for growth in data center AI hardware. The available text is a short summary, and the full article is restricted to paid subscribers, so most of the detail is not visible.

The report indicates that the strategy is tied to the expanding market for AI computing, with China Mobile's US$75 billion 2027 procurement plan cited as a sign of a major shift toward AI infrastructure. The summary does not spell out specific product timelines, revenue targets, or the size of investment either company plans to commit. It also does not give a figure for the expected smartphone decline beyond describing it as potentially the sharpest on record. Readers should treat the claims about the scale of the shift as coming from the article's framing rather than from confirmed company filings.

The reporting names Qualcomm and MediaTek as the parties making the change, and describes both as the two leading smartphone system-on-chip makers. The visible text does not include direct statements from executives at either company, so no company responses can be paraphrased from this material. Digitimes, the outlet that published the piece, is the source of the framing and is the only named organization in the available text. Any direct quotes or attributed comments would need to be checked in the full paywalled article.

Related coverage on the same site points to a broader AI compute race, including Nvidia's expanding role in AI infrastructure and continuing supply pressures in AI chip materials. Those items suggest the cloud AI push by Qualcomm and MediaTek is taking place in a crowded market dominated by larger players. The available text does not say how the two companies plan to compete with those rivals or what their next steps will be. More to follow.

Articles.Title: MediaTek, Qualcomm shift focus to cloud AI as smartphones stall

stories.Headline: Wistron October revenue more than doubles as AI server demand surges
stories.Summary:
Wistron reported that its October 2026 revenue more than doubled, driven by strong demand for AI servers. According to the article, the Taiwanese company posted revenue of NT$402.6 billion, or about US$12.2 billion, for the month. That figure rose 5.73% from September and was 1.18 times the level of October 2025. The report was published by Digitimes on November 8, 2026.

The article's figures are the core of the story, and they show a steep climb in a single month. The growth reflects how much AI server orders are contributing to the company's sales. Beyond the monthly and yearly comparisons, the article does not spell out any further requirements or changes tied to these results. The article does not name a specific spokesperson or official statement from Wistron about the results.

Responsibility for the reported revenue rests with Wistron, which the article identifies as the company behind the numbers. The article gives no direct quotes from company leadership. The piece is short and sits alongside other Digitimes coverage on AI computing demand, including a note on China Mobile's large planned procurement for 2027. Beyond the figures given, the article offers no further detail on what comes next for Wistron.

Articles.Title: Wistron October revenue more than doubles as AI server demand surges

stories.Headline: Opinion: Why using AI saves doctors time but won’t fix physician burnout
stories.Summary:
AI scribes, tools that listen to clinical visits with patient consent and draft physicians' notes, are spreading quickly. More than 12,000 primary care clinicians have enrolled in Canada Health Infoway's national program, about 5,000 Ontario physicians use them, and roughly one in five Canadian physicians use some AI tool. Almost 60 per cent of those users report less administrative time. The article is an opinion piece by Ali Abdalvand, an emergency physician and associate professor at the University of British Columbia, and Ehsan Etezad, an organizational psychologist at Saint Mary's University.

The authors argue that the time saved is often absorbed by new demands and that AI brings new work of its own. In Canada's national program, half of clinicians put saved time into other administrative tasks and one in five used it to add appointments. A U.S. study of five health systems found adopters saved 13.4 minutes of daily record-keeping time and delivered 0.49 more visits per week. The piece also says that many AI tools sit outside core clinical systems, forcing copy-and-paste work and constant logins. It names change fatigue and what it calls AI fatigue as additional strains.

On safety, the article cites Ontario's auditor general, who tested 20 government-approved AI scribes in two simulated runs and found most made errors. Twelve recorded the wrong drug, nine invented treatment steps and 17 missed key mental-health details in at least one test. The province reported no known patient harm. OntarioMD, which helps physicians adopt digital health tools with provincial funding, said physicians know they must review every note the scribe produces, a step the authors call essential but also extra work. The authors say physicians shift from writing notes to editing them and watching for rare but serious errors.

The authors contend that burnout comes from mismatches in workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values, not from any single task. One study found electronic health record design and use explained 6.8 per cent of differences in burnout between clinicians, rising to 36.2 per cent when work conditions were included. In emergency medicine, physicians are interrupted 7.9 times an hour, and the article notes prescribing error rates nearly triple with interruptions. The authors propose GRACE, a five-principle framework co-developed by Etezad for responsible AI adoption by health-care organizations. The article does not describe the framework's principles in detail, and it does not report any planned policy changes or deadlines.

Articles.Title: Opinion: Why using AI saves doctors time but won’t fix physician burnout

stories.Headline: SPH Media looks to plug into AI channels without losing its place in the news
stories.Summary:
SPH Media, the Singapore publisher, is seeking a place in the channels through which people increasingly find news rather than trying to resist artificial intelligence, according to executive chairman Chan Yeng Kit. He has voiced concern that publishers could lose their role between reporting and audiences if AI services become a main route to information. The article, published on 9 November 2026 by Tomorrow's Publisher, frames this as part of a wider shift in which news organisations have depended on technology platforms for distribution. Earlier reliance on search and social media left publishers exposed when platform priorities changed, and AI services that summarise journalism may add to that pressure. The risk is that readers take in information without visiting or recognising the outlets that produced it.

SPH Media's response includes a partnership with Google meant to extend the reach of its journalism through Google's channels. The partnership also aims to strengthen newsroom capabilities in areas including generative AI verification and AI-enabled workflows. The two companies have named talent development and audience engagement as areas of cooperation. The article stresses that these are stated aims, and that their practical effect on publisher control and sustainable revenue remains uncertain. Alongside this, the Chinese-language publication Lianhe Zaobao has launched an English-language website using AI-assisted translation with human proofreading and editing.

The initiative is meant to reach younger readers and other language communities while keeping its Chinese-language edition. Malay and Tamil offerings are expected to be considered progressively as the operation develops. Chan has argued that technology can extend the audience for existing journalism but that reporting still depends on people's ability to build trust, draw out personal accounts and make editorial decisions. The article cites the Associated Press, whose standards say AI may assist newsroom work but does not replace journalists' responsibility for gathering and assessing facts.

Staff must verify AI-generated material and remain accountable for published work. ProPublica is also quoted as saying AI-assisted journalism must receive human review and meet the newsroom's usual editorial standards. The article notes that the tools and their effects are still developing, leaving publishers to balance access to new distribution systems against the risk of becoming less visible to audiences. SPH Media presents its approach as adaptation, alongside investment in a range of products and the fundamentals of journalism.

Articles.Title: SPH Media looks to plug into AI channels without losing its place in the news

stories.Headline: Essential Reading in an Era of AI Doomsaying
stories.Summary:
Shannon Vallor, a professor of ethics of data and artificial intelligence at the University of Edinburgh, published a reading list on Nautilus on November 9, 2026, recommending ten books as a response to what she calls the current wave of AI doomsaying. She describes doom predictions as everywhere, spreading from the media into everyday conversation and shaping how people think about the future. The list is organized as five pairs of fiction and nonfiction titles, each chosen to offer a vision of how broken situations can be repaired rather than how the world ends. Vallor says the books are meant to help readers think about the future and technology with more love, courage and wisdom.

Vallor is clear that she does not dismiss the risks. She says today's AI technologies are dangerous to human agency, to self-understanding, to relationships, to people's ability to think for themselves, and to prospects for living sustainably. Her case rests on the distinction between doomsaying and calls to action. Doomsaying, she argues, produces decision paralysis, apathy and resignation, while calls to action restore a sense of agency, purpose and moral urgency. She notes that her own book, The AI Mirror, published in 2024, comes from the same concern that reasonable fears cannot be avoided by looking away from them.

The selections include Imagining AI, edited by Stephen Cave and Kanta Dihal, which gathers essays on AI from many regions, and Becky Chambers's A Psalm for the Wild-Built, a gentle story about humans and machines learning when to stop. Vallor pairs Adam Becker's Everything Forever with N.K. Jemisin's The Fifth Season, and Carissa Véliz's Prophecy with Samuel Butler's Erewhon. Other picks include Ruha Benjamin's Imagination, Ursula K. Le Guin's The Lathe of Heaven, David Karpf's Vaporware, Inc, due in 2027, and Neal Stephenson's The Diamond Age. Vallor characterizes Karpf's book as a critique of "digital futurism," a pattern of promised technological abundance that she says keeps failing to arrive.

Articles.Title: Essential Reading in an Era of AI Doomsaying

stories.Headline: FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (FFR) and Faraday Future Announce FF OmniMind and Its Model Achieve No. 1 in RoboColiseum Embodied AI Model Ranking; Advance Sales with Several Leading U.S. Integrators of Security and Inspection Robotics Solutions
stories.Summary:
FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (NASDAQ: FFR), a California-based physical AI robotics company, announced on November 8, 2026 that its EAI Brain, called OmniMind, and its underlying model ranked first overall on RoboColiseum's global leaderboard as of November 6. RoboColiseum tests embodied AI models in simulation, and the OmniMind model scored 0.8698 out of 1, ahead of models including NVIDIA GR00T N1.7, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and π0.5. The same update reported that the company has advanced sales with several leading U.S. integrators of security and inspection robotics solutions. The announcement was made by YT Jia, the company's founder and global CEO, in a weekly business update.

The company says the ranking reflects progress on the EAI Brain core in Phase One of its "Built in USA" program, which it describes as now complete. According to the published scores, OmniMind reached about 0.99 in instruction following, 0.92 in spatial reasoning and 0.96 in robustness to disturbances. The company credits a layered architecture with programmatic execution, which breaks a task into separate steps for interpreting instructions, locating targets with 3D perception and planning motion, so each step can be checked and optimized separately. On the business side, the update said the company has signed sales contracts with several North American integrators and distributors of security and inspection robotics, and it is working with Pinnacle in Southern California on a home security proof of concept. It also reported that RoboShare sold a Master humanoid robot in Las Vegas.

Jia is the executive who attributed the progress to the company's teams and its four-core full-stack strategy, saying the feedback from these evaluations will guide future improvements to the brain, models and skills. The company also said it will hold its third-quarter 2026 earnings call for FFR on November 12 at 4 p.m. Pacific Time, which will be its first earnings call since listing, and a call for affiliate FFAI on November 16 at the same time. The release includes standard cautionary language that its forward-looking statements carry risks, including whether guidance and projections are achieved, the ability to commercialize its technologies, and the need for additional financing and continued Nasdaq compliance.

Articles.Title: FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (FFR) and Faraday Future Announce FF OmniMind and Its Model Achieve No. 1 in RoboColiseum Embodied AI Model Ranking; Advance Sales with Several Leading U.S. Integrators of Security and Inspection Robotics Solutions

stories.Headline: New Falcon Cloud Security Innovations Secure the Cloud AI Runs On
stories.Summary:
New Falcon Cloud Security innovations, announced by CrowdStrike on November 4, 2026, aim to help organizations secure the cloud infrastructure that AI applications depend on. The company says AI coding agents and automated pipelines are pulling in open source packages, launching workloads, and creating identities faster than security teams can review them manually. CrowdStrike positions its Falcon Cloud Security product, which draws on adversary intelligence covering more than 290 adversaries, as a response to this pressure. The updates are all described as generally available.

The announcement centers on stopping compromised software before it reaches production. CrowdStrike cites one observation in which its researchers saw ALTERED SPIDER compromise more than 300 software dependencies in a single day. The company says Supply Chain Security for Cloud extends its endpoint detection of malicious packages into container images, identifying compromised npm and PyPI packages during build and registry scanning. The Falcon Kubernetes Admission Controller can then alert on or block affected images at deployment. Expanded Cloud Risks coverage now reaches Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, and agentless vulnerability scanning is added for Linux-based Google Compute Engine instances.

CrowdStrike, which is the company behind the Falcon platform, presents these features as part of a single platform that links endpoint, identity, and SOC operations with cloud protection. Brett Shaw is listed as the author of the post. The company says proactive exposure work and real-time cloud detection and response share context, so information gathered before an attack can help analysts stop one. The articles describe Real-Time cloud detection and response being extended to Microsoft Azure and Kubernetes, building on existing coverage for AWS and Google Cloud.

The announcement also covers application context and runtime protection. Expanded Application Security Posture Management brings containerized applications into Application Explorer, and new package exports map vulnerable dependencies to the applications that use them. Enhanced third-party API findings identify external payment-service integrations and help teams assess exposure if a provider is compromised. The articles cite these changes as a way to help defenders interrupt attacks in progress and protect AI workloads, though the excerpt provided is cut off before the full runtime details appear.

Articles.Title: New Falcon Cloud Security Innovations Secure the Cloud AI Runs On

stories.Headline: Seoul AI pavilion generates $3.52 mil. in export opportunities at Barcelona expo
stories.Summary:
The Seoul AI Foundation said on Monday that Seoul's pavilion at the Smart City Expo World Congress 2026 in Barcelona had generated $3.52 million, or about 4.7 billion won, in export consultations. The pavilion ran from November 3 to 5 at Fira Barcelona Gran Via and recorded 398 business consultations. The foundation organized it for the seventh straight year together with Gangnam District and 11 Seoul-based technology firms under the theme "AI City Seoul." The approximately 180-square-meter space showed AI tools aimed at urban problems.

The companies represented were active in energy, urban safety, mobility and spatial information. The participants named were Tilda, LBS Tech, Inpera, Ninewatt, Desen Korea, Archisketch, Kairos Lab, Innonet, PiaSpace, SaveTree and GroundOne. Gangnam District ran its own separate space under the slogan "Gangnam, Smarter With AI," which included five companies based in the district or tied to its pilot projects. Each participating firm averaged 36 consultations, up from 32 last year.

Average consultation value reached $320,000 per company, compared with about $300,000 in 2025. The exhibition also hosted the sixth Smart City Seoul Forum on Wednesday, where domestic and international experts discussed applying AI policy to public services, urban safety and city governance. Foundation Chairman Kim Man-ki said the real value of AI lies in creating opportunities, and that the AI city Seoul envisions is one dense with possibilities for citizens and businesses. He framed that vision as the foundation's aim rather than a measured result.

The foundation said it will widen international partnerships through Seoul Smart Life Week and help local technology companies pursue business overseas. The article notes that it was produced with generative AI assistance and edited by The Korea Times. Its report is based on figures the foundation released, and it does not describe how the consultation values were calculated or whether any of them have turned into signed contracts. The reporting also does not say what specific partnerships or support programs will follow beyond the general plans announced.

Articles.Title: Seoul AI pavilion generates $3.52 mil. in export opportunities at Barcelona expo

stories.Headline: Debate Over ‘Conscious’ AI Divides Industry as Microsoft AI Chief Takes Firm Stance
stories.Summary:
Mustafa Suleyman, chief executive of Microsoft's AI division, has sparked a major debate across the technology industry with comments on AI rights. In an essay titled A Warning About ‘Model Welfare’, he stated that AI systems are not conscious. He later said on X that he would reconsider his position if evidence to the contrary emerged. The issue was examined in an article by Futurism.

Suleyman's starting point is that AI systems do not feel, experience, or suffer. His view is not that AI could never become conscious, but that current systems are not and should remain that way. He said he has seen no evidence that AIs are conscious or deserve welfare. He added that a surprisingly large number of people on X think AI rights should be taken seriously, which prompted him to clarify his stance.

Futurism noted that his reasoning may still give too much credence to the idea, since scientists remain divided on whether current architectures could support anything like human experience. The debate comes at a time when companies worth billions and even trillions of dollars, including Anthropic, are openly discussing the possibility that their language models may show signs of consciousness. Futurism observed that the discussion is increasingly shaped by what it called "sci-fi primed paranoia" rather than rigorous scientific analysis. Significant sections of the AI industry nonetheless take such ideas seriously.

Suleyman has taken a clear ethical position that such synthetic beings should not be created, whether or not the technology makes it possible. In his essay, Suleyman wrote that developing conscious AI would be reckless if it is possible based on everything he knows, and that AI should not be built that way. He argued that AI developers have no right to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world, even if some want to do so with AI welfare as a top priority. The articles provided do not describe any formal policy changes, regulatory measures, or further steps Microsoft plans to take on the question.

Articles.Title: Debate Over ‘Conscious’ AI Divides Industry as Microsoft AI Chief Takes Firm Stance

stories.Headline: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months
stories.Summary:
Nominal, a four-year-old Austin-based startup that makes an AI platform for engineering and testing complex hardware such as aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has tripled its valuation to $3 billion. The company announced on Monday that it raised a $240 million Series C, led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners. The round follows a $155 million Series B extension announced in March at a $1 billion valuation, led by Trae Stephens of Founders Fund. That earlier deal was a preemptive offer, meaning the investor initiated it rather than the startup. Other backers include Sequoia, General Catalyst, and Lux Capital.

Nominal says it counts 80 commercial and government organizations as customers, including Anduril, the defense company co-founded by Stephens. In October, the U.S. Air Force selected Nominal for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase, known as STRATFI, a program that requires matching funds from outside the Air Force. The article does not say what the matching funds must total or how that requirement will be met. The funding is aimed at helping the company expand its work with the military and other large buyers of complex hardware. The article does not provide further details on how the money will be deployed.

Nominal's chief executive and co-founder, Cameron McCord, is a former U.S. Navy submarine officer who previously worked at Anduril. The company's rapid rise in valuation reflects strong investor interest in AI tools for building and testing physical systems, a category that sits alongside software for defense and industrial customers. The article does not describe any plans for future rounds, public offerings, or product launches. It also does not indicate whether the valuation increase signals changes in the company's revenue or headcount. The story was reported by TechCrunch's Julie Bort, and the information comes from the company's announcement and the investors involved.

Articles.Title: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months

stories.Headline: AI adoption creates new market for compliance startups
stories.Summary:
