Democrats secured majorities in both the House and Senate, and Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, has said the state should pause data center buildout until new protections are in place. Yahoo Finance reported that prospective buyers discussed lowering Anthropic's valuation to a range of $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, with some considering as low as $1.1 trillion, citing Bloomberg. Those figures sit far below estimates as high as $2 trillion projected in early October. Anthropic confidentially filed its IPO prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June.

Analysts quoted by Yahoo Finance said the company faces a difficult choice either way. Anna Rathbun, founder and CEO of Grenadilla Advisory, said it would be difficult to go public in this environment. Kevin Mahn, chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh, said a delay could be read as a bearish signal for the AI trade, while a weak debut could also be taken that way. Willy Lee of Neostellar said investors want to know whether Anthropic can sustain long-term growth and secure a meaningful share of the AI market. Yahoo Finance also reported that Anthropic's revenue grew to $33.2 billion through the first nine months of the year.

Investors will look for further signals on Nov. 17, when Nvidia reports earnings. Yahoo Finance noted that hyperscalers including Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta have already reported, and that expectations are high Nvidia will again beat estimates and raise its guidance. Shay Boloor of Futurum said he gave a 1% chance that Nvidia would miss. CNBC reported that the Nasdaq and S&P 500 attempted a rebound on Friday, though Micron and Nvidia shares remained well below their recent highs after steep losses. Whether the sell-off deepens or fades will likely determine if Anthropic goes ahead with its listing this year.

Articles.Title: Anthropic's IPO dilemma after the AI sell-off: 'Damned if you do, damned if you don't'

stories.Headline: South Dakota Mines professor earns NSF-backed award for AI research
stories.Summary:
A South Dakota Mines professor has received an award to help make artificial intelligence tools that convert speech into text more accurate. Nirmalya Thakur, an assistant professor in the university's Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, was awarded 200,000 ACCESS Credits through a program funded by the National Science Foundation. The story was reported by KOTA, with Mary Francis Witte as the author, and was published on November 8, 2026. The award comes through the Explore category of the ACCESS program, which gives researchers computing resources they may not have at their home institutions.

The credits give Thakur and his research team access to advanced computing resources for studying how different computer systems affect speech recognition technology. The technology is commonly used to create captions and transcripts. Researchers will examine whether different graphics processing units, or GPUs, affect how accurately and consistently these AI systems interpret spoken words. The stated goal is to identify what influences transcription quality and to find ways to make the technology more dependable. Better speech recognition could improve accessibility for people who are deaf or hard of hearing, as well as others who rely on speech-to-text tools.

Thakur said the award will help expand his work in artificial intelligence and high-performance computing. He said it will also support the development of more reliable AI systems. The article does not include any further statements from him about the project's timeline or findings. The ACCESS program, whose name stands for Advanced Cyberinfrastructure Coordination Ecosystem: Services & Support, launched in 2022 and supports research across a wide range of scientific fields. The article does not say when the research is expected to produce results.

Articles.Title: South Dakota Mines professor earns NSF-backed award for AI research

stories.Headline: AI art on Philly’s walls? | Mike Newall
stories.Summary:
Mural Arts, the Philadelphia public art program, unveiled designs last month for mesh banners that will hang on a fence at the Bellwether District development in South Philly. Social media users and at least one AI scholar said the imagery looked AI-generated, and one design showed a skyline that looked more like Chicago than Philadelphia. The designs came from muralist Kelley Prevard, and the banners are part of the citywide Throughlines installation. Mural Arts has not explained its internal review process, and the artist has declined to comment.

Mural Arts executive director Emily Mello did not answer questions from Inquirer reporter Rosa Cartagena about whether AI tools were used or how the designs were approved. The organization has said it will install the banners later this month despite the criticism. A spokesperson said the Chicago skyline will be altered to look more like Philadelphia. The dispute has also raised concerns about the organization's commitment to local artists and its lack of a formal AI policy.

Mural Arts is scheduled to hold a town hall on Thursday where local artists will review a working draft of an AI policy. Cartagena said the responsibility for the commission rests with Mural Arts because the work was unveiled with its approval. She also said the questions extend beyond this one organization and concern how arts groups in the city and elsewhere will use these tools. Some social media users have predicted the banners will be vandalized, and Cartagena described a sense that the work does not reflect Philadelphia.

Articles.Title: AI art on Philly’s walls? | Mike Newall

stories.Headline: This Stock Is a Nearly Guaranteed Winner From the AI Infrastructure Buildout
stories.Summary:
This article is an opinion piece, not a breaking news report, so the story is a Motley Fool analysis published on Yahoo Finance on November 8, 2026, by Keithen Drury, arguing that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company is a near-certain beneficiary of the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure. The author says that investing in the AI buildout can be difficult because there are many options, including computing companies, application providers and energy firms. He names Taiwan Semiconductor, traded as TSM on the New York Stock Exchange, as a single company that cuts through that noise. The piece was published with a note that the author holds positions in Broadcom, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor.

The author explains that Taiwan Semiconductor manufactures chips designed by its clients, most of which lack foundries of their own. Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom are among the major AI chip designers that rely on its services. The article cites the company's share of chip foundry revenue, which it says was 72.5 percent in the second quarter, as evidence that no rival has enough capacity to serve as a viable alternative. It also says clients have little reason to switch because the company offers best-in-class technology and strong production yields.

As demand for computing capacity grows, the author expects large chip orders to continue. The article reports that the company projected its AI chip revenues would grow at a compound annual rate in the mid-to-high 50 percent range from 2024 to 2029. During its third-quarter conference call, chief executive C.C. Wei reportedly said that growth probably would be higher than that projection. The author also argues the stock is not priced expensively, trading at 23 times forward expected earnings, which he describes as a discount to its typical level at this time of year.

He calls it a timely buy, while conceding that it may not deliver the best long-term AI returns. The article is promotional in nature and carries a standard disclaimer that the Motley Fool has positions in and recommends several of the stocks discussed. It also includes marketing material for the Motley Fool's Stock Advisor service, citing past returns for picks such as Netflix and Nvidia, and reports Stock Advisor's total average return at 852 percent against 203 percent for the S&P 500. The page lists related articles on the same company, though the articles provided do not indicate any subsequent corporate announcement, regulatory action or shift in the company's outlook beyond the projections quoted above.

Articles.Title: This Stock Is a Nearly Guaranteed Winner From the AI Infrastructure Buildout

stories.Headline: What Is Meta Platforms (META) Facing As Legal Risks Rise And AI Deals Expand?
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and other apps, faces a set of legal and business pressures that were reported on November 8, 2026. Meta joined Google and TikTok in suing California to block a new law aimed at users under 16. Separately, police in India registered a First Information Report against Meta over complaints about alleged child sexual abuse material on Instagram and Facebook. The same period brought disclosures that AMD agreed to terms under which Meta may gain rights to about 320 million AMD shares as part of AI chip related deals. The California law targets young users of social media, and the lawsuits seek to block it before it takes effect.

The Indian complaint centers on content found on Meta's two main platforms and has led to a formal police report. For investors, the article frames these matters as a test of how expensive new compliance rules could become and how much control regulators might seek over algorithms that decide what younger users see. Its focus is on how these pressures could affect the way Meta handles feeds and advertising for younger audiences. The article describes these developments as occurring alongside Meta's heavier spending on artificial intelligence, including its AMD arrangement and new fixed rate bonds and preferred securities used to fund infrastructure. It suggests the company is weighing the cost of that buildout against legal and child safety obligations, with the risk that both could strain free cash flow if new AI products fail to earn enough.

The article notes that guidance for 2026 capital spending falls in the US$130 to 145 billion range, though it does not state how management will present these items. Meta Platforms is discussed as a company that runs social apps, virtual reality devices and AI hardware partnerships at global scale. The article's stated checkpoint is how Meta explains its funding needs and legal exposure in its next major update, including comments on the California case and the Indian report. Observers will look for whether management ties its spending and regulatory situation to revenue from AI advertising, AI agents and messaging in upcoming earnings commentary. The article is general in nature, was produced with AI automation, and is not financial advice.

Articles.Title: What Is Meta Platforms (META) Facing As Legal Risks Rise And AI Deals Expand?

stories.Headline: Five9 (FIVN): Evercore ISI Downgraded the Stock Despite AI Revenue Growth Rate of 91%
stories.Summary:
Evercore ISI cut its rating on Five9 (FIVN) to In Line from Outperform on November 6, 2026, while keeping its price target at $24. The move came as the broader market was reeling, with the Nasdaq Composite falling 5.52% on November 5, its deepest one-day drop in 19 months. The index closed more than 10% below its October 6 record, confirming a technical correction. The S&P 500 slid 4.36% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 3.44% that day. Chipmakers and other AI-linked stocks took the heaviest losses.

The firm said that a clear turning point in Five9's growth is not yet visible and that near-term positive catalysts are missing. The company's third-quarter results contained real strength, with revenue rising 13% to $323.3 million and subscription revenue growing 16%. AI revenue reached roughly $45 million, up 91% from a year earlier, and management raised its full-year AI growth outlook to at least 75% from at least 60%. The weak spot was profit guidance, with fourth-quarter non-GAAP earnings per share guidance of $0.88 to $0.92 falling below estimates. Full-year guidance of $3.17 to $3.21 implies a lower midpoint than the $3.26 cited in prior quarters, and GAAP gross margin slipped to 53.4% from 55.0%.

The report ties the selloff to politics and to the Federal Reserve. Democrats won control of Congress in that week's elections, and investors worried that tougher rules on data centers could slow the buildout of AI infrastructure, according to Reuters. Separately, a hot jobs report showed employers adding 165,000 jobs in October, more than twice what economists expected, while the unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%. Traders then raised their bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike, with markets pricing about a 78% chance of a quarter-point increase at the December 8-9 meeting. Five9 also has a pending acquisition of Level AI, which it expects to close in the fourth quarter, and its guidance excludes that deal.

Articles.Title: Five9 (FIVN): Evercore ISI Downgraded the Stock Despite AI Revenue Growth Rate of 91%

stories.Headline: Stocks will drop further as AI investment slows next year then falls in 2028 and drags GDP down too
stories.Summary:
Capital Economics, a research firm, has forecast that stock prices will fall further as spending on artificial intelligence slows, with the drop reaching the broader economy by 2028. In a note published on Friday, November 6, 2026, the firm's chief economic adviser, Vicky Redwood, said AI investment will keep rising next year but at a slower pace before falling outright by around 10% in 2028. A handful of hyperscalers are expected to spend $800 billion this year, roughly double the year before, and an estimated $1 trillion or more in 2027. The note also describes stock market losses that have already been significant.

Redwood calculated that annual AI-related revenue from outside customers would need to grow tenfold by 2030 to justify that level of spending. She said that outcome is possible but would imply a far faster and more severe disruption to existing businesses and jobs than is currently visible. Higher AI investment added 0.3 percentage points to U.S. GDP growth last year, so a slowdown should trim a similar amount from recent growth, and a 10% capital spending drop could subtract about 0.1% from GDP. She expects the S&P 500 to sit 12% below its current level by the end of 2027, which would be 17% below its early-October peak. Tech-heavy indices, she added, could fall considerably more.

Redwood also said that a stock selloff would weigh on the economy through the wealth effect, which drives consumer spending. She estimated that the market's rally over the past year lifted GDP by about 0.4%, so a comparable decline would act as a drag of similar size. Taiwan's real GDP growth next year could be about 3 percentage points lower and South Korea's about 1 point lower, with further drag in 2028, since those economies depend more heavily on AI. Redwood did not describe a sudden collapse in investment or a deep downturn in the United States. She wrote that the economy should see slower growth in 2028 but not a major downturn.

Redwood also said AI should keep spreading and raising productivity, which she estimated will rise by about 1% per year for several years. Capital spending could stay relatively high even as it declines, because companies need to replace equipment, gain scale and compete in what she called a winner-takes-most race. Any reduction could also be spread over several years rather than arriving all at once. She noted that past capital spending booms have sometimes been followed by recessions, including after the dotcom bust in the early 2000s, but a fall in capital spending alone has generally not been enough to cause one. Her expectation is that investment will settle at a more sustainable pace rather than collapse.

Articles.Title: Stocks will drop further as AI investment slows next year then falls in 2028 and drags GDP down too

stories.Headline: ‘Let’s Talk’ series to hold session 2: ‘AI’s Moral Dilemma: AI and Ethics’
stories.Summary:
The Friends of the Solana Beach Library will hold a session titled "AI's Moral Dilemma: AI and Ethics" on Tuesday, Nov. 17, from 5:30 p.m. to 6:45 p.m. This is the second of four sessions in a series focused on artificial intelligence. The event is part of the group's "Let's Talk" series, which aims to build awareness and promote discussion on topics shaping the world. The talk was announced in a news release published November 8, 2026.

The session will examine the ethical concerns that have grown alongside the rapid expansion of AI. According to the announcement, AI development and use should account for transparency, accountability, sustainability, bias, and human agency and wellbeing. The release frames the central question as whether something should be done simply because it can be. Organizers say the talk will also cover moral questions raised by the development and the very large scale of AI systems. A recap of how people can use AI rather than having AI use them is also planned.

Two speakers will lead the discussion. Shelly Skinner is chief of AI Solutions and Governance at Salience AI, and Tulay Muezzinoglu is an AI engineer working in the public sector. The "Let's Talk" format features local experts and includes a question-and-answer period. The release describes the sessions as a way to demystify topics that are shaping the world.

The series will continue in the coming months with two additional sessions. The third session, "Taming the beast: AI and regulation," is set for March 16, 2027, from 5:30 p.m. to 6:45 p.m. The fourth, "Teaching the A(I)BCs: Tackling AI in Education," is scheduled for April 20, 2027. The announcement came from the Friends of the Solana Beach Library and was distributed as a news release.

Articles.Title: ‘Let’s Talk’ series to hold session 2: ‘AI’s Moral Dilemma: AI and Ethics’

stories.Headline: Replace all your AI subscriptions with this one $60 lifetime bundle
stories.Summary:
The article is a sponsored product promotion, not a news report, and it describes a bundle of five AI tools sold for a one-time price. According to Popular Science, published on November 8, 2026, the Lifetime AI Software Stack Bundle is on sale for $59.99, down from a listed value of $1,811.99. The bundle includes lifetime access to 1ForAll AI Pro, AskAnyModel AI, PromptBuilder Starter, Voibe Custom Plan, and Leelo AI Personal Plan. The article notes that the page may earn revenue from products it features and that it takes part in affiliate programs.

The bundle is described as a way to replace several separate AI subscriptions with one purchase. 1ForAll AI Pro handles text, voice, image, and video generation using models from OpenAI, Google, AWS, Azure, and Luma, and supports voice cloning, PDF-to-speech, and processing of an entire book at once. AskAnyModel AI sends a single query to as many as six models at the same time and shows the answers side by side, including results from Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini. PromptBuilder Starter, a Chrome extension, turns rough drafts into prompts for ten AI tools and allows up to 5,000 queries a month for life. Voibe provides voice-to-text dictation for Word, Outlook, Gmail, Google Docs, Slack, and other apps on Mac and Windows, while Leelo AI turns text into speech in 142 languages with authentic accents.

The article is written by the publication itself in promotional form, and it does not name an individual author or a company behind the five tools beyond the product names. It presents the bundle as a simplifying choice for people who pay for several AI services, and it says the bundle "handles all of that for you." The article does not offer independent testing, reviewer findings, or comments from the tool makers, so its claims about performance and value rest on its own description. It also does not state how long the sale price will last or what happens to buyers if any of the underlying services change.

Articles.Title: Replace all your AI subscriptions with this one $60 lifetime bundle

stories.Headline: ABNB Q3 2026 deep dive: AI-driven product expansion accelerates growth and margin gains
stories.Summary:
Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) reported third-quarter 2026 results that beat Wall Street expectations, with revenue rising 18.9% year on year to $4.87 billion, about 2.6% above analysts' estimates of $4.75 billion. Non-GAAP profit came to $3.16 per share, roughly 10.7% above consensus, and adjusted EBITDA reached $2.51 billion, a 51.5% margin that beat estimates of $2.36 billion. The stock reacted strongly, and the company's shares were reported to have jumped about 11.7% after the release. Management said the quarter reflected accelerated growth across all major regions, the rollout of new features, and an expanding product lineup.

Management tied the results to artificial intelligence and product work. The company launched more than 50 new features in the quarter, nearly 70% more than a year earlier, and AI tools resolved 40% of customer support issues without a human agent. All five of its core markets posted double-digit growth in nights booked, with Brazil up more than 30% and India up more than 60%. Gen Z was described as the fastest-growing guest segment, and the hotel pilot, now in more than 60 destinations, is growing faster than the core business. Airbnb also pointed to dynamic pricing tools, the single service fee, guest travel insurance, and a new exclusive deal with American Express Travel as contributors.

Chief executive Brian Chesky credited years of investment in technology and organizational structure, saying the results did not happen overnight and that the company had spent years changing how it operates. Chief financial officer Ellie Mertz said the company would keep investing in growth while staying profitable, describing continued momentum as the top priority. The company also hired Pepijn Rijvers as Chief Business Officer to strengthen international expansion and performance marketing. These remarks are paraphrased from management's comments on the earnings call.

Looking ahead, Airbnb plans to launch custom travel-focused AI agents in the first half of next year, which it expects will let users book a wider range of travel services inside its platform. Management projects multi-billion-dollar revenue potential from hotels in coming years and is integrating car rentals and meal delivery, while a loyalty program is under consideration. The article notes that analysts will watch the rollout of the AI agents, the pace of hotel and service expansion, and the effect of the American Express partnership on customer acquisition. Airbnb shares were trading at $188.91 at the time of the article, up from $170.13 before the earnings.

Articles.Title: ABNB Q3 2026 deep dive: AI-driven product expansion accelerates growth and margin gains

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang is living proof that AI’s rockstar CEOs are also a hidden risk
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board said on Sunday, November 8, 2026 that it is investigating reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair with an executive who, according to reports, was working with Chinese intelligence, and US officials reportedly suspect that person passed intelligence to China and helped smuggle advanced AI chips into the country. Huang said he was unfaithful, that his conduct hurt his wife and children, and that he takes full responsibility and accepts the criticism that follows. He also said he supports the board's investigation, and he did not name the other person involved.

The article's central point is that the fortunes of many leading AI companies depend heavily on a single leader, a risk often called "key man risk." Analyst Dan Ives told CNN that such powerful CEOs are both a blessing and a curse, and Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld said these companies have built a "solar system model" of leadership that can be problematic and needs deeper bench strength. Sonnenfeld noted that Nvidia has no obvious board succession plan, and that Huang has bragged about having 60 direct reports. The article contrasts this with JPMorgan Chase, which has built a deep roster of talent behind Jamie Dimon. Nvidia's annual filing says the company is "highly dependent" on its executive team and acknowledges that failure to ensure effective succession planning could hinder its long-term success.

The article describes Huang as central to Nvidia's rise into a company valued at $4.5 trillion, and as the industry's most prominent voice in Washington and abroad. It cites his role at a White House meeting in September 2026 on AI safety, his help in assembling a $500 billion plan to keep money flowing into AI chips, and his promotion of "sovereign AI" in European capitals. Nvidia disclosed $99 billion in equity investments across the AI ecosystem in September, up from $2.2 billion two years earlier. Sonnenfeld estimated only a 50/50 chance that Huang keeps his job, given the multiple investigations from the board and congressional committees, and suggested the board could move him into a symbolic role or bring in an experienced outside leader such as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. The article's account ends there, so the outcome of the investigation is not yet known.

Articles.Title: Jensen Huang is living proof that AI’s rockstar CEOs are also a hidden risk

stories.Headline: How Big Oil Became the AI Industry's Favorite Customer
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence companies are deepening ties with the fossil fuel industry, as major tech firms sign large deals with energy companies to power their data centers and to build AI into energy operations. On November 2, OpenAI, Abu Dhabi's ADNOC, and G42 signed a multi-year agreement to apply AI across ADNOC's operations, according to reporting from Semafor and Reuters. The deal was the most prominent example of a wider push at the ADIPEC energy conference, where tech companies pitched AI tools for running drilling rigs, refineries, and other oil assets. The reporting describes the OpenAI deal as one step in a growing relationship between the ChatGPT maker and the United Arab Emirates.

The trend also runs the other way, with fossil fuels supplying power to AI. Microsoft signed a 20-year deal with Chevron for 2.67 gigawatts of natural gas-fired power for a proposed West Texas data center. Amazon is building a gas-fired plant in Texas that, under its current plan involving seven natural gas plants, would become the single largest source of power-related emissions in the United States. In August, Nvidia said it would partner with Japan's SoftBank and the federal government to build the largest fossil fuel plant in the country to power an OpenAI project in Ohio. The article notes that legislation under the Trump administration has pushed tech companies to supply their own power, which has led many of them to sign large natural gas contracts.

The article cites a peer-reviewed study published in NPJ Climate Action that questions the claim that AI will save more energy than it uses. The study found that if fossil fuels gain economically from AI at all, the emissions enabled by AI would exceed the emissions avoided. Even if both fossil fuels and renewables benefited equally, global CO2 emissions would still rise by between 0.47 billion and 1.8 billion metric tons a year. Holly Alpine, a co-author of the research, told the Wall Street Journal that the low end is roughly comparable to Mexico's annual emissions. The article argues that the OpenAI-ADNOC deal signals where both sectors are heading.

Articles.Title: How Big Oil Became the AI Industry's Favorite Customer

stories.Headline: AI used to predict cavities
stories.Summary:
Researchers from New York University and several Brazilian universities used artificial intelligence to identify groups of people at high risk for tooth decay, and published their findings in the journal Caries Research on November 9, 2026. The team, led by Fernando Neves Hugo, chair of the Department of Epidemiology and Health Promotion at NYU College of Dentistry, analyzed existing data from the Brazilian Oral Health Survey, a national study coordinated by the Brazilian Ministry of Health. The data covered 23,726 people who took part in the 2023 survey, including children, adolescents and adults. The researchers ran several machine learning models on this data, which captures demographic details, social factors such as wealth, household density, private dental insurance and water source, behaviors such as time since the last dental visit, and clinical exam results for tooth decay.

The traditional analysis found that wealth and household density were the strongest predictors of cavity risk, with non-white populations at higher risk in every age group. Private dental insurance and recent dental visits were protective, and water source mattered a great deal: 62.5% of 12-year-olds without access to fluoridated water had cavities, compared with 35.5% of those who had fluoridated water. The AI models were able to predict cavity risk and severity by age group by weighing how much each factor contributed. Hugo said the approach can flag individuals whose profiles signal elevated risk that would otherwise be hidden inside community averages. The article does not describe any change to clinical practice or policy that the study requires.

Hugo said the tools could help target resources and preventive care to the groups that would benefit most, and he framed the approach as a way to make better use of limited public health funds. The researchers caution that the findings may carry over to other middle-income countries, but that local factors such as access to dental care and benefits would likely change which variables matter most elsewhere. Their stated goal is to repeat the analysis with factors specific to other countries. Hugo and his colleagues are preparing a similar analysis using data from the United States National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Additional authors are Jessye Melgarejo do Amaral Giordani, Orlando Luiz do Amaral Júnior and Maria Laura Braccini Fagundes of the Federal University of Santa Maria, and Juliana Balbinot Hilgert of the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul.

Articles.Title: AI used to predict cavities

stories.Headline: Lived Experience Advocacy Hub Webinar Opportunity: AI in Oncology
stories.Summary:
AICANcer, a patient-led non-profit that advocates for ethical, equal, safe and patient-centred artificial intelligence in cancer care, is offering an interactive online webinar on the use of AI in oncology. The session is hosted by the group's founder and president, Adiba Zeito, and features guest expert Dr. Douglas Flora. The listing was published by OncoDaily on November 8, 2026. The webinar is meant to connect clinical and technical AI expertise with patient-centred advocacy goals. The session will cover four topics: real-world applications of AI that are already helping cancer patients and care teams, strategies for building trust and inclusion so patients stay informed and confident about the technology, health equity in AI so that advances benefit all cancer communities rather than a few, and patient-centred policy that aligns clinical innovation with ethical, safe and patient-guided standards.

The format includes a live question-and-answer session. The organisers say the target audience includes patient advocates and cancer advocacy leaders, management teams and board members of cancer non-profits, and clinicians, oncology researchers and other healthcare professionals. Dr. Flora is described as the Executive Medical Director of Oncology Services at St. Elizabeth Healthcare, Editor-in-Chief of AI in Precision Oncology, and president of the Association of Cancer Care Centers. He is also the author of Rebooting Cancer Care, a co-founder of TensorBlack, the host of the OncologicAI podcast, and a cancer survivor. Ms. Zeito leads AICANcer, and the listing gives a contact email address for the organisation.

The listing does not give a date, time or registration details for the session. The webinar is presented as a discussion of how AI can progress responsibly in oncology, with the stated aim of keeping patient experience central to that progress. OncoDaily's page also links to other news on its site, including an item on lessons from the ESMO Congress 2026 focused on equity and patient advocacy. The listing does not say whether the webinar will be recorded or what outcomes or recommendations, if any, will follow it.

Articles.Title: Lived Experience Advocacy Hub Webinar Opportunity: AI in Oncology

stories.Headline: AI-assisted atomic models reveal how protective shells regulate aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Tohoku University have used a newly developed AI agent, called MLP Copilot, to build atomic models that show how protective oxide shells control the oxidation of aluminum nanoparticles. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on October 15, 2026, and the team's findings were reported on November 9, 2026. Aluminum nanoparticles store a large amount of chemical energy, but the thin oxide shell on their surface can limit how quickly they react with oxygen. Understanding how that shell changes could help future efforts to control oxidation and the release of energy.

The framework learns atomic energies and forces from quantum calculations, and the resulting models make larger simulations feasible. Across roughly 80 active-learning iterations, the team assembled 88,833 atomic configurations, with uncertain cases guiding additional quantum calculations and model training. Before using the model in oxidation simulations, the researchers checked it against reference results, thermodynamic properties and independent cluster tests. The coordination methods can be reused across other materials systems, with calculations, training data and validation adjusted for each application. Throughout the workflow, AI agents organized project knowledge and retrieved evidence, while computational tools kept datasets, model versions and evaluation reports.

The lead researcher, Hao Li, a distinguished professor at the Advanced Institute for Materials Research at Tohoku University, said the framework is meant to make materials science more efficient while keeping humans in control. The authors of the paper include Yiming Lu and colleagues. According to the researchers, human scientists still decided which models to accept, where to use them and how to interpret the results. Li compared the system to an autopilot that eases the work of pilots without replacing them.

The simulations found two behaviors in particles with an existing oxide shell. At moderate temperatures within the study, temporary nanoscale pathways let oxidation continue while limiting material transport, a behavior the team called a "breathing mode." At higher temperatures, the shell ruptured, exposing the aluminum core to oxygen and speeding up oxidation. The analyses pointed to outward aluminum transport as the dominant pathway under the conditions studied. The researchers also said that this kind of workflow could support future research into recursive self-improvement, though that idea remains a possibility rather than a demonstrated result.

Articles.Title: AI-assisted atomic models reveal how protective shells regulate aluminum nanoparticle oxidation

stories.Headline: Texas Just Became a Swing State for the AI Economy
stories.Summary:
Texas has become a fault line in the artificial intelligence economy after voters elected Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who ran on halting new data centers, over Gov. Greg Abbott by a lead of more than 700,000 votes in unofficial returns. Hinojosa wants an immediate statewide moratorium on new facilities that would last until lawmakers write protections giving communities a say, end industry subsidies and guarantee that households will not pay higher electric bills. She is due to be sworn in on Jan. 19, after the Legislature convenes earlier that month. The article notes that the freeze did not begin with her, since Abbott already started it.

Abbott acted first. On Aug. 3 he ordered the Public Utility Commission and the grid operator, ERCOT, to audit every data center in the interconnection process before any advanced, with projects that fell short to be refused a connection. His office put the pending requests at roughly 474 gigawatts, more than five times the grid's record peak demand, and said about 90 percent came from data centers. On Sept. 21 he widened the freeze with a letter ordering the state environmental regulator to stop granting data center permits until the review was finished, and the regulator said on Oct. 19 that it was complying. A 2025 law already requires large new customers to pay at least $100,000 for an initial screening study and contribute to connection costs, and Abbott has pledged to work with lawmakers to strip the industry's financial incentives.

The audit is advancing. In a preliminary summary presented on Nov. 5, ERCOT said all 245 large loads of 75 megawatts or more had answered its questionnaire, representing about 166 gigawatts of requested capacity, with 33 projects each seeking more than a gigawatt and making up about 36 percent of the total. West Texas holds the largest share, about 73 gigawatts, and ERCOT aims to publish a final report on Dec. 10. The gap between the 474 and 166 gigawatt figures reflects different counts, since the larger one covered every big request while the smaller covers only the data center projects that responded, and neither should be read as a guarantee that projects will be built.

The article's author argues that delay is the central cost, because projects waiting for connections still bear land, equipment and financing expenses, and developers will price that risk and some may move to friendlier states. The author adds that Long Island readers feel the exposure through retirement accounts, pension funds and lenders backing the AI buildout, since a large share of that investment is placed in Texas. The article concludes that the boom is not ending but that the industry must now win permits and elections rather than only customers. How long the pause lasts depends on how quickly lawmakers act, and a moratorium tied to future legislation could extend well into 2027.

Articles.Title: Texas Just Became a Swing State for the AI Economy

stories.Headline: Enterprise AI is waiting for its Transformer moment
stories.Summary:
A professor of innovation argues in a November 2026 Fast Company essay that enterprise AI is still waiting for its equivalent of the 2017 Transformer breakthrough. He opens with the Google paper "Attention Is All You Need," which eight Google researchers published in 2017 to define the Transformer architecture. That architecture later underpinned GPT and much of the generative AI wave that followed. The author notes that Google incorporated the design into products such as Translate and Search but did not turn it into the defining product of the era, while OpenAI built GPT and ChatGPT on top of it.

The essay argues that today's enterprise AI rests on individual capability rather than organizational design. It cites McKinsey's 2026 survey, in which 80% of respondents reported better personal productivity but only 37% reported a positive contribution to enterprise EBIT, with no significant change from the prior year. It adds that high performers tend to redesign their workflows instead of inserting AI into existing ones. The author says the industry is starting from the agent and treating coordination of agents as the main problem, which he sees as different from building an intelligent organization. He also points to Gartner's forecast that more than 40% of agentic projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027 because of cost, unclear value or inadequate risk controls.

As the author describes it, the missing layer would be a persistent, goal-directed organizational system that owns the company's representation of its business, including its state, objectives, constraints, authority and accumulated experience. Agents and models would supply reasoning or execution, while the system would hold them to deterministic authorization outside the model, escalation paths and an append-only record linking intent, action and outcome. He says recent NIST guidance and a Microsoft reference architecture both separate reasoning from policy and keep immutable audit evidence. He argues that a true breakthrough would make coordination, governance, memory, accountability and continuous learning simpler to manage because a single design handles them.

The author places responsibility for the current gap with today's AI leaders, whom he says are repeating the mistakes that incumbents made in earlier cycles. He recalls that Google's hurried Bard response led to errors and about $100 billion in lost market value in February 2023. He also recounts how Yahoo! declined to meet with Larry Page and Sergey Brin about PageRank and Excite doubted its business value. He concludes that whoever supplies the organizing principle for intelligence at organizational scale could reshape the industry, and that this architecture may come from a company other than today's model leader.

Articles.Title: Enterprise AI is waiting for its Transformer moment

stories.Headline: Elvis Presley rights holders sue AI music generator over licensing, copyright violations
stories.Summary:
Elvis Presley Enterprises leads a group of plaintiffs who have sued Suno, an artificial intelligence music generator, claiming the company used The King's name, image and likeness along with copyrighted works without permission. The complaint was filed on a Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, and the article, published November 9, 2026, reports it. The plaintiffs say Suno trained its models on protected materials and let users generate songs that imitate Presley's distinctive voice. A second group, known as the Raleigh plaintiffs, who control hundreds of other songs including Chubby Checker's 1955 hit "Let's Twist Again," joined the suit. Together the two groups say Suno infringed on 859 combined works.

The plaintiffs rely on Tennessee's Ensuring Likeness, Voice, and Image Security Act, commonly called the ELVIS Act, which extends state protection against unauthorized use of a person's likeness to include their voice. They also allege direct copyright infringement, violations of Tennessee's common law right of publicity, circumvention of copyright protection measures, and removal or alteration of copyright management information. They ask the court for an injunction barring further infringement, an order requiring Suno to destroy unauthorized copies, including those in data sets, and a complete record of its training data, plus damages for both groups. The complaint includes nearly 50 recorded examples that the plaintiffs say show Suno's outputs directly infringing on Presley's likeness and their copyrights.

The plaintiffs argue that Suno made false public statements, saying the platform does not reproduce specific melodies from others' songs and has never allowed prompts for specific artists or copyrighted songs. Their complaint contends the recorded examples contradict those assertions, and it accuses Suno of acting intentionally, maliciously and fraudulently for financial gain. Suno did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A representative for the plaintiffs, Lark-Marie Antón, said the complaint and its exhibits speak for themselves and that the rights to Presley's name, image, likeness and music are protected vigorously. Attorneys from Adams & Reese and Skaggs Faucette represent both groups.

The same attorneys also represent Eight Mile Style, the publisher that administers songs by Eminem, which filed a separate copyright suit against Suno the same day in the same court. That complaint accuses Suno of training on copyrighted works and using copyrighted lyrics in its outputs. Earlier, in late October, Elvis Presley Enterprises had sued the AI developer Anthropic over alleged direct copyright infringement. The article does not say how the court will rule on these claims or when any hearings are scheduled.

Articles.Title: Elvis Presley rights holders sue AI music generator over licensing, copyright violations

stories.Headline: AI Model Distinguishes SLE Immune Profiles from Healthy Controls
stories.Summary:
A study published in Clinical and Experimental Medicine reports that an artificial intelligence model could tell apart the immune profiles of people with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) from those of healthy people. The research team, led by P.-Y. Li and M.-H. Chen, analyzed blood samples from 18 SLE patients and 21 healthy controls. The article's date is November 8, 2026, and it was reported by Scienmag and bioengineer.org. The researchers examined granulocytes, B cells, T lymphocytes, and regulatory cells to look for changes linked to the disease.

The model reached a precision, recall, and area under the curve of 1.00 in this group, which the article describes as a perfect separation between patients and controls. The researchers found that SLE patients had higher levels of effector memory and terminal effector CD4+ T cells, marginal zone B cells, and IgMhi B cells. Patients had lower levels of memory, follicular, and IgMdim B cells. The authors describe this pattern as an active primary humoral response, meaning an imbalance in which some B cell groups are expanded and others are reduced. The model relied most heavily on five subsets, namely follicular, IgMhi, and IgMdim B cells, CTLA4+PD-1+ cells within FoxP3+ CD4+ Treg cells, and effector memory CD8+ αβ T cells.

The article stresses that the sample was small, and it says the generalizability of the findings to a larger and more diverse population remains to be determined. The study was designed to assess immune cell profile changes and the role of specific subsets in separating the groups. The authors and the article's writer say future studies in larger cohorts will need to validate the AI model before its robustness can be confirmed. The research is presented as adding to the understanding of how SLE develops by linking particular immune cell changes to the disease state. The article does not describe any clinical use or diagnostic deployment of the model.

Articles.Title: AI Model Distinguishes SLE Immune Profiles from Healthy Controls

stories.Headline: Suno AI Music Generator Sued Again For Copyright Infringement
stories.Summary:
Two groups that hold music rights have filed separate lawsuits against Suno, the AI music generator, accusing it of copyright infringement. One group owns the rights to Elvis Presley's music, and the other is Eight Mile Style, a music publishing company that owns hundreds of Eminem recordings. According to the reporting, both suits include examples of songs made with Suno that allegedly sound like Presley or copy Eminem's lyrics. The articles do not give the filing dates.

The plaintiffs' attorneys argued that Suno's tools make human creativity obsolete by copying, without a license, what takes artists years to learn and refine. Suno responded that it does not permit any unauthorized use of an artist's work and that it bans the use of specific artists' names and songs. The company also said it works with third-party firms to screen for potential misuse. The articles do not say what remedies the plaintiffs are seeking in these two suits.

The group that controls Presley's music rights has been pursuing AI copyright claims more broadly. It recently sued Anthropic, seeking $41 million in damages over allegedly training its AI models on Presley's works without permission. These new suits add to a growing list of complaints against Suno. Earlier this year, Sony Music Entertainment and Universal Music Group jointly sued Suno, alleging that its latest v6 models still infringe their copyrighted material. Warner Music Group, by contrast, dropped its lawsuit against Suno last year and agreed to a licensing deal instead.

Articles.Title: Suno AI Music Generator Sued Again For Copyright Infringement

stories.Headline: Shift in Aussie job market as AI begins to show up for these professions: 'The end of the beginning'
stories.Summary:
The Australian Bureau of Statistics has begun asking employers whether artificial intelligence is leading them to hire more or fewer staff, and the first results suggest some professions are already feeling the effects. The latest job vacancy data, released by the ABS in the week before the article was published, shows an overall decline in available jobs. The survey finds the sharpest drop in information, media and telecommunications, where 16 per cent of businesses report fewer vacancies. Wholesale trade follows, with a net 8 per cent of companies reporting fewer openings.

The article says the falls may reflect more than automation, since AI can also reduce demand for the services companies sell, as people turn to chatbots instead of search engines. It notes the survey shows the share of organisations with fewer or more vacancies, not the number of positions lost, so a few large employers could be hiring while many smaller ones cut back. Public administration and safety show mixed signals, with AI likely to streamline government information work while also driving new policy and cyber-defence roles. The electricity, gas, water and waste services sector is the clear exception, with many vacancies tied to building the data centres that AI requires.

The author, Jason Murphy, writes that the national decline is small, at 0.9 per cent over the three months to August and 1.2 per cent over the year. He argues that the broader fall owes more to the Reserve Bank of Australia's recent interest rate rises than to AI, at least for now. He describes the current period as the end of the beginning, meaning the stage where AI's effect on jobs is being measured rather than guessed at. He adds that past technologies such as electricity and the internet eventually created new jobs, though the transition may be painful for some workers in the meantime.

Articles.Title: Shift in Aussie job market as AI begins to show up for these professions: 'The end of the beginning'

stories.Headline: Capital Economics Warns AI Investment Boom Is Fading, Sees S&P 500 Falling 12% by End of 2027
stories.Summary:
On Friday, research firm Capital Economics issued a note warning that the AI investment boom is losing momentum and that stock markets will fall further. In it, Chief Economic Adviser Vicky Redwood said AI can still raise productivity but questioned whether the revenue from AI will be enough to justify current spending levels. A small group of hyperscalers is projected to spend $800 billion this year, double the previous year's figure, with about $1 trillion or more expected in 2027. Redwood calculated that annual AI-related revenue from outside customers would need to rise roughly tenfold by 2030 to support that level of spending. Redwood expects AI investment to keep rising next year but more slowly, then fall by about 10% in 2028.

Because higher AI investment added 0.3 percentage point to U.S. GDP growth last year, she estimated a slowdown would subtract a similar amount from recent growth. A 10% drop in capital spending might cut GDP by about 0.1%, which she described as a modest effect. She contrasted this with more AI-dependent Asian economies, where Taiwan's growth next year is expected to be about 3 percentage points lower and South Korea's about 1 point lower. Redwood expects the S&P 500 to be 12% below its current level by the end of 2027, which would leave it 17% below its early-October peak. She also expects tech-heavy indices to fall much more than the broader index.

She noted that tighter financial conditions, such as higher energy prices or term premia, could make it harder to finance investment. She added that a market selloff would weigh on consumer spending through the wealth effect, with last year's market rally having lifted GDP by around 0.4%. Despite these warnings, Redwood expects AI to keep spreading through the economy and improving productivity, supported by infrastructure already built. She said capital spending could stay relatively high even after declining, since hyperscalers must replace depreciating equipment and remain competitive in a race where the biggest players tend to win. She also suggested that companies could spread any cuts over several years rather than making them all at once.

Articles.Title: Capital Economics Warns AI Investment Boom Is Fading, Sees S&P 500 Falling 12% by End of 2027

stories.Headline: How agentic AI models could (finally) open the door for agent-based modeling in economics
stories.Summary:
The only article provided is an opinion blog post by an economist, published November 8, 2026, on the website Economist Writing Every Day. It is the third in a series and argues that agentic AI, meaning large language models that can pursue goals and adjust their behavior with little human input, could help revive agent-based modeling in economics. The author describes agent-based models as computer simulations of economic systems in which heterogeneous agents such as consumers, firms and workers follow behavioral rules and interact to produce aggregate outcomes. The post does not report a new event, a decision by any institution, or a finished study.

The author's central concern is the curse of dimensionality. Agent-based models are parameter rich, so a researcher facing thousands of possible parameter combinations cannot test every one, and a full grid search could take an impractically long time. The author's example model has five attributes per agent type, three statistical properties per attribute, several functional variants per rule, and a grid of at least 5,000 combinations before timing, sequencing and environment are even considered. The proposed remedy is to narrow the search with a golden section approach, which iteratively shrinks the interval toward an optimum, and to have an agentic AI make the decisions about what to vary and what to assume.

The author proposes that a base model be handed to an agentic AI, which would recursively revise it until the results met four conditions set by researchers: a falsified theoretical prediction, outcomes generated through observable mechanisms, dependence on a maximal set of modeler decisions, and independence from unlimited but fully observable decisions. To keep the result transparent, the author suggests constraining the AI to a pre-defined modeling language or library, capping the amount of code, and requiring it to itemize and defend every deviation from the base model. The author writes in the first person and presents the ideas as advice to graduate students, while also saying they are not fully convinced of AI's promise in other fields. The article does not describe any implementation, data, or results, and it does not indicate what researchers or institutions have said or done in response.

Articles.Title: How agentic AI models could (finally) open the door for agent-based modeling in economics

stories.Headline: AI-Managed Hybrid Solar-Wind-Battery System Cuts Grid Import in Simulation
stories.Summary:
A simulation study published in Discover Energy describes a grid-connected hybrid system that pairs solar, wind and battery storage with artificial intelligence managing how energy is dispatched. The research was authored by V. A. Sawant, S. S. Chaugule and D. Daphale, and the article was published on November 8, 2026, with the lead report carried by Scienmag. The system combines a 100 kW PV array, a 50 kW wind subsystem and a 60 kWh lithium-ion battery, all connected through a common 800 V DC bus. The AI layer runs on a 60-second cycle and uses forecasting plus a reinforcement learning dispatcher, while fast device-level controls handle power quality beneath it.

The design separates the AI dispatch from the converter switching, so a bounded supervisory layer limits the AI commands and keeps grid-code compliance even if the AI fails. In a 24-hour test using data for a spring day in Pune, India, the dispatcher cut daily grid import from 190 kWh to 162 kWh, a 14.8% reduction against a rule-based baseline. Across four seasonal days, import reductions ranged from 11.9% to 16.2%, averaging 14.6% when weighted by season, with the largest gains in summer and monsoon periods. The study also estimates that cycling fell from 1.4 to 1.1 full cycles per day, pushing battery end-of-life from year 11.2 to year 13.0, and it projects a levelized cost of energy of 0.057 USD/kWh against 0.063 USD/kWh for the baseline, a 9.5% reduction.

The authors report the figures as model-based predictions built in MATLAB/Simulink, and they state that hardware validation has not yet been carried out. The power-quality results, measured against IEEE-519 limits, showed grid-current total harmonic distortion of 2.18% at full bandwidth and 1.60% up to the 50th order, with fifth-harmonic content at 0.84% against a 4.0% limit. The authors also noted that the system's negative-sequence detection met IEEE-1547-2018 but missed the stricter 10 ms target of IEEE-2800-2022, taking 8 ms to detect the fault. They describe the study as a step toward integrating AI dispatch with robust inverter control, and they plan next to test the controller on a hardware-in-the-loop platform and a 10 kVA prototype, along with grid-forming operation and cybersecurity studies.

Articles.Title: AI-Managed Hybrid Solar-Wind-Battery System Cuts Grid Import in Simulation

stories.Headline: Sakana AI Targets Record Japanese IPO, Seeking to Top Mercari's 2018 Benchmark
stories.Summary:
Sakana AI, a Japanese generative AI startup, is preparing for a possible initial public offering as early as fall 2027, according to a November 10, 2026 report from BusinessKorea. The listing could become one of the largest IPOs in Japan's startup history and would be the first by a Japanese company specializing in generative AI. Market expectations cited in the report suggest its market capitalization on the first day of trading could exceed 680 billion yen, about $4.3 billion, the benchmark set by Mercari in 2018. The venue, timing, offering size and valuation have not been finalized.

The company has selected Goldman Sachs as an IPO adviser and is in discussions with Daiwa Securities and SMBC Nikko Securities. It is considering a listing on the Tokyo Stock Exchange or Nasdaq. Sakana AI says it will use the proceeds to develop its own Japanese AI models, recruit talent and expand sales. Its model, tentatively named Sakana Sawara, is slated for a smaller release in spring 2027 before a larger version follows, and the company aims to lift annualized revenue above 30 billion yen in 2027, roughly ten times its projected 2026 figure. The report notes that annualized revenue is an extrapolation of a period's revenue over a full year rather than actual revenue earned.

The article identifies Sakana AI's leadership as the company's founders, David Ha and Llion Jones, former Google AI researchers, and Ren Ito, a former Mercari executive. Their stated strategy centers on "AI sovereignty," keeping technology and operations within Japan, and on combining existing open-source models with evolutionary techniques to reach high performance with fewer computing resources. The report says the company's current product, Sakana Fugu, depends on overseas foundation models, which is why it is building Sawara to conduct its own pre-training. Clients named include MUFG Bank, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp. and Sumitomo Corp., and in July 2026 the company signed a proof-of-concept contract with Japan's Ministry of Defense.

The company was founded in 2023 and became a unicorn about a year later. In November 2025 it was valued at about 400 billion yen in a funding round involving Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group and other investors, and it has drawn investment from Nvidia and Google. The article warns that global investor sentiment is a risk to the IPO, pointing to uncertainty over AI regulation and data center investment following the U.S. midterm elections, along with possible shifts in funding and listing plans at companies such as Anthropic. It adds that the company's ability to show its own model performs well and is commercially viable is likely to be a key factor in its prospects.

Articles.Title: Sakana AI Targets Record Japanese IPO, Seeking to Top Mercari's 2018 Benchmark - Businesskorea

stories.Headline: In March 2000, Cisco Briefly Became The World's Most Valuable Company As Its Stock Closed At $80.06. Buyers That Day Waited More Than 25 Years For It To Close Higher. Here's What AI Investors Need To Know
stories.Summary:
In March 2000, Cisco Systems briefly became the world's most valuable company when its shares closed at $80.06 on March 27, pushing its market value to $555.5 billion on basic shares, according to the Associated Press. That put it just ahead of Microsoft, which stood at $541.6 billion. Buyers who paid that closing price waited more than 25 years for the stock to close higher. The shares then collapsed as the Nasdaq came apart, and the recovery took until December 2025.

The fall was severe. From the March 27, 2000 close to the October 11, 2002 close, Cisco shares dropped 87.11%, with the low at $10.32. Cisco first paid a quarterly dividend in 2011, and buybacks have shaped its market value since then. Investors who held on have since collected dividends, though the company's market value at the December 2025 high still sat roughly $250 billion below its 2000 peak, according to Matt Phillips of Sherwood News.

Cisco's business kept growing through the decline, with revenue, profits and earnings per share rising sharply since 1999, as the Financial Times noted. Today the company sells AI infrastructure, reporting fiscal 2026 revenue of $63.3 billion and AI infrastructure orders from hyperscalers of $9.3 billion. Chair and CEO Chuck Robbins said Cisco is well positioned as critical infrastructure for the AI era. The company expects $7.5 billion in AI infrastructure revenue in fiscal 2027.

The comparison to Nvidia, the leading supplier of AI chips, has drawn attention from analysts. Nvidia trades at roughly 37 times earnings, far below the multiple above 200 Cisco carried at its peak, yet its shares have still fallen 21.14% over the past month. Cisco is expected to report again on November 12, a date the company has not confirmed, while Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results on November 17. Writers at 24/7 Wall St. argue the lesson is that the price paid for growth matters as much as the growth itself.

Articles.Title: In March 2000, Cisco Briefly Became The World's Most Valuable Company As Its Stock Closed At $80.06. Buyers That Day Waited More Than 25 Years For It To Close Higher. Here's What AI Investors Need To Know

stories.Headline: AI hub push 'risks hurting green goals'
stories.Summary:
Thailand's push to become a regional artificial intelligence hub could undermine its sustainability goals unless data centre growth is matched by cleaner energy and more efficient technology, according to an AI expert. Asst Prof Etienne Mueller of CMKL University raised the concern at the Sustainability Expo 2026 in Bangkok, speaking on a talk stage about AI and green data centres. The remarks were reported on November 8, 2026. CMKL, Thailand's AI-focused university, was founded through a collaboration between Carnegie Mellon University and King Mongkut's Institute of Technology Ladkrabang. Mueller's warning centred on the rapidly growing power needs of AI infrastructure.

Thailand is drawing AI and data centre investment, partly because building restrictions in Singapore have pushed hyperscalers toward the kingdom. In early 2026, 88 AI and data centre projects worth US$27 billion were approved, and investment is projected to reach 570 billion baht by 2030. Electricity demand from the sector is expected to hit 6 terawatt-hours by 2030, equal to 2.5% of national consumption. Each AI server rack can draw up to 80 kilowatts, which is 16 times the power of a standard configuration. Mueller warned that this expansion is outpacing the buildout of solar and wind power, making operators more likely to rely on natural gas.

Mueller also described a "Green Squeeze," in which corporate demand for certified renewable energy could take up Thailand's limited clean power supply, leaving households and local industries more dependent on fossil fuels. He urged more efficient AI algorithms and software, citing methods such as model quantisation, model distillation and Mixture-of-Experts architectures. He also pointed to the potential of Thai-language AI models to offer greater accuracy with less computing power. On the operations side, he suggested closed-loop water recycling, electronic waste recovery and waste heat reuse, and said corporate clean power purchases should add new generation rather than simply redirect existing supply.

At the same event, Mueller presented AI as a tool that could also support sustainability. He said AI could help balance electricity grids, monitor emissions, deforestation, biodiversity and forest-fire risks, speed up the discovery of materials for clean technologies, and improve precision agriculture. His overall message was that these benefits depend on how the expansion is managed. The articles do not describe any government response or binding measures arising from the talk.

Articles.Title: AI hub push 'risks hurting green goals'

stories.Headline: New AI Model Classifies Wheat Leaf Diseases with High Accuracy
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Koneru Lakshmaiah Education Foundation in India have developed a lightweight deep learning model called ACCM-Net to classify wheat leaf diseases, and their study was published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence. The model was reported on November 8, 2026, by bioengineer.org and Scienmag, and it is built to tell apart healthy wheat leaves, Septoria tritici blotch, and Stripe rust. The authors describe both fungal diseases as among the most economically damaging to wheat crops. The model is intended as a practical diagnostic tool, since early symptoms of the two infections look alike to the eye.

The team says earlier deep learning systems struggled with class imbalance, complex lesion patterns, and uneven field conditions such as shadows, leaf folding, and background clutter. ACCM-Net instead concentrates on improving the features extracted from leaf images rather than simply making the network deeper. Images pass through a three-stage preprocessing pipeline that includes contrast enhancement and edge detection before reaching the classifier. The model uses a frozen MobileNetV2 backbone followed by an attention module called CBAM, which helps the network focus on the regions of a leaf that show disease. The authors say this design keeps the model compact, with about 3.98 million parameters and an inference time of 40.58 milliseconds per image on their workstation.

The model was tested on 407 original wheat leaf images from Kaggle, distributed as 102 healthy, 97 Septoria, and 208 Stripe rust images. The training set was balanced to 200 images per class through augmentation, and a separate test set of 40 images was held out before augmentation to avoid data leakage. ACCM-Net reached an overall accuracy of 97.56 percent, an F1-score of 97.60 percent, a sensitivity of 98.41 percent, and a specificity of 98.92 percent. The authors report that across five training runs with different random seeds, the average accuracy was 97.50 percent with a standard deviation of 1.77 percent. They also say the model outperformed several comparison models, including MobileNetV2, InceptionV3, VGG19, and a baseline CNN trained from scratch, which reached only 0.67 accuracy.

The authors themselves caution that the evaluation was small, with only 40 images in the independent test set, so the strong results may not hold on larger or more varied datasets from different locations, seasons, and imaging equipment. They note that generalizability has not yet been verified and that hardware-specific testing for handheld or sensor-based deployment remains future work. The article does not describe any planned trials, commercial release, or farmer adoption timeline. It does say that further research with large-scale, multi-location data is needed before the model can be confirmed for real-world field use.

Articles.Title: New AI Model Classifies Wheat Leaf Diseases with High Accuracy

stories.Headline: AI chatbots can flip-flop on false claims when users keep repeating them
stories.Summary:
A study published in Scientific Reports found that large language models can flip-flop on false claims when the same misinformation is repeated within a conversation. The research, led by Jordan Rodriguez of the University of Arizona with colleagues, tested seven models, including ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama-3-70B, and DeepSeek-R1. Under repetition, the models affirmed false statements in between 0.08% and 12.3% of their responses, depending on the model. Some models moved back and forth between accepting and rejecting the same claim across successive exchanges.

The researchers wrote 100 false statements, mostly by altering or inverting well-known facts, and ranged from easily spotted errors to more obscure ones. In the first experiment, each statement was repeated 50 times in a single conversation, and ChatGPT 3.5 drifted toward accepting more falsehoods, rising from affirming 3 statements on the first prompt to 18 by the 50th repetition. A second experiment used 33 increasingly forceful prompts, from mild disagreement to direct insults, and most models resisted this pressure. DeepSeek was the exception, with its affirmation rate rising from 1.0% under repetition to 22.2% under argument, though its sarcastic replies made it hard to judge whether it truly agreed. In a third experiment, the researchers resubmitted the models' earlier errors in fresh conversations, and most models corrected them, with Llama-3-70B fixing 96% and ChatGPT 3.5 only 32%.

The authors described the findings as showing that conversational dynamics reveal failure modes that standard tests miss, with consequences for choosing and using models in settings where truth is critical. The researchers caution that generative AI changes quickly, so the tested models have largely been superseded and the results may not carry over to newer versions or updates. They also noted that providers' default settings differ, so the models were not tested under identical conditions. Annotators were members of the research team and affiliated graduate students, and it remains unclear how often real users apply this kind of sustained pressure, a question the team plans to explore.

Articles.Title: AI chatbots can flip-flop on false claims when users keep repeating them

stories.Headline: Best AI Chatbot for Customer Support: $1 vs $4 [2026]
stories.Summary:
The Tech Insider article compares four AI models for customer support chatbots as of 8 November 2026, covering Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Terra, Gemini 4 Argon and GLM-5.3-Flash. Its main point is that the model behind a chat window often matters more to the bill than the software product itself. The four options shipped or changed price within roughly ten weeks, with Anthropic releasing Opus 5.5 on 22 September, OpenAI launching GPT-6.1 Terra on 26 October, Google making Gemini 4 Argon generally available on 13 October, and Z.ai open-sourcing GLM-5.3-Flash on 26 August. The article is aimed at teams building directly on a model, and it says it leaves out packaged helpdesk products such as Intercom Fin or Zendesk AI.

The article gives the prices it could confirm, all in US dollars per million tokens and excluding Irish VAT. GPT-6.1 Terra is listed at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, while Gemini 4 Argon's introductory price ends on 30 November and then rises to $4 for input and $20 for output. Claude Sonnet 5 is listed at $2 input and $10 output, and the article notes that its introductory price became permanent on 10 August 2026. GLM-5.3-Flash is priced at one-tenth of GLM-5.3, with secondary reports putting it at $0.15 and $0.50, though the author treats those figures as unconfirmed. To illustrate the cost, the article assumes 2,000 input tokens and 400 output tokens per chat, and it stresses that these are assumptions to be replaced with a team's own transcripts.

The article attributes the pricing and capability figures to the vendors' own announcement pages, and it says Anthropic states that Opus 5.5 charges 20% less per token than Opus 5. It also reports Anthropic's claim that the model costs 40% less to run on typical workloads. Google, Z.ai and OpenAI each appear through their own published descriptions of their models, and the article notes that where a vendor has not published a figure, its table says so rather than guessing. It also points out that no neutral, support-specific benchmark covers all four models, so the vendor-run tests it collects should be read as signals rather than verdicts.

The article's wider argument is that caching and conversation length can shift costs more than headline prices. It says that support bots resend the same system prompt on every turn, so cached input rates can reduce the bill sharply, with Terra's cached rate at one-twentieth of its input rate and Argon's introductory cached rate at a 95% discount. It adds that escalations to human agents and the cost of wrong answers sit outside the token table. The article states that GLM-5.3-Flash is the only one of the four that can be self-hosted, which changes the data-protection conversation, and it advises building the bot so the model name is a configuration value.

Articles.Title: Best AI Chatbot for Customer Support: $1 vs $4 [2026]

stories.Headline: AI Model Predicts Fertilizer Spread Width from Video
stories.Summary:
A team at the University of Regina and its collaborators has built a computer vision system that estimates how wide a fertilizer spreader distributes material, using only video of the spreading. The work, published in Smart Agricultural Technology, pairs a ResNet-18 convolutional neural network with a Transformer encoder to read sequences of frames. The approach removes the need for collection trays placed on the ground or analysis of the field after the spreader has passed. The authors frame it as a way to assess spreading performance while the machine is running.

The problem being addressed is that swath width, the spacing between passes, controls how much adjacent passes overlap and therefore how evenly fertilizer lands. Uneven spreading can waste nutrients, raise costs and contribute to runoff and leaching. The standard tray-based methods in ISO 5690 and ASAE S341.2 are accurate but must be run offline and consume material, while Discrete Element Method simulations are too computationally heavy for field use. Because labeled footage of real fertilizer spreading was scarce, the team trained the model on synthetic video produced by a simplified Python model of particles moving under gravity and aerodynamic drag. The training set covered variations in disk diameter, disk speed, disk height, wind speed and wind direction.

The model extracts a 512-dimensional feature vector from each frame, and a Transformer encoder with two layers and eight attention heads reads the sequence to output one value in meters. The training set contained 297 simulation scenarios, 162 under baseline conditions and 135 with varying wind, and was fitted with the Adam optimizer over 30 epochs. On held-out synthetic data, the wide-field-of-view version reached a mean absolute error of 0.529 meters and an R² of 0.996. Against independent EDEM simulations, the error was 0.535 meters with an R² of 0.954. In laboratory tests with a Scotts Elite Spreader and a ZED 2 stereo camera, using real image sequences, the model recorded an error of 0.11 meters and a mean absolute percentage error of 7.26 percent against collector-bin measurements.

The researchers attribute the model's performance to its wide field of view, which captured the full spreading pattern, and to a pre-processing pipeline that applied lens undistortion, gamma correction and contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization to the real images. A full 25-frame sequence was processed in 1.318 seconds, or about 18.96 frames per second on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 GPU, and the authors say further optimization is needed before the system could drive closed-loop control. The study also notes limits: the lab test used a small spreader and few conditions, the training data was built for commercial-sized spreaders, and field factors such as soil, vegetation, shadows, dust and changing light remain untested. The authors call for commercial-scale field validation, estimates of distribution uniformity, and faster inference on embedded hardware.

Articles.Title: AI Model Predicts Fertilizer Spread Width from Video

stories.Headline: I Let AI Redesign a Key Living Room Feature (the Results Surprised Me!)
stories.Summary:
The only article supplied is a lifestyle piece from Apartment Therapy, republished on AOL on November 8, 2026, by writer Cori Sears. In it, Sears describes struggling to style the built-in shelves in her living room, a space that also holds an internet modem, TV remotes, and her husband's PlayStation. Ahead of the holidays, she tested ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude with the same prompt, asking for a minimalist, timeless winter or holiday look and uploading a photo of the shelf. Sears found the three tools gave very different results.

ChatGPT produced several inspiration images that she found the most useful, though she noted that its renderings distort proportion and look heavily filtered. Gemini generated mockups she disliked, and she said they focused too heavily on the word "minimalist." Claude's free version could not generate images, so it offered written guidance and web inspiration photos instead, which she found less helpful as a visual learner. Sears chose ChatGPT's suggestions and rebuilt her shelves using decor she already owned, with no shopping trips.

She kept the lamp, a framed picture, a potted plant, and a wicker basket, then added brass candlesticks, wintry artwork, tonal books, vases, white ceramic Christmas houses, and greenery she foraged from her backyard. She kept the PlayStation and modem on the middle shelf because they are part of daily life. She concluded that the AI blueprint helped her past a creative block, though she noted that she already owned many of the suggested items. The article does not say what, if anything, happens next beyond her plan to use the approach for future seasonal vignettes.

Articles.Title: I Let AI Redesign a Key Living Room Feature (the Results Surprised Me!)

stories.Headline: AI Vehicle Maintenance System Merges Environmental Context With Internal Sensor Diagnostics
stories.Summary:
The study was published in the journal Discover Vehicles by researchers Kushal Khemani and Anjum Nazir Qureshi, who introduced an artificial intelligence system that predicts when connected vehicles will need maintenance.
