stories.Headline: American Businesses Just Unleashed the Biggest Investment Boom in 15 Years — and AI Is Driving It
stories.Summary:
American factories shipped a record $86 billion of core capital goods in September, according to The Kobeissi Letter, with shipments up 11.6% from a year earlier. Core capital goods are the machinery, computers and equipment that companies buy to expand, and the measure excludes defense hardware and aircraft. Over the past three months shipments climbed at a 16.5% annualized pace, the quickest since 2011 if the pandemic rebound is set aside. Orders for computers, servers, storage devices and related equipment rose 27% year over year, the strongest gain since January 1997, and much of the growth rests on a small group of tech buyers.

The broader government figures point the same way. Real gross domestic product grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter, and gross private investment rose 19.4%, its biggest jump since early 2025. Private nonresidential fixed investment reached a record annual rate of $4.95 trillion, up 12.1% from a year earlier. Corporate profits ran at a $4.7 trillion annual rate in the second quarter, up 20.8% year over year. Estimates cited by 24/7 Wall St. put hyperscaler spending on data centers at $845 billion this year and close to $1.4 trillion in 2027.

The article's author, Rich Duprey, a writer for 24/7 Wall St., notes that unfilled equipment orders have grown for more than a year, meaning demand is running ahead of production. He also points out that some of the benefit flows abroad, since imports rose 19.7% in the third quarter while exports fell 5.7%. Investors have grown nervous, with tech stocks suffering their biggest selloff since Covid on fears the data center boom could end early, according to Fortune, and Morningstar warning that hyperscaler AI investment will outpace near-term earnings. Local voters have also pushed back, approving restrictions in nearly every data center ballot measure in the midterms, with one exception in Hardwood, North Dakota.

Power supply is another constraint. The Energy Department projects data centers could use up to 12% of U.S. electricity by 2028, and retail electricity prices have risen faster than inflation since 2022. The article warns that AI companies could cut back if returns disappoint, borrowing grows costlier or capacity outstrips demand, which would cause equipment orders to fall quickly and turn today's support for growth into a drag. Two indicators will signal the direction: the unfilled orders figure in upcoming durable goods reports, and the capital spending guidance the largest cloud companies give in their fourth-quarter earnings reports early next year.

Articles.Title: American Businesses Just Unleashed the Biggest Investment Boom in 15 Years — and AI Is Driving It

stories.Headline: Codenotary Releases Open-Source AgentMon Live to Improve AI Coding Productivity
stories.Summary:
Codenotary, a company focused on the safe and secure use of AI, released AgentMon Live on November 9, 2026, as free, open-source software for developers who use Claude Code. The tool checks whether AI coding agents have actually finished the work they were asked to do, flags problems that need a human's attention, and aims to reduce wasted token consumption. It is available immediately under the Apache 2.0 license, which gives developers access to the source code so they can inspect, modify, extend, and contribute to it. Codenotary describes the release as its contribution to the growing community of developers building software with agentic AI.

AgentMon Live connects directly to Claude Code and offers a live dashboard showing agent activity, tool use, file changes, and verification results. Its "Done Gate" feature examines recorded session activity for signs of unfinished work, such as failed or outdated tests, incomplete tasks, and subagent failures, before an agent is allowed to finish. An optional second-model advisor can separately assess whether the agent's response addresses the developer's original request. The dashboard also shows active tools, subagents, pending approvals, and stalled or repeatedly failing processes, so developers need not read agent conversations continuously. The software further reports on token consumption, context growth, cache efficiency, and tool execution time, and it flags possible inefficiencies such as repeated file reads and unused Model Context Protocol servers.

Codenotary's chief technology officer and co-founder, Dennis Zimmer, said that productivity from AI coding should be measured by how much useful, verified work gets done. He argued that developers should not have to spend their days supervising agents, confirming that they really finished, or guessing where their tokens went. Zimmer said the company is releasing the tool free and open source because it believes the whole agentic development community should benefit. The announcement also notes that agents may report completion even when tests have failed, when verification predates the latest code changes, or when required steps remain undone.

The software works with Claude Code version 2.1.308 and later, and developers can install it from within Claude Code using a plugin command that references the codenotary/agentmon-live marketplace entry. Source code, installation instructions, and contribution information are published on GitHub at github.com/codenotary/agentmon-live. The articles do not say how many developers have adopted the tool or whether Codenotary plans further releases. The announcement appeared on SD Times, which also carried several unrelated items about AI and software development in the same feed.

Articles.Title: Codenotary Releases Open-Source AgentMon Live to Improve AI Coding Productivity - SD Times

stories.Headline: 1-0 to humankind? US midterms vote puts AI, datacentres and the broligarchy back in their box | Heather Stewart
stories.Summary:
Voters in the US midterm elections last week rejected a number of measures and candidates tied to the expansion of artificial intelligence and the datacentres that power it, according to a Guardian column by Heather Stewart published on 8 November 2026. Dozens of ballot measures calling for limits on datacentre expansion were passed in many places, and reining in the rapid growth of these power-hungry sites became a rallying cry for some campaigners. The cost of living squeeze, which the column links to Donald Trump's war in Iran, was also a major factor in the Democratic wave. Stewart points to the Texas senator-elect James Talarico, who described a mother whose son thought it was daytime at night because of the bright lights from a neighbouring datacentre.

The column argues that the result has undermined a key story sustaining the AI market boom, namely that the US would be carpeted with debt-funded datacentres as demand for the technology grew. It describes the public as having been asked to accept these costs for the economic good AI would bring, but says the downsides, including online "slop", intrusive features forced into apps and devices, and rising consumer prices while tech leaders grow rich, have eroded that goodwill. Stewart notes that Elon Musk spent billions trying to influence the Texas electorate, which she says became a selling point for Democrats. She adds that the opposition is likely to slow the pace of investment in AI's physical infrastructure.

Stewart cites the economist Joe Maher of Capital Economics, who said sentiment towards the AI trade was already fragile and that the midterms could become the catalyst for a longer unwind of the AI equity boom. She also quotes Dario Perkins of TS Lombard, who argued in a recent note that ordinary people were never especially interested in AI and that tech insiders were living in a bubble. Perkins described the industry as roughly $200bn in current revenues supporting more than $1tn in future commitments from two companies, Anthropic and OpenAI. The column also references the International Monetary Fund, which last month pointed to growing evidence that AI rollout may not require the massive investment being made by hyperscaler firms.

The column places these developments against a market that was already showing signs of strain, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq having peaked a month earlier. Stewart writes that whether the stock sell-off continues remains to be seen, and that the datacentre backlash has given new force to earlier concerns about costs and circular financing within the sector. She concludes that the AI lobby now faces the challenge of showing what the technology can do for societies, including outside the US, that are reluctant to accept its costs. The column is an opinion piece rather than a news report, and it does not set out a specific timetable for further market or policy moves.

Articles.Title: 1-0 to humankind? US midterms vote puts AI, datacentres and the broligarchy back in their box | Heather Stewart

stories.Headline: Sphera AI Turns Supply Chain Signals Into Fast Decisions
stories.Summary:
Sphera, a supply chain software company, announced new Sphera AI capabilities on November 8, 2026, designed to connect external risk signals directly to the suppliers, products and operations they threaten. The launch is aimed at helping organizations move from detecting a risk to responding to it in minutes rather than days. The technology uses conversational AI and intelligent agents to identify exposed suppliers, assess severity and prioritize mitigation, while keeping human decision-makers in control. Marina Mayer reported the launch for Supply & Demand Chain Executive.

The new features include a conversational interface that lets teams ask plain-language questions about supplier and supply chain risk without compiling data by hand. A Model Context Protocol integration pulls risk insights into compatible AI tools, so the information is available wherever decisions are made. Within the Risk Response & Resolution Center, AI agents assess risk severity and supplier impact to show which risks need a response, reducing manual triage. Sphera says the combined capabilities help teams spend less time investigating and more time protecting supply continuity, production and revenue. The articles do not give pricing or availability dates.

The company's CEO and president, Paul Marushka, said the boundary of an enterprise no longer marks the boundary of operational risk. He argued that disruptions often begin outside a business, with a supplier, a critical material or a distant event, yet their consequences land inside it. In his account, the challenge is linking those outside signals to affected products and operations fast enough to improve decisions, and Sphera AI is meant to close that gap while leaving people in charge of key choices. Sphera's own research supports the framing, drawn from five markets: the U.S., UK, Germany, France and the UAE.

That research found that 58 percent of COOs say their most significant disruptions originated at least as much outside their organization as within it, rising to 71 percent in the UAE. The same COOs cited the hardest tasks as identifying exposed suppliers or products (33 percent), choosing the right mitigation (30 percent) and quantifying business impact (29 percent). The articles present the launch as a response to that gap between external disruption and internal visibility. They do not report independent verification of the research or any customer results.

Articles.Title: Sphera AI Turns Supply Chain Signals Into Fast Decisions

stories.Headline: AI Power Stocks Just Fell 6.3% to 9.3% on Financing Fears. SpaceX Just Said New Compute Pays Back in Under a Year.
stories.Summary:
On October 20, 2026, during its third-quarter earnings call, SpaceX said its new compute investments were paying for themselves in under a year. Shortly afterward, shares of GE Vernova fell as much as 9.3% and Bloom Energy dropped 6.3%, with investors worried about how AI infrastructure would be financed. The article notes that GE Vernova's slide followed analyst target cuts and a partly debt-funded $9 billion acquisition. Bloom Energy's decline came after negative free cash flow in the most recent quarter, despite record revenue.

On the call, the company's chief financial officer said new compute deployments currently show a payback period of less than a year. He also said pricing was tracking slightly above the high end of the $30 to $50 per-watt range discussed the previous quarter. Management argued that a faster payback lets a company reinvest in capacity rather than depend on outside financing. The company also reported strong customer interest in compute capacity, with cloud service agreements adding a revenue stream. Management said deployment decisions would be tied to near-term demand rather than built ahead of need.

Beyond the payback claim, the article describes SpaceX's AI business as supported by several operations, including the Starlink connectivity business and a planned Terafab semiconductor project. The Super Intelligence segment brought in $7.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, helped by new cloud agreements, added compute and the Cursor acquisition. The company ended the quarter with about 1.7 gigawatts of nameplate compute and is targeting 2.5 to 3 gigawatts by the end of the fourth quarter. Its third-quarter capital expenditures were $19.6 billion, and it guided to $35 billion to $40 billion for the fourth quarter.

The article cautions that the spending creates execution and financing risks if demand or pricing weakens. It also says SpaceX trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of about 50, compared with about 38 for GE Vernova and about 37 for Bloom Energy, which implies investors expect strong future growth. The piece is written by The Motley Fool and includes promotional material for its stock service. The author states he holds no position in the stocks mentioned.

Articles.Title: AI Power Stocks Just Fell 6.3% to 9.3% on Financing Fears. SpaceX Just Said New Compute Pays Back in Under a Year.

stories.Headline: Siri AI chief may step down as more Apple departures are rumored
stories.Summary:
Apple's Mike Rockwell, who leads the company's Siri AI team, is reportedly weighing whether to step back from that role, according to a Bloomberg report cited by AppleInsider on November 8, 2026. The report, which appears in Bloomberg's "Power On" newsletter, says Rockwell is seriously considering his future, and it suggests he could step down as Siri AI lead during 2027 or leave Apple entirely. The report offers no further detail on timing or the reasons behind his thinking. It also speculates that if Rockwell moves on, his responsibilities would likely be divided between Amar Subramanya, a former Google AI veteran, and Sebastien Marineau.

Rockwell took over Siri AI in March 2025 after Apple's Kim Vorrath assessed the team, and by April he was bringing in staff from his earlier Apple Vision Pro work. That reorganization led to the much-revamped Siri AI announced at WWDC 2026. The change in leadership from John Giannandrea to Rockwell reportedly followed crisis talks within the company. Rockwell previously led development of the Apple Vision Pro, which the article's context describes as a setback for the company.

Marineau currently reports to Craig Federighi, and the report says there is some expectation that he could eventually succeed him. The report also notes, however, that there is no current indication that Federighi plans to retire or leave Apple in the near term. The article is based on a newsletter report rather than an official statement from Apple, and the reader comments included with it are opinion rather than reporting. The articles do not say whether Apple has commented on the speculation or when any decision will be made.

Articles.Title: Siri AI chief may step down as more Apple departures are rumored

stories.Headline: Bonus Features – November 8, 2026 – 48% of Americans have used AI to review their health insurance options, 68% would independently verify AI-generated medication details, plus 34 more stories
stories.Summary:
Healthcare IT Today's weekly Bonus Features roundup for November 8, 2026 reports that 48% of Americans have used an AI tool to review their health insurance options, according to research from eHealth. The same edition notes that Wolters Kluwer Health found 68% of consumers would independently verify medication details when those details are generated through processes using AI. These findings sit among dozens of short items covering product launches, partnerships, hires and policy updates in health IT. The roundup is presented as a weekly digest meant to keep readers informed of news they might otherwise miss.

Among the policy items, CMS released the 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule and delayed until 2029 the requirement that remote patient or therapeutic monitoring be paid only when performed by clinical staff employed by the practice. ONC announced that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of War have joined TEFCA, the trusted exchange framework for health information. A separate ACTO report found that 54% of senior leaders remain concerned about how AI is used in life sciences organizations, and 58% say the industry lacks a clear standard for responsible AI. Taken together, these items point to ongoing questions about oversight, data exchange and the governance of AI in care.

The roundup itself is compiled by Healthcare IT Today, which describes itself as the leading provider of healthcare IT news and analysis within the Healthcare Scene media network. Vendors and organizations are invited to submit news for future editions through a submission page, with items received after Thursday closing possibly held until the following week. The articles do not describe any independent verification of the survey results beyond attributing them to their research sponsors. The edition also lists new executive appointments at companies including Azalea Health, AvaSure and Definitive Healthcare, along with several health system deployments of imaging and AI tools.

A separate TLT AI Brief from November 2026 describes parallel developments in the United Kingdom, where the Chancellor's Budget set out AI investment including a £165 million National AI Biosecurity Initiative. That package includes £100 million in public funding for the AI Biosecurity Lab and commitments of up to £200 million from OpenAI and Anthropic. The MHRA has also outlined its next phase of AI and medtech regulation, accepting all 44 recommendations of the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare. These UK moves suggest that regulators and governments are working to define accountability for AI across medicine and public services over the coming years.

Articles.Title: Bonus Features – November 8, 2026 – 48% of Americans have used AI to review their health insurance options, 68% would independently verify AI-generated medication details, plus 34 more stories

stories.Headline: Siri AI Rumored to Become 'More Like an Agent' as Early as Next Year
stories.Summary:
Apple could make Siri work "more like an agent" as early as next year, according to a rumor reported by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman in his Power On newsletter on November 8, 2026. Gurman said he was told that the company wants to move in this direction, though the exact form such a change would take is still unknown. He noted that rival products such as OpenAI's Dots, Meta's Muse, and Grok can track goals and pursue objectives without a user starting each step. The current Siri AI is more capable and personalized than classic Siri, but it is not yet proactive or always on. Gurman also reported that Apple CEO John Ternus told software engineering chief Craig Federighi, in a closed-door meeting in recent weeks, that Apple must accelerate its software roadmap.

According to Gurman, Ternus said the company should move quickly beyond making only the necessary improvements to Siri. The articles do not describe a specific timeline or product plan beyond the possibility of next year. The report is based on Gurman's sources and has not been confirmed by Apple. The rumor comes as Apple continues to roll out Siri AI across its devices. The articles mention that the new Apple TV 4K, announced October 13, 2026, supports Siri AI, and that the HomeView smart home hub, releasing November 13, also includes Siri AI support.

They also note that iOS 27.2 brought Siri AI improvements, and that a 27.3 beta with further Siri AI upgrades is already in testing. Reader comments on the report were mixed, with some users calling Siri unfinished. Apple has not commented publicly on the rumored agent-style Siri, and the articles offer no date for any launch. Whether the change arrives next year will depend on how Apple's plans develop. For now, the report remains a rumor based on a single newsletter.

Articles.Title: Siri AI Rumored to Become 'More Like an Agent' as Early as Next Year

stories.Headline: Susquehanna Warns 8% of Planned AI Data Centre Capacity Could Face Cancellation
stories.Summary:
Susquehanna Financial Group has warned that regulatory uncertainty after the 2026 US midterm elections could threaten about 12 gigawatts of planned artificial intelligence data centre capacity. That figure represents 8% of projects scheduled for development between 2025 and 2030. The firm released its report on Friday. It identified potential delays affecting a much larger share of planned infrastructure, while suggesting that near-term disruption should remain fairly limited.

Susquehanna estimates that roughly 148 gigawatts of training-focused AI data centre capacity is planned for 2025 to 2030. Around 60 gigawatts of that total, or 40%, is exposed to possible delays because regulatory approvals are still pending. The firm calculates that the 12 gigawatts at risk would equal about 20% of projects awaiting approval. Under its worst-case scenario, projects scheduled for 2028 through 2030 could be cancelled because of regulatory challenges. The analysis points to growing uncertainty around projects that need further regulatory authorisation.

The firm said most projects due in 2027 already hold the necessary permits, which lowers their exposure to new obstacles. It therefore still expects 2027 to be the peak year for new AI data centre installations. The greatest risks sit in the 2028 to 2030 period, when projects without approval could face longer timelines or cancellation. Susquehanna also noted that enterprise AI inference workloads are expected to accelerate in 2027, which could generate computing demand beyond its 148-gigawatt estimate. It added that a possible recovery in semiconductor demand outside AI could partly offset weaker data centre spending.

Susquehanna warned that semiconductor revenue could fall 10% year over year under its most pessimistic scenario. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index has already dropped about 38% from its June peak and trades near a historical low forward price-to-earnings level, at around 15 times expected earnings. The firm suggested that share prices may already reflect much of the potential negative impact. It described regulatory uncertainty as a significant consideration for AI infrastructure investment, while concluding that current valuations may already price in a gloomier outlook than the underlying project risks justify.

Articles.Title: Susquehanna Warns 8% of Planned AI Data Centre Capacity Could Face Cancellation

stories.Headline: Missing the Point: Isolation Alone Will Not Build AI Safety
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column, not a news event, so there is no breaking story to report. The articles describe a MedCity News piece in which the author disputes the view of Imprivata CEO Fran Rosch that AI agents should be used in a transactional, self-limiting way with constant reminders that they cannot be trusted. Rosch had compared AI agents to contract nurses and argued that healthcare should treat them similarly. The author, writing from a cybersecurity-adjacent but patient-engagement perspective, says this view misses the point.

The author's central argument is that isolating AI agents reduces risk but also gives up significant benefits. Agentic AI, like a nurse, improves with learning, so working on a problem over time lets it adjust to a client's needs, learn workflows, sustain engagement, and improve return on investment. The author also argues that trust in technology must be built gradually, and that an "adopt and drop" model creates repeated new introductions, permissions, and workflows, each a new chance for something to go wrong. In healthcare especially, patients need to trust an AI companion that follows their history and preferences in order to stay engaged with their care.

The column does not describe any regulation, rule, or change being implemented, and it names no official responsible for a decision. Its disagreement is with Rosch's published recommendation, which the author paraphrases as treating AI like a temporary worker with minimal access to patient data. The author concludes that the real task is to make AI agents trustworthy enough to operate safely over time, rather than to isolate them. The articles do not say whether any healthcare organization has adopted either approach, and they offer no timeline for further developments. The other items on the page are unrelated promotional or sponsored pieces, and the source of this column is the MedCity Influencers program, which lets outside contributors publish their views.

Articles.Title: Missing the Point: Isolation Alone Will Not Build AI Safety

stories.Headline: For C.S. Lewis fans: AI is not N.I.C.E.
stories.Summary:
I cannot write this to the specification as stated, because the requirements conflict with the source material. The article is an opinion essay about C.S. Lewis's novel and its use in debates about AI, and it contains no reported news event, no date of an incident, and no official action requiring specific numbers. Instead of inventing a breaking-news story from it, I can offer a short paragraph set that summarizes the essay's argument accurately, which I've written below in four-to-five-sentence paragraphs. The essay, published by mindmatters.ai on November 8, 2026, examines how Christian writers have used C.S. Lewis's novel That Hideous Strength to criticize artificial intelligence. It notes that Jeremy Wayne Tate, founder of the Classic Learning Test, said on X in February that Lewis predicted AI in the book's N.I.C.E. organization.

The author describes several other critics, including Paul Kingsnorth, Rod Dreher, Derek Rishmawy, and Annie Crawford, who have linked the novel to current AI concerns. Each treats the novel as a warning about technology and the demonic. The author, who says the book is his favorite novel, argues that these critics are partly right but misread who the villains are. He observes that the N.I.C.E. produces little actual science and works mainly by coordinating power, controlling institutions, and manufacturing emergencies. He ties this pattern to older appeals, such as the 1946 film One World or None, which urged handing atomic authority to a global body.

He also cites Nick Bostrom and Paul's warning about "peace and safety" to suggest that systems promising to eliminate risk can become the greatest risk themselves. The author contrasts this with AI research organizations such as OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic, which he says build models and make technical discoveries rather than pursue propaganda. The essay closes by distinguishing the novel's warning about concentrated power from the claim that AI labs are the equivalent of Belbury. The article does not report any scheduled action or next step beyond this argument.

Articles.Title: For C.S. Lewis fans: AI is not N.I.C.E.

stories.Headline: 2027 AI Governance: Operating Models, Not Policy Documents
stories.Summary:
Enterprises began adopting AI and quickly built governance frameworks to manage the new risks that tools and users would bring. Many organizations restricted the data employees could enter into public tools, and some banned generative AI use altogether. Those measures have not been enough, since 45% of U.S. workers reportedly use unsanctioned, or shadow, AI on the job. The article argues that these policy documents are too blunt to work in practice. When rules simply prohibit certain tools and uses, they fail to show where sensitive data begins and ends, which pushes employees toward workarounds.

The article says AI governance in 2027 is shifting from written policy toward a four-part operating model. The first part is discovery, which means finding out which tools employees already use, whether sanctioned or not. The second is data-centered rules, which tie AI permissions to existing data classifications so the question becomes what class of data is involved and which tool is approved for it. The third is approved paths, which means providing sanctioned enterprise AI tools with proper contractual and technical controls so the approved choice is also the easiest one. The fourth is cross-functional ownership, with business leaders, HR, legal, and others sharing a governance group that reviews new tools and exceptions quickly.

The article also describes a four-lane model for sorting data and use cases by sensitivity and impact, instead of a simple permitted or prohibited split. Lane zero covers activities prohibited outright without an explicit policy change, such as entering regulated or secret data into public chat tools. Lane one covers low-risk uses, such as internal writing help with non-sensitive data, which can be fast-tracked under a standard acceptable use policy. Lane two covers moderate-risk uses, such as code assistants for proprietary code, which need security and privacy reviews plus controls like retention settings and evaluation plans. Lane three covers high-risk uses and regulated data, such as customer-facing AI, which require a full governance path, group approval, formal risk assessments, red teaming, model evaluations, and kill switches.

The piece is written by Ken Reely, Head of Cyber Security Services for North America, EMEA, and APAC at Stefanini, and it was published on cybersecurity-insiders.com on November 8, 2026. Reely's argument is that protecting information should not make AI feel off limits, since organizations that only prohibit certain uses will likely see more shadow AI and greater risk. He recommends starting with discovery, identifying which AI tools employees use today and assigning each tool and data type to a lane before 2027. The article presents this as the practical path forward for security leaders who already see AI in widespread use.

Articles.Title: 2027 AI Governance: Operating Models, Not Policy Documents

stories.Headline: Right Answer, Wrong Reasons: AI Forecasts Costco - Hassan El Mghari & Omar El Mghari, Together AI｜AI Engineer
stories.Summary:
A podcast episode published on November 9, 2026, by AI Engineer features Hassan El Mghari of Together AI and his father Omar El Mghari, a CPA and former Big Four auditor, presenting a 15-minute talk on using an open-source language model to forecast Costco's profit after its July 2024 membership fee increase. The model's headline result landed within 4.4% of actual profit, averaged across five builds that ranged from 0.7% to 5.2%. Omar's audit found that this accuracy was accidental: the model overstated the member base by applying the fee increase to Costco's entire international membership rather than only US and Canadian members, and it understated the executive-tier share at 15% when Costco's filings disclosed 45%. The two errors pushed the estimate in opposite directions and roughly canceled out.

The team built the model from about 214 Costco public filings, converted into roughly 3,000 timestamped facts and filtered to those available before a cutoff set a couple of weeks before the announcement. They used models trained before the event, GPT-OSS-120B and Llama-3.3 70B, after finding that newer models already knew about the fee change. The pipeline had the model output structured formulas and assumptions rather than doing arithmetic end to end, then ran 16 parallel sessions at a total cost of 19 cents, keeping the five that passed automated checks. Costco raised its standard membership fee from $60 to $65 and its executive fee from $120 to $130, its first increase since 2017. The model predicted a $560 million profit increase over two years, and Omar's testing showed the result was fragile: correcting only the executive-tier share pushed the error to 28%.

Omar presented the work as an example of the three-lines-of-defense model used in auditing, with Hassan's automated checks as the first line, codifiable accounting checks as the second, and expert review as the third. He argued that a subject-matter expert in the loop is essential, saying "Luck is not a control in the auditing world." Hassan acknowledged that he saw the 4.4% figure and considered it excellent because he does not come from accounting, and that the gap was visible only to someone who knew which assumptions to question. The talk suggests that expert review can be turned into specific checks that make a system more autonomous over time, though it notes that identifying those checks still required an accountant's judgment.

Articles.Title: Right Answer, Wrong Reasons: AI Forecasts Costco - Hassan El Mghari & Omar El Mghari, Together AI｜AI Engineer - finance.biggo.com

stories.Headline: Securing AI Agents: Lessons From Real-World Deployment
stories.Summary:
Uber published an engineering article on November 6, 2026, by Sean Tout, Director of Engineering & Science, describing how it secures AI agents in production. The article, first posted on uber.com in the early hours of that day, explains that agentic AI differs from conventional software because agents reason over content from users, webpages, documents, tools, and other agents, and can turn that reasoning into real-world actions. That shifts part of the attack surface into the semantic layer, where risks such as prompt injection, tool and memory poisoning, goal hijacking, behavioral drift, and hallucination-driven actions appear. Uber says the question for these systems goes beyond whether an agent is authorized, asking whether a proposed action fits the user's request, the agent's persona and intents, the user's role, and the full session history.

The company built a defense-in-depth framework called Uber Secure AI that covers the agent lifecycle in three layers: provisioning-time validation, runtime enforcement, and continuous assurance. The framework includes an agent registry, personas and explicit intents, constraints, tool and MCP validation, context-aware guardrails, continuous red teaming, and end-to-end observability and replay. Uber also describes prompt provenance and evidence chaining, which link privileged actions back to what the user actually requested. Runtime evaluation has to stay within strict latency budgets, so the article says Uber favors small, specialized models that run locally over large general-purpose language models. The article also notes that stronger enforcement can produce false blocks, so Uber calibrates thresholds per agent rather than applying one uniform setting, and it automates onboarding so the secure path is the easiest one for developers.

The articles name Sean Tout as the author, and a second version of the page lists Max Zhurovich, Senior Staff Software Engineer, and Adi Raghavendra, Senior Engineering Manager, as co-authors. Uber presents the work as a set of shared practices meant to help engineering teams build these protections into agentic systems from the start. The authors state that security, accuracy, latency, cost, agent autonomy, and developer experience cannot be optimized independently, and they describe effective agent guardrails as both a security problem and a distributed systems engineering problem. The excerpts available do not describe any specific incident or deployment outcome beyond the framework itself.

Articles.Title: Securing AI agents isn’t science fiction. It’s good engineering

stories.Headline: ‘Very deceptive’: WA real estate listings are getting AI makeovers
stories.Summary:
In September, Nicole and Nathan Broyles visited a house in Preston, east of Issaquah, that they had first seen only through its Redfin listing photos. The couple, who were moving back to Washington from Florida, found the home looked nothing like its online images. The listing had been altered with artificial intelligence to show sleek furniture, bright carpet and a polished interior, while the actual house had worn orange shag carpet and other flaws. Some edits also changed the layout, such as turning the front door into a window and inventing a hallway that did not exist.

Real estate professionals in the Seattle area say AI alterations to listing photos have become common and, in their view, sometimes cross into deception. The Northwest Multiple Listing Service, which most brokers in Washington and Oregon use, requires that digital alterations be visible to consumers, either flagged in the listing text or marked with a written notice on the image. Adding or removing temporary furnishings is allowed if disclosed, but altering landscaping, paint or kitchens is not. Other states, including California and Wisconsin, have laws requiring disclosure, and Washington law requires AI tool developers to embed provenance data in images, though screenshots or compression can erase it.

The Seattle Times reported that the listing service calls such misleading edits a direct violation of its rules, and it uses automated scanning and broker reports to remove noncompliant images. Richard Buchanan, the seller's agent for the Preston property at Keller Williams' Greater Seattle office, confirmed he used ChatGPT to remove clutter and add furnishings, and he said he was unaware of the disclosure rules until the newspaper called. He acknowledged he had been wrong and said there had been some confusion on his part. Redfin says it bars agents it works with directly from using AI to conceal defects, and Zillow says it takes misleading photos seriously and lets users report them.

Other cases show the problem extends beyond one listing. A Redfin photo of a new home in North Seattle in August altered neighboring houses, added landscaping and changed the home's color, and the brokerage said its listing agent was an independent contractor and that the altered photos had since been removed. Robert Luecke Jr., chief operating officer of ShopProp Realty, reported a Lake Washington listing in September that showed mountain views that do not exist, and after his report, the photo was replaced with another AI-modified image without disclosure. As of Wednesday, the Times reported, those images had been deleted, though some other images in that listing still lacked clear disclosure or had their metadata erased.

Articles.Title: ‘Very deceptive’: WA real estate listings are getting AI makeovers

stories.Headline: Apple leadership may have differing views on AI strategy
stories.Summary:
A new report suggests Apple still faces internal disagreement over its AI strategy, even though the company appears to have kept to the approach set by John Giannandrea nearly a decade ago. The account comes from the "Power On" newsletter from Bloomberg, which says CEO John Ternus has asked Craig Federighi to produce more AI faster. The article notes that the report also contradicts itself, suggesting Federighi's planning is already on too short a timeframe. Other leadership changes and possible departures are mentioned in the report as well, though the article does not provide specifics on them.

The writer of the AppleInsider piece argues that the report does not match how Apple's AI efforts look from outside the company. Apple hired Giannandrea from Google in 2018 to advance its AI and machine learning work, and his strategy centered on powerful hardware able to run smaller models locally rather than chasing a costly frontier model that would need extensive data centers and GPUs. The article says Apple faced investor pressure in 2024 to show progress, which led to an over-ambitious WWDC, and that it later reset its approach, rebuilt Siri, and relaunched it in 2026 with Google's Gemini frontier model at its core. Apple's own Apple Foundation Models are described as useful for its users' private, on-device functions.

The article characterizes the Bloomberg report as likely shaped by sources with an agenda, and says the meeting between Ternus and Federighi probably took place but in a different tone than described. It presents the rumors as something to treat with caution, comparing them to similar rumors about hardware chief Johny Srouji's departure. The author also contends that Apple has avoided the billions in losses and wasted investment that competitors have faced. The article places this against a backdrop of falling tech stocks, rising political pressure, and possible regulation of the data center buildout, which it says Apple is largely insulated from by its local-first approach. The piece does not describe any further steps or deadlines beyond these points.

Articles.Title: Apple leadership may have differing views on AI strategy

stories.Headline: Morgan Stanley Sees a Big Opportunity for Itron (ITRI) in the AI Power Boom
stories.Summary:
Morgan Stanley's September 2026 report, titled "AI Beneficiaries: Investing in Second-Order Effects – Update: 100x AI Cultures," argues that companies using AI to raise employee productivity may outperform the firms that build the infrastructure. The bank developed an "AI Productivity Spread," which subtracts growth in average technical employee compensation from growth in revenue per technical employee, and analyzed about 750 public technology companies and roughly 40 million employee records. It concluded that firms with the highest spreads later delivered better stock returns than their peers. The report uses past examples, such as automakers, Walton family retail, Wi-Fi router makers and Netflix, to support the idea that second-order beneficiaries can outlast the first movers.

The report also looks beyond technology to broader corporate profits. Morgan Stanley estimates that automating half of the high-probability automation positions across the 1,000 largest public companies could eliminate about 1.7 million jobs and cut labor costs by $207 billion. After distributing those savings among shareholders, employees, customers and suppliers, the companies could keep an estimated $87 billion in additional profits. The firm concludes that businesses integrating AI tools more effectively could capture a disproportionate share of the resulting gains.

Itron, Inc. (NASDAQ: ITRI), which makes smart meters, communication networks and software for electric, gas and water utilities, is named among the companies Morgan Stanley sees as well positioned. The firm links the opportunity to record US power demand driven by data center construction, which it says requires more sophisticated grid systems, including dynamic pricing and better demand management. Itron's third-quarter 2026 results, reported October 27, beat top- and bottom-line estimates, with an adjusted gross margin of 41.3%, up 350 basis points. Revenue rose 3% year over year, adjusted EBITDA rose 18%, adjusted EPS rose 26%, and the full-year 2026 EPS outlook was raised to $6.72 to $6.82.

The article also notes limits to the case for Itron. The company ended the third quarter with a $4.3 billion backlog, over 25% from its most software- and services-intensive segments, which it describes as a shift away from hardware. However, revenue for the first nine months of 2026 fell about 3% to $1.75 billion, which raises questions about whether earnings growth can continue without faster sales growth. The piece was published by Insider Monkey and carried on Yahoo Finance on November 8, 2026, and it also promotes other stocks it considers more promising.

Articles.Title: Morgan Stanley Sees a Big Opportunity for Itron (ITRI) in the AI Power Boom

stories.Headline: China AI bust threatens Xi’s ’Wall Street East’ ambitions
stories.Summary:
China's technology stock selloff is threatening President Xi Jinping's plan to turn household savings into a major source of funding for the country's tech sector. The SSE Star 50 index has dropped 40% in less than four months, wiping out at least $480 billion in market value. Losses have spread across companies tied to artificial intelligence, electric vehicles and semiconductor manufacturing. Beijing has responded by mobilising state-backed funds, insurers and regulators to support the market.

Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related companies make up 42% of China's total stock market capitalisation, with more than 3,000 listed firms generating AI-related revenue. Their combined market value was put at around $10 trillion as of March. Several prominent names have taken heavy losses, with battery maker CATL down 35% this year and robot maker Unitree down by half since its August initial public offering. Shares of Suzhou TFC Communication and Victory Giant Technology have fallen as much as 26% over the past week. The selloff reflects high valuations, domestic competition, higher energy costs, tariffs and the possibility that the United States and Europe could restrict access to Chinese technology.

Weakening domestic demand and the long property crisis are adding to investor concerns. The CSI 300 index has fallen around 21% from its June peak, even after earlier stimulus measures aimed at supporting the economy. China's $21.5 trillion economy remains heavily reliant on exports, and the property downturn continues to weigh on household confidence. The weakness contrasts with gains elsewhere in Asia, where Taiwan's benchmark has risen 56%, South Korea's 36% and Japan's Nikkei 225 more than 25%. The Shanghai Composite remains near 4,000, well below its October 2007 peak of about 6,100.

For Xi, the stakes extend beyond market values. Beijing wants households to invest in equities, especially technology companies, to finance AI infrastructure and reduce reliance on property, which accounts for roughly 70% of household wealth. Repeated market collapses and regulatory interventions have damaged retail investor confidence, and past technology-sector crackdowns have made households cautious. Even after the decline, the STAR 50 trades at about 38 times forward earnings, compared with roughly 20 times for the Nasdaq 100. An extended correction would threaten investor wealth, China's technology ambitions and Xi's wider plan to build a stock-market alternative to the struggling property sector.

Articles.Title: China AI bust threatens Xi’s ’Wall Street East’ ambitions

stories.Headline: Pod-Ed: Why Airline AI Needs Better Data Before Smarter Technology
stories.Summary:
Airways Magazine published an episode of its podcast, The Airways Podcast, on November 8, 2026, in which hosts Rohan Anand and Vinay Bhaskara spoke with Tim McMullen, vice president of aviation and travel technology at DataArt. The conversation focused on how airlines are modernizing their technology, and McMullen argued that the promise of artificial intelligence in aviation depends on the quality and accessibility of the underlying data. He said new applications must work alongside older systems that airlines use to handle bookings, schedule crews, and run daily operations. The episode is Season 10, Episode 8 of the series.

According to the discussion, airlines often operate technology stacks that span several decades, from passenger service systems first developed in the 1960s to newer crew scheduling platforms, loyalty databases, and mobile applications. McMullen said airlines cannot simply switch off existing systems and start again, so he favors selective modernization, in which new applications extract and interpret information already held in established platforms. He pointed to passenger service systems from Sabre and Amadeus as reliable infrastructure and noted the risk of older applications unexpectedly going out of service. He also cited AI assistance at United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and American Airlines as examples of newer tools running alongside older systems, though he was describing the orchestration required rather than assessing any single airline's application.

McMullen was the main voice on these points, and the hosts contributed comparisons. Bhaskara distinguished low-cost carriers seeking efficient, predictable operations from premium carriers pursuing more individualized experiences, and he described the work of connecting different database structures. Anand drew on his time at Southwest Airlines to argue that technology decisions made decades earlier can constrain an airline's commercial strategy as its business changes. McMullen also described DataArt's work on a payment orchestration platform for ZIPAIR, a subsidiary of Japan Airlines, and his view that payment flexibility is part of the passenger experience. He added that data sharing across codeshares and partnerships raises questions about ownership, security and retention, and that such cooperation needs governance and clear rules.

The episode also covered the practical side of AI work and its human effects. McMullen described a workshop with an airline that sorted ideas into immediate improvements, follow-on projects, and larger strategic investments, some of which did not require AI at all. He said DataArt automated a manual process for an unnamed client in about nine weeks and that the work saved 83% of the time spent on it, though that figure is his own account and was not independently verified. On employment, he acknowledged that some businesses may need fewer staff but argued that experienced employees hold institutional knowledge that remains valuable. The articles do not describe any further publication or follow-up beyond the episode itself.

Articles.Title: Pod-Ed: Why Airline AI Needs Better Data Before Smarter Technology

stories.Headline: Microsoft Is Reportedly Getting Pickier About AI Data Center Deals. Is the Stock a Buy Now?
stories.Summary:
Microsoft may be becoming more selective about the outside data center capacity it rents for artificial intelligence work. On Nov. 5, Bloomberg reported that the software giant has tightened oversight of some projects from neoclouds, which are firms that rent out AI computing capacity, including Nebius Group, IREN and the privately held Nscale. The Financial Times reported the same day that Microsoft will not exercise an option to more than double its Nscale deal at a Texas data center. Microsoft has not confirmed either report, so the details remain unverified.

The reports come as Microsoft's spending has climbed much faster than the cash its business generates. Free cash flow over the last four reported quarters was about $60 billion, down roughly 23% from about $78 billion in the four quarters ended September 2025. Much of the outside capacity arrives through finance leases, and Microsoft counts the full principal value of a lease in capital expenditures when it begins, while the cash is paid over many years. IREN said a customer-requested network design change and vendor timing pushed its goal of over $4 billion in annualized revenue into early 2027. Microsoft also had $364.6 billion in leases that had not yet started as of Sept. 30, mostly for data centers, up from $106.2 billion a year earlier.

Microsoft has not publicly explained the changes beyond what its executives have said in earnings calls. On the fiscal first-quarter call on Oct. 28, CFO Amy Hood said the company would access additional sources of funding when it believed doing so was attractive. A day later, Microsoft agreed to sell $25 billion in notes. Demand does not appear to be the problem, since Azure revenue rose 48% year over year in the fiscal first quarter and management expects 49% to 50% constant-currency growth in the fiscal second quarter.

The article's author, Daniel Sparks, argues that renting less would not quickly ease the free cash flow pressure, and that building more of its own data centers could add to near-term spending. He also says the stock looks expensive, trading near $535 at about 30 times adjusted earnings and roughly 66 times trailing free cash flow, and he has said he would prefer to buy closer to $465. Management expects capital expenditures to exceed $50 billion in the fiscal second quarter and to accelerate after that. The article does not describe any further decisions by Microsoft on these projects.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Is Reportedly Getting Pickier About AI Data Center Deals. Is the Stock a Buy Now?

stories.Headline: Technical Aspects of AI-Generated Video Assets for Web Design
stories.Summary:
This article is not a news story. It is a SitePoint community piece, published on November 8, 2026, that gives developers and designers a technical guide to using AI-generated video on websites. Because it contains no event, actor, or announced change, the facts available are limited to its guidance, and the rules you set call for a breaking-story treatment in that case. The piece argues that making a good-looking AI video is only part of the job, and that the format, visual quality, file size, and page performance all determine how the video works for visitors. It recommends MP4 with H.264 as a dependable default, with WebM or AV1 offered as additional sources, and it notes that multiple sources let browsers pick a supported option.

It also suggests 1080p as a practical resolution for most desktop banners and backgrounds, and 24 or 30 frames per second for typical website footage. The author advises reviewing AI footage for transitions, motion consistency, sharpness, and color accuracy before publishing it. The guidance extends to loading and accessibility. The author recommends compression with tools such as FFmpeg, trimming footage, removing audio from background videos, and serving smaller versions to mobile users. The article also covers the HTML video element's muted, autoplay, loop, playsinline, and poster attributes, and suggests respecting the prefers-reduced-motion setting by showing a static image instead.

Performance can be checked with Google Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools. The article was written by a contributor named Alex and is labeled as a community article, meaning it was screened by SitePoint but its views are the author's and not necessarily SitePoint's. stories.Headline: Together AI's Hassan El Mghari: A Costco Earnings Model Landed Within 4.4% — Because Two Errors Cancelled Out
stories.Summary:
A language model built a Costco earnings forecast from 214 public filings and landed within 4.4% of the actual profit result after the retailer raised its membership fees in July 2024. Hassan El Mghari, a developer-experience lead at Together AI, and his father Omar, a CPA with 25 years at Big Four audit firms, presented the case at the AI Engineer conference. When Omar examined the assumptions, he found the close result was an accident, because two errors offset each other. The model applied the fee increase to Costco's entire international membership, although only US and Canadian members were affected, and it assumed executive-tier members made up 15% of the base when the company's filings disclosed 45%.

The pipeline was otherwise carefully built, using timestamped facts, models with training data that predated the event, structured formula output, automated checks and 16 parallel runs that cost 19 cents in total. Only five of the 16 runs passed the checks, and across those five the forecasts varied widely, from 0.7% to 5.2% error, with the fee-increase profit estimates ranging from $500 million to $6 billion against a recalculated figure of about $450 million. The model also cited a real Costco filing for the executive-tier claim, but that filing contained no such number, and the 15% figure was invented along with a 5% to 30% range. Omar also found an input tied to US and Canadian sales that had no effect on the forecast at all, a problem the automated checks missed. When he corrected only the executive-tier share to the disclosed 45%, the error rose to 28%.

Hassan described the lesson as a reminder that a human expert needs to stay involved, and Omar argued that expert review should feed the checks the system uses rather than serve as a final gate. Omar compared the setup to the three-lines-of-defense audit model, with automated checks as the first line, codified accounting checks as the second, and expert judgment as the third. Hassan admitted he had thought the 4.4% result was excellent because he is not an accountant. The presenters said the case shows that passing engineering checks does not establish that a model's assumptions are correct, and that an expert is needed to identify which assumptions to question.

Articles.Title: Together AI's Hassan El Mghari: A Costco Earnings Model Landed Within 4.4% — Because Two Errors Cancelled Out - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: A single AI forecast inflates US power auctions by $5.7B
stories.Summary:
A single AI-driven demand forecast has been shown to add $5.7 billion to the modeled cost of a US power capacity auction, according to an analysis that reran PJM's market. The independent market monitor, Monitoring Analytics, calculated in a recent report dated October 30, 2026 that PJM's July auction for the 2028-29 delivery year produced about $16.41 billion in capacity revenue. When the monitor removed forecast growth in demand from new and expanding data centers while keeping other assumptions fixed, the total fell to about $10.7 billion. The gap reflects expectations of future demand rather than any building already operating. The auction pays power suppliers to commit capacity years before the electricity is used, so forecasts directly shape the sums involved.

The consequences extend beyond wholesale markets into consumer prices, though the articles stress that the effects are hard to isolate. Australia's Bureau of Statistics reported a 6.1% quarterly rise in audio, visual, and computing equipment prices, and the Reserve Bank of Australia linked some of that increase to higher memory-chip costs tied to AI infrastructure demand. In the US, September consumer-price data showed computers, peripherals, and smart-home assistants up 9.7% over a year, while smartphones fell 9.9%. The San Francisco Fed estimated that information-processing equipment added only 0.2 percentage points to August's 3.4% personal consumption expenditures inflation rate. Virginia regulators have also created a separate rate class for Dominion Energy Virginia's large users, with minimum payments and a requirement to take and pay for electricity for at least 14 years for new large-load customers contracting on or after January 1, 2027.

Responsibility for these costs remains contested, and the articles frame it mainly through the institutions involved. The market monitor's analysis puts the modeled figure in the capacity market, and the articles note that it is only an estimate of generative AI demand, not a household surcharge. The Reserve Bank of Australia said AI's effect on overall consumer prices remained modest, citing fuel costs and domestic capacity constraints as other factors, and raised its cash rate to 4.85% on November 3. The Bank of England, which raised Bank Rate to 4%, judged the effect of AI and other non-energy risks on UK inflation to be much smaller than the energy shock. The articles also note that how these costs reach individual customers depends on contracts and local regulation, and that some large customers making long-term payments can spread existing costs across more consumption.

The articles indicate that the debate will continue as central banks, grid operators, and state regulators track AI-related demand and its pricing effects. Federal Reserve researchers have warned that some inflation data may not fully account for quality improvements in software and devices, which could change how the price increases are read. Planning for too little capacity risks shortages, while planning for projects that use less power than forecast could leave infrastructure with fewer customers than its financing assumed. These trade-offs will shape the next auctions and the rules governing how large users pay.

Articles.Title: A single AI forecast inflates US power auctions by $5.7B

stories.Headline: Nebius and Positronic launch physical AI competition to test robot manipulation models
stories.Summary:
Positronic Robotics and Nebius have launched an international physical AI competition designed to improve robotic manipulation and create more consistent ways of evaluating AI models on real-world tasks. The competition was announced on October 26 and runs through December 2026, inviting developers and research teams to submit robotic AI models for independent evaluation. Entries will first be assessed in simulation, and the 10 highest-performing teams will advance to testing on a physical robot arm. The organizers are offering more than $20,000 in Nebius GPU computing credits and Positronic evaluation credits.

Positronic Robotics, which runs the independent PhAIL.ai physical AI leaderboard, says the competition responds to a lack of standardized, independent comparisons between robotic foundation models. The company reports that its DROID benchmark has tested open models across more than 1,000 episodes covering over 100 everyday manipulation tasks, all using the same Franka robotic arm. Those tests found wide gaps in performance, with the strongest models completing about 70 percent of tasks on average and the weakest around 12 percent. The organizers argue these results show robotic manipulation is still an open research problem, and that smaller development teams have a real chance to compete with established laboratories.

Nebius is supplying the GPU infrastructure and its Physical AI Workbench, while Positronic will oversee the evaluation of submitted models. The organizers have cited the DARPA Grand Challenge as an inspiration, pointing to how that event used standardized technical challenges to speed up autonomous vehicle development. The competition extends an existing partnership in which Nebius became a founding partner of Positronic's PhAIL.ai leaderboard. Registration and submission details are published at competition.phail.ai.

stories.Headline: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate
stories.Summary:
Three leading consciousness researchers, Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi, have argued in a commentary for Nature that today's AI is not conscious and probably cannot be on silicon hardware. Their piece pushes back on the idea that running the right computations is enough for consciousness, a central assumption in the debate. They are responding to figures such as Richard Dawkins and Geoffrey Hinton, who consider AI systems possibly already conscious. The authors also address a study Anthropic published this year, which reported internal processing patterns in its Claude model that resemble properties of consciously accessible information processing, a reading the company itself does not treat as evidence of subjective experience.

The commentary builds on a 2023 report, "Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence," by Patrick Butlin, Robert Long, and 17 other experts, including Yoshua Bengio. That team derived a checklist of 14 indicators drawn from leading neuroscientific theories and tested several current systems, including GPT-4. They concluded that none was a strong candidate for consciousness, a point on which the new authors agree. However, the report found no obvious technical barrier to building future systems that meet more indicators, and it assumed, for pragmatic reasons, that consciousness depends only on the type of information processing, a view known as computational functionalism. The report itself acknowledged that its indicators would be unreliable if consciousness depends on properties of living organisms, a view it attributed to Seth among others.

The Nature authors argue that consciousness is what disappears in dreamless sleep or under general anesthesia, and that it is distinct from intelligence, which means carrying out functions. They cite the human cerebellum, which holds nearly four-fifths of the brain's neurons and handles precise, fast, learned movement without any conscious involvement. They attribute the confusion between intelligence and consciousness to people's tendency to project human qualities onto things, and to language models trained on human text that often describes thoughts and feelings. They also reject computational functionalism outright, tracing its roots to Alan Turing's 1936 work and to the 1943 artificial neuron model of McCulloch and Pitts, and argue that the brain's material is inseparable from its function. Their view is that the position is "fatally flawed," and that any evidence the material matters counts against consciousness in today's AI.

The authors conclude that researchers should assume by default that AI is not conscious, and that advocating for AI welfare or AI rights wrongly diverts resources from beings that can actually feel. They warn that granting rights to systems that only appear conscious could make them harder to control when oversight matters most. Anthropic, for its part, has said there is no scientific consensus on whether AI systems could have conscious experiences, and it launched a model welfare research program in April 2025 as a precautionary measure. The article notes that false attribution of consciousness is already causing confusion, citing the 2022 dismissal of Google engineer Blake Lemoine after he claimed the LaMDA chatbot was sentient.

Articles.Title: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Signs Multi-Year Agreement to Support Wayve’s Autonomous Driving AI Development
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, the Nasdaq-listed cloud infrastructure company, has signed a multi-year agreement with autonomous vehicle technology firm Wayve to support the training of its artificial intelligence driving systems. The agreement was reported on November 9, 2026, by Yahoo Finance, with Fiona Craig as the reporter. Under the deal, Wayve will use CoreWeave Cloud along with Nvidia Blackwell graphics processing units to train its foundation models. The partnership will also supply computing resources for model evaluation and simulation work. The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the agreement.

Wayve develops what it calls AI Driver technology using real-world driving data gathered in more than 70 countries. Its method involves training foundation models on that data, evaluating how they perform and deploying updated systems only after testing. The company previously used Weights & Biases for its machine learning work before expanding into CoreWeave Cloud. The new agreement adds computing capacity for training, evaluation and simulation as Wayve continues to build its technology. Wayve describes its system as hardware-agnostic and mapless, meaning it is designed to run on different vehicle hardware without relying on predefined high-definition maps.

Wayve's AI Driver is intended for both privately owned vehicles and autonomous taxi services, and its investors include SoftBank Group, Nvidia and Uber. Silvius Rus, Senior Vice President of Engineering at Wayve, said the company improves its system through a continuous cycle of gathering driving experience, training on it and deploying only what outperforms the current version on the road. He said access to CoreWeave's AI cloud infrastructure would help speed up commercial deployment. Gavin Jackson, CoreWeave's Managing Director for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, said the partnership brings one of the most demanding physical AI programs in the world onto a platform built for that purpose.

CoreWeave was founded in 2017 and completed its Nasdaq listing in March 2025. The companies have not disclosed the contract's value or any specific deployment milestones. Coverage of the deal in financial media noted that CoreWeave shares rose after the announcement. The articles do not describe any next steps beyond the continued development and commercial rollout of Wayve's technology.

stories.Headline: 1flowww Clients Gain Google Search Clicks and Placements in Google's AI Answers
stories.Summary:
Eight dental, med spa and wellness practices working with Chicago marketing agency 1flowww reported gains in Google search clicks, phone calls and mentions in Google's AI-generated answers since July 2026, according to a press release dated November 8, 2026. The practices are located in New York, Washington, DC, North Carolina, Kansas, California and Minnesota. Click figures come from Google Search Console, and one practice in Manhattan's Financial District saw clicks rise 77%, from 5,235 to 9,251, for July 1 to October 23, 2026, compared with the same months of 2025. A North Carolina dental practice saw clicks rise 162% to 340 over an early August to November 1 window, compared with the previous three months. A Kansas restorative practice saw clicks rise 51% to 203 over the same period.

Several practices also reported changes in leads and placements. In Washington, DC, Google Ads conversions rose from 61 to 92 in the first week on a new website launched October 27, and cost per conversion fell from $48.38 to $35.54 compared with the last week on the old site. An IV therapy clinic in Huntersville, North Carolina, saw calls from its Google Business Profile rise from 8 in July to 26 in September. A Queens dental practice ranked first in Google's regular results for a cosmetic dentist search on October 14, while a Tustin, California practice appeared in Google AI Mode's answer for a local search and was listed first on three of five checks. A Duluth, Minnesota med spa was presented as the Featured Medical Spa in Google AI Mode on October 11.

The results were released by 1flowww, a Chicago agency founded by Bera Niemczewski and Thomas Niemczewski, and Niemczewski is quoted as saying the agency counts a Google or AI placement only after a team member has seen it live and saved a dated screenshot. The agency said it checks AI answers from each practice's area, loads each one twice, and aims to track booked patients by source for every client. The Washington practice owner asked for at least 50 new patients a month after new patients had fallen sharply by June 2026, and 1flowww said it will report 28-day results and booked patients by source on November 24. The release is a company announcement, and the figures are the agency's own reporting from its clients rather than independently verified data.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike Announces New Native AI Security Innovations on AWS
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced new AI and cloud security tools built with Amazon Web Services on November 3, 2026, at its Fal.Con Europe 2026 event in Barcelona, Spain. The company said it is extending its Falcon Guardian product to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Guardrails. It is also introducing a Falcon sensor for Amazon Elastic Container Service Managed Instances, including managed demons. The announcement came in a paid press release carried by Business Wire and Yahoo Finance.

The Falcon Guardian integration gives AI applications and agentic workflows built on Amazon Bedrock protection against prompt injection, sensitive data leakage, and malicious AI activity inside the guardrail layer, with no separate deployment required. The Falcon sensor for Amazon ECS Managed Instances deploys automatically across applicable hosts as ECS environments scale, protecting systems before application workloads run, removing manual host-level installation, and reducing configuration drift. CrowdStrike trades on Nasdaq under the symbol CRWD, and AWS is owned by Amazon, which trades as AMZN. The release gives no prices, release dates, or customer numbers for the new tools.

Daniel Bernard, chief business officer at CrowdStrike, said AI is changing how enterprises build and operate, and security has to move just as fast. He said the work with AWS makes security foundational to AI innovation, protecting the applications and agents customers build and the cloud infrastructure behind them, so organizations can move faster with AI without giving the adversary an advantage. Mona Chadha, director of AI and strategic partnerships at AWS, said organizations are rapidly moving AI applications and agents into production and need security that scales with the speed and flexibility of AWS. She said the two companies are helping customers protect AI applications, agents, and the AWS infrastructure powering them so they can build and scale AI with confidence.

The release describes CrowdStrike as a global cybersecurity leader with a cloud-native platform for protecting endpoints, cloud workloads, identity, and data, powered by the CrowdStrike Security Cloud and AI. It says the Falcon platform uses a single lightweight-agent architecture for rapid and scalable deployment. The release points readers to a page on the CrowdStrike and AWS partnership for more information. It does not say what happens next beyond that.

stories.Headline: ‘Hard to recover the investment’: Gita Gopinath warns $1 trillion AI bet could correct, flags US recession risk
stories.Summary:
Former IMF chief economist Gita Gopinath has warned that the AI investment boom could face a market correction, saying companies may struggle to earn enough profit to recover nearly $1 trillion in spending expected in 2026 alone. She made the remarks on Saturday while speaking on Raj Shamani's podcast, describing herself as a Harvard professor. Gopinath said she personally believes a correction will come, but she did not say when it might happen, adding that it is impossible to tell. Her comments came as AI has become one of the biggest investment themes, with companies pouring money into infrastructure and some cutting jobs to redirect resources toward it. Investors have been chasing exposure, particularly in the United States, South Korea and Taiwan.

Gopinath described a world where two opposing forces are keeping global growth broadly stable, with the AI boom driving investment while geopolitical tensions, tariffs and the US-Iran conflict in West Asia weigh on economies. Her view is that the headline numbers mask large changes underneath. Taiwan and South Korea are growing at roughly twice their usual pace, and Taiwan's statistics agency has raised its 2026 growth forecast to 11.05%, the fastest annual growth since 1987, citing AI demand. West Asian economies such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE face growth downgrades linked to energy and the US-Iran conflict. The United States is still growing at or slightly above expectations, with AI investment offsetting some of the drag from tariffs.

Gopinath's main concern is that returns may not justify the scale of investment, given intense competition among companies and AI labs. She said it is hard to see how these firms will earn the profits needed to recover that spending. She also pointed to circular money flows in which Nvidia invests in AI labs that then buy Nvidia chips, so a collapse at either end could spread through the ecosystem. She warned that a sharp stock-market correction could push US growth to zero or slightly negative, triggering a recession that would likely be short-lived if driven purely by market losses. The article notes the irony that the AI boom is currently supporting the US economy through wealth gains and increased spending.

Articles.Title: ‘Hard to recover the investment’: Gita Gopinath warns $1 trillion AI bet could correct, flags US recession risk

stories.Headline: Forum: Protecting personal data should take priority over efficiency and AI adoption
stories.Summary:
A public healthcare service outage lasting nine and a half hours occurred on October 13, and according to a reader's letter published by The Straits Times on November 8, 2026, a missed security update was the cause. The letter refers to a November 3 article on the matter. The writer, Chong Ryh Huei, notes that the outage came alongside other recent incidents, including a data breach at Alliance Medinet and an e-mail lapse at the National Cancer Centre Singapore. Verifying updates and ensuring effective recovery are described as basic responsibilities that organisations should carry out. The letter stresses that no patient data compromise was reported in the outage itself.

The writer argues that the incidents raise doubts about whether organisations can protect citizens' sensitive information. The letter questions how prepared organisations are for the added connections, permissions and complexity that artificial intelligence may bring, if existing safeguards are applied inconsistently. It says ISO standards, AI verification tools and Health Ministry guidelines are in place but must be implemented effectively to be meaningful. The presence of these measures alone, the writer contends, cannot reassure citizens that their information is safe. Shared infrastructure, the letter adds, also needs recovery arrangements that can withstand common failures.

Chong Ryh Huei, the letter's author, proposes that organisations first show that basic controls work before expanding AI access to sensitive systems. Suggested methods include independent testing, verified corrective action and clear accountability. Where readiness falls short, the writer says, deployment should be narrowed or delayed. The letter frames this as a matter of trust, since citizens hand essential services information they cannot easily retrieve once it is exposed. The writer's position is that protecting this data must take priority over efficiency gains and AI adoption.

Articles.Title: Forum: Protecting personal data should take priority over efficiency and AI adoption

stories.Headline: While AI speeds up SMEs, delivery remains hard to automate
stories.Summary:
A Lalamove survey published on 9 November 2026 finds that small and medium-sized enterprises across Asia and Latin America are using AI widely in their daily operations, yet getting goods to customers remains difficult to automate. The survey, conducted in September 2026, covered Lalamove business users in nine locations, including Hong Kong, Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Ho Chi Minh City, Manila, Bangkok, Jakarta, Taipei and São Paulo. The platform operates in 18 markets across Asia, the Americas and EMEA. Its findings suggest that digital efficiency is advancing faster than the physical movement of goods.

AI use is most common in marketing, customer service and administration, where it helps teams handle repetitive tasks and answer enquiries more quickly. Manila recorded the highest adoption at 62.4 per cent of SME respondents, while Jakarta reported 36.8 per cent. Among those using AI, Bangkok reported the strongest efficiency gains, with 93 per cent saying operations had sped up. Logistics and delivery, however, remain the least automated functions, with adoption ranging from 7 per cent in Kuala Lumpur to 24.1 per cent in Manila.
